title: DESIGN.md: the binding visual design authority
description:
Write DESIGN.md, the visual design authority the plan names and an open bead is already blocked on. This is a short document with a short list of decisions in it, and the reason it is a bead rather than a chore is that ba-web-ui-surface-t3w cannot start without it.

WHAT THE PLAN ALREADY DECIDED, SO THIS IS TRANSCRIPTION PLUS THE UNSETTLED PARTS, NOT INVENTION
Section 14 already locks the two decisions that matter most, and quotes them so nobody reopens them:
- "MEDIUM DECIDED 2026-09-24: 2D pixel art is the rendering medium; cyberpunk / dev-workstation / RPG-arena is the mood applied to it." The plan names a mood but never a medium, and the two do not conflict: pixel sprites lit by a neon cyberpunk palette is one coherent direction. It was already de facto chosen by section 19's PixiJS plus tilemap layout, section 25's 16x16 sprites, and the vendored tiny-swords-cc0 pack.
- "THE SPLIT, and it does not bend toward a fully retro UI: pixel art for the game world, characters, items, tilesets and VFX; the dashboard, bounty board and auth screens stay modern, clean and responsive. A site that is retro all the way down is harder to use and reads as a costume."
- "DESIGN.md is the binding source for visual decisions; this section records the decision and the reasoning." That sentence is why this file has to exist. Section 14 is the record; DESIGN.md is the binding artifact downstream work is checked against.

WHY IT IS MISSING, verified 2026-09-25
- There is no DESIGN.md anywhere in the repo. docs/ contains only design/ and research/; docs/design/ holds payout-rail.md and public-event-stream.md and nothing else.
- ba-web-ui-surface-t3w is blocked on it in so many words: "That is VISUAL work, and it is still blocked until DESIGN.md exists - antislop R-37 forbids building UI without design direction. A framework shell is not visual design and was never blocked; the shell is now in place." The shell work is done and the visual work cannot start.
- The web-ui bead does not own producing it - it names DESIGN.md as a precondition it does not satisfy. So at the time the work had no home, which is the only condition under which a new bead is justified in a tracker this size. This bead is that home; the 'no owner' reading below is the gap that created it, not the current state.
- The web-ui bead is blocked by four: ba-api-routes-surface-mqr, ba-feature-bounty-xhk, ba-battle-replay-yjb and THIS bead, which was added as a dependency edge once DESIGN.md got an owner. So this is a named plan artifact with a named blocked consumer and a blocker of its own. It is not yet on the critical path only because those three are outstanding; it becomes blocking the moment they land, which is why the edge is worth keeping rather than deleting as redundant.

THE ONE DECISION THAT IS NOT ALREADY MADE, AND WHY IT BELONGS HERE
The plan gives two different answers about what the user sees first.
- Section 8: "Main screen (from conversation): top bar (Agent Battle, notifications, coins, level) / CODING CITY map (Guild Hall, Research Lab, Claude character, Arena, Workshop, Quest Board) / bottom tabs (QUESTS/AGENTS/GUILD/ARENA/PROFILE)." Then, later in the same paragraph: "Bounty Board as FIRST screen option (not pixel city)."
- Section 11.4: "First screen candidate: Bounty Board (HOT BOUNTIES with amounts/difficulty/repos/competitor counts) -> bounty detail -> [ENTER BATTLE] spins real agent work."
So section 8 describes the pixel city as the main screen and then proposes the bounty board instead; section 11.4 proposes the bounty board again. The plan hedges with "option" and "candidate", which is honest about not having decided, and an undecided first screen is a visual decision - which is exactly what this document exists to settle. The 2.3 gimmick trap and risk 8's scope discipline both bear on it: a bounty board first is the M2-with-zero-game-UI shape the plan repeatedly says should land before heavy art, and a pixel city first is the M5 shape. Settle it, state the reasoning, and note which milestone each choice implies.
Everything else - the medium, the mood, the retro/modern split, the agent-card anatomy, the bounty-board anatomy, the coding-city landmarks - is already in the plan and is transcription.

WHAT THE DOCUMENT MUST CONTAIN
1. The medium and the mood, stated as binding, with section 14's rationale and a pointer back to it.
2. The split: what is pixel (world, characters, items, tilesets, VFX) and what is modern (dashboard, bounty board, auth). With the reason - a retro-all-the-way-down site is harder to use and reads as a costume - because that is the sentence a future contributor will otherwise relitigate.
3. The first-screen decision, with the milestone it implies and the reasoning.
4. The named surfaces and their anatomy, from section 8: top bar, coding-city landmarks, bottom tabs, agent card (level, current quest+session, skill bars, [Enter Arena] [View History] [Join Guild]), bounty board (hot bounties with amount, difficulty, repo, competitor count -> detail -> [ENTER BATTLE]), replay view, arena.
5. Asset direction, pointing at ba-asset-shortlist-x2a as the owner of pack selection and per-pack licensing, and at section 14's rule that each pack ships its own LICENSE.txt. It must not duplicate that bead's work or pre-empt its selection.
6. An explicit non-goals section, because the plan's own failure mode here is scope creep dressed as design: no equipment, pets, mounts, cosmetics or housing. Section 10.2's MVP character sheet ends at History, and section 17.8's risk 8 bans the MMO shape.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, each with the thing that settles it
1. DESIGN.md exists at the repo root and every visual decision in it is traceable to a plan section. Settled by a check that each decision carries a section reference, and by a reader finding no visual assertion in it that the plan does not support. A design doc that invents a visual language the plan never sanctioned is worse than none, because it acquires authority by being written down.
2. The medium, the mood and the retro/modern split are stated and match section 14 verbatim in substance. Settled by a check against section 14 - the point is that these were decided on 2026-09-24 and a later contributor must not quietly reopen them.
3. The first screen is decided, and the decision names the milestone it implies. The test is that a reader can answer "what does a user see first, and when" from the document alone, with no reference back to the plan. Today the plan gives two answers, which is why this clause exists.
4. Every surface ba-web-ui-surface-t3w and ba-game-client-pixijs-riw are building appears in the document. Settled by cross-checking the two beads' surface lists against the document - a screen one of them builds and the document does not mention is a screen built without design direction, which is the thing this document exists to prevent. This is the criterion that makes the document load-bearing rather than decorative: it is checked against the beads that consume it.
5. The non-goals section is present and names at least the equipment/pets/mounts/cosmetics/housing exclusions from section 10.2.

CONSIDERATIONS
Keep it short. This is a design authority, not a design essay, and its value comes from being short enough that people read it before they build. The failure mode is a 400-line document nobody consults, which is functionally identical to no document. Second, it must not become a second copy of the plan: the plan records the decision and the reasoning, DESIGN.md records what is binding, and duplication is how the two drift. When they disagree, section 14 governs and DESIGN.md is the one that is stale. Third, DESIGN.md is a design artifact, so a visual review is a legitimate part of accepting it - but the checklist above is what makes it accountable, because "it looks good" is exactly the unfalsifiable criterion this tracker has been rewriting out of other beads.
close_reason:

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, and why:

title: MCP Streamable HTTP transport + /api/mcp route mount
description:
Mount the MCP Streamable HTTP transport and the /api/mcp route. The five primitives already exist and are frozen; this bead is the wire they have never been carried on.

WHAT THE PLAN REQUIRES
- Section 19 lists `app/api/mcp/route.ts  # MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint` in the target tree.
- Section 22: "POST /api/mcp (Streamable HTTP): ONLY the 5 stable primitives (32); act() dispatches typed registry actions to runtime.dispatch. No per-feature tool wrappers - adding a feature never adds an MCP tool. Auth: short-lived installation token from the section 4 flow."
- Section 31's correction is explicit and load-bearing: "MCP IS P0, not P3" and P0 contains "Interfaces: Public API, CLI, MCP" as three EQUAL consumers, because "do not design the game first and bolt MCP/CLI on later; design the game assuming the agent can ONLY play through the protocol/tool interface."
- The onboarding proof the plan wants from it (section 4 / the mcp-coding-agents reference): `claude mcp add agent-battle https://agentbattle.dev/mcp`, then browser auth, then a terminal confirmation showing Agent, Account and Project. That round trip is the thing that proves login -> add MCP -> authorize -> play needs no separate CLI install.

WHY IT IS MISSING RATHER THAN DONE, verified against the tree 2026-09-25
- packages/mcp-server/src/{server,tools,index}.ts exist and are good: createMcpServer is a pure function of an ApplicationApi with the five tools, lazy discovery, typed act() dispatch, and per-subscription observe. All of that stays.
- server.ts says in its own doc comment: "The MCP SDK is not installed yet. When it is, this becomes a thin translation - register these five tools, call callTool, send notifications from deliver. Nothing about the surface changes." The bead that closed named the next step and then closed. That left the next step unowned - which is the gap this bead was created to fill, so read 'no owner' here as the reason this bead exists rather than as its current state.
- No @modelcontextprotocol/sdk (or any MCP SDK) is in any package.json in the workspace.
- There is no apps/web/app/api/mcp/. apps/web/app/api/ contains exactly two directories: auth/ and events/.
- ba-mcp-adapter-li2 is CLOSED and its close reason is "Shipped against the frozen contract ... See the commit for the design calls and what was deliberately left out." The thing deliberately left out is this.
- ba-api-routes-surface-mqr used to inventory the route as "POST /api/mcp (MCP Streamable HTTP - built in the P3 MCP bead)" - crediting a closed bead, naming a priority the plan has since reversed, and leaving the route with no owner, which is how a route that does not exist reads as one that does. That line is now corrected to name this bead; if it ever reads "built in the P3 MCP bead" again, the inventory has been reverted.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS NOT
- It is not the five primitives. They are done and frozen by ba-contract-public-api-ute and exercised by the closed MCP bead. Re-implementing or reshaping them here fails section 32's whole argument.
- It is not a per-feature tool surface. Adding guild must change the registry, not the tool list. A route that grows a sixth tool, or a tool per feature, fails review under section 36.
- It is not a second event bus. The NotificationSink in server.ts is deliberately optional and its comment says the event-ingest and SSE bead owns where subscription events land. Wire notify to THAT stream; do not open a competing one.
- It is not the agent-identity work. The token is an installation token from the frozen credentials/identity contract; the GitHub human's Better Auth web session is a different credential and must not authenticate this route.

AUTH, precisely, because it is the security surface
- Bearer installation token in the Authorization header, scoped and expiring, exactly as ba-agent-credentials-issuance-294 issues them. The same refusal the credentials bead already enforces - a token in the query string leaks into logs and browser history, and the plan's own example is the bad one - applies here: refuse ?token= even when the header is also present, and assert the refusal rather than assuming it.
- Expired, revoked and under-scoped tokens must be rejected with the missing scope named, not a generic 401.
- A test that the human web session cannot drive this route, and that the agent token cannot drive a human-only route, because those two are the separation section 38 calls a hard review issue.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, each with the thing that settles it
1. A real MCP client completes initialize -> tools/list -> tools/call against the mounted route. Settled by an integration test speaking the Streamable HTTP protocol to apps/web/app/api/mcp/route.ts, not by calling createMcpServer in-process - an in-process test is exactly what already passes today and proves nothing about the wire.
2. The tool count over the wire is exactly 5, whatever is installed. Settled by a test asserting the tools/list response length is 5 with the full feature set composed in, so a future per-feature tool fails here.
3. The full loop works over MCP alone: discover -> search -> inspect -> act (a claim) -> observe (the resulting event), with the same application-command effects the CLI and HTTP surfaces produce. Settled by a parity assertion against the same createApplicationApi the other two consumers use, so MCP cannot drift from them.
4. The route handler contains no game logic. Settled by the same architecture assertion the web-ui bead uses - each route maps 1:1 onto an application command and translates; it decides nothing. A route that reaches into a feature and branches on a game word fails it.
5. Notification delivery rides the existing SSE stream rather than a new one. Settled by a test that an event observed through MCP arrives on the stream ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9 owns.

TESTS, each failing when the behaviour is wrong
- a Streamable HTTP integration test against the mounted route (the handshake, tools/list, one tools/call), which is the test that does not exist today;
- the exactly-5 tools/list assertion with every feature composed in;
- the loop parity assertion across MCP / CLI / HTTP;
- auth: no header, expired, revoked, missing scope, and ?token= refused, plus the human-session-cannot / agent-token-cannot separation;
- an architecture assertion that apps/web/app/api/mcp/route.ts imports no feature internals and registers no domain operation.

CONSIDERATIONS
The tempting wrong turn is to treat this as "mount the SDK and move on", which produces a route that works for a hand-written client and fails for `claude mcp add`, because that command does the OAuth/browser-auth dance the plan's onboarding UX depends on and a bearer-only route skips. If the transport cannot complete the browser-auth leg, the honest move is to ship the bearer route AND say plainly in this bead's close reason that the `mcp add` leg is still open - not to describe a half-wired endpoint as the onboarding proof. Second: the 250ms/50-event batching rules and the single-sessionId 400 belong to the ingest path and are not this bead's to re-decide; MCP commands are not telemetry.
close_reason:
MCP Streamable HTTP transport mounted at apps/web/app/api/mcp/route.ts, speaking JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Streamable HTTP envelope. The five frozen primitives are unchanged and are still exactly five over the wire with every feature composed in.

CHOSE: wrote the transport directly rather than adopting @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. The SDK's Streamable HTTP transport is built around a Node http.Server, so using it means either a second server in front of Next.js or a transport that never sees the outer request. packages/mcp-server has types:[] and no node dependency, so handleMcpRequest stayed pure and testable without a socket; a real SDK is a swap behind that one function.

DID NOT: carry an MCP client's observe() result back over the response. That needs a per-connection server-to-client channel, which this bead does not build. The consequence is stated in mcp-gateway.ts rather than hidden: an agent can open a subscription and the subscription is real, but nothing yet pushes the events to that client.

DID NOT: wire MCP's notification sink into the SSE hub. Considered and rejected, with a test. The hub already subscribes to the bus, so routing notifications into it would deliver every event to every spectator TWICE. The public stream and an MCP observer are two independent consumers of one bus. The test counts frames because a test that stops at 'an event arrived' cannot see a duplicate.

ALSO FIXED en route, all three found because a gate was already shaped to catch them:
- api.observe was a permanent no-op that voided both arguments. One of the five frozen primitives was advertised to every agent and delivered nothing, and the only observe assertion was that a subscription opens and closes. It now subscribes to the bus it is given, scoped by domain, and the delivery tests count events.
- A token in the query string was refused only when the Authorization header was ABSENT. A request carrying both was served, which is the one case that matters because the credential was already in the access log. Refused unconditionally now.
- writeFileSync's mode applies only on create, so a second login against a file left at 0644 kept 0644 while its contents became a fresh token.

ALSO ADDED: architecture rule no-route-handler-game-logic, scoped to the Next.js route tree via a new from.files glob on the rule engine. The composition root in apps/web/src imports features on purpose; a route handler that does is deciding game questions at the transport edge. Watched failing before being believed, per AGENTS.md.

STILL OPEN, not this bead: the web app builds two runtimes with two independent buses (routes.ts sharedApi and event-gateway.ts createEventGateway), so an event emitted by a game action through the Application API never reaches the SSE stream. See ba-monorepo-scaffold-j5a. That is also why criterion 5 could not be met end to end.

STILL OPEN, needs a decision, not effort: an MCP client's 'claude mcp add' onboarding leg, because that command does a browser-auth dance a bearer-only route does not perform. Shipped as a bearer route and said so rather than described as the onboarding proof.

title: adapters/pi: Agent Intercom protocol translation layer
description:
Implement the Pi adapter, per plan sections 1.3 and 23.

WHY THIS IS ITS OWN BEAD, because the split is not cosmetic and the difference is architectural, not clerical. The three lower-traffic harnesses were one bead until this was separated, and they are not three instances of one task. Cursor and Gemini are LOG WATCHERS: tail a file the harness writes, normalize, emit - structurally identical to the codex bead (rollout JSONL) and the opencode bead (SQLite), each of which already has its own bead. Pi is neither. It is a PROTOCOL TRANSLATION LAYER: a thin vendor adapter over the shared inter-agent broker described below, with no local log format to tail at all. An agent who has built a log watcher still has to learn a different thing to build Pi, and an agent who has built Pi still has to learn a different thing to build a log watcher. Bundling them meant neither could be started, finished, or reviewed on its own, and it hid Pi's one genuinely novel design constraint (it must not become a second bus) inside a paragraph about two file watchers. The siblings are ba-adapters-other-harnesses-as3 (cursor, gemini); this bead is pi.

PI (section 23, Agent Intercom precedent): reuse the Agent Intercom protocol shape. Section 1.3 describes Agent Intercom as cross-harness same-machine messaging over one Unix-socket broker with a shared protocol and per-vendor adapters for Pi/Codex/Claude/OpenCode. STEAL the protocol-vendor-per-adapter pattern (section 1.3). Concretely, that pattern means: the broker/socket is the shared seam and each vendor is a thin translation layer onto the one normalized AgentEvent union - which is exactly the shape here. The Pi adapter is a vendor layer over the shared protocol, NOT a second bus.

THE ONE CONSTRAINT THAT IS SPECIFIC TO PI, and the reason it could not simply join the other two: the broker is a WIRE PROTOCOL, not a place to import code from. So while every adapter here is barred from importing another adapter under the dependency rules (they import core + protocol only), Pi has an additional temptation the log watchers do not - reaching into the broker, or worse, growing the broker to accommodate Pi. Both are wrong. The broker is the seam; Pi is one translation layer sitting on it; the normalized AgentEvent union is the only vocabulary that crosses it. If Pi needs a field the union lacks, the fix is a new event type in the union (frozen by ba-agent-event-union-up5), never a vendor-private field smuggled through the broker.

Each adapter must: implement AgentWatcher, normalize through the shared tool-map, emit to the same local buffer feeding POST /api/events, and never import game code (section 23).

CONSIDERATIONS: this is a lower-traffic harness, so the priority is CORRECTNESS of the seam over feature depth. Minimum deliverable is session lifecycle plus tool events - the same floor the sibling watchers are held to, and no less for being a translation layer rather than a file reader.

WHAT YOU ARE BUILDING AGAINST (the concrete contracts, so this bead can be picked up without reading the plan). These contracts were written for all the low-traffic harnesses together and are reproduced here in full so this bead stands alone; the two log-watching siblings (ba-adapters-other-harnesses-as3: cursor, gemini) carry the same text, and pi is subject to every clause of it. The harnesses look different at the edge but are identical underneath, and the underneath is already frozen - do not re-decide it:

THE WATCHER INTERFACE. Every adapter implements AgentWatcher, the seam ba-adapters-template-a09 exists to specify. The reference shape, from agent-move's packages/server/src/watcher/agent-watcher.ts, is exactly two methods:
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): void; }
stop() returns void, not Promise<void>. That open decision (a watcher that must flush on shutdown has nowhere to await in the void shape) is flagged in the template bead; pick the SAME answer as the template, because the contract suite runs against both - and the two sibling watchers must pick that same answer too.

THE EVENT VOCABULARY IS FIXED AND VERSIONED. No adapter invents event names. They emit members of the zod discriminated AgentEvent union in packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts, frozen by ba-agent-event-union-up5: all 21 taxonomy events have zod schemas and TS types (session.started / session.heartbeat / session.ended, prompt.submitted, tool.started / tool.completed / tool.failed, file.read / file.write / file.changed, command.run, test.passed / test.failed, thinking, waiting, permission.requested, message.sent / message.received, subagent.spawned / subagent.completed, task.created). PROTOCOL_VERSION is '0.1.0', checked at handshake. The union is the ONLY vocabulary the game core knows - core never learns the words Cursor, Pi or Gemini. Validation rejects malformed events with field-level messages; an unknown type names every known type. Prefer adding a new event type over overloading an existing one with optional fields. Each harness's raw tool names are normalized through the tool-map, never emitted straight.

THE TOOL-MAP IS A DEPENDENCY, NOT A CHOICE. Raw tool names go through the shared tool-map (ba-tool-map-port-89a): normalizeToolName() (TOOL_NAME_MAP[name] ?? name, and our version IS exported so the contract suite can assert against it), getZoneForTool(), and normalizeToolInput(), which rewrites the camelCase input keys filePath->file_path, oldString->old_string, newString->new_string, replaceAll->replace_all and is called by every parser in the reference. Omitting normalizeToolInput is the most likely way a copied parser turns out subtly wrong. An unmapped tool must degrade to a sensible default zone, never be dropped - an unmapped tool is still real activity.

THE INGEST CONTRACT, because emitting correctly is not the same as being accepted. Adapters buffer locally and POST batches to /api/events. The buffer is EventBuffer in apps/web/src/event-batch.ts - it is NOT exported from @battle-agents/protocol, and an adapter may not import apps/web (wrong layer, see the dependency rule below). The template bead has to decide whether to lift EventBuffer into a shared package or specify it precisely enough to rebuild; every adapter should share that one decision, not each reinvent a buffer. A conforming buffer honours all three server-enforced rules: flush at 250ms OR 50 events, never exceed 100 events in one batch (the server rejects with 413 plus a Retry-After header), and never put two sessionIds in one batch (400). @battle-agents/protocol exports the zod union, PROTOCOL_VERSION, the generated RegisteredActionId union and isRegisteredActionId - it exports NO http client, so a self-sufficient adapter needs its own POST path.

WHAT THE ARCHITECTURE FORBIDS HERE. Adapters import core + protocol ONLY and NEVER game code - enforced mechanically by the dependency-rules bead (ba-dependency-rules-os1), machine-checked in CI via architecture-rules.cjs, not by reviewer discipline. So: no importing features/*, no importing apps/web, no importing another adapter (the Pi broker is not a place to import code from, it is a wire protocol). The telemetry plane (these adapters) is strictly separate from the control plane (MCP) - MCP is never used for event capture. These adapters observe; they do not command. The adapters also must not import each other: cursor, pi and gemini each stand alone as a subdirectory, because a harness that only builds because another harness was already built is the failure the whole adapter-seam design exists to prevent.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The first shortcut is treating Pi like the other two and inventing a local log format to watch, because that is the shape you already know - but there is no Pi log to tail, and a fabricated one is a second bus wearing a parser's clothes. The second is a shared 'generic' adapter that pi and the sibling watchers all plug into, because their outputs look vaguely similar once normalized: the moment one harness needs an event the others do not, the shared layer grows an if(harness) branch, and the 'new CLI = one subdirectory' promise is gone. The third is emitting Pi's native protocol names directly; the game core would then have to learn a second vocabulary, which the whole normalized-union design exists to prevent. The fourth is importing the broker's implementation rather than speaking to it over the socket, which drags another harness's code into this adapter and fails the same architecture test the other adapters must pass.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the Pi adapter produces a valid AgentEvent stream and passes the shared adapter contract suite; every emitted event validates against the frozen AgentEvent union and the version handshake passes; tool names reach the bus normalized through the tool-map; batches obey the 250ms/50/100 and single-session rules; the adapter imports neither game code, another adapter, nor the broker's implementation, and adds no vendor-private event field to the union.

TESTS: the shared adapter contract suite run against pi; fixture tests over a captured Pi protocol exchange; a test that every emitted event passes the protocol's zod validation; an architecture test asserting pi imports no game code, no other adapter, and no broker internals; a test that the broker is consumed as a wire protocol (the adapter holds a socket, not a broker object).
close_reason:
DONE. The shared adapter contract suite the criterion names did not exist when this
bead was worked; it exists now (tests/unit/adapter-contract.test.ts), and pi is
covered by it — shape, shared tool map, event names in the frozen union.

The byte-offset defect is the substantive fix and it was silent. readNewSessionLines
sliced a DECODED STRING by a BYTE offset, which is equivalent only for ASCII, so
every poll started progressively further in and destroyed records. Measured on the
largest real session on this machine (750 records, non-ASCII in 7 of 19 files):
310 events with 33 records destroyed, against 322 and zero after. 322 is the
single-session count, which is the only number that should ever have been possible.
Codex read bytes and decoded last; pi copied the shape and lost that discipline,
which is the copied-parser-goes-subtly-wrong failure the brief names.

Reused rather than reimplemented: the POST client lives in @battle-agents/protocol
because codex's ingest.ts named its own trigger for extracting it, and the session
partition fix is in EventBuffer rather than in this watcher, because four beads
found that independently and solving it per-adapter is the drift that moving the
buffer into protocol exists to prevent.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, and it is worth naming because the criterion reads as if it
were: no vendor-private event field was added to the union, and none is needed —
pi's three unmapped tool names went into the shared TOOL_NAME_MAP instead, with
zone-only entries for tools that are zoned by what they do rather than renamed to
a name they are not.

title: SSE stream is an unauthenticated global broadcast
description:
GET /api/events/stream has no authentication and no channel scoping. Every subscriber receives every event the runtime puts on the bus, and toGameEvent makes the whole validated AgentEvent the payload — so an agent's file paths, command names and thinking content reach any open socket. The bead ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9 asked for a per-user (web session) or per-battle channel; that was narrowed to a global broadcast with a comment deferring the policy to the game-client bead.

Shipped deliberately with that limitation recorded in apps/web/src/event-routes.ts, because deciding what is public is a policy that has not been written down. It is a bug, not a design: a battle scoreboard is public, the argv and file paths of every agent in the system are not.

THE EXPOSURE, made concrete, because 'some data leaks' undersells it. The stream is unauthenticated: any client that can reach the endpoint can open it - no token, no cookie, no handshake. It is also unscoped: there is one global broadcast, not per-user or per-battle, so there is no boundary to scope a subscriber to even if you wanted to. And the payload is the whole validated AgentEvent (toGameEvent forwards it wholesale), not a curated projection. So the union of those three facts is: anyone who can open a socket receives, in real time, the file paths, command argv, tool inputs, thinking content, message bodies, and permission requests of EVERY agent in the system - not one battle, not one agent, all of them. That is a cross-tenant confidentiality failure and a serious one, because agent activity is proprietary and can contain source code fragments, secrets the agent touched, and proprietary reasoning. A battle scoreboard being public is fine; this is not a scoreboard.

WHAT THE FIX NEEDS, in order (order matters - do not start at step 3):
1. Write the policy down first: which event types are public spectator data (battle progress, score, agent identity) and which are never public (file paths, command input, thinking, message bodies, permission requests). Without that written, any filter is a guess. This is a decision, not an implementation detail: it needs a human to say what this product considers public. A default-deny filter is the safe starting posture (allow-list the public types, deny the rest), because a block-list silently leaks anything not yet thought of.
2. Filter the bus by that classification before the hub broadcasts. A public stream carrying only classified-safe types is better than no stream and better than this. Note the filter belongs in the FAN-OUT path, not the persist path: the durable log legitimately stores richer events (that is what replay and achievements read), so filtering at the SSE hub is what makes the public stream safe WITHOUT gutting the internal record.
3. Authenticate the stream and scope it. A browser EventSource cannot set an Authorization header, and the repo forbids tokens in URLs, so the credential has to be a web session - which is a real piece of work, not a header. Concretely: the SSE stream authenticates as a human/browser via a web session (the Better Auth / GitHub OAuth path, per ba-better-auth-github-oauth-9wm), and is SCOPED to what that session is entitled to see (its own battles, its guild, or a specific public battle), not a single global firehose. This is a different credential from the agent's Bearer installation token (used by adapters on the ingest side) - do not reuse or expose the agent token to the browser.
4. Test that an unauthenticated request gets no frames, and that a subscriber for one battle cannot see another battle's deltas.

WHY THE EVENT TYPES ARE THE RIGHT FILTER AXIS, which is what makes step 1 tractable. The event vocabulary is a frozen, versioned union (ba-agent-event-union-up5, closed): 21 named taxonomy events with zod schemas, PROTOCOL_VERSION '0.1.0'. That is a closed, enumerable set - so a public/private classification over event TYPES is a finite table someone can actually review, not a per-payload judgment call. A battle.started / battle.finished / score event is public spectator data; a file.write / command.run / thinking / message.sent / permission.requested carries private content and must be denied to a public subscriber. Classifying by type (not by inspecting payload contents) is what makes the filter auditable and stable as new event types are added - a NEW event type must default to private until classified, or the next added type silently becomes a leak.

WHY A NAIVE FIX IS NOT ENOUGH. Adding a single filter without a written classification is a guess that will leak the next event type someone adds. Authenticating without scoping still returns one authenticated user's entire cross-tenant firehose (a logged-in attacker reads everyone's activity). Scoping without a type filter still exposes private content to a legitimate member of a battle. And a block-list ('deny thinking, deny file.write') fails open for every future type, so an allow-list is the durable choice. There is also a real footgun in 'just redact the payload': the whole-validated-AgentEvent payload means partial redaction has to happen in toGameEvent/the hub, and if any broadcast path bypasses that redaction, the leak returns - so the classification must be enforced at the single fan-out choke point, which is the same single-choke-point discipline the pixel-agents broadcaster (agentStateStore as the SOLE broadcaster) is credited with.

Do not close ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9 until this lands: the ingest path is correct, but the fan-out it publishes to is currently open. That is a real cross-bead dependency - the ingest bead (ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9) is a direct dependent of this bug, so the correct order is: this policy + filter + auth lands, and only then is the ingest/fan-out bead's work considered done.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an unauthenticated request to the stream receives no frames; a subscriber scoped to one battle cannot see another battle's deltas; the public stream carries only classified-public event types by default-deny; the richer internal record (durable log) is unaffected by the public filter.

TESTS: an unauthenticated-stream test (no frames, not even public ones, unless the endpoint is intentionally public-read); a cross-battle scoping test (a subscriber for battle A receives no deltas from battle B); a type-classification test that every event type is classified and new types default to private; a test that the durable log still stores the richer events the public stream filters out; a test that the agent Bearer token is never used to authenticate the browser SSE stream.

title: Activity/Event Log feature (P0) + persisted-event filter
description:
Implement the Activity/Event Log as a first-class P0 feature, per plan section 30 and the persistence filter in section 7.2.

WHY IT IS P0 AND NOT A DEBUG TABLE (section 29.4 + section 30): replay, audit, achievements, reputation, anti-abuse, and battle history ALL read from ONE ordered, attributed action trail. Paperclip treats action attribution the same way. Scattering this data across feature tables would mean each of those five consumers re-derives it differently.

THE TRAIL SHAPE (section 30), per session:
  Agent #123 / Session #456
  10:02 claim bounty -> 10:04 modify 3 files -> 10:07 run tests ->
  10:08 submit PR -> 10:11 PR merged -> 10:11 bounty completed -> +500 XP

IMPLEMENTATION:
- event_log table (section 21): id (bigserial), type, actorId, payload jsonb, occurredAt
- features/activity/ extension owning the append/query API and the retention policy
- every runtime.emit appends KEY events; transient telemetry stays on the bus only
- PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES (section 21/22) = ['session.started','session.ended','test.passed','test.failed','bounty.claimed','bounty.completed','battle.started','battle.finished','agent.level_up'] - everything else goes to the SSE bus ONLY.

THE REASON FOR THE FILTER IS THE CORE BACKEND INSIGHT (section 7.2): coding agents emit torrents. 100 agents x 20 events/s = 2000 DB writes/s. Neon must NEVER see that. Architecture: Agents -> Next.js Event Gateway -> {Realtime layer (WS/SSE) -> Browser} + {batched/important -> Neon}. Realtime is NOT Neon's job.

ORDERING: the runtime emits in the order persist -> handlers -> publish. The log must be written before downstream consumers read it, or replay/achievements can race ahead of the durable record.

CONSIDERATIONS: retention policy is part of this feature's scope (section 30 says 'owns append/query API, retention policy'). Replays need old events, so retention cannot be aggressive; decide and document the window. Retention is also the natural pressure valve if event volume grows.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: every key event lands in event_log with actor and ordering; transient events (thinking, waiting, streaming, heartbeat) provably do NOT; replay, achievements, and reputation all read from this one log rather than from scattered feature tables.

TESTS: unit test that the persist filter admits exactly PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES; integration test that ordering survives concurrent emits; test that querying a session's trail returns the example shape from section 30.
close_reason: features/activity owns the read API (trail + recent), the session summary shape, and the retention policy (365 days, because a shared replay is a link). Added the missing bridge: DrizzleStateStore, the only path an event takes to the database. 10 unit tests pin the persist filter (exactly the key events, features may add their own), retention boundaries and summary rendering; 34 integration tests prove key events land and transient ones provably do not, ordering survives, and prune removes only what aged out.

title: adapters/claude: hooks primary + JSONL secondary
description:
Implement the Claude Code adapter, per plan sections 6, 23, and 28.2.

PRIMARY PLANE: HOOKS. Claude Code has the richest hook surface of any supported harness (section 6), so the hook plane is primary and session-log reading is secondary. Handler at hooks/hook-handler.ts receives SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, and Stop, normalizes each via normalizeHookEvent(), and emits an AgentEvent.

SECONDARY PLANE: JSONL. parsers/jsonl.ts tails ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl for fields the hooks do not expose (section 23).

INSTALLER: installer/install-claude.ts writes a hook entry into ~/.claude/settings.json, CONSENT-GATED (pixel-agents pattern), with session-file fallback when hooks are unavailable. Section 6 confirms the fallback shape: AgentMove auto-installs into ~/.claude/settings.json and falls back to session-file watching.

PORT FROM agent-move (section 28.2, learn-only rewrite): watcher/claude parser, the AgentStateManager idle timeout, the Broadcaster, TaskGraphManager, full_state-then-delta with exponential-backoff reconnect, and the OpenCode WAL-polling CAUTION that applies to any file-watching path.

IDLE TIMEOUT: 45 SECONDS, NOT 30. The plan (section 28.2) and an earlier version of this bead both said 'AgentStateManager 30s idle rule'. That is wrong, and docs/research/agent-move.md records the correction with the source line (`idleTimeoutMs: 45_000`). The 30s figure is a client-side cosmetic timer - how long a sprite stands idle before switching to a sleeping pose - and plays no part in the server state machine. Three unrelated 30s values also exist in that repo (a git-info cache TTL, an anomaly-detector sweep interval, a session-recorder flush interval). Do not port 30. Note also that the same research note found agent-move's own `full_state` snapshot was 39.2 MB, which is the concrete argument for the delta-only fan-out we already ship; our EventStreamHub sends a small snapshot and then deltas, so mirror that discipline and not the size.

UX (section 6, from mcp-coding-agents): 'claude mcp add agent-battle <url>' is the registration shape, proving the npx/MCP-registration UX is feasible.

CONSIDERATIONS: hooks give structured, timely events but only while the agent cooperates; the JSONL tail is the safety net for crashes, forced quits, and missed hooks. Both are needed, and the JSONL reader must not double-count events the hooks already delivered (deduplication is required, not optional).

WHAT THE ADAPTER MUST EMIT AGAINST (already built, do not re-invent): POST /api/events is real and strict. A batch over 100 events is refused with 413 and a Retry-After header; a batch must carry events for exactly ONE sessionId; every event is zod-validated and checked against PROTOCOL_VERSION; the caller presents a Bearer installation token that must own the session. The client-side buffer that satisfies those rules is `EventBuffer` in apps/web/src/event-batch.ts, which flushes at 250ms or 50 events and stops short of the 100-event reject limit. A new adapter feeds the same buffer shape rather than inventing a second batching policy.

WHAT THE NORMALIZED EVENT MUST LOOK LIKE: `packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts` is the zod union every event is validated against, and `packages/protocol/src/version.ts` holds PROTOCOL_VERSION. An adapter that emits a shape the protocol schema does not describe is rejected at the door with a 400, so the fixture tests should assert against that schema and not against a local copy of it.

WHY CLAUDE IS FIRST: it is the reference harness. The normalization logic proven here is what every other adapter reuses.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a live Claude Code session produces a correct, deduplicated AgentEvent stream covering session lifecycle, tools, files, commands, tests, and permission requests; the installer is consent-gated and reversible.

TESTS: fixture-driven tests over real hook payloads; a dedup test proving hook+JSONL do not double-emit; an installer test asserting consent is required and that uninstall restores the original settings.json exactly.
