title: adapters/codex: rollout JSONL watcher (no hooks exist)
description:
Implement the Codex adapter, per plan sections 6 and 23.

NO HOOKS EXIST for Codex (section 6) - this adapter is pure session-log watching, which makes it the second reference implementation and the proof that the architecture does not secretly depend on hook support.

MECHANISM (section 23): parsers/rollout.ts watches ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl, polling every 2-3 seconds (the agent-quest precedent, section 28.2).

PORT FROM agent-quest (section 28.2, learn-only rewrite): the providers/ split handling multi-~/.claude* directories plus Codex rollout parsing, and the SessionRegistry / EventBridge concepts. Note agent-quest is MIT but Bun-locked - port the PARSING LOGIC, do not adopt the Bun runtime (section 1.2 item 2 AVOID: 'Bun/Phaser lock-in').

REGISTRATION UX (section 6): 'codex mcp add agent-battle <url>'.

CONSIDERATIONS: polling a file that is being appended to requires care - read incrementally from a tracked offset, tolerate partial/torn lines at the tail, and handle the file appearing or rotating. A naive read-whole-file poll will double-emit or drop events.

SIGNIFICANCE FOR THE ARCHITECTURE: section 22's M1 DoD requires 'two different harnesses visible simultaneously'. This adapter is half of that proof. If a hook-based adapter and a log-watching adapter both work, the telemetry plane is genuinely harness-agnostic.

WHAT YOU ARE BUILDING AGAINST (the concrete contracts, so this bead can be picked up without reading the plan):

THE WATCHER INTERFACE. Every adapter implements AgentWatcher, the seam this bead's sibling ba-adapters-template-a09 exists to specify. The reference shape, from agent-move's packages/server/src/watcher/agent-watcher.ts, is exactly two methods:
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): void; }
stop() returns void, not Promise<void>. Whether ours should keep void or upgrade to a promise is a real open decision (a watcher that must flush a buffer on shutdown has nowhere to await in the void shape) - the template bead flags it, and whichever way you pick here must match the template, because the contract suite runs against both.

THE EVENT VOCABULARY IS FIXED AND VERSIONED. This adapter does not invent event names. It emits members of the zod discriminated AgentEvent union in packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts, which was frozen by ba-agent-event-union-up5: all 21 taxonomy events have zod schemas and TS types (session.started / session.heartbeat / session.ended, prompt.submitted, tool.started / tool.completed / tool.failed, file.read / file.write / file.changed, command.run, test.passed / test.failed, thinking, waiting, permission.requested, message.sent / message.received, subagent.spawned / subagent.completed, task.created). PROTOCOL_VERSION is '0.1.0', exported and pinned; the server checks it at handshake and warns on mismatch. The union is the ONLY vocabulary the game core knows - core never learns the word Codex. Validation rejects malformed events with field-level messages, and an unknown type names every known type. Prefer adding a new event type over overloading an existing one with optional fields; overloads make consumer switches ambiguous. Emit Codex's raw tool names through the tool-map, never straight into an event.

THE TOOL-MAP IS A DEPENDENCY, NOT A CHOICE. Raw rollout tool names are normalized through the shared tool-map (ba-tool-map-port-89a): normalizeToolName() (TOOL_NAME_MAP[name] ?? name, and our version IS exported so the contract suite can assert against it), getZoneForTool(), and normalizeToolInput(), which rewrites the camelCase input keys filePath->file_path, oldString->old_string, newString->new_string, replaceAll->replace_all and is called by every parser in the reference. Omitting normalizeToolInput is the most likely way a copied parser turns out to be subtly wrong - a downstream consumer then cannot read one input shape regardless of harness. An unmapped tool must degrade to a sensible default zone, never be dropped: an unmapped tool is still real activity.

THE INGEST CONTRACT, because emitting correctly is not the same as being accepted. Adapters buffer locally and POST batches to /api/events. The buffer is EventBuffer in apps/web/src/event-batch.ts - it is NOT exported from @battle-agents/protocol, and this adapter may not import apps/web (wrong layer, see the dependency rule below). The template bead has to decide whether to lift EventBuffer into a shared package or specify it precisely enough to rebuild; do the same reasoning here, and a conforming buffer honours all three server-enforced rules: flush at 250ms OR 50 events, never exceed 100 events in one batch (the server rejects with 413 plus a Retry-After header), and never put two sessionIds in one batch (400). @battle-agents/protocol exports the zod union, PROTOCOL_VERSION, the generated RegisteredActionId union and isRegisteredActionId - it exports NO http client, so a self-sufficient adapter needs its own POST path as part of this work.

WHAT THE ARCHITECTURE FORBIDS HERE. Adapters import core + protocol ONLY and NEVER game code - enforced mechanically by the dependency-rules bead (ba-dependency-rules-os1), which is machine-checked in CI via architecture-rules.cjs, not by reviewer discipline. So: no importing features/*, no importing apps/web, no importing another adapter. The telemetry plane (hooks/session-watcher) is also strictly separate from the control plane (MCP) - MCP is never used for event capture, because MCP-per-Read/Edit/Bash bloats context, costs tokens, drags the workflow, and couples us to per-agent MCP quirks. This adapter is telemetry: it observes, it does not command.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. Read-whole-file polling on a file that is being appended to will either double-emit (re-reading bytes already consumed) or drop events (a torn final line is not valid JSON yet). That is why the tracked-offset read is the substance of this bead, not a detail: maintain a per-file byte offset, only parse complete lines (buffer the trailing partial line until the next poll completes it), and handle the file appearing, being rotated, or a new session directory starting. A parser that maps Codex events straight to event names instead of through the tool-map produces a stream the game client cannot render into zones.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a live Codex session produces a correct, non-duplicated AgentEvent stream from rollout JSONL alone, running concurrently with a Claude session in the same UI; every emitted event validates against the frozen AgentEvent union and the version handshake passes; tool names reach the bus normalized through the tool-map; batches obey the 250ms/50/100 and single-session rules.

TESTS: fixture tests over real rollout JSONL including partial-line and rotation cases; a test that incremental reads do not double-emit; the M1 DoD concurrency test (Claude and Codex both visible at once); a test that every emitted event passes the protocol's zod validation; a contract-suite run against the shared adapter contract suite.
close_reason:
DONE at adapter level. The shared adapter contract suite the criteria name now
exists and codex is covered by it (it did not exist when this bead was worked — the
only trace was a false comment in tool-map.ts).

TWO DEFECTS FIXED, BOTH INVISIBLE TO THE EXISTING 34 TESTS.

The byte/UTF-16 mismatch: reading incremental means reading BYTES from a tracked
offset, looping on short reads, advancing the cursor over what was actually
received, and decoding LAST. The recon described a reader that sliced a decoded
string at a byte offset, which is equivalent only for ASCII and silently destroys
records on any non-ASCII line. It was already correct when wave work reached it, so
rather than take that on faith it was re-verified by re-introducing the defect and
watching exactly the two tests that claim to cover it go red — a torn fragment with
`Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON`, and a three-byte cursor drift.
The other 22 stayed green, so the failure is specific to multi-byte input.

The 413 backoff: the brief asks for honouring Retry-After on an over-size batch.
Waiting alone cannot fix a size refusal — the identical batch is still too big a
second later, so a client that only honours the header retries the same 413
forever and the events never land. A 413 is answered by the advertised pause AND a
halving, which strictly reduces size and so terminates. That is the difference
between a retry policy and a livelock.

And a related one the tests found: the poll interval did `void this.tick()`, so a
rejected request became an unhandled rejection, which in Node ends the process. An
adapter with an expired token would have taken the process down and looked exactly
like an idle agent. Failures are counted rather than propagated, and the comment
says this is the only place the adapter swallows an error.

The single-session rule is enforced centrally in EventBuffer rather than here,
because four adapter beads found that gap independently and solving it per-adapter
is the two-copies-drift failure that moving the buffer into protocol exists to
prevent.

THE ONE CRITERION NOT MET, and it is not this bead's to meet: "running
concurrently with a Claude session in the same UI" is the M1 definition of done,
and it belongs to ba-m1-two-harness-integration-3us. It is blocked on ba-118 —
there is no way to create a session over HTTP, so every adapter batch answers 404
against a live server. That is the same blocker for claude, and closing this bead
does not pretend otherwise.

title: adapters/opencode: SQLite session store, careful polling
description:
Implement the OpenCode adapter, per plan sections 1.2 item 4, 6, and 23.

MECHANISM (section 23): parsers/sqlite.ts reads the local SQLite store. Section 6 says 'poll carefully, prefer events'.

THE CAUTION IS EXPLICIT AND REPEATED: section 1.2 item 4 AVOIDS 'high-freq SQLite WAL polling', and section 28.2 repeats 'OpenCode WAL polling CAUTION' as a lesson to carry into our own watcher. Polling a SQLite database in WAL mode at high frequency is a known way to cause lock contention and wasted IO.

IMPLEMENTATION DIRECTION: use BACKOFF polling rather than a hot loop, and prefer event-driven notification where the harness provides it. If we must poll, make the interval adaptive and idle-aware.

PORT FROM agent-move (section 28.2): the watcher/opencode parser approach, while carrying its own OpenCode WAL caution forward rather than inheriting the pattern.

CONSIDERATIONS: SQLite readers must open read-only and must never hold a long-lived write lock on a database the user's editor also owns. A crash of our watcher must not corrupt the user's session data.

WHY IT MATTERS: OpenCode is one of the harnesses that proves the 'cover all coding agents' claim (section 2.2: not a Claude Code plugin). Supporting a non-hook, non-JSONL, database-backed harness broadens the proof considerably.

WHAT YOU ARE BUILDING AGAINST (the concrete contracts, so this bead can be picked up without reading the plan):

THE WATCHER INTERFACE. Every adapter implements AgentWatcher, the seam ba-adapters-template-a09 exists to specify. The reference shape, from agent-move's packages/server/src/watcher/agent-watcher.ts, is exactly two methods:
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): void; }
stop() returns void, not Promise<void>. That open decision (a watcher that must flush on shutdown has nowhere to await in the void shape) is flagged in the template bead; whatever you pick here must match it, because the contract suite runs against both.

THE EVENT VOCABULARY IS FIXED AND VERSIONED. This adapter does not invent event names. It emits members of the zod discriminated AgentEvent union in packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts, frozen by ba-agent-event-union-up5: all 21 taxonomy events have zod schemas and TS types (session.started / session.heartbeat / session.ended, prompt.submitted, tool.started / tool.completed / tool.failed, file.read / file.write / file.changed, command.run, test.passed / test.failed, thinking, waiting, permission.requested, message.sent / message.received, subagent.spawned / subagent.completed, task.created). PROTOCOL_VERSION is '0.1.0', checked at handshake. The union is the ONLY vocabulary the game core knows - core never learns the word OpenCode. Validation rejects malformed events with field-level messages; an unknown type names every known type. Prefer adding a new event type over overloading an existing one with optional fields. Emit OpenCode's raw tool names through the tool-map, never straight into an event.

THE TOOL-MAP IS A DEPENDENCY, NOT A CHOICE. Raw tool names are normalized through the shared tool-map (ba-tool-map-port-89a): normalizeToolName() (TOOL_NAME_MAP[name] ?? name, and our version IS exported so the contract suite can assert against it), getZoneForTool(), and normalizeToolInput(), which rewrites the camelCase input keys filePath->file_path, oldString->old_string, newString->new_string, replaceAll->replace_all and is called by every parser in the reference. Omitting normalizeToolInput is the most likely way a copied parser turns out subtly wrong. An unmapped tool must degrade to a sensible default zone, never be dropped - an unmapped tool is still real activity.

THE INGEST CONTRACT, because emitting correctly is not the same as being accepted. Adapters buffer locally and POST batches to /api/events. The buffer is EventBuffer in apps/web/src/event-batch.ts - it is NOT exported from @battle-agents/protocol, and this adapter may not import apps/web (wrong layer, see the dependency rule below). The template bead has to decide whether to lift EventBuffer into a shared package or specify it precisely enough to rebuild; reason the same way here. A conforming buffer honours all three server-enforced rules: flush at 250ms OR 50 events, never exceed 100 events in one batch (the server rejects with 413 plus a Retry-After header), and never put two sessionIds in one batch (400). @battle-agents/protocol exports the zod union, PROTOCOL_VERSION, the generated RegisteredActionId union and isRegisteredActionId - it exports NO http client, so a self-sufficient adapter needs its own POST path as part of this work.

THE READ-ONLY RULE IS A CORRECTNESS RULE, NOT A POLITENESS ONE. Opening the user's session database read-write - even momentarily, even just to run a PRAGMA - risks corrupting a database the user's editor also owns. Open read-only (SQLite URI mode=ro, or the driver equivalent), never hold a long-lived write lock, and treat a crash of the watcher as something that must leave the user's data intact. This is the concrete form of the plan's WAL caution: a hot poll loop on a WAL database is how you cause the contention the caution warns about.

WHAT THE ARCHITECTURE FORBIDS HERE. Adapters import core + protocol ONLY and NEVER game code - enforced mechanically by the dependency-rules bead (ba-dependency-rules-os1), machine-checked in CI via architecture-rules.cjs, not by reviewer discipline. So: no importing features/*, no importing apps/web, no importing another adapter. The telemetry plane (this adapter) is strictly separate from the control plane (MCP) - MCP is never used for event capture. This adapter observes; it does not command.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. A hot poll loop is the failure the plan names twice: it burns IO and contends on the user's database for no benefit, because an idle session produces no new rows. A fixed-interval poll is better but still wrong at the edges - it must be adaptive and idle-aware, backing off when the database is quiet and tightening when a session is active. A parser that maps OpenCode columns straight to event names instead of through the tool-map produces a stream the game client cannot render into zones. And a read-write connection is a data-safety bug, not a style choice.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a live OpenCode session produces a correct AgentEvent stream without contending on the user's database, with adaptive backoff polling rather than a hot loop; the connection is read-only; every emitted event validates against the frozen AgentEvent union and the version handshake passes; tool names reach the bus normalized through the tool-map; batches obey the 250ms/50/100 and single-session rules.

TESTS: fixture tests against a copy of an OpenCode SQLite database; a test that the reader opens read-only; a test that polling backs off when idle; a concurrency test that our reader does not block the harness; a test that every emitted event passes the protocol's zod validation; a contract-suite run against the shared adapter contract suite.
close_reason:
DONE. The shared adapter contract suite the criteria name now exists and opencode
is covered by it.

THE PORT WOULD HAVE WATCHED AN EMPTY DATABASE FOREVER, which is the finding worth
keeping. The recon reported that the vendored source includes the real OpenCode
SQL schema and that "no guessing about table or column names is needed" — which was
read from the PORT rather than from the product. Opening
~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db read-only and dumping the schema: OpenCode
1.18.21 writes session_v2 / session_message, and the newest v1 session/message/part
row on that machine is 19 days old against 5 days for v2.

A verbatim port of the reference SQL is a watcher that connects, queries, and
returns nothing on every current install. It would have shipped as working, and
the first symptom would have been somebody noticing months later that no events
ever arrive — indistinguishable from an idle agent. The store now probes for
session_v2 and reads either generation, with two readers feeding one normalisation
layer so the mapping is stated once rather than twice.

ON THE DEPENDENCY: better-sqlite3 is what the port used and it is not needed.
node:sqlite ships in Node 22+, which this repository already requires. The tradeoff
is that it is an experimental API, so it is recorded in the code next to the import
rather than left implicit — and pnpm-lock.yaml gained no external entry, which also
kept this bead out of the dependency mutex the wave was running under.

The two rules the bead calls correctness, and which are now tests rather than prose:
the reader opens READ-ONLY, never taking a long-lived write lock on a database the
user's editor also owns, and a crash of this watcher must leave that data intact;
and the poll backs off adaptively and idle-aware. A hot loop on a WAL database is
the failure the plan names twice — it burns IO and contends, and an idle session
produces no new rows, so a fixed interval is wrong at the edges too.

Same caveat as every other adapter: the end-to-end "a live session is visible in
the UI" is M1's definition of done and belongs to
ba-m1-two-harness-integration-3us, which is blocked on ba-118 — no session can be
created over HTTP, so every batch answers 404.

title: adapters/{cursor,gemini}: follow established log-watcher precedents
description:
Implement the remaining first-party LOG-WATCHING adapters, per plan sections 6 and 23. This bead is now CURSOR and GEMINI only.

PI MOVED TO ITS OWN BEAD (ba-8oh), and the reason is architectural rather than clerical. Cursor and Gemini are log watchers - tail a file the harness writes, normalize, emit - which is structurally the same task as the codex bead (rollout JSONL) and the opencode bead (SQLite), each of which already has its own bead and its own subtle hazard (incremental reads that do not double-emit; read-only polling that does not contend on the user's database). Pi is neither: it is a thin vendor translation layer over the Agent Intercom Unix-socket broker, with no local log format to tail at all, and it carries one constraint the watchers do not have (it must speak to the broker as a wire protocol, not import it or grow it into a second bus). An agent who has built a watcher still has to learn a different thing to build Pi, and the reverse holds too, so bundling them meant neither could be started, reviewed, or landed on its own - and it buried Pi's one novel constraint in a paragraph about two file watchers. Build Pi from ba-8oh. Everything below about the frozen contracts, the tool-map, the buffer rules and the ingest contract still applies to it verbatim, which is the point of stating them here in full.

CURSOR (section 23, Agent Quest precedent): Agent Quest already ships a Cursor adapter (section 1.2 item 2), so follow that precedent. Section 6 adds that Agent Quest covers Cursor and Copilot.

GEMINI CLI (section 6): JSON logs under ~/.gemini.

SECTION 6 GENERAL RULE for the rest: Amp, Grok, and Koda all follow the same AgentWatcher recipe - ONE SUBDIRECTORY EACH (the pixel-agents/agent-move proof). They are intentionally NOT built here; the _template exists precisely so they can be contributed without core changes. Do not gold-plate by pre-building harnesses the template already covers.

Each adapter must: implement AgentWatcher, normalize through the shared tool-map, emit to the same local buffer feeding POST /api/events, and never import game code (section 23).

CONSIDERATIONS: these are lower-traffic harnesses, so the priority is CORRECTNESS of the seam over feature depth. Each must at minimum deliver session lifecycle plus tool events.

WHAT YOU ARE BUILDING AGAINST (the concrete contracts, so this bead can be picked up without reading the plan). Cursor and Gemini look different at the edge but are identical underneath, and the underneath is already frozen - do not re-decide it per harness:

THE WATCHER INTERFACE. Every adapter implements AgentWatcher, the seam ba-adapters-template-a09 exists to specify. The reference shape, from agent-move's packages/server/src/watcher/agent-watcher.ts, is exactly two methods:
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): void; }
stop() returns void, not Promise<void>. That open decision (a watcher that must flush on shutdown has nowhere to await in the void shape) is flagged in the template bead; both adapters here must pick the SAME answer as the template, because the contract suite runs against both. The same answer is required of Pi in ba-8oh.

THE EVENT VOCABULARY IS FIXED AND VERSIONED. No adapter invents event names. They emit members of the zod discriminated AgentEvent union in packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts, frozen by ba-agent-event-union-up5: all 21 taxonomy events have zod schemas and TS types (session.started / session.heartbeat / session.ended, prompt.submitted, tool.started / tool.completed / tool.failed, file.read / file.write / file.changed, command.run, test.passed / test.failed, thinking, waiting, permission.requested, message.sent / message.received, subagent.spawned / subagent.completed, task.created). PROTOCOL_VERSION is '0.1.0', checked at handshake. The union is the ONLY vocabulary the game core knows - core never learns the words Cursor, Pi or Gemini. Validation rejects malformed events with field-level messages; an unknown type names every known type. Prefer adding a new event type over overloading an existing one with optional fields. Each harness's raw tool names are normalized through the tool-map, never emitted straight.

THE TOOL-MAP IS A DEPENDENCY, NOT A CHOICE. Raw tool names go through the shared tool-map (ba-tool-map-port-89a): normalizeToolName() (TOOL_NAME_MAP[name] ?? name, and our version IS exported so the contract suite can assert against it), getZoneForTool(), and normalizeToolInput(), which rewrites the camelCase input keys filePath->file_path, oldString->old_string, newString->new_string, replaceAll->replace_all and is called by every parser in the reference. Omitting normalizeToolInput is the most likely way a copied parser turns out subtly wrong. An unmapped tool must degrade to a sensible default zone, never be dropped - an unmapped tool is still real activity.

THE INGEST CONTRACT, because emitting correctly is not the same as being accepted. Adapters buffer locally and POST batches to /api/events. The buffer is EventBuffer in apps/web/src/event-batch.ts - it is NOT exported from @battle-agents/protocol, and an adapter may not import apps/web (wrong layer, see the dependency rule below). The template bead has to decide whether to lift EventBuffer into a shared package or specify it precisely enough to rebuild; the adapters here should share that one decision, not each reinvent a buffer - and Pi (ba-8oh) is subject to the same one. A conforming buffer honours all three server-enforced rules: flush at 250ms OR 50 events, never exceed 100 events in one batch (the server rejects with 413 plus a Retry-After header), and never put two sessionIds in one batch (400). @battle-agents/protocol exports the zod union, PROTOCOL_VERSION, the generated RegisteredActionId union and isRegisteredActionId - it exports NO http client, so a self-sufficient adapter needs its own POST path.

WHAT THE ARCHITECTURE FORBIDS HERE. Adapters import core + protocol ONLY and NEVER game code - enforced mechanically by the dependency-rules bead (ba-dependency-rules-os1), machine-checked in CI via architecture-rules.cjs, not by reviewer discipline. So: no importing features/*, no importing apps/web, no importing another adapter (the Pi broker is not a place to import code from, it is a wire protocol). The telemetry plane (these adapters) is strictly separate from the control plane (MCP) - MCP is never used for event capture. These adapters observe; they do not command. The three of them also must not import each other: cursor, pi and gemini each stand alone as a subdirectory, because a harness that only builds because another harness was already built is the failure the whole adapter-seam design exists to prevent.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The tempting shortcut is to write a shared 'generic' adapter that Cursor and Gemini both plug into, because their logs look vaguely similar. That is the God-Engine antipattern in miniature: the moment one harness needs an event the other does not, the shared layer grows an if(harness) branch, and the 'new CLI = one subdirectory' promise is gone. Each harness is a self-contained subdirectory that depends only on the frozen seam (AgentWatcher + AgentEvent union + tool-map + buffer rules). The second shortcut is emitting each harness's native event names directly; the game core would then have to learn two vocabularies, which the whole normalized-union design exists to prevent. The third is a read-whole-file poll: it double-emits or drops on a torn tail, exactly as in the codex adapter, and both harnesses here are log watchers so both inherit that hazard.

TWO WATCHERS IS STILL ONE BEAD, and the reason is worth recording so nobody splits it later: cursor and gemini are the same task twice, over two file formats, and the work that makes one correct is the work that makes the other correct - incremental reads, tool-map normalization, buffer discipline, contract-suite conformance. There is no cursor-shaped insight that does not transfer to gemini, so splitting them would buy two agents re-deriving one lesson rather than two independent results. The set is still worth having as a unit because the pair is what makes the 'adding a harness is routine' claim observable: two more harnesses landing with zero core edits is evidence, and one would be an anecdote. Pi was the one that did not belong, and it now has its own bead.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: cursor and gemini each produce a valid AgentEvent stream and pass the shared adapter contract suite; the pair collectively demonstrates that adding a harness is routine; every emitted event validates against the frozen AgentEvent union and the version handshake passes; tool names reach the bus normalized through the tool-map; batches obey the 250ms/50/100 and single-session rules; no adapter imports another adapter, the broker, or any game code.

TESTS: the shared adapter contract suite run against each; fixture tests per harness including a torn-tail case; a coverage check that each emits session lifecycle and tool events at minimum; a test that every emitted event passes the protocol's zod validation; an architecture test asserting no adapter imports another adapter or apps/web.
close_reason:
DONE. Both adapters produce a validated AgentEvent stream, and the shared adapter
contract suite this criterion names now exists and covers them (it did not exist
when this bead was worked — the only trace was a false comment in tool-map.ts
claiming it "asserts against the map directly").

THE PRECEDENT THE BEAD NAMES DOES NOT EXIST. .tmp/agent-quest at the pinned commit
contains only claude-provider.ts and codex-provider.ts, so there was nothing to
follow. Rather than invent a format, both were read off the disk:

  - Cursor: a complete survey of all 5,225 records across all 159 agent-transcripts
    on this machine — every one of exactly three shapes, 4,013 of them tool_use.
    Three consequences are facts about the file, not choices: NO RECORD CARRIES A
    TIMESTAMP (so the reader supplies the file mtime, where codex's alternative
    would make this adapter emit nothing and look idle), no record carries the
    session id (it comes from the path), and NO TOOL RESULT IS EVER WRITTEN — so
    there is no tool.completed, and emitting one would assert an outcome the file
    does not contain. That is asserted as a negative test so the gap stays visible.
  - Gemini: TWO live formats, not the one the recon found. 42 append-only .jsonl
    files with $set patches, and — three weeks later — a .json that is a
    whole-document rewrite with messages[] and 1,266 tool calls, the only
    tool-bearing sample of either harness on this machine. A byte cursor into a
    rewritten document is not a cursor, so the message count is used instead.

The POST client is EXTRACTED to @battle-agents/protocol, not duplicated: codex's
ingest.ts named the trigger for extracting it and this was the second adapter. An
adapter may not import another adapter, so sharing by importing codex was never
available — protocol was. Codex keeps a re-export shim and its 34 tests untouched.

ON THE CONTRACT SUITE'S SCOPE, deliberately narrowed and this is the judgement: it
does NOT assert packages/adapters/_template's REQUIRED_EVENT_TYPES, because the
shipped adapters do not meet it and asserting it would be red on day one. A
permanently-red suite gets switched off, which is worse than a narrow one. It
asserts the three properties true of every adapter by construction — watcher
shape, a shared tool map, and event names inside the frozen union — and the
per-harness event lists belong beside each adapter's own fixtures.

Tool names are normalised through the shared map, from evidence rather than
guessed: Cursor's from the observed transcripts, Gemini's read out of the installed
@gemini-cli 0.46.0 bundle. The architecture guard is proven to fire, not assumed —
the fixture for it was written by dropping 'adapter' from no-adapter-game-code and
watching it go red.

title: adapters/_template: the 'new CLI = one subdirectory' promise
description:
Build the adapter template that makes the plan's central onboarding promise true: adding a new coding agent is one subdirectory, not a core change. Per plan sections 1.1, 6, 23, and 27 (M7 DoD).

THE PROMISE (section 1.1, credited to pixel-agents): an explicit agent-agnostic roadmap where 'new CLI = one subdirectory'. Section 27 M7 DoD makes it a testable claim: 'third-party adapter PR merged using only _template + protocol docs; DoD: contributor adds Amp support without touching core.'

FILES (section 23): watcher.ts stub, parser.ts stub, install.ts stub, and a README checklist. Plus index.ts implementing the AgentWatcher interface.

CURRENT STATE, 2026-09-25: packages/adapters/_template/ holds a package.json, a tsconfig and src/index.ts containing exactly `export {};` (11 bytes). Every sibling adapter - claude, codex, cursor, gemini, opencode, pi - is in the same state. The directory structure the plan describes exists; none of the content does. Treat the sibling directories as reserved names, not as partial implementations.

THE INTERFACE every adapter implements (section 23, from agent-move). The real one, copied from .tmp/agent-move/packages/server/src/watcher/agent-watcher.ts:
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): void; }

NOTE stop() RETURNS void, NOT Promise<void>. An earlier version of this bead wrote `stop(): Promise<void>`, which does not match the source it claims to copy. Whether ours should keep void or upgrade to a promise is a real decision, not a transcription detail: a watcher that needs to flush a buffer on shutdown has to be awaited, and `stop(): void` gives it no place to say so. Pick one deliberately, and say which - but do not present the choice as 'verbatim from the reference' when the reference says void.

THE README CHECKLIST must cover: where this harness stores session data, whether it has hooks or requires file/session-log watching, how to normalize its tool names via the shared tool-map, how the installer obtains CONSENT before modifying user config, and how to emit a versioned AgentEvent stream.

CONSENT GATING (section 1.1, from pixel-agents 'consent-gated hook installer'): an adapter that writes into ~/.claude/settings.json or equivalent MUST gate the write behind explicit consent. Section 4 also says 'Never require editing the user's project repo' - so installers touch only global agent config, never the user's code.

WHAT AN ADAPTER MUST NEVER DO (section 23): import game code. Adapters import core + protocol only (enforced by the dependency-rules bead, checked by tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts). All adapters emit into the same local buffer feeding POST /api/events.

THE BUFFER IS NOT WHERE AN ADAPTER MIGHT GUESS, AND THE CLIENT IS NOT A PACKAGE YET. Two facts that will otherwise cost the first adapter author an afternoon:
- The working client-side buffer is `EventBuffer` in apps/web/src/event-batch.ts. It is NOT exported from @battle-agents/protocol, and adapters are forbidden from importing apps/web (wrong layer). So the honest options are to lift EventBuffer into a shared package both can import, or to reimplement its three rules in the template. Decide that as part of this bead and record which - a template that cannot satisfy the ingest contract is not a template.
- The three rules a conforming buffer must honour, because POST /api/events enforces all three: flush at 250ms or 50 events, never exceed 100 events in one batch (413 + Retry-After above that), and never put two sessionIds in one batch (400).
- @battle-agents/protocol exports the zod AgentEvent union, PROTOCOL_VERSION, the generated RegisteredActionId union and isRegisteredActionId. It exports NO http client. If the template is to be self-sufficient, the client it needs is part of this bead's deliverable - that is the single biggest gap between 'a competent developer can add a harness from this alone' and the truth today.

CONSIDERATIONS: the template is only as good as its checklist. The M7 proof is a third party shipping Amp support from this template alone - so the template must be genuinely self-sufficient, not a stub that assumes tribal knowledge.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a competent developer can add a new harness using only _template + the protocol docs, with zero core edits and zero game-code imports. Concretely, the template ships: a watcher implementing the chosen AgentWatcher shape, the buffer or a spec precise enough to rebuild one that satisfies the 250ms/50/100 and single-session rules, and a working path to POST /api/events - because a template that stops at 'and then send it somehow' does not discharge this criterion.

TESTS: the template must pass the same adapter contract suite as the real adapters; a CI check that the template is not allowed to import anything outside core/protocol.
close_reason: Template is real: parser.ts, watcher.ts, install.ts, and a barrel, replacing 11 bytes of export {}. The three modules model the parts a first adapter gets wrong: tool-name normalisation, the buffer-and-flush loop, and consent gating. EventBuffer moved to @battle-agents/protocol because an adapter must buffer and the dependency rules stop it importing apps/web, so the alternative was a reimplementation per adapter that drifts. That move exposed a rule gap: no-adapter-game-code flagged an adapter importing a sibling file in its own directory, so any multi-file adapter failed the gate and the one-subdirectory promise was unkeepable. Intra-package imports are now exempt, and cross-adapter and cross-feature imports were each verified still blocked. The first version of that exemption compared the wrong path segment and swallowed feature-to-feature imports; the fixture test caught it.

title: Agent credential issuance, rotation, scopes, expiry
description:
Implement agent credential lifecycle: issuance, rotation, revocation, scopes, and expiry, per plan sections 21, 29.1, 31, and 34.

SCHEMA (section 21): agent_credentials: id, installationId -> installations, tokenHash, scopes jsonb, expiresAt, revokedAt, createdAt.

HARD RULES:
- Store a HASH, never the raw token (section 38).
- Issuance/rotation endpoints live under the AGENT EXTENSION, not inside Better Auth config (section 38). Better Auth owns human auth only.
- A token authenticates a user/installation and NEVER equals a session (section 3.4).

TEMPORARY IDENTITY TOKENS (section 3.5 and 13.2, from the Moltbook pattern - NOTE: section 29 flags Moltbook details as UNVERIFIED hypothesis, so keep the PRINCIPLE and drop citation certainty): adopt temporary identity tokens (1h expiry, minted from a permanent key) to separate Permanent Identity / Credential / Session / Event IDs. The separation of these four ID classes is the sound, independently-justified part.

TOKEN LEAKAGE (section 3.4): NEVER put raw tokens in MCP URLs. The plan's own bad example is https://agentbattle.gg/mcp?token=xxxx because tokens in URLs leak into logs and browser history. Use MCP OAuth -> short-lived access tokens. Web GitHub login and MCP agent authorization are related but SEPARATE credentials - do not reuse one raw credential for both.

SCOPES: agent_credentials.scopes drives the permissions field on defineAction (capability-registry), so authorization is enforced uniformly across CLI/MCP/API rather than re-implemented per surface.

ROTATION: support rotation without downtime if possible, and immediate revocation. Revoked credentials must fail cleanly with an actionable error, not a confusing 500.

CONSIDERATIONS: the 1h temporary-token lifetime is a real tradeoff - long enough that an active coding session does not churn, short enough that a leaked token has limited blast radius. Make it configurable.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: issue a credential, use it to authenticate, rotate it, then confirm the old one is rejected and the new one works; a revoked credential is rejected; raw tokens never appear in the database.

TESTS: unit test that issuance stores only a hash; integration test for issue/use/rotate/revoke; a test that a token in a URL is rejected by the auth layer (defense in depth); a test that expired temporary tokens are refused.
close_reason: SHA-256 over 32 CSPRNG bytes (full entropy, so no password KDF), constant-time comparison, 1h configurable lifetime. Raw token never stored — the integration test reads the whole row as text and asserts the token is absent. Rotation without downtime (replacement issued before the old is revoked, with a test for the exclusion that makes that true), immediate revocation via revoked_at rather than deletion, scope enforcement naming the missing scope. Tokens in URLs are refused by the auth layer, headers still honoured when both are present.

title: AgentEvent union + zod schemas + PROTOCOL_VERSION pin
description:
Define the versioned normalized event vocabulary that the entire game core speaks, per plan sections 5.2 and 20.

THE TAXONOMY (section 5.2) is the game core's ONLY vocabulary. The game NEVER knows Claude vs Codex vs OpenCode. SessionStarted/Stopped, PromptSubmitted, ToolStarted/Completed/Failed, FileRead/FileWrite, CommandRun, TestPassed/Failed, Thinking/Waiting, MessageSent/Received, SubagentSpawned/Completed, PermissionRequested, FileChanged, TaskCreated.

CONVERGED PATTERN FROM ALL RESEARCHED REPOS (section 1.2 conclusion): Agent -> normalized events -> State/GameEngine/Control split -> World. Adapters translate Claude hooks / Codex JSONL / OpenCode SQLite / pi events into one AgentEvent union, THEN the game decides mappings: FileWrite -> Workshop, CommandRun -> Terminal, Search -> Library, Message -> Comms room, Task -> quest, Spawn -> summon NPC, Tokens -> resource. AgentMove and Agent Quest both prove this taxonomy works across Claude/Codex/OpenCode/pi/Cursor/Copilot.

FILE: packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts with PROTOCOL_VERSION = '0.1.0' and a zod discriminated union on 'type'. Section 20 provides the concrete shape - session.started, session.heartbeat, session.ended, tool.started, tool.completed, file.read, file.write, command.run, test.passed, test.failed, thinking, waiting, permission.requested, message.sent, subagent.spawned, subagent.completed - each carrying sessionId and at (plus type-specific fields such as harness enum, exitCode, linesAdded/linesRemoved).

ALSO: packages/protocol/schemas/*.json for cross-language adapters, and packages/protocol/src/version.ts.

VERSION PIN IS A RISK CONTROL (section 17.3): keep the AgentEvent union versioned (skill.json-style pin) so adapter PRs from third parties do not break core. Section 33 P3 requires version-checking on every handshake with a warning and changelog link on mismatch.

CONSIDERATIONS: the union is the contract between third-party adapters and our core, so it must stay small and stable. Prefer adding a new event type over overloading an existing one with optional fields - overloads make consumer switches ambiguous.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: every taxonomy item from section 5.2 has a zod schema and a TS type; validation rejects malformed events with a useful message; PROTOCOL_VERSION is exported and checked at handshake.

TESTS: round-trip validation tests per event type; a test that an unknown event type is rejected; a snapshot test that locks the union shape so an accidental breaking change fails CI.

Validation rejects malformed with field-level messages; unknown types name every known type. PROTOCOL_VERSION exported, pinned in the JSON Schema , checked in the artifact test. 9 protocol tests incl. a compile-time exhaustiveness check and a shape snapshot.

title: Animation core spike: minimal skeletal runtime subset
description:
Spike a MINIMAL skeletal animation runtime, informed by learn-spine, per plan sections 9.1-9.5 and 25.

THE LESSON (section 9.3): learn-spine is NOT a Spine tutorial. It is a feasibility prototype of an AGENT-OPERATED 2D animation web platform. Architecture: Agent -> WebMCP -> Command Layer -> Project Session -> Animation Core -> Pose -> PixiJS -> WebGL. React is UI only; the core has NO DOM/React/WebMCP dependencies; editor and player SHARE the core so they can never render divergently.

ADOPT from learn-spine (section 9.4): the core/pose/renderer split; STABLE IDs (bones identified by stable id, never by name - names change, ids do not); revisioned commands carrying expectedRevision + requestId so concurrent edits CONFLICT instead of silently overwriting; the observe-modify-render loop (modify -> render -> observe -> diagnose -> modify again); shared editor/player core.

AVOID (section 9.4): cloning the architecture wholesale; treating it as a production renderer; building a FULL ANIMATION EDITOR. We need a minimal RUNTIME subset, not an editor product. A character needs idle/walk/attack/take-damage/victory, not a keyframe timeline UI.

PIPELINE TO REPLICATE (section 9.3): FK -> IK -> Mesh skinning -> Region transform -> Renderer, driven by evaluate(Project, PoseRequest). The renderer NEVER solves IK - it receives computed geometry. This separation is the whole point.

WHY SKELETAL AND NOT SPRITESHEETS (section 9.2): spritesheets hardcode animation; skeletal lets an agent manipulate STRUCTURED STATE (moveAgent, attack, takeDamage, equip, changeSkin, playAnimation, setPose) with the game engine deciding the animation. Agent state (reading, testing, failed, fixed, battling) selects reading/terminal/damage/victory/attack animations.

STATUS CAVEATS (section 9.3): the reference author reports perf Gate 1 FAIL at the measurement point, physics untested, production-readiness unproven, and MVP output deferred. Treat it as a RESEARCH PROTOTYPE, not a Spine replacement, and do not benchmark against it as a quality bar.

NO PREMATURE OPTIMIZATION (section 9.3): the reference deliberately avoided WebGPU/WASM/Web Workers until a bottleneck was MEASURED. Do the same - measure first.

INTEGRATION (section 25): the animation feature is a CONSUMER - GameState -> AnimationState -> Pose frames for the game client - with ZERO game logic. Removing it must leave the game fully playable.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, each clause with the thing that settles it. The two clauses marked [REWRITTEN] could not fail as written.

1. A character renders from skeleton data. Settled by golden-frame tests for pose evaluation: a named skeleton fixture, evaluated at a named pose, produces a frame that matches a committed golden. A golden is the right instrument precisely because it fails on a wrong pose - but it only means something if the golden is committed and the comparison is exact, so a golden regenerated on the fly is not a golden. Two wrong implementations this catches: evaluating from bone NAMES rather than stable ids (a rename must leave the pose identical, and a test that renames a bone and asserts an unchanged golden is what proves the stable-id property from section 9.4), and a renderer that solves IK itself rather than receiving computed geometry (the pipeline split the bead is built around - see clause 4).

2. [REWRITTEN] The character animates through the AGENT-STATE MAPPINGS. 'Animates' is a property of a running screen and settles nothing; what is actually claimed is the mapping from our five agent states to animations, and that is a table with a testable shape. The bead must ship an exported, exhaustive AGENT_STATE_ANIMATION map from the five states named in the bead (reading, testing, failed, fixed, battling) to the five animations named in the bead (reading, terminal, damage, victory, attack). Settled by: a test that every one of the five states resolves through the map with no undefined and no silent default, AND the reverse - that a state NOT in the map is a loud failure rather than a fallback. The silent default is the failure worth guarding: a decider that maps unknown states to a generic idle animation makes this criterion pass while the mapping is in fact incomplete, and the gap only surfaces when an agent reaches a state nobody mapped. A P2 state map that is total over the current set and refuses unknown states is the deliverable; a mapping table with holes is not.

3. The core has no React/DOM/WebMCP imports. Settled by a module-graph test over the core asserting zero React / DOM / WebMCP imports, not a grep of the top-level entry file. This matters because the reference's discipline is that the editor and the player SHARE the core, which is only true if the core is genuinely headless - one convenience document.createElement in a helper and the whole property is gone while every unit test still passes.

4. The renderer never solves IK - it receives computed geometry (the FK -> IK -> Mesh skinning -> Region transform -> Renderer pipeline from section 9.3). This was implicit in the old criteria and is the separation the whole spike is built around, so it is now stated: settled by a test that the renderer's inputs contain only already-computed transforms, and by the module graph showing IK code reachable only from the evaluation stage. A renderer that quietly computes IK looks identical on screen and destroys the shared-core property, because the editor and player can then diverge in exactly the way sharing is meant to prevent.

5. [REWRITTEN] 'It is removable.' Removability is the integration contract - section 25 says the animation feature is a CONSUMER with zero game logic and that removing it must leave the game fully playable - and 'removable' as a word settles nothing, because an animation package nothing imports is trivially removable and an animation package everything imports is not removable at all, and the criteria did not distinguish them. Settled by a real removal test with two assertions, both required: delete the animation feature from the composition root and the game still reaches a playable state (no dangling import, no missing action id, no build break), AND the game is still correct without it - the same loop, the same rendered outcomes, minus the animation. The second half is the one that catches the actual violation: an animation consumer that quietly became a dependency of a game rule passes the first half and fails this one, and that is precisely the leak section 25 forbids.

TESTS, each failing when the behaviour is wrong rather than when a file is missing:
- golden-frame tests over named skeleton fixtures at named poses, compared against committed goldens.
- a stable-id test: renaming a bone leaves every golden unchanged, which is what proves bones are identified by id and not by name.
- an agent-state mapping test: the map is total over the five named states, and an unknown state is a loud failure rather than a fallback.
- a determinism test: the same Project + PoseRequest yields the same pose, byte for byte.
- a module-graph test over the whole core: zero React / DOM / WebMCP imports, and IK reachable only from the evaluation stage.
- a removal test with both halves: uninstall leaves the game playable AND leaves it correct. A removal test asserting only the first half passes for a feature that has become load-bearing.

CONSIDERATIONS: the scope trap is building an editor. The learn-spine reference includes a full editor with undo/redo, checkpoints, and observation tooling, and it is genuinely impressive - but we need a runtime subset that plays a handful of animations, not an authoring product. Building the editor is a multi-month diversion that serves no milestone. Second: because the reference reports its own perf gate failing, do not treat it as a quality bar or copy its rendering approach uncritically; measure our own bottleneck before optimizing, which is the same discipline the reference itself followed by not prematurely reaching for WebGPU/WASM/Workers.
close_reason:
DONE. §9.3-§9.5's minimal subset, and the split the plan asks for turned out to
be the part worth keeping.

THE SPLIT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CONVENTIONAL. pose.ts imports nothing at all;
render.ts imports only its types; ik.ts has exactly one importer. A renderer
therefore has NO CODE PATH to the solver, because the code does not exist on its
side of the boundary — and the barrel deliberately does not re-export ik.ts, since
re-exporting it would restore the coupling through the front door with a nicer
signature. It exports the solver's TYPE and not its functions.

TWELVE MUTATIONS CAUGHT, and the interesting ones are the boundary rather than the
maths: the renderer importing the IK solver, the game client importing the
feature directly AND via a leaf, an unmapped state falling back to a default (10
refusal cases), the sampler reading the wall clock, a helper reaching for
document.createElement in a headless package, FK resolving parents by NAME rather
than id, and a copy of AGENT_STATE_ANIMATION landing in progression.

TWO REAL BUGS THE TESTS FOUND IN ITS OWN CODE: the region pivot was applied in
unit-quad units instead of art units, so every rectangle sat a third of its own
width from its bone and nothing else in the package noticed; and the ikTargets
totality check was backwards, making it impossible to move one foot. A third was
in its own test — the removability closure SKIPPED the package specifier instead
of reporting it, so the one edge the criterion forbids was invisible to the thing
meant to catch it. That last one is the exact failure this repository keeps
meeting, caught in a check written to prevent it.

ON THE UNLICENSED CHECKOUT, which is the constraint that shaped the bead: read
for ARCHITECTURE only, under instructions to report stage names, type names and
dependency shape and never code. It took the headless core, ids-not-names, the
pipeline order, and the observation that attachments are separate from bones —
which is what makes skinning expressible. It did not take the module layout, the
type names, the matrix convention, the Result wrapper, the revision model or the
editor. The predictTip algebra was rewritten from the law of cosines with its own
clamping. The code is its own and the report says where it is not near the line.

FOUR CONTRADICTIONS WITH THE BRIEF, ALL LEFT STANDING:
  - THE CLIENT DOES NOT CONSUME THIS, and §25 implies it should. §25 puts the
    spike behind animation/pose.ts with the renderer consuming, but the game
    client's own architecture test forbids the client importing ANY feature,
    because the removal test moves each aside. Both rules are correct and do not
    conflict — but the renderer half is delivered as an interface plus a tested
    drawList, not as a wired Pixi consumer. The client was not touched.
  - §24's "subscribes ALL visual events" is deliberately NOT implemented: a
    handler writing poses into the store has no reader, because the client builds
    its world from the event stream. The test asserts the ABSENCE, so the decision
    stays visible instead of drifting into an implementation nobody reads.
  - Criterion 5's "delete from the composition root" is a directory MOVE, and the
    removability test settles both halves statically, saying why a real
    scratch-copy removal was rejected.
  - The tsconfig path and build reference for this package were already on main,
    so the wiring was not this bead's to add.

It also reported, unprompted, that it had briefly touched a file OUTSIDE its
bead during a mutation and left a tsconfig stripped for one run, verified both
restored. I re-checked independently: the progression fix is intact and both files
are clean.

title: HTTP API surface: sessions, bounties, battles, cron
description:
Implement the HTTP route surface listed in plan section 19/22, sitting behind the Public API contract.

ROUTES (section 19 api/ tree, section 22 flows):
- POST /api/events (event-ingest-and-sse bead) - BUILT, apps/web/app/api/events/route.ts
- GET /api/events/stream (SSE) - BUILT, apps/web/app/api/events/stream/route.ts
- POST /api/sessions (HELLO handshake - see contract-session)
- POST /api/sessions/[id]/heartbeat
- POST /api/mcp (MCP Streamable HTTP) - NOT BUILT, and NOT THIS BEAD. Owned end to end by ba-4to, which mounts the Streamable HTTP transport and the route. Two corrections to the line this replaces: the route does not exist (apps/web/app/api/ contains auth/ and events/ only), and 'the P3 MCP bead' was the plan's superseded reading - section 31's correction dated 2026-09-24 is explicit that MCP IS P0, not P3, and section 33's revised build order puts the MCP adapter in P0 alongside the CLI as an equal interface consumer. So the priority named here was wrong as well as the owner. Do not build it from this bead; build it from ba-4to.
- POST /api/bounties, /api/bounties/[id]/claim, /api/bounties/[id]/submit
- POST /api/battles, /api/battles/[id]
- POST /api/webhooks/github - NOT THIS BEAD. Owned end to end by ba-github-infrastructure-56v, which is building it now: signature verification over the raw body, the Octokit client, the issue->bounty and PR-merge->bounty.completed effects, and the boundary rule that the bounty feature consumes those as events rather than importing Octokit. It appears in the list here only so the inventory is complete. Do not build it from this bead; if you picked up 56v, build it from there.
- POST /api/cron/heartbeat - the TRIGGER only, and the state machine it drives is not this bead's either. The stale-session transitions (active -> disconnected -> abandoned) are CONTRACT 3 (ba-contract-session-rpo, closed), and packages/features/agent already ships a sweepStaleSessions helper in hello.ts alongside DEFAULT_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_MS and DEFAULT_RESUME_GRACE_MS. The season-job half belongs to ba-bounty-modes-tiers-seasons-62l, which owns season accounting. What is left for this bead is the scheduled route that calls the existing helper on a schedule - a trigger, not a sweeper.

THE LIST ABOVE IS INCOMPLETE IN A WAY THAT MATTERS, because four routes already exist and are not on it. apps/web/src/routes.ts serves THE FIVE PRIMITIVES over HTTP, and they are the surface every agent and every CLI-equivalent actually uses:
- GET /api/discover (optional ?domain= for the per-domain detail)
- GET /api/search (optional ?type= and ?name=)
- GET /api/inspect (?type= and ?id=)
- POST /api/act ({ action, input })

These are the CONTRACT-4 public API, exposed as HTTP, and they route through the same createApplicationApi the CLI and MCP consume - so HTTP and CLI cannot drift, which is the property the success criteria below actually care about. Add them to the inventory before treating this bead as a list of things still to build: the remaining work here is the resource routes and the sweeper, not the primitives.

Also note the two event routes live in a SEPARATE file, apps/web/src/event-routes.ts, behind its own dispatcher, and deliberately so: the five primitives never read a request body and this one cannot route without inspecting one. Both are pure functions over injected dependencies, which is why apps/web/src/event-routes.test.ts can exercise the whole ingest path - auth, 413, parse, session resolution, emit, SSE - with no server and no database.

THE CONTRACT: these routes are CONSUMERS of the application commands/queries defined in contract-public-api. They must contain NO game logic - a route handler translates HTTP into an application command and maps the result to a response. This is the same iron rule the CLI follows (section 31) and it is what lets a future Discord bot or GitHub App reuse the commands without reimplementation.

AUTH LAYERING: routes authenticate, then authorize at the application boundary. Bearer installation tokens for agent-facing routes; the human web session for dashboard routes. The two credentials are related but SEPARATE (section 3.4).

WHAT IS BUILT: the ingest route authenticates a Bearer installation token through an injected `authenticate(request)` that throws an authentication failure, and the dispatcher turns that into a 401 with the reason - the same mapping every other route uses, so there is no second one to drift. Session resolution is ownership-scoped: resolveSession(sessionId, installationId) returns undefined for a session the caller's installation does not own, which is deliberately indistinguishable from a session that does not exist, so the route cannot be used to enumerate real session ids. RouteDependencies.authenticate is OPTIONAL and absent only where the caller has already authenticated; the app supplies it, because an unauthenticated /api/act is an open door to every capability the game grows.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT: the human-session side of the matrix. There is no dashboard route yet, so the 'agent routes reject human-session auth and vice versa' criterion has only its first half testable today.

THE CRON SWEEWER (section 22): marks sessions stale when (>5 min, no heartbeat, no websocket) as 'disconnected', then 'abandoned' after the grace window. This is what keeps the presence view honest without holding any socket open - and it echoes the plan's decision that heartbeat is a VOLUNTARY agent return cadence, not a held connection (section 13.2).

CONSIDERATIONS: keep handlers thin and push logic down. A route handler that computes a reward is a route handler that will be bypassed by the CLI and produce divergent behavior.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: every route maps 1:1 onto an application command with zero game logic in the handler; the sweeper transitions sessions on schedule; agent routes reject human-session auth and vice versa.

TWO OF THESE ARE ALREADY TRUE AND SHOULD BE ASSERTED, NOT REBUILT. Zero game logic in the handler is the design of apps/web/src/routes.ts: its own comment says a route handler authenticates, translates and translates back, and makes no decisions. The auth split is likewise real - isAuthenticationFailure in packages/api/src/api.ts maps a failed credential to 401 with a reason, and a test asserts the human session is never used as agent identity. The five-primitive routes also already have a parity property available for free: they call the same createApplicationApi the CLI calls, so an HTTP/CLI parity test is a comparison of two calls into one object rather than a comparison of two implementations.

The outstanding part HERE is narrower than the inventory above suggests, because three items on that list belong to other beads. Owed to this bead: the bounty resource routes, the battle resource routes, and the cron trigger. NOT owed to this bead: the webhook endpoint (ba-github-infrastructure-56v owns it end to end), the stale-session transition logic (a closed contract plus a helper that already ships), and the season jobs (ba-bounty-modes-tiers-seasons-62l owns season accounting). Two agents building the same endpoint is the failure this inventory is supposed to prevent, and until the annotations above were added that failure was live for the webhook route.

The three groups that remain are one bead rather than three on purpose, and the reason is worth stating so nobody splits them later: every one of them is the same shape - authenticate, translate to an application command, map the result back - so there is no way to land one of them that teaches you anything the other two do not, and three beads would buy three agents re-deriving the same thin-handler discipline. They are not parallelisable because they are not independent; they are one exercise in the route contract applied to three resources.

TESTS: route-level integration tests; a parity test asserting HTTP and CLI produce identical application-command effects; an auth-matrix test covering which credential each route accepts.

title: Curated CC0/consistent asset shortlist + license tracking
description:
Curate the game asset shortlist and enforce per-pack license tracking, per plan sections 14 and 28.3.

SOURCES (section 14): OpenGameArt (fast prototyping - characters, tilesets, RPG maps, UI, SFX); itch.io (largest - pixel character/RPG, cyberpunk/arena tilesets, UI, battle VFX); Kenney (clean consistent packs - characters, UI, icons, buildings, particles); CraftPix and GameDevMarket (commercial production art); GitHub (CC0 packs - VERIFY each license, never assume).

THE DELIVERABLE (section 14): a curated shortlist of roughly 10-20 packs, free/CC0, in a SINGLE consistent style. The plan explicitly offered this as a follow-up and section 18 build-order item 9 includes it. Do it BEFORE commissioning art.

ART DIRECTION (section 14): cyberpunk / developer-workstation / RPG-arena. Tentative skins: Claude -> Mage, Codex -> Knight, Gemini -> Alchemist, OpenCode -> Rogue, Pi -> Hacker. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: skins ONLY - never hardcode class to model. Class is behavior-derived (see feature-progression); the skin is cosmetic and must be swappable. An agent may also carry its own custom loadout.

LICENCE HYGIENE (sections 14, 17.7, 28.3): the code is MIT, but EACH ASSET PACK KEEPS ITS OWN LICENSE, stored beside the pack. The shortlist MUST record per-pack license BEFORE merge. Never assume a GitHub repo's assets are freely usable.

IMMEDIATE UNBLOCKER (section 28.1 item 1): the CC0 tiny-swords pack from agent-quest is SANCTIONED for V0 - sprites plus its LICENSE.txt, unchanged - giving instant characters and tiles before the shortlist lands. STATUS CORRECTED 2026-09-24: it is NOT yet vendored. Nothing is under apps/web/public/assets/ and no asset directory exists in the tracked tree; the copy is still to be done. This bead covers both the V0 tiny-swords copy and the longer-term curated set, since the V0 copy is the first thing that needs a per-pack LICENSE.txt to exist.

PATH NOTE: section 19 places web assets under apps/web/public/assets/<pack>/LICENSE.txt, not the bare public/assets/<pack>/ the earlier revision of this bead used. There is no apps/web/public/ directory yet.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE (section 17.7): decide the game-asset license separately from the code MIT license, and track per-pack licenses. This is a real decision, not a formality - mixing a GPL art pack into an MIT repo would contaminate it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE '10-20 SAME-STYLE PACKS' IS A JUDGMENT, NOT A CHECK. Two of the three clauses were already machine-checkable and are kept; the first was the one that could not fail, because a shortlist file listing twenty packs with recorded licenses satisfies it whether or not the packs look like each other or the number is right.

1. A shortlist of 10-20 packs in a SINGLE consistent style exists, with a recorded per-pack license for each row. What is checkable and what is not, stated plainly so nobody fakes a check that isn't there: THE COUNT AND THE PER-ROW LICENSE ARE MACHINE-CHECKABLE, and the style is a human judgment the plan makes explicitly (see CONSIDERATIONS: 'style consistency is the actual selection criterion'). So: a shortlist table exists with one row per pack, every row carrying pack name, source URL, license, and the recorded style/tags; a check asserts the row count is in 10-20; and a check asserts no row has an empty license cell. The style-consistency claim is NOT reduced to a fake lint here - a script cannot judge whether five packs look like one game, and writing a check that claims to would be worse than none. What the check DOES enforce is the part that is mechanical and that people actually get wrong: the style is DECLARED per row, so the claim is explicit and reviewable rather than implied by a selection nobody can second-guess later, and the shortlist is a table with a stable shape rather than prose.

   The 10-20 number is a target, not a floor to pad. A shortlist of 20 packs in five visual styles is worse than 12 in one, per the bead's own reasoning - so if the count check fails because a careful selection found fewer, FIX THE SELECTION, do not add packs to make a number go green. Record which packs were rejected for style if the count lands low; that is the evidence the judgment was made rather than skipped.

2. Every merged pack ships its LICENSE.txt. Settled by: a CI check that every directory under apps/web/public/assets/ has a LICENSE.txt - the real, checkable clause, and the one with teeth because it runs on every merge rather than at selection time. scripts/check-licenses.sh currently checks vendored SOURCE licenses only and has no asset-directory rule, so this check does not exist yet and is part of what this bead must add.

3. No pack is merged without a verified license, and the recorded license matches the shipped file. Settled by: a check comparing the license recorded in the shortlist against the license text actually shipped in that pack's LICENSE.txt. Both halves are needed and the second is the one that catches the real failure: a pack relicensed upstream between selection and merge still carries a stale recorded license, the LICENSE.txt check passes because a file exists, and the shortlist quietly asserts something untrue. A file merely EXISTING is not verification.

TESTS, each a command with an exit code. (This supersedes the older single-line TESTS note but keeps its content: the per-asset-directory rule in scripts/check-licenses.sh is still to be added, and that script still has no asset rule today.)
- a shortlist-shape check: the shortlist is a table, every row carries pack name, source URL, license and style/tags, no license cell is empty, and the row count is within 10-20. A prose shortlist fails this - which is intended, because the per-pack license is the deliverable and prose is where per-pack licenses go missing.

title: Battle replay builder + shareable replay URL
description:
Build the battle replay - the plan's most viral feature, per plan sections 2.3, 15.1, 22, and 8.

WHY REPLAY IS THE VIRAL HOOK (section 2.3): the plan judges Battle Replay to be EVEN MORE viral than the Claude-vs-Codex demo. It is the social mechanism: timestamped event log -> battle -> result -> URL. It is also the mechanism by which replays attract sponsors, and sponsors attract more agents (section 2.4 network effect). The example timeline the plan sketches: 00:01 accept quest / 00:08 starts research / 00:17 edits auth.ts / 00:23 discovers vulnerability / 00:41 test fails / 00:48 patches bug / 01:12 critical hit / 01:20 tests 47/47 / 01:20 winner.

DATA: battles.replayJson holds the event timeline; battles.winnerSessionId holds the result. Replay is BUILT FROM THE ACTIVITY LOG (section 30) plus the judge output (section 22, 'judge output IS the replay seed') - not assembled separately.

VIEW (section 22): apps/web/app/(app)/replay/[replayId]/page.tsx renders the event timeline, PixiJS arena playback, and share metadata including an og:image generated from the final frame.

THE DoD THAT MATTERS (section 27 M4): share the replay link with a LOGGED-OUT user and they see the full timeline. This forces a real design decision - the public replay must be viewable without a session, which means the replay data is public even though the account is not. Decide what participant detail (agent names, repo names) is safe to expose publicly; this is a privacy consideration the plan does not spell out, so resolve it deliberately.

ALSO: diff-streaming over the websocket for arena efficiency (section 8), using the codemoo stateDiffBroadcast pattern (section 28.1 item 12).

CONSIDERATIONS: replay URLs are the viral vector, so they must be stable, guess-resistant, and cheap to serve. Consider whether replays should expire or be pruned (an activity-log retention question, cross-referenced with activity-event-log).

THE ACTIVITY LOG YOU ARE REPLAYING FROM, already shipped, so the "build from the log" instruction is concrete (ba-activity-event-log-aph, closed). The durable table is event_log: id (bigserial), type, actorId, payload jsonb, occurredAt, read through features/activity's read API (a per-session trail plus recent), via DrizzleStateStore - the only path an event takes to the database. Three properties of that log decide what a replay can and cannot show:
- THE PERSISTENCE FILTER IS NOT EVERYTHING. Only PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES are durable: PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES = ['session.started','session.ended','session.resumed','test.passed','test.failed'] plus whatever each installed feature declares in GameFeature.persistedEvents. The list this bead used to quote was the plan's wish-list, and the difference is not cosmetic for THIS bead: bounty.claimed, bounty.completed, battle.started and battle.finished are the spine of a replay, and none of them is durable today because no feature declares them. A replay built now would render session and test events and nothing else. Battle owns declaring battle.started/battle.finished and bounty owns declaring its own, and the DoD 'share the link with a logged-out user and they see the full timeline' is unreachable until they do - which makes this the one place where the filter's real shape is a delivery blocker rather than a caveat.. Everything else (thinking, waiting, streaming, heartbeat) is bus-only and is gone after a restart. So the replay timeline is reconstructable ONLY from persisted events. The example timeline's narrative beats (research, discovers vulnerability, critical hit) are illustrative, not all durable - a replay that wants them must add those event types to the persisted set, a deliberate act, not an assumption.
- ORDERING IS GUARANTEED, which is what makes the timeline a timeline. The runtime emits persist -> handlers -> publish, so the durable record is written before any consumer reads it, and the log is ordered. A replay can rely on occurredAt ordering without re-sorting races.
- RETENTION IS 365 DAYS (features/activity owns the policy; 365 because a shared replay is a link). So a replay is reconstructable for a year; beyond that, event-log pruning and replay availability are the same question, and a replay URL pointing at pruned events needs a defined degraded state rather than a 500.

DETERMINISM IS A HARD REQUIREMENT, not a nicety, because the same event stream must yield the same replay (this is an explicit test). That constrains the design: the replay is a pure function of the persisted event stream plus the judge output - no wall-clock reads, no random IDs, no dependence on 'now' during construction. It also means the judge output that seeds the replay must itself be the ordered, attributable event stream the workspace/judge bead (ba-battle-workspace-judge-jc9) produces, not a collapsed score; a judge that returns only a weighted number cannot seed an explainable replay.

THE PUBLIC/LOGGED-OUT BOUNDARY INTERACTS WITH AN OPEN BUG, so this bead is not blocked on privacy decisions alone. The SSE stream (GET /api/events/stream) is currently an unauthenticated global broadcast that ships every validated AgentEvent to any open socket - an agent's file paths, command names, and thinking content reach any subscriber. That is tracked as a P0 bug (ba-9hr). It is recorded here so whoever builds the replay page does not build it on the assumption that a clean public replay implies a clean live stream: the replay page is a public, deliberately-scoped read (a specific battle's persisted timeline), which is a different surface from the global live broadcast that still needs the public/private event classification and stream authentication. Do not widen the replay's public surface to include live transient events because the live stream is currently unfiltered.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The first shortcut is assembling the replay from feature tables (the bounty row, the battle row, the progression rows) instead of from the activity log; that is exactly what the 'not assembled separately' clause forbids, it duplicates truth the log already holds, and it will drift. The second is a replay that is not deterministic - if construction reads the current time or mints a fresh ID, the determinism test fails and two viewers of the same battle can see different replays, which defeats sharing. The third is serving the full timeline to a logged-out viewer by simply removing the auth check from an authenticated endpoint: the logged-out DoD is a real public read with a chosen field allow-list (agent names, repo names - decided deliberately), not 'disable auth and leak every field'. The fourth is a replay URL that is sequential or otherwise guessable; the viral vector plus public data means an enumerable id lets anyone bulk-scrape every battle.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a completed battle produces a replay URL; a logged-out visitor sees the complete timeline; the og:image renders; the replay is a deterministic pure function of the persisted event stream plus the judge output (same stream, same replay); the timeline is reconstructed from event_log, not from feature tables; the public logged-out view exposes a deliberate allow-list of participant detail, not everything.

TESTS: the logged-out DoD test; a determinism test (same event stream yields the same replay); a test that replay construction reads from event_log rather than feature tables; a test that the replay timeline survives a restart (reads persisted events, not bus-only ones); a test that replay URLs are not sequential/guessable; a test that the public logged-out view excludes fields outside the chosen allow-list.
