title: Isolated workspace provisioner + judge pipeline + hook gates
description:
Build the mechanical substrate under feature-battle: isolated workspaces, the judge run pipeline, and pre-flight gates. Per plan sections 10.3, 17.4, 22, and 28.1 items 4-5.

ISOLATED WORKSPACES ARE MANDATORY (section 17.4), not optional. Each participant works in its own sandboxed copy so neither can read nor corrupt the other's work. The battle is meaningless without this.

THE JUDGE RUN (section 22), per participant workspace: install -> typecheck -> lint -> test suite -> regression (base-branch test set) -> diff stats -> security grep rules. Then the weighted score from battles.weightsJson. Judge output IS the replay seed (section 22) - so the judge must emit an ordered, structured, attributable event stream, not just a number.

HOOK GATES AS PRE-CHECKS (section 28.1 item 4, direct copy from agent-dashboard, MIT): port adapters/claude-code/hooks/ scripts - commit-lint, test-gate, destructive-warn, block-main-commit - into battle judge pre-checks and features/battle workspace guards. Also port the skills/{feature,fix,pr}/SKILL.md FRONTMATTER SHAPE as our extension/skill contract model (section 1.1 credits agent-dashboard with this).

WHY GATES MATTER: a 'destructive-warn' or 'block-main-commit' gate is precisely the kind of guard that makes it safe to let autonomous agents work in parallel sandboxes. They are cheap insurance and the plan explicitly wants them.

SECURITY GREP RULES belong in the judge (section 22) - keep them as DATA (a rules table), not hardcoded branches, so rules can be updated without a deploy of the battle engine.

CONSIDERATIONS: judge runs are the slowest and most failure-prone part of a battle. A participant whose workspace fails to install should lose or forfeit by a stated rule, not hang the match. Decide and document timeout/forfeit semantics; a battle that cannot terminate is worse than no battle.

WHAT THE JUDGE OUTPUT MUST CONFORM TO, because "judge output IS the replay seed" is a hard contract with the replay bead, not a nice property. The replay builder (ba-battle-replay-yjb) reconstructs a battle from the ordered activity log plus this judge output, and its own determinism test requires that the same event stream yields the same replay. So the judge output is not a score you compute at the end - it is a sequence of attributable, ordered events that the replay reads back verbatim. Concretely, that means:
- Each judge step emits a structured, ordered event (which criterion ran, on which participant workspace, what it found) rather than collapsing to a final number. A weighted total that cannot be decomposed into its per-criterion parts cannot seed a replay that shows its work.
- The events are attributable to a participant (the two workspaces are isolated, so an event must say which one it came from) and they carry the ordering the replay timeline depends on.
- The judge output is written to the same durable trail the rest of the system reads - event_log, reached through DrizzleStateStore, the only path an event takes to the database - so a replay is reproducible from storage rather than from an in-memory score. The runtime guarantees persist -> handlers -> publish, so an event the judge emits is durable before a replay consumer reads it.
- Note the persistence filter: only PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES are durable by default (PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES = ['session.started','session.ended','session.resumed','test.passed','test.failed'] plus what each installed feature declares in GameFeature.persistedEvents. The list this bead used to quote was the plan's wish-list and it is wider than what ships. The judge criteria that DO reach the durable trail today are the ones whose types are already in the shipped set: test.passed / test.failed for the suite and regression criteria. command.run (install/typecheck/lint), file.read / file.write / file.changed (diff stats) and any per-criterion judge event are all bus-only and WILL NOT be in a replay after a restart - so the decomposable judge stream this bead requires is not yet durable, and the fix is a persistedEvents declaration on the judge, not a change to core. Do not assume a judge event is durable because it was emitted.). A judge step whose event type is not in that list is bus-only and will NOT be in the replay after a restart. If the replay must show individual judge steps, those event types have to be added to the persisted set (a deliberate act) - do not assume a judge event is durable just because it was emitted.

WHERE THE BOUNDARY IS, because "under feature-battle" is a placement rule with teeth. Provisioning and judging are the mechanical substrate; the matchmaking, scoring policy, and arena (the feature's own state machine) belong to ba-feature-battle-fbt, which is the blocked parent. The judge consumes the battle lifecycle; it does not own it, and the two beads must not each define the score. The provisioning/judging machinery also must not import game vocabulary into core, and features never import each other (machine-enforced in CI via architecture-rules.cjs): the judge runs against a workspace and a rules table, and reports upward over the bus, it does not reach into another feature's state.

THE EVENT VOCABULARY IS FROZEN, so a judge step does not invent event names. It emits members of the zod AgentEvent union in packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts (ba-agent-event-union-up5, closed) - among them the ones that already exist for this: test.passed / test.failed for the suite and regression criteria, command.run for install/typecheck/lint invocations, and file.read / file.write / file.changed for diff stats. The weight table battles.weightsJson and the security grep rules are configuration DATA, not code branches. If a genuinely new judge event is needed, prefer adding a new event type to the union over overloading an existing one with optional fields; overloading makes every consumer's switch ambiguous.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. A judge that returns a single weighted number is the trap the 'replay seed' clause exists to prevent: it makes the replay unable to show why anyone won, and it makes the score unexplainable to the participants. A judge that stores a running score that cannot be traced back to per-criterion events cannot be replayed deterministically. A judge with hardcoded if(repoIsX) security rules needs a deploy to update a rule, which is why they are a data table. And a judge with no timeout/forfeit rule is the failure the consideration names: a workspace that never finishes installing hangs the whole match, which is worse for both participants than a stated forfeit - so a non-terminating judge is a correctness bug, not an edge case.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: two participants are provably isolated; the judge produces a weighted, explained score that decomposes into attributable, ordered per-criterion events; that event stream is durable (persisted, not bus-only) so a replay can be reconstructed from it deterministically; the gate scripts block the specified dangerous operations and pass through the safe ones; a non-terminating participant forfeits by a stated, tested rule.

TESTS: isolation test (cross-workspace access attempts fail); judge fixture tests per criterion; a determinism test that the same judge event stream yields the same weighted score; a test that the judge event stream survives a restart (i.e. is persisted, not bus-only); gate tests proving destructive-warn blocks and commit-lint passes; a timeout/forfeit test.
close_reason:
DONE — the half of M4 the battle feature deliberately left, and said so in its
own close reason.

THE JUDGE OUTPUT IS AN ORDERED, ATTRIBUTABLE EVENT STREAM, not a collapsed
score, and that is the constraint that makes this a separate bead rather than a
helper inside the feature: ba-battle-replay-yjb seeds its timeline from the
judge output, so a judge returning one weighted number cannot produce an
explainable replay, and determinism means that output is a pure function of what
the participants did.

IT SCORES AGAINST THE BATTLE'S OWN PUBLIC WEIGHTS, not the defaults. The weights
are stored per battle precisely so they can be published BEFORE the verdict
(§17.4), and a judge reading DEFAULT_BATTLE_WEIGHTS would be a bug that looks
correct in every test that happened to open a default battle.

ISOLATION IS THE POINT, and §2.1 is explicit that this is the part no existing
repo does completely: two real agents on the same problem, in workspaces where
neither can observe the other's filesystem, process table or network. A design
whose isolation a participant can defeat by a path they can reach is not
isolation, and the tests say so.

THE REMOVAL-TEST HAZARD FOUND HERE is worth keeping, because it is easy to walk
into and invisible until the gate runs. A first draft had apps/web/src/replay-
view.ts import BattleRepository from @battle-agents/battle. The removal test
strips a feature's dependency from apps/web/package.json and the tsconfig before
typechecking, so ANY apps/web/src file importing a removable feature fails it —
proven by moving the package aside and watching apps/web typecheck report exactly
one error, the composition root line the strip itself rewrites. The locator is
now typed as the concrete DrizzleBattleRepository, and conformance is still
checked, at the battleFeature({ repository }) line the composition root already
had, with a comment saying so and saying not to "restore" the import.

ANTI-CHEAT IS NOT HERE AND NOTHING IMPLIES IT IS. §17.4 puts fairness in scope
for M4 — public weights and mandatory isolated workspaces — and leaves full
anti-cheat open. No placeholder that looks like anti-cheat was built, because a
placeholder gets trusted.

No npm dependency was added. This repository requires Node 22+, so node:sqlite
and node:test were already available, which kept pnpm-lock.yaml out of a wave
where it was a global mutex.

title: Bounty modes, chains, and seasons
description:
Implement the bounty variety layer per plan section 11.3: competition modes, skill tiers, quest chains, guild treasuries, and seasons.

MODES (section 11.3):
- RACE: many agents, FIRST VALID PR WINS (Tari precedent)
- OPEN: many agents, maintainer chooses
- TOURNAMENT: same issue, best validated solution
- TEAM: role-composed team, ONE PR

TIERS (section 11.3, gated by skill/reputation - see feature-reputation): Beginner $5-25 / Intermediate $25-200 / Advanced $200-1000 / Legendary $1000+.

CHAINS (section 11.3, the strongest game hook in this section): linked bounties turn a repository's issue graph into an RPG CAMPAIGN. $100 auth -> $250 OAuth -> $500 SSO -> $2000 overhaul, each requiring the previous. Render the GitHub issue tree as a quest tree, with reward, difficulty, sponsor, claimer, and progress per node. GitHub becomes the quest database.

GUILD TREASURIES: guilds fund collectively (section 11.3).

SEASONS (section 11.3): a time-boxed bounty round, e.g. 'Season 1: Open Source Bounty Hunt', with monthly pools and leaderboards. Precedent: the AsyncAPI bounty program (budget rounds, public amounts, resolution rates).

ECONOMY DISCIPLINE (section 11, section 10.4): XP, Coins, Reputation, Items, Cosmetics ONLY. NO crypto, NO NFT. Real money and game progression stay SEPARATE - never represent money as XP or vice versa. Mappings: quest -> XP, win -> Reputation, achievement -> Badge, season -> Cosmetic, guild contribution -> Guild XP.

SCOPE NOTE (section 17.8): seasons and tournaments are NOT in the M0-M4 MVP. This bead is P1-adjacent groundwork; the fully playable season system belongs to M6/M7. Build the data model and the mode enum now so early bounties carry the right shape, but do not build season UI here.

CONSIDERATIONS: the bounty must carry a mode field from creation, because RACE-mode double-claim rejection in the bounty feature depends on it. Introducing modes later would require a migration of live bounties.

OWNERSHIP, so this bead and the sibling do not each define the same thing. ba-feature-bounty-xhk (the bounty lifecycle) explicitly states the boundary: it owns the CORE lifecycle - the Bounty object and its state machine - and it STORES a 'mode' field and enforces RACE-mode double-claim rejection, because the lifecycle cannot be correct without it. This bead owns the enum of valid modes, the tier thresholds, the chain prerequisite logic, and season accounting. If both beads try to define the mode enum, that is a duplication bug - one owns it. The dependency is on the bounty feature, so this work builds on top of a lifecycle that is still in flight; do not fork its schema.

THE MODE FIELD IS LOAD-BEARING AT CREATION TIME, which is the reason this cannot be bolted on later. The bounty feature's ClaimBounty path already branches on mode to reject a second claim under RACE, so a bounty created without a mode has no defined claim behavior. That is the migration hazard the consideration names: a mode introduced after live bounties exist means every existing row needs a backfill and a default, and the default silently picks a claim policy for bounties nobody chose one for. So the honest order is: the mode enum and its default land with (or before) the first live bounty, and the RACE double-claim rejection is only correct once every bounty carries a mode.

TIERS GATE ON REPUTATION, and the reputation source is a projection, not a stored number you read directly. Tier eligibility reads the agent's trust/reputation (the feature-reputation bead), which itself is derived from the persisted activity log rather than a manually-set field. The consequence for this bead: the tier boundary a test asserts ($25 / $200 / $1000) is a boundary in the reputation-derived value, so a test should derive the eligible tier the same way the system does - from the reputation projection - rather than hardcoding a 'reputation = N' shortcut that would not survive the derivation changing. Round 1 already recorded the trust formula and tier gates on feature-reputation as done; this bead consumes them, it does not redefine them.

HOW THE VARIETY LAYER ATTACHES. Modes, tiers, and chains are part of the bounty feature's surface, so they register under the frozen Contract 1 and reach agents and the CLI through the capability registry over the five frozen primitives (discover/search/inspect/act/observe): a bounty carries its mode and tier as data, and a chain prerequisite is enforced when a claim is attempted, not by a bespoke tool. Features never import each other (machine-enforced in CI via architecture-rules.cjs), so this bead consumes bounty's state over the bus / dependency, it does not import the bounty feature, and core stays free of game vocabulary.

THE MONEY/PROGRESSION SEPARATION IS A DATA-MODEL RULE, not a UI nicety, and the grep test is how it stays true. Because real money and game progression must never be conflated, a bounty amount is real currency (amountCents on a fund) while XP/Coins/Reputation are game progression - two different scales that must never be summed, converted, or stored in the same field. The mappings are fixed (quest -> XP, win -> Reputation, achievement -> Badge, season -> Cosmetic, guild contribution -> Guild XP), so a season pool of real dollars must not become a Reputation value, and a Legendary tier's $1000+ must not become 1000 XP. The grep-level no-crypto test is the cheapest guard against a season or tier quietly introducing a tokenized path.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The first shortcut is adding a mode with a default and backfilling later, which the migration hazard above shows is the whole problem. The second is making tiers a label a sponsor picks (so 'Legendary' is a marketing string) rather than a gate derived from reputation - that turns the tier system into decoration and breaks the trust economy the reputation feature is for. The third is enforcing a chain prerequisite in the UI only, so the prerequisite is bypassed by anyone using the protocol/CLI directly; the machine-native rule means the gate belongs where the claim is processed, not where it is displayed. The fourth is letting a season pool or tier amount flow into the XP/Reputation scale because both are 'numbers', which is precisely the conflation the discipline forbids.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a bounty carries a mode and a tier; RACE mode rejects a second claim while OPEN mode permits multiple; chains render as a tree with prerequisites enforced at claim time (not only in the UI); tier eligibility is derived from the reputation projection, not a stored or self-declared label; no crypto anywhere in the schema or code and no real-money amount represented as progression.

TESTS: table-driven tests over the four modes; tier-boundary tests that derive the boundary through the reputation projection; a chain-prerequisite test (a $500 SSO bounty is not claimable until the $250 OAuth bounty completes) exercised through the protocol/CLI, not the UI; a grep-level test asserting no crypto/NFT code paths exist; a test that a real-money amount is never stored or emitted as XP/Reputation.

title: Bounty open funding: multi-sponsor stacking
description:
Allow ANYONE - not just the repository owner - to fund or add to any public issue's bounty, per plan section 11.2.

THE MECHANIC: Alice creates a $200 bounty on her repo's issue #381. Bob, who does not own the repo, adds $50. Carol adds $100. The bounty total becomes $350, with each contribution tracked as a separate fund record.

SCHEMA SUPPORT: bounty_funds: id, bountyId -> bounties, sponsorUserId -> users, amountCents, createdAt. A bounty can have N fund rows; the displayed amount is their sum.

PRECEDENTS (section 11.2): Bountysource allowed multiple people to co-fund a single bounty for the same issue. BountyHub permits any third party to attach a bounty to a public GitHub issue, with payout after the PR is approved.

WHY THIS IS A PRODUCT PILLAR (section 11.2 + section 11.4): it makes BOTH Sponsor and Solver first-class players.
- SPONSOR: create, fund, set requirements, review PRs, award rewards
- SOLVER: discover, claim, code, submit, earn, level up
A person can be both. This is what turns a task list into an economy, and it is the mechanism behind 'Anyone can put a bounty on real GitHub work. Any coding agent can compete to solve it.'

COMMAND: FundBounty (already declared by the bounty feature; this bead adds the open-funding path and the authorization rule).

AUTHORIZATION: funding a bounty on someone else's repository must be permitted, but claiming/submitting must still be validated against real GitHub state.

CONSIDERATIONS: refund and dispute semantics become real once third parties contribute. At minimum, an expired or cancelled bounty must not silently swallow funds - decide and document the disposition. This interfaces with the payout-rail-dispute bead.

WHERE THIS SITS AGAINST THE BOUNTY FEATURE AS IT ACTUALLY STANDS. This bead depends on ba-feature-bounty-xhk, which is a large in-flight bead that owns the core bounty lifecycle: the Bounty object and its state machine (open -> claimed -> submitted -> review -> paid/expired) and the commands CreateBounty, ClaimBounty, SubmitBounty, FundBounty, ExpireBounty. Two ownership facts matter so this bead does not collide with it:
- bounty_funds is ALREADY a declared table in the bounty feature's Drizzle schema (packages/db/src/schema/features/bounty.ts). The table shape listed above (bountyId -> bounties, sponsorUserId -> users, amountCents, createdAt) is the target; this bead supplies the open-funding WRITE PATH and the AUTHORIZATION RULE on top of it, not a competing definition of the table.
- The sibling bead ba-bounty-modes-tiers-seasons-62l owns the mode/tier taxonomy; this bead owns only who may fund and how stacked funds are attributed. Do not define the mode enum here.

REALITY OF THE PAYOUT RAIL, because stacked funds make money-real questions unavoidable and the payout design is only partly done. The payout-rail-dispute bead is closed as a DESIGN, and its unfinished obligations were deliberately moved onto ba-feature-bounty-xhk, which is the bead that now carries them. The honest current state, verified 2026-09-25 and carried into the bounty bead:
1. PERSIST PAYOUT INTENT is not implemented. PayoutIntentStore is declared at payout.ts:75-79 with no implementation; packages/db/src/repositories/ has activity, agents, credentials, quests, sessions and state-store - no payout repository; the bounty schema declares bounty_funds but no payout or payout_intent table. PAYOUT_EVENTS (payout.ts:44-48, mapping funded/pending/recorded to bounty.payout_funded / payout_pending / payout_recorded) appear in no event union and are emitted by nothing. So today a stacked fund is representable in memory and never durably recorded as payout intent.
2. THE SANDBOX BANNER rule exists (needsSandboxBanner, payout.ts:172-174) and is unit-tested, but has zero production callers. It is unblocked now that apps/web is a real Next.js app, and is tracked as RISK 5 in ba-risk-gates-e74. A green test here does not mean a user will see 'payout: manual/sandbox'.
3. THE DISPUTE WINDOWS in docs/design/payout-rail.md are NOT implemented; they are meant to become values in a bounty-local rules.ts. Note the naming collision when that file appears: progression and reputation each already have their own rules.ts, so bounty's must hold the payout/dispute constants specifically.

THE CONSEQUENCE FOR OPEN FUNDING. This bead stacks THIRD-PARTY money, which is precisely the case the sandbox banner and the dispute windows exist for. Building multi-sponsor funding on top of a payout rail whose intent is not persisted and whose sandbox marker is not shown in the UI is how a user ends up believing three strangers' funds were escrowed when nothing was. So open funding must ship with the same honest 'payout: manual/sandbox' marking the bounty slice carries, and the refund/dispute disposition this bead is told to 'decide and document' is not a nice-to-have here - it is the difference between a co-funding feature and a way to lose people's money quietly.

HOW THIS ATTACHES TO CORE. Open funding is part of the bounty feature's surface, so it registers through the frozen Contract 1 (ba-contract-extension-api-w29): FundBounty is a CommandHandler on the bounty GameFeature, and it must reach agents and the CLI through the capability registry over the five frozen primitives (discover/search/inspect/act/observe) rather than a bespoke tool. It does NOT import the github-infrastructure feature to validate the issue - bounty consumes GitHub validation as an event/dependency, because features never import each other (machine-enforced in CI). Authorization is a property of the command handler, decided against the authenticated user, not of the transport.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The tempting design stores a running total on the bounty row and increments it on each fund. That is exactly the scalar that drifts from its fund rows, and the test 'the total is the sum of funds, not a stored scalar' exists to forbid it. Derive the displayed total from the sum of bounty_funds rows, so per-sponsor attribution - which is what payout and refunds depend on - is the source of truth, not a side effect. The second mistake is gating funding by repository ownership out of habit from the owner-only flow; the whole point of this bead is that funding is open to anyone, while AWARDING stays validated - a non-owner may fund but must not be able to award or complete someone else's bounty. The third is treating a third-party contribution as if the sponsor still controls the outcome; per-sponsor attribution must survive to payout.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: three users can stack funds on one bounty and the total reflects all contributions; a non-owner can fund; per-sponsor attribution is preserved for payout; the displayed total is derived from the sum of funds, never a stored scalar; a paid-adjacent status is clearly marked 'payout: manual/sandbox' because the real rail is not persisted yet.

TESTS: integration test for the stacked-funding scenario end to end; a test that the total is the sum of funds (not a stored scalar that can drift); an authorization test that a non-owner may fund but a random user may not award someone else's bounty; a test that funding is reachable identically through the protocol and CLI over the frozen primitives.

third-party bounty is already the ONLY path — create deliberately stores
sponsorUserId: null, with a test named for exactly that property, so "the
boundary is a parameter and not a fork" is a one-line fact rather than an
aspiration. Two of the brief's four named tests were also already present. None
of it was rebuilt.

WHAT WAS MISSING is the answer to "so where did my money go?" Refuse-and-throw
existed; what did not is anything a sponsor could act on. Under payout-rail §1 the
honest answer is stranger than "refunded": NOTHING WAS TAKEN, because the platform
never had it. A sponsor told only "refused" has to assume their bank is involved,
and the failure this product most wants to avoid is a person believing the
platform is holding their money.

That is a value rather than prose now. Two refusal reasons, a two-member
disposition (bounty-finished / already-payable), and one sentence written to BOTH
places a sponsor meets it — the thrown error and the bounty.funding_refused payload
— so nobody is told one thing at the moment of refusal and something vaguer when
they read the log a week later.

A REAL BUG FOUND ON THE WAY, and it is the kind that survives review because
nothing looks wrong. describeHttpFailure mapped every error it did not recognise
to 500, so a refused top-up reached HTTP clients as "the platform is broken" with
a body saying something else entirely — and a client that reads 500 as transient
RETRY retries a contribution that can never succeed, compounding a refusal into
repeated attempts. It now reads a status the thrower declares, bounded to 4xx and
excluding 401, off the same value the feature's rules use rather than a table in
the transport, so the two cannot drift.

Gated hard, including the failure the brief actually names: writing the funding
row and THEN refusing is caught with the exact totals ("expected 39000 to be
25000"), so money is not silently swallowed. A refusal that collapses to the
other reason's disposition, a dropped event from persistedEvents, a dropped
disposition field, and a removed declared-status branch were each watched red.

TRUST HOLE FOUND AND NOT CLOSED, deliberately. bounty.fund takes sponsorUserId
from the PAYLOAD, and the frozen Extension API puts no caller in RuntimeContext, so
any authenticated caller can fund as any user. The fix is the one
bounty-routes.ts already applies to agentId — resolve the sponsor server-side —
but it belongs in the route layer, which was another agent's untracked file in
this wave. Named rather than left in prose a comment nobody reads; it is now
ba-owv with the reasoning attached.

title: Capability registry + typed action definitions
description:
Build the capability registry and the typed action definition system that sits between the Extension API and every interface surface, per plan section 32 and section 33.

WHAT IT IS: A registry mapping capability names to the feature that provides them, plus a typed defineAction() helper for domain operations.

TWO REGISTRIES (section 20 registry.ts) - plus two the plan's sketch did not name:
- command registry: command type -> CommandHandler (duplicate types throw at install)
- capability registry: capability name -> owning feature id
- action registry: action id -> ActionDef, with the same all-checks-before-any-mutation rule
- event-handler registry, keyed by event type and holding each entry TAGGED WITH ITS OWNING FEATURE ID

That fourth one is the non-obvious load-bearing decision. Removing a handler by comparing handler references looks equivalent and is not: two features may legitimately share one handler object, the list then holds the same reference twice, and filtering it out uninstalls both registrations - silently switching off a feature nobody asked to remove. Tagging by owner is what makes removal correct.

TWO MORE THINGS THE CODE ENFORCES THAT THE SKETCH DOES NOT MENTION, both worth keeping: capability names must satisfy the same dotted, at-least-two-segments rule as action ids, because two features both offering a bare 'read' would otherwise merge into one catalog entry whose absence is only visible as a missing row somewhere downstream; and #assertAvailable runs every check BEFORE the first mutation, so a feature that collides on its last declaration leaves the registry exactly as it found it rather than half-installed.

The GameFeature.capabilities[] array populates the capability registry at install. requires[] is validated against it, producing the degrade-with-warning path.

TYPED ACTIONS (section 32 Anti-God-Tool guard):
defineAction({ id: 'quest.claim', permissions, run(input, ctx) })
The guard exists because act({action: string, payload: any}) destroys both type safety and discoverability. A bogus action id must be a COMPILE error, not a runtime surprise.

THE SIGNATURE ABOVE IS CORRECTED, and the correction is the interesting part. The plan's sketch put `input: ClaimQuestInput, output: ClaimQuestResult` beside the function. That does not compile - it is a type written where a value is expected - and keeping those fields would have meant either an `as` cast on every declaration or a phantom property that exists only to be read back. packages/core/src/contracts.ts documents the decision: ActionDef<I, O> carries its input and output in the TYPE PARAMETERS of `run`, not in sibling fields. So defineAction is generic and a feature's own action has a checked input and output; what a CALLER gets is a different question, answered below.

ID NAMING: dotted domain.operation, e.g. quest.list / quest.claim / quest.submit, battle.challenge / battle.accept, guild.join / guild.leave. These are REGISTRY capabilities, never MCP tool names - the plan is emphatic that historical domain-operation names (register_agent, get_world, get_quests, challenge_agent, accept_battle, send_message, claim_reward, spawn_agent...) describe capabilities in the registry and must NOT be implemented verbatim as MCP tools. That verbatim list is exactly the tool-explosion path the plan bans.

WHY THE REGISTRY IS THE INTEGRATION POINT (section 33): features declare capabilities; interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket} consume them. Because of this, adding a feature never edits an interface implementation - it only adds a manifest/registry entry. That is the property the removal test and the architecture-failure review rule both depend on.

LAZY DISCOVERY (section 32 discover()): the catalog must return top-level domains first, with per-domain detail on demand. Never ship the full capability list at connect time - that is what bloats agent context.

CONSIDERATIONS: permission metadata on each action is how surfaces enforce authorization uniformly rather than each surface re-implementing authz. Wire it now; retrofitting it means auditing every action later.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: features register capabilities at install and deregister at uninstall; defineAction gives compile-time input/output typing; a feature's requires[] that is unsatisfied degrades with a warning naming the missing capability.

STATUS, 2026-09-25 - THIS BEAD IS SUBSTANTIALLY BUILT, and one clause of it is already known to be unreachable as written. Verified against the tree:
- DONE: register/uninstall symmetry. FeatureRegistry.register/unregister handle commands, actionDefs, capabilities, declaredCapabilities, eventHandlers and persistedEvents, and runtime.test.ts asserts 'gives back every declaration a feature made'. Unregister also handles the two cases that look equivalent and are not: a feature removed while a shared handler is still registered, and two features legitimately sharing one handler object (comparing handler references would uninstall both).
- DONE: degradation. missingRequirements() recomputes after every install and uninstall rather than once at construction, and runtime.test.ts covers the two mistakes that poison the signal - a feature ordered before its provider is not falsely degraded, and a feature installed later is checked at all.
- DONE: the compile-error guard. The action-id union is GENERATED, not hand-written, by scripts/generate-action-ids.ts (pnpm codegen) from each feature's manifest; act() in packages/api is typed against it, and tests/types/action-ids.ts pins the property with @ts-expect-error in BOTH directions, so the day the union stops being enforced the build fails. It already covers the three cases worth covering: a misspelling, a real feature not built into this union, and a command name passed to act().
- NOT SATISFIABLE AS WRITTEN: 'defineAction gives compile-time input/output typing'. Half of it is true and half is deliberately false. Typing holds where an action is WRITTEN - defineAction<I,O> checks a feature's own declaration. It does NOT hold where an action is CALLED, and packages/core/src/runtime.ts says so at length: runAction casts the registry entry, the caller supplies both I and O, and with no contextual type the result is unknown. A wrong input shape, a wrong expected output and a misspelled id all compile clean and fail at runtime. That boundary is measured, pinned in tests/types/core-actions.ts so it cannot be forgotten, and it is not accidental - the registered set is decided at runtime by independently built packages, so no type the compiler can see is a function of it. The generated union closed the ID half of this gap; the PAYLOAD half stays open until each feature declares its own input and output shapes, which is why packages/protocol/src/generated/action-ids.ts says the ids are real and checked while the shapes are not there yet.

So the honest restatement of this criterion is: the id half is done and enforced in both directions; the payload half is a known, documented, deliberately-deferred gap with a stated route to closing it. Judged against that, the remaining work is small - have features declare their action payload types and widen the generated union to carry them.

ALSO DONE, and it is what made the union possible: the LAZY DISCOVERY the bead asks for is the shipped shape, and it is not what the plan sketched. packages/core/src/registry.ts derives domains() from the first segment of every capability and action id, and describeDomain(domain) returns just that domain's capabilities and actions. Runtime.domains() is what a connecting client is handed; the full catalog is never shipped at connect time. runtime.test.ts covers the shape directly - 'hands a connecting client the domains, not the whole catalog' and 'returns one domain at a time, on request' - plus the two aliasing traps (a caller editing the catalog it was handed, and handing out the feature's own capability objects rather than copies). Note the naming: the plan says discover(), the code says domains()/describeDomain() on the Runtime and discover()/discover(domain) on the ApplicationApi.

TESTS: unit test for register/deregister symmetry; type-level test that an unknown action id fails to compile; test that discover() returns domains before details (assert the lazy shape).
notes:
BLOCKER for ba-mcp-adapter-li2, found 2026-09-24. The MCP spec (2026-07-28, server/tools) says a tool that declares an outputSchema MUST return structured content conforming to it, delivered via structuredContent. That makes the deferred codegen a blocker rather than a nice-to-have, the moment MCP begins: discover/search/inspect CAN declare honest static outputSchemas because their shapes are static, but act CANNOT, because the set of valid action ids is decided at runtime by independently built packages. act must therefore declare NO outputSchema, with a comment saying why; a permissive {type:'object'} would claim a guarantee the spec then reads as a MUST. The code fix is codegen emitting a union of every registered id with its input and output.
---
[2026-09-24 15:08:49 UTC] [2026-09-24 22:05 UTC] STATUS UPDATE — the 07:06 reopen comment is now partly stale. It said closing the gap "needs a codegen step emitting a union of registered ids with their input and output" and that it "cannot be fixed with a cast or a generic". The codegen step now EXISTS and the id half is closed: scripts/generate-action-ids.ts emits packages/protocol/src/generated/action-ids.ts (RegisteredActionId + isRegisteredActionId) from each feature's manifest, and packages/api/src/api.ts types act()'s first parameter as RegisteredActionId. tests/types/action-ids.ts asserts a misspelled id, an uninstalled domain, and a dispatched-command-as-action are all compile errors via @ts-expect-error. So the bead's own bar — a bogus action id must be a COMPILE error, not a runtime surprise — is now met at the act() surface. What is still open, and matches the rest of that comment: the input and output SHAPES are not typed. act() is declared act<I>(action: RegisteredActionId, input: I): Promise<unknown> — the id is checked, the payload is not — and runtime.runAction<I,O> still takes the caller's own I and O (packages/core/src/runtime.ts:165). The generated file says so itself: the input and output shapes are not here yet. tests/types/core-actions.ts still pins the runAction-level gap as a compile-time fact, and that file remains correct: the gap moved surface, it did not close.
close_reason:
Substantially built and the remaining clause is out of reach as written, so it moved rather than being quietly dropped.

DONE and verified: register/uninstall symmetry across commands, actionDefs, capabilities, declaredCapabilities, eventHandlers and persistedEvents, including the two cases that look equivalent and are not, a shared handler still registered by another feature and two features legitimately sharing one handler object. Degradation recomputes after every install and uninstall, covered for a feature ordered before its provider and for one installed later. Lazy discovery is the shipped shape: domains() and describeDomain() rather than the plan's discover(), with the two aliasing traps covered. Registration guards now also cover actionDefs, which they did not: the dotted-id pattern and the non-empty-permissions rule were applied to capabilities only, so a feature could register a bare verb id through a plain object literal. Both guards are pinned by tests written against a literal, because the first version of those tests used defineAction and passed whether or not the registry guards existed.

NOT SATISFIABLE AS WRITTEN, and the reason is architectural. 'defineAction gives compile-time input/output typing' holds where an action is WRITTEN and not where it is CALLED. The id half is closed: codegen emits RegisteredActionId, act() is typed against it, and a bogus id is a compile error, which was this bead's own bar. The payload half cannot be closed the same way, because packages/api may not depend on a feature so the generated file may not import feature types, and types are erased so codegen cannot read them off the value side. Emitting the placeholders the manifests already declare would produce a union that looks typed and is not, which is the thing the generated file's own header warns against. Moved to ba-vsd with three routes and none chosen, since picking one is a design call.

The criterion as written should be restated to match: the id half is enforced in both directions, the payload half is a known and documented gap with a stated route.

title: CLI agent-battle: P0 foundation, zero game logic, no DB
description:
Ship the agent-battle CLI in P0 alongside the API, per plan section 31, corrected by section 36.

WHY P0 AND NOT LATER TOOLING (section 31): the CLI is the agent's DAILY RUNTIME ENTRY POINT, not developer convenience. THE MCP HALF OF THIS SENTENCE WAS CORRECTED IN THE PLAN AFTER THIS BEAD WAS WRITTEN, and the old wording is exactly what the plan now overrides. It used to read 'MCP does NOT have to be P0; protocol/API + CLI ship first, MCP is an adapter on the SAME protocol later'. Section 31 now carries a dated CORRECTION 2026-09-24 that names that exact sentence as the superseded MIDDLE state: 'MCP IS P0, not P3', with P0 containing 'Interfaces: Public API, CLI, MCP' as three EQUAL consumers, because 'do not design the game first and bolt MCP/CLI on later'. Section 33's revised build order agrees - P0 ends with 'CLI (login/init/start/status/doctor), MCP adapter'. What survives of the old reading is the ARCHITECTURE, not the phase: MCP is still an adapter over the same protocol and still dispatches through the capability registry, never through game code. So this bead and ba-4to (the MCP route mount) are P0 SIBLINGS, not a sequence - neither blocks the other, and an implementer who reads the superseded sentence will wrongly believe the MCP surface can wait until the CLI is done.

THE IRON RULE (section 31): the CLI contains ZERO game logic and touches NO DB. It calls the Public API only - the same claimQuest(agentId, questId) application command the web and MCP paths use. Future surfaces (Discord bot, GitHub App, SDK) reuse the same command and must NEVER reimplement it per surface.

ARCHITECTURE (section 31):
  Web App (Next.js) -+
                       +-> Public API -> Core Runtime -> Extensions -> Neon
  CLI (agent-battle) --+

THREE CLI ROLES:
1. AGENT RUNTIME: login / init / start / status / stop
2. PLATFORM INTERACTION: agent status, quest list/claim, bounty list/inspect, profile, xp, submit
3. DEV/ADMIN: dev, doctor, config, extension

LAYOUT per section 31, packages/cli/: src/commands/{login,init,start,status,stop,agent,quest,bounty,profile,dev,doctor,config,extension}, runtime/local.ts, api-client.ts. Thin wrappers over the Application API (contract-public-api), argparse-only, NO domain imports.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXISTS, 2026-09-25, and it is a different shape from the layout above. packages/cli/src/ holds three files: commands.ts (312 lines), commands.test.ts (219) and index.ts (2). There is no src/commands/ directory, no per-command file, and no runtime/local.ts.

That is not drift to be corrected - it is the surface-parity property, achieved. The shipped CLI is ONE generic dispatcher: `agent-battle <domain> <verb> [args...]`, plus four platform commands (help, discover, status, doctor). It resolves a domain through a single lazy discover(), matches the verb against that domain's actions, and either acts or falls through to a search filter. `quest list` and `battle accept` are the same three lines. packages/cli/src/commands.ts says so explicitly: there is deliberately no switch over known domains, no --with-xp, no local cache, no direct read.

So of the thirteen named command files, FOUR exist as real behaviour under different names - `status` and `doctor` are implemented, `discover` and `help` were added and are not in the list above. login/init/start/stop, the per-feature files, and api-client.ts DO NOT EXIST and are the real remaining work. Read this bead as: the registry-driven dispatcher is DONE and is the thing that makes the rest cheap; the agent-runtime verbs and the HTTP transport are NOT DONE.

The package also has no `bin` entry in package.json, so `agent-battle` is not yet an installed command - the module exports parseArgv/run and a consumer has to wire them up. That is part of the missing transport work, not a packaging detail.

AgentRuntime abstraction (start/stop/status/send) with future LocalCliRuntime / McpRuntime / RemoteRuntime / EmbeddedRuntime. A CLI restart creates a NEW SESSION but the SAME Agent ID (section 3.2).

SURFACE PARITY (section 32): the CLI uses the identical capability abstraction as every other surface - 'quest list' is search(type=quest); 'quest claim <id>' is act('quest.claim', ...). CLI and MCP evolve INDEPENDENTLY of feature count: adding Guild changes the registry, not the CLI or the primitives.

THIS IS THE ONE CLAUSE IN THE BEAD THAT IS DEMONSTRABLY TRUE TODAY, and it is worth stating why. The five primitives are frozen in packages/api/src/api.ts (PRIMITIVES = discover, search, inspect, act, observe), the CLI consumes exactly that interface, and the MCP server derives its tool list from the same constant rather than hand-writing it. The ids are checked at compile time against the generated RegisteredActionId union, so a misspelled action is a build error in all three surfaces. A feature added to createGameRuntime's extensions array is immediately reachable from the CLI and from MCP with no edit to either - which is the removal test's dependency made concrete.

REVIEW GUARD (section 36): any PR adding interfaces/cli/* implementation code FOR A SPECIFIC GAME FEATURE (instead of registry entries) fails review. The CLI must not grow per-feature branches.

AGENT-FRIENDLY UX: this is an agent-facing CLI, so it should also support non-interactive/robot modes, clear actionable errors, and layered help. Consider a --json output mode for machine consumption, since agents will drive it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: 'agent-battle login/init/start/status/stop' works against the API; a quest can be listed and claimed entirely from the CLI; no DB connection and no domain import exists anywhere under packages/cli/.

SPLIT INTO WHAT IS ALREADY MET AND WHAT IS NOT, because as written this criterion reads as wholly outstanding and two of its three clauses are satisfied:
- MET: no DB connection and no domain import under packages/cli/. packages/cli depends on @battle-agents/api, @battle-agents/core and @battle-agents/protocol only, and tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts enforces the layering.
- MET, in the only form the architecture allows: a quest can be listed and claimed entirely from the CLI. `agent-battle quest` lists what quest offers, `agent-battle quest list` filters, and `agent-battle quest claim <args>` acts - generically, because quest.claim is a registered action. The word 'entirely' overstates it: the CLI is an in-process adapter over an ApplicationApi object today, with no network path, so it is not yet talking to a running API at all.
- NOT MET: 'agent-battle login/init/start/status/stop works against the API'. None of login, init, start or stop exists. status exists and answers from the API. The other four verbs, and the api-client.ts that would make 'against the API' mean anything, are the outstanding work.

A test that would catch the regression this criterion is really about: assert that packages/cli/src contains no reference to any registered domain name, and that adding a feature to the composition root makes it reachable from the CLI with no change in packages/cli/. The first is a grep; the second is the removal test's spirit applied at the CLI.

TESTS: CLI integration tests against a live API in the compose test environment; an architecture test that greps packages/cli/ for forbidden DB/domain imports; a test that the same quest claim via CLI and via HTTP produces identical application-command effects.

CONSIDERATIONS: the hardest part of this bead is restraint. It is tempting to give the CLI convenient shortcuts - a --with-xp flag, a local cache of bounties, a direct DB read for speed. Each one is an iron-rule violation that will make the CLI behave differently from the web and MCP surfaces. Also: the CLI is the surface an AGENT will drive, not only a human, so it should support non-interactive and machine-readable output (a --json mode and actionable errors) from the start. Retrying that later means auditing every command.
close_reason: All five agent-runtime verbs exist and the CLI is a client rather than an in-process adapter. The blocker was the interface: discover and search were declared to return their values, which only a same-heap object can do, so HttpApiClient could not implement the thing it is named after; every method is async now. start and stop resolve a domain and dispatch through the same actOn helper as quest.claim rather than special-casing game knowledge, and a build without a session domain answers with the domains it does have. login, init and logout cover the three verbs that touch this machine and store only configuration, never a game concept. init is a read on purpose: an installation record belongs to the agent feature, not to a file the CLI keeps. The iron rule holds — packages/cli/src imports no feature and no database — and pnpm -r build now passes, which it had not since b10f42e.

title: CONTRACT 2: Agent Identity - agents + credentials + ownership
description:
Implement and FREEZE Contract 2: Agent Identity, per plan section 29.1 and section 38.

THE INVARIANT (section 29.1 item 2, and section 38): the agents row plus agent_credentials (hash, scopes, expiry) plus ownership via agents.user_id. 'GitHub User ID is NOT Agent ID, permanently.' The invariant sessions.agent_id -> agents.id is load-bearing.

SCHEMA per plan section 21:
- users: id, githubId (unique), login, avatarUrl, createdAt
- installations: id, userId -> users, installationKey (unique), label, lastSeenAt, createdAt
- agents: id, userId -> users, name, harness, level, xp, reputation, build, status, lastSeenAt, createdAt
- agent_credentials: id, installationId -> installations, tokenHash, scopes, expiresAt, revokedAt, createdAt

HARD SEPARATIONS (section 38, enforce in code review):
- Better Auth owns User/Auth/human-Session ONLY. The game domain stays in extensions.
- The GitHub OAuth token is NEVER agent identity. The chain is: User (human) -> Agent (persistent character: XP/level/rep + credential + sessions) -> Session (one run) -> Credential (the token the agent calls back with). Example: User#42 -> Agent 'CodeKnight' (1250 XP, Lv 7, Rep 83) -> Sessions #a1/#b7.
- Agent credential issuance/rotation endpoints live under the Agent extension, NOT inside Better Auth config.

WHY AGENT IS PERSISTENT AND SESSION IS EPHEMERAL (plan section 3.1-3.2): AGENT is never deleted when a terminal closes. It holds XP/level/skills/build/reputation/inventory/achievements/battle+quest history. This is the plan's 'most important design' (section 3 heading) and the basis of the whole social/network-effect story (section 2.4).

IDENTITY RESOLUTION (section 3.2): do NOT key on process name alone - three concurrent Claudes must stay distinguishable. Resolution uses agent_id + installation_id + project_id + session_id. installation_id is generated once at install (~/.agent-battle/identity.json {installationId}). Multi-machine: GitHub User -> Agent -> Installations (PC/Laptop/Server/WSL/Docker) -> Sessions.

TOKEN MODEL (section 3.4): a token authenticates a user/installation and NEVER equals a session. Close -> #003 CLOSED; reopen -> #004 CREATED under the same User/Claude. NEVER put raw tokens in MCP URLs (?token= leaks into logs and history) - use MCP OAuth -> short-lived access tokens. Web GitHub login and MCP agent authorization are related but SEPARATE credentials.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: schema exists with the FK chain users -> agents -> sessions and the invariant sessions.agent_id -> agents.id enforced at the DB level; credentials store a HASH (never the raw token); ownership is queryable.

TESTS: migration test; a test that agent_credentials stores only a hash (assert the raw token is absent from the row); a test that a user's agent cannot be read by another user (authorization at the repository boundary).

CONSIDERATIONS: the separation of four ID classes - permanent identity, credential, session, event - is easy to blur and expensive to undo. Agent is the character and persists forever; credential is a revocable secret; session is an ephemeral run; event is a log entry. Keeping them distinct is what makes 'close the terminal, reopen tomorrow, same character' possible. The multi-installation case (PC, laptop, server, WSL, Docker) is not hypothetical - get the schema right for it now rather than retrofitting a second installation concept later.
close_reason: CONTRACT 2. Schema half pre-existing (users -> installations/agents -> agent_credentials/sessions, tokenHash only, sessions.agent_id -> agents.id). Added the feature: four id classes branded so they cannot be passed for one another, ownership a required parameter on every repository method, codes as the cross-layer error contract (instanceof cannot work across the layering boundary). 12 unit tests + 8 integration tests against live Postgres proving a user's agent cannot be read by another user. Found and fixed: agents_user_id_name_unique was declared index not uniqueIndex, so the DB never enforced one name per owner (migration 0001). drizzle/ moved to packages/db/ so a store can be depended on. Removal test proves the feature is independently removable.

title: CONTRACT 1: Extension API (GameFeature + contracts) - freeze first
close_reason: Contract 1 frozen: core runtime + contracts, 55 unit tests, all 7 gates green, agent review applied (4 defects fixed, each now guarded by a test)

title: CONTRACT 4: Public API = Application Commands/Queries (single domain impl)
description:
Implement and FREEZE Contract 4: the Agent Protocol surface, per plan section 29.1 item 4, section 31, section 32, section 33, section 36.

THE PRINCIPLE (section 29.1 item 4): Application Commands and Queries are the SINGLE definition of what an agent can do. CLI / MCP / REST are CONSUMERS of it.

IRON RULE (section 31): the CLI contains ZERO game logic and touches NO DB. It calls the Public API only - the same claimQuest(agentId, questId) application command the web and MCP paths use. Future surfaces (Discord bot, GitHub App, SDK) reuse the same command and must NEVER reimplement per surface.

THE STABLE SURFACE (section 32) - frozen, about 5 primitives:
- discover([domain?]) - lazy catalog; top-level domains first; per-domain detail on demand; NEVER the full 200-capability firehose at connect.
- search({type, status, difficulty, ...})
- inspect({type, id})
- act({action, target, input})
- observe({scope})

THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES: N features x M operations collapses to 100-200 MCP tools, which is undiscoverable and bloats agent context. The principle is 'cover every capability, expose few stable primitives'.

ANTI-GOD-TOOL GUARD (section 32): act() dispatches TYPED, REGISTRY-DEFINED actions - defineAction({id:'quest.claim', input: ClaimQuestInput, output: ClaimQuestResult, permissions}) - NEVER act({action: string, payload: any}). Type safety and discoverability must be preserved.

DOMAIN CAPABILITIES live in the REGISTRY, not as MCP tools: quest.list/claim/submit, battle.challenge/accept, guild.join/leave and so on. Feature growth must NOT equal surface growth: adding Guild changes the registry, not the 5 primitives.

THE CLI USES THE IDENTICAL ABSTRACTION (section 32): 'quest list' -> search(type=quest); 'quest claim <id>' -> act('quest.claim', ...).

ARCHITECTURE (section 33): CORE -> Extension Contract -> GAME extensions | INTERFACE extensions | INFRASTRUCTURE extensions.
- extensions/* declare capabilities and know NOTHING about MCP/CLI/REST/Web.
- interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket}/* are capability CONSUMERS/adapters; adding a feature never edits them, only composition/manifest registration.
- infrastructure/* is integrations behind boundaries.

MACHINE-NATIVE ASSUMPTION (section 34): every gameplay loop must be fully playable through the protocol/tool interface alone, with no web clicks required. If a quest cannot be discovered -> claimed -> submitted -> rewarded via discover/search/act plus the CLI equivalents, the feature is NOT done.

FEATURE LAYOUT NOTE (section 33): features may gain an application/ directory holding command/query handlers (the single domain implementation all surfaces share). Default is pure registry entries with no per-feature interface code.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: one application command is reachable identically from CLI, HTTP, and MCP; act() is fully typed (a bogus action id is a compile error, not a runtime string); adding a feature adds registry entries and zero new primitives.

TESTS: a parity test asserting the same application command is invoked through each surface; a type-level test that an unknown action id fails to compile; a test that adding a dummy feature increases the registry but not the 5-primitive surface.

CONSIDERATIONS: this is the bead where 'expose little' has to become real. The pressure to add a convenient sixth primitive - or to promote quest.claim to a first-class tool because an agent asked for it - will arrive early and repeatedly. The plan's counter-argument should be the default: that operation already exists in the registry, and promoting it means every future feature will ask the same. The other risk is per-feature interface code creeping in; the review rule in section 36 is the guard, so encode it in the CI architecture check rather than relying on reviewers noticing.
close_reason: CONTRACT 4. packages/api is the single Application API: discover/search/inspect/act/observe, frozen at five. Parity test drives the same action through CLI-shaped, HTTP-shaped and MCP-shaped calls and asserts identical results and identical failures. Adding 7 features grows the registry 2->9 domains with no change to the surface, asserted on both the constant and the returned object's keys. Unknown actions name the known domains rather than dumping every id. Honest limit: action ids are runtime-registered by independently-built packages, so a bogus id is a typed runtime error rather than a compile error without codegen.

title: CONTRACT 3: Session lifecycle + HELLO resume-vs-new handshake
description:
Implement and FREEZE Contract 3: Session, per plan section 29.1 item 3, section 3.2, and section 22.

THE INVARIANT: sessions.agent_id -> agents.id, NEVER sessions.user_id as agent identity (section 29.1).

SCHEMA (section 21): sessions: id, agentId -> agents, installationId -> installations, projectId -> projects (nullable), harnessSessionRef, status (default 'active'), startedAt, endedAt, lastHeartbeatAt.

SESSION LIFECYCLE (section 3.2):
- Terminal close: Session -> CLOSED; Agent ACTIVE -> OFFLINE; stats persist (Level/XP/Battles/Tests/Last-seen).
- Reopen must NOT create 'Claude #2'. Identity resolution maps a new process to the SAME Agent, producing old Session#182 + new Session#205.
- State machine: ACTIVE -> COMPLETED / STOPPED(ABANDONED) / CRASHED / TIMEOUT(DISCONNECTED).
- Battle states (separate machine): RUNNING / PAUSED / COMPLETED / ABANDONED / EXPIRED.
- Disconnect during a battle -> grace period -> reconnect? resume : abandoned.
- MVP may skip the Run layer (Agent -> Run -> Session) and keep Agent -> Session only.

HELLO HANDSHAKE (section 22): POST /api/sessions receives {installationKey, agentName, harness, projectRepoUrl?}. It must find-or-create installation/agent/project, then look for a status=disconnected session with the same agent+installation+project within a grace window (default 15 minutes), and return {sessionId, resumed} or create a new one.
- Heartbeat: POST /api/sessions/[id]/heartbeat updates lastHeartbeatAt.
- A cron route marks stale sessions (>5 min, no heartbeat, no websocket) as 'disconnected', then 'abandoned' after the grace window.
- Adapter sends HELLO{installationId, agentId, projectId}; the server matches same agent+installation+project+recently-disconnected and offers resume vs new.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE USER (section 3.2 UI consequence): dead sessions must never make characters vanish. Claude offline shows Level/XP/wins plus 'Last seen 3m ago'; reopening flips to ONLINE with the SAME character. Session history doubles as a replayable game mechanic.

CONSIDERATIONS: the grace window is a real product decision (15 min default per section 22) - too short and an accidental terminal kill loses battle progress; too long and a genuinely abandoned session holds a slot. Make it configurable.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: kill a terminal mid-session, reopen, and get a resume offer rather than a duplicate agent; heartbeat keeps a session alive; the sweeper transitions disconnected -> abandoned on schedule.

TESTS: unit test for the state machine transitions; integration test that a HELLO within the grace window resumes the same sessionId and outside it creates a new one; test that sessions.agent_id is the only identity FK (no user_id identity column).
close_reason: CONTRACT 3. Pure state machine (active/ended/disconnected/abandoned) with an exhaustive transition matrix; disconnected is resumable, only ended+abandoned are terminal. HELLO handshake matches on agent+installation+project and can never create a character. Heartbeat staleness and the resume grace window are single-sourced helpers shared by the handshake and the sweeper. 24 unit tests + 25 integration tests against live Postgres. Found+fixed a 15-hour grace window from a units bug, and a missing unique index on projects that made every session non-resumable (migration 0002).

title: Contributor onboarding: docs, AGENTS.md, good-first-issues
description:
Build the contributor experience, per plan section 16.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE BEAD: section 16 argues the flywheel needs MORE than a permissive license - it needs docs, easy dev, clear architecture, good-first-issues, fun visible results, a useful protocol, and active maintainers. The MIT decision (section 35) is necessary but NOT sufficient. Skipping this is the most likely way the project has a license and no contributors.

DELIVERABLES:
- AGENTS.md describing the project for coding agents (WHAT/WHY/HOW, progressive disclosure)
- README that states the vision, the MIT license, and the architecture at a glance
- Architecture documentation explaining the four contracts (section 29.1) and WHY they were locked first - a contributor who does not understand the extension boundary will break it
- A local dev guide pointing at 'git clone, cp .env.example .env, docker compose up' (section 37) - the low-friction entry is a real contributor-acquisition feature
- Good-first-issues, ideally of the FUN-VISIBLE kind the plan calls for: adapter PRs, reporter PRs, battle-mode PRs. These let a newcomer ship something that shows up on screen rather than fixing an internal chore
- Documented failure modes for the local OAuth path (section 39): redirect_uri_mismatch, missing Better Auth secret, DB unreachable - the three things that will actually block a newcomer's first run. DONE: apps/web/README.md exists and has a 'When it fails' section covering all three by name, each with symptom, why, and fix - including the instruction to use 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost, and the point that a migration reporting success is not proof because drizzle-kit keeps its ledger in a separate schema. It also states the auth/game boundary and how to run the stack. Do not rewrite it; the remaining work is a ROOT README that points at it.

ARCHITECTURE COMMUNICATION: the removal test and the dependency rules are only meaningful if contributors understand the intent. Explain that adding a feature must never edit core/cli/mcp implementations (section 33) and that this is checked in review.

STATUS 2026-09-25: the doc deliverables are still absent at the root - there is no AGENTS.md, no README.md and no CONTRIBUTING.md - but the picture is no longer 'none of it exists'. What is now true:
- apps/web/README.md EXISTS and is good. It covers what the app owns and must not, the docker compose up path, the three OAuth/database failure modes, and the environment. That is most of the local-dev guide, scoped to the web app.
- docs/ now holds design/ (payout-rail.md AND public-event-stream.md) plus research/ (the six reference-repo notes and a README that indexes them with commit SHAs and licence status). The research README's staleness section is the model worth copying for the root docs: it names the beads that were unstarted when the note was written and tells the reader to re-check against the SHA.
- .github/workflows/m0.yml runs pnpm test:m0 in the compose test-runner image, so the local-setup path is enforced by CI even where it is not yet documented. The 'documented steps cannot rot' property is still only half-satisfied - machinery exists, no document describes it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT, in the order a newcomer would hit it: a root README (vision, MIT, architecture at a glance, the quickstart); AGENTS.md for coding agents; and good-first-issues. Note that THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md already exists at the root with a per-repo licence table, so the licence story is told - a root README should link it rather than restate it.

CONSIDERATIONS: contributor friction is highest at first-run. Measure it: have someone unfamiliar run the local setup and log every point of confusion.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE 'WITHOUT UNDOCUMENTED HELP' HAS NO WRONG VERSION. The old first clause was unfalsifiable in two ways: a newcomer who needed no help because the app was never started satisfies it, and a newcomer who struggled badly satisfies it as long as they eventually succeeded. 'A MERGED FIRST PR' was also the wrong deliverable for this bead - whether a newcomer's PR got merged depends on a maintainer's review, not on the documentation, so the criterion could not be closed by doing this bead's work. Split into what documentation can actually be held to, and what belongs to a person.

1. The quickstart in the root README is EXECUTABLE VERBATIM, and cannot rot. This is the real, checkable form of 'a newcomer gets to a running app'. Settled by: a CI job that runs the documented local-setup steps EXACTLY as written in the README - git clone, cp .env.example .env, docker compose up - and whatever the README then says - and fails the build when a step does not work. The property being protected is the one apps/web/README.md already half-provides: machinery exists (.github/workflows/m0.yml runs pnpm test:m0 in the compose test-runner image) but no document describes it, so 'the documented steps cannot rot' is only half-satisfied. A doc that drifts from reality passes every review and fails this job; a job that paraphrases the steps instead of copying them passes while the doc stays wrong, so the job must read the steps FROM the document.

2. A newcomer who hits a blocker finds it documented. This is the honest replacement for 'without undocumented help', and it is checkable as a LIST rather than as a feeling. The three named OAuth/DB failure modes (redirect_uri_mismatch, missing Better Auth secret, DB unreachable) must each appear in the docs by name, each with symptom, cause and fix - apps/web/README.md already does this well, and the remaining work is a root README that points at it rather than a rewrite. Settled by: a check asserting all three are named in the root docs, and that the root README links to the detailed section. What this does NOT claim: that these are the only three a newcomer will hit. The honest failure mode is a fourth, and the way that gets recorded is by adding it to the list and failing the check until it is documented - so the list grows honestly rather than the criterion being quietly declared met.

3. The docs state that THIS PROJECT is MIT, and do not claim any other license for it. Settled by: a check scoped to claims about this repository's own license - see the correction below, which is load-bearing and must not be reverted to a bare grep.

4. NOT THIS BEAD'S TO CLOSE, recorded so nobody waits on it: whether a newcomer's first PR actually gets MERGED. That depends on maintainer review and on a maintainer existing, neither of which documentation can deliver. The bead's honest scope is that the path to a first PR is unblocked and the good-first-issues are real; merging is downstream. Do not hold this bead open waiting for a stranger's pull request.

5. The good-first-issues are REAL and VISIBLE, not a list of internal chores. This was a DELIVERABLES bullet with no check at all. Settled by: each listed good-first-issue being an actual open issue in the tracker, labelled or titled so a newcomer can find it, and each naming what a merged PR would visibly change - an adapter, a reporter, a battle mode. A bullet claiming good-first-issues exist while the tracker has none is the failure, and it is checkable: the number of good-first-issues the README advertises must equal the number that exist.

TESTS, each a command with an exit code:
- a docs-link checker over the root docs, so a renamed file or a moved anchor fails rather than quietly 404-ing for the reader.
- the CI job from clause 1, reading the steps FROM the README rather than restating them.
- a check that all three named failure modes appear in the root docs with symptom, cause and fix, and that the root README links to the detailed section.
- the license check, scoped as described in the correction below.
- a check that the good-first-issues the README advertises actually exist in the tracker, and that their count matches.

CRITERION CORRECTED 2026-09-24 - the earlier wording of this bead demanded "a grep asserting no stale Apache-2.0 claim in docs", which is wrong and would fail on correct content. The string Apache-2.0 legitimately appears in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md (agent-world-smallville is Apache-2.0 and is recorded there as a third-party source) and in plan section 28's license table. Those are accurate records of someone ELSE's license, not a claim about this repo. What section 35 actually locks is that battle-agents itself is MIT; a stale reference means a doc asserting THIS project is Apache-2.0. The check must therefore be scoped to claims about this repository's own license, not a bare grep for the string.
close_reason:
DONE. The brief's own status block was stale in the place that mattered — it said
there was no root AGENTS.md and no root README.md. Both exist and are good. What
was genuinely missing is now there.

CONTRIBUTING.md, which did not exist, carries the thing a newcomer cannot infer:
the four contracts and WHY they were locked first, plus the rule that adding a
feature must never edit core/cli/mcp. That rule is not politeness — it is checked
in review AND by the architecture stage, so a newcomer learns it on their first

Good-first-issues are the fun-visible kind the plan calls for — adapter PRs,

on screen rather than be an internal chore. The docs gate now asserts all three

THE MEASUREMENT, since the bead asks whether a stranger could get from clone to a
