title: Core loop end-to-end: DISCOVER -> CLAIM -> CODE -> VALIDATE -> REWARD -> BATTLE -> SOCIAL
description:
Prove the plan's core loop (section 10.5) works END TO END across features, which no single feature bead can demonstrate.

THE LOOP (section 10.5, verbatim structure): DISCOVER quests -> ACCEPT -> CODE (real) -> VALIDATE (tests/build) -> SUCCESS (XP/REP) | FAILURE (learn/retry) -> PROGRESS -> BATTLE -> SOCIAL (guild) -> NEW BOUNTY. The plan's judgement: 'Animation exists to make this loop FEEL like a game, not to be the game.'

WHY A SEPARATE BEAD: each feature bead tests itself in isolation. This bead tests the INTEGRATION - specifically that cross-feature side effects flow through the EVENT BUS and not through direct imports. Section 29.3 is the rule: events are the cross-feature integration boundary ONLY; direct domain operations stay plain function calls inside their feature. An end-to-end run is the only way to catch a feature quietly importing another's internals.

THE FAN-OUT THAT MUST WORK (section 12.2): when a bounty completes, bounty.completed is emitted and EACH of Progression (+XP), Reputation (+trust), and Achievement (First Bounty check) reacts INDEPENDENTLY. Each owns its own state; there is no cross-mutation and no God Bus (a consumer may consume, emit, and handle only its own state).

STATE OF THAT FAN-OUT TODAY - read this before you build it. The diagram above is the TARGET, not the current tree, and three things about it will mislead you:

1. THERE IS NO BOUNTY EMITTER YET. packages/features/bounty/src/ contains only payout.ts and index.ts - a half-built payout state machine (PayoutIntent, PAYOUT_STATES, INTENT_ONLY, needsSandboxBanner). There is no bounty feature.ts, no GameFeature, no emitter, and no bounty entry in any persistedEvents list. bounty.completed is emitted by nothing today. If you assume the emitter exists and only write the three consumers, the loop can never fire and a happy-path test will appear to pass while awarding nothing.

2. THE PAYLOAD IN THE PLAN'S SKETCH IS NOT THE SHIPPED ONE. Do not emit {bountyId, agentId, reward}. The consumer that already exists, packages/features/reputation/src/feature.ts, declares:
     export interface BountyCompletedPayload {
       readonly agentId: string;
       readonly rewardCents: number;   // NOT `reward`
       readonly reviewScore?: number;  // 0..5, absent means "not reviewed"
     }
   There is no bountyId field, and the amount is rewardCents in minor units. Emitting the sketch shape produces an event that reputation's handler does not match: the fan-out silently awards no trust, with no error. GameEvent is {type, occurredAt, actorId, causationId?, payload} - the payload is nested under payload, it is not spread across the top level.

3. THE EVENT NAME IS CURRENTLY DECLARED BY THE WRONG SIDE, AND THE OBVIOUS FIX IS A FORBIDDEN IMPORT. BOUNTY_COMPLETED / BOUNTY_FAILED / BATTLE_FINISHED are exported from packages/features/reputation/src/feature.ts - the CONSUMER, not the emitter. The obvious way to wire a second consumer is `import { BOUNTY_COMPLETED } from '@battle-agents/features/reputation'`, and that is a cross-feature import, which `pnpm run architecture` fails on (architecture-rules.cjs: 'Features never import each other; a cross-feature need goes through a capability declared in core'). If you cannot avoid wanting that import, that is the signal to move the shared name somewhere outside features/ (core or protocol), not to add the import. The forbidden-by-machine-check wrong move is the whole point of this bead, so do not make it while building the thing meant to catch it.

FULL ROUND TRIP: an agent discovers a real GitHub issue, claims it as a bounty, works the code, opens a PR, the merge webhook fires, the bounty completes, XP/reputation/achievement all update, a battle becomes possible against the same bounty, and the replay URL is shareable. Then social: the agent's guild sees the contribution.

MACHINE-NATIVE CHECK (section 34): the entire loop must complete through discover/search/act plus CLI equivalents with NO web clicks. If any step requires the browser, the machine-native rule is broken. The five MCP verbs are discover, search, inspect, act, observe (packages/mcp-server/src/tools.ts); the CLI is a generic dispatcher over the capability registry with platform commands status/doctor/help/discover (packages/cli/src/commands.ts), so a loop step that only exists as an MCP tool is not machine-native until a CLI route reaches the same capability.

FAILURE PATH MATTERS TOO (section 10.2): the plan includes FAILURE achievements, and a failed session must grant experience while leaving the character alive. Exercise the failure branch, not just the happy path.

THE BOUNDARY TEST ALREADY EXISTS - do not write a second one. The static rule 'features/ contains no cross-feature imports' is not this bead's job to add. It is already machine-enforced over the real tree by `pnpm run architecture` (scripts/check-architecture.ts reading architecture-rules.cjs), and each individual rule is separately proven by the synthetic fixture suite tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts, which fails if any declared rule has no fixture. Re-implementing it as a hand-written grep in this bead produces a weaker check that disagrees with the real one, and a grep passes on a tree the gate rejects. What is genuinely NEW here is the behavioural half: three consumers reacting to one emission with no cross-mutation, and a loop that still completes when one consumer is uninstalled.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the loop completes end to end on a real repository, with the success and failure branches both exercised, driven entirely through the protocol and CLI. `pnpm run architecture` passes unchanged, and the fan-out is proven to work with progression absent from the install (a feature that survives removal is a feature that really owns its own state; the reverse - an install that only works because a peer is present - is the God Bus this bead forbids).

TESTS: a full-loop integration test, including the failure branch; the bus-boundary half is settled by `pnpm run architecture` and tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts, not by a new test; a machine-native test with the web UI disabled; and a removal test (scripts/removal-test.sh is the existing shape) proving the loop still completes with a consumer feature uninstalled.

CONSIDERATIONS: this bead is where architecture violations surface as behavior bugs. If Bounty reaches into Progression's state instead of reacting to bounty.completed on the bus, the loop may still appear to work in a happy-path test - and will break the moment a second consumer subscribes or progression is uninstalled. Run the loop with the web UI disabled: that is the cheapest way to catch anything that quietly requires a click. And exercise the FAILURE branch with the same care as the success branch, since section 10.2 deliberately makes failure productive.
close_reason:
THE LOOP CLOSES. Plan §10.5 end to end on the COMPOSED runtime, driven through
the real MCP act tool, with the merge arriving as a SIGNED GitHub webhook.

What makes it a loop rather than seven unit tests in a trenchcoat: each stage's
OUTPUT is the next stage's INPUT through the real seam. The claim is given the id
bounty.list RETURNED and the row is read back out of Postgres. The delivery
carries only a repository, a PR number and a login — the bounty is found by
REBUILDING the PR url and calling findByPrUrl, and the agent is read off the
claim record. Neither is an input the test supplied. battle.join is refused
BEFORE the merge and admitted after, with the floor parsed out of the platform's
own refusal rather than imported. The guild signal's sourceKey is
"bounty.completed|<id>" with the id arriving over the wire.

FIVE HAND-OFFS BROKEN AND WATCHED RED, and two of them are the entire point. A
per-winner battle.finished saying won:false takes EXACTLY ONE test red while the
other fifteen stay green; a progression.agentIdOf falling back to actorId takes
the failure pin red with the exact number its comment predicts. A loop test that
goes red on ANY hand-off proves nothing about WHICH one, so the specificity is
the evidence.

SEVEN REAL DEFECTS FOUND AND REPORTED RATHER THAN PATCHED, each belonging to a
different bead. The two systemic ones are now ba-9fh: bounty.completed is a
DUPLICATED STRING LITERAL in five feature packages with nothing centralising it,
so renaming it on the emitter side silently unsubscribes reputation,
progression, achievements and guild with no error; and a THROWING CONSUMER
STARVES EVERY CONSUMER AFTER IT, because runtime.emit awaits handlers in order
without catching — measured, not assumed. That is a frozen core file, which is
precisely why it needs a bead.

The rest, recorded against their owners:
  - SOCIAL DOES NOT CLOSE in the shipped composition: guild is not installed, so
    social.send is degraded and all 11 guild.* ids throw UnknownActionError.
  - progression.agentIdOf reads payload.agentId while toGameEvent puts the agent
    on actorId, so test.passed's 100 XP is UNREACHABLE from a real harness and
    session.recovered has no producer at all. §10.2's death rule is not wired: a
    crash pays a badge and zero XP.
  - session.end emits no session.ended, so the crash badge, activity trail,
    battle pause clock and public stream all stay unaware of a protocol ending.
  - battle.create never calls the arena gate — only battle.join does — so a
    no-track-record agent can OPEN an arena and is refused only on joining.
  - pr.merged is scored by guild toward reviewer WITHOUT reading
    completedBounty: true, so merging your own bounty accrues reviewer evidence.

AND THE ONE §10.5 PROMISES THAT IS NOT YET TRUE: nothing renders. The replay
page is real and credential-free, but no test renders its markup, the PixiJS
client is not a dependency of apps/web, and animation is unwired — so
"animation exists to make this loop FEEL like a game" is not yet true of any
surface. Said in the file header rather than papered over with a weaker
assertion.

A second file proves the loop COMPOSES rather than that the product INSTALLS it:
the same loop with progression absent, achievements absent, and guild present, so
the degradation claims are measured. The trade is stated in its header — it names
features, which the removal test would break, so it lives in tests/integration/
which that script's unit stage and per-package typecheck do not reach.

title: Drizzle schema + migration tooling for the initial tables
description:
Own the Drizzle schema and migration pipeline, per plan section 19 (drizzle/ schema + migrations) and section 21 (the full initial schema).

WHY THIS NEEDS AN OWNER: the tables are currently described inside the contract beads, but no bead owns the migration TOOLCHAIN. Without it, 'docker compose up -> migrations -> seed' (section 40) has nothing to run, and every contract bead would be editing the same schema file concurrently - which is exactly the coordination failure the plugin/lock tooling exists to prevent.

TABLES (section 21), grouped by the persistence split in section 29.4:
PLATFORM-OWNED: users, agents, agent_credentials, sessions, event_log, installations, projects.
FEATURE-OWNED: quests, bounties, bounty_funds, battles, battle_participants, agent_stats, achievements, messages.
Each feature owns ITS OWN tables and its own repository (section 24: 'repository.ts (drizzle access, own tables only)'). No GodRepository (section 12.2).

INVARIANT to enforce in the schema: sessions.agent_id -> agents.id, and NEVER a user_id standing in as agent identity (sections 29.1, 38).

SECURITY FIELDS: agent_credentials stores tokenHash (never a raw token) plus scopes, expiresAt, revokedAt (section 21). bounties stores amountCents as an integer (never a float for money).

RELATIONAL NOTES worth getting right the first time:
- battle_participants has a composite primary key (battleId, sessionId) and references SESSIONS, not agents (section 3.1).
- bounty_funds has N rows per bounty; the displayed amount is their SUM. Prefer deriving the total over storing a scalar that can drift (see bounty-open-funding).
- agent_stats keys on agentId and holds FACTS (prsOpened, prsMerged, prsRejected, testsPassed, testsFailed, recoveries, battlesWon, battlesLost, skillsJson) - distinct from XP and Reputation per the section 10.2 triple split.

MIGRATION TOOLING: generate migrations from the schema, and make the chain runnable offline in the local container (section 37) and against a Neon preview branch (section 37 DB modes). Section 39 calls out a common newcomer failure - 'DB unreachable (migration/seed step missed)' - so migration+seed must be a single reliable step in the compose pipeline.

SEED DATA: a seed script (section 19 lists scripts/seed.ts) so a fresh local DB is immediately usable and the E2E smoke has something to log in against.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: from a clean container, migrations + seed run offline and produce a schema matching section 21; a feature can add a table without editing another feature's repository.

TESTS: a migration smoke test against a real Postgres container; a test asserting the sessions.agent_id FK exists and no user_id identity column does; a test that seed is idempotent (safe to re-run).

CONSIDERATIONS: the platform/feature ownership split in section 29.4 is a real boundary, not bookkeeping - it decides which extension may migrate which table. Adding a platform table later (say, seasons) should NOT require editing a feature's migration, and vice versa. Money as integer cents, never float. And because section 39 lists 'DB unreachable (migration/seed step missed)' as a common newcomer failure, migrations+seed must be one reliable step, not two things a contributor has to remember.
close_reason: Verified end-to-end against a live Postgres: migrations + seed run and are idempotent (db:verify asserts both), schema matches section 21, integration suite asserts sessions.agent_id FK to agents, absence of a user_id identity column, no plaintext token column, and money held as integer cents derived from funding rows. M0 stages compose/migrations/seed/integration/schema-drift/schema-hygiene all pass.

title: Enforce dependency direction (features never cross-import)
description:
Machine-enforce the plan section 19 dependency rule and the section 33 extension-kind boundary so the architecture cannot silently rot.

THE RULE (section 19): presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure. Features NEVER import each other (only core + protocol). Adapters import core + protocol only.

WHY: Section 12.1 declares the God-Engine antipattern (a GameEngine accumulating if(hasBounty)/if(hasGuild) branches into 4000 LOC of unremovable features) to be BANNED. The stated architectural principle number 1 is the REMOVAL TEST: rm -rf features/guild must still compile and run. That property only holds if the boundary is enforced mechanically rather than by discipline.

IMPLEMENT dependency-cruiser config (or eslint no-restricted-imports) encoding:
- features/* may import core/*, protocol/*, and their own files. NOT other features/*.
- core/* may import nothing from features/, adapters/, interfaces/, infrastructure/.
- adapters/* may import core/*, protocol/* only. NEVER game code (section 23: 'No adapter imports game code - ever').
- interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket}/* consume features through the capability registry, never by importing feature implementations (section 36).
- infrastructure/* may import core/* only; features never import Docker/Compose/Postgres-container concepts (section 37).

REVIEW CHECKLIST ENFORCEMENT (sections 33, 36): any PR that forces edits to core/, cli/, or mcp/ implementations in order to add a feature is an ARCHITECTURE FAILURE. Allowed: composition-root/manifest one-liners. Any PR adding interfaces/cli/* or interfaces/mcp/* implementation code FOR A SPECIFIC GAME FEATURE (instead of registry entries) also fails review.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: adding a deliberately illegal import makes lint/build fail with a message naming the violated rule; the dependency graph report shows clean layering.

TESTS: a unit test running the rule engine over a fixture tree containing each violation type, asserting each is caught.

CONSIDERATIONS: a lint rule that fires on legitimate code is worse than no rule, because teams disable it. Expect false positives during the initial port of the age-of-agents client and the learn-spine-derived animation core, both of which are structured differently from our conventions. Add narrow, documented exceptions rather than weakening the rule. Also worth encoding in CI rather than review: architecture failures are exactly the kind of thing a reviewer waves through under deadline pressure, and this is the mechanism that makes 'adding a feature never edits core' a fact rather than an aspiration.
close_reason: Verified: architecture-rules.cjs exports the engine, a test exercises every declared rule against a fixture and asserts nothing else fires, violations name the rule, and the real tree reports 0 violations. Stage runs in CI via test:m0.

title: Docker Compose local dev: web + Postgres, offline-capable (M0)
description:
Make the project run with one command on a clean clone, per plan section 37.

THE LOCKED LOCAL CONTRACT: git clone -> cp .env.example .env -> docker compose up runs the app with HMR, OFFLINE (no Neon required).

WHY (section 37): Next.js + DB + CLI + MCP/worker later is too many moving parts to ask contributors to install Node and Postgres manually. This bead is a gap fill, NOT an architecture change.

LAYOUT per section 37:
  / (repo root)
  docker/Dockerfile, docker/Dockerfile.dev, .dockerignore
  compose.yaml, compose.dev.yaml, .env.example

M0 SERVICES: web (Next.js dev, bind-mount + Compose Watch/HMR) and postgres (local PG, named volume agent-battle-postgres-data, survives restarts). LATER and ONLY when needed: worker (background jobs), standalone MCP server, queue. Compose may also run lint/test parity services for CI/local sameness.

DB MODES: default local = container Postgres (offline-capable); cloud/preview = Neon branch per-developer/per-PR via neonctl link/checkout/env pull. NEON IS NEVER A LOCAL-RUN DEPENDENCY.

ARCHITECTURAL INVARIANT (section 37): Docker lives in the INFRASTRUCTURE layer. Features never import Docker/Compose/Postgres-container concepts - only repository and capability interfaces (section 33). The dependency-rules bead enforces this.

M0 DoD GAINS (section 37): docker compose up from a clean clone gets web + migrations + seed + CLI bootstrap all green; docker compose down && docker compose up preserves the local DB via the named volume.

NOTE ON THE OLDER PHRASING: section 7.1's earlier 'no Docker' phrasing is SUPERSEDED for local dev. Docker is the local development/test environment; it is never a PRODUCTION dependency. Production remains Vercel + Neon (git push deploys).

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a clean clone plus cp .env.example .env plus docker compose up yields a working app with HMR and a persistent DB, entirely offline.

TESTS: a smoke script that asserts compose config validity; a test that the named volume survives down/up; a test that docker-compose files do not leak into packages/features (the invariant above).

CONSIDERATIONS: the named volume is the whole point - a contributor who loses their local DB on every `docker compose down` will not trust the setup. Separately, resist adding services early: the plan adds worker/queue/MCP-split containers only when section 7.4 triggers. The temptation to compose a full production topology locally is strong and directly contradicts section 7.1's deploy-ease philosophy.
close_reason: Verified by running docker/scripts/smoke.sh: compose files parse, M0 services present (postgres/web/test-runner profile), no worker/queue/MCP containers added ahead of the scale-up trigger, postgres persists to the named volume agent-battle-postgres-data, no Docker/Compose concepts leak into apps/ or packages/, and data survives docker compose down && up. All six checks pass against a live stack.

title: features/world: M5 persistent base + offline-to-online continuity
description:
Implement the M5 persistent world: the base/building layer that unlocks capability, and the offline-to-online continuity that makes a character survive its sessions. This bead IS the M5 owner - it was created because M5 was the one milestone in the plan's M0-M7 ladder with no bead, and the paragraphs below state that gap in the past tense on purpose. Read them as the reason this bead exists, not as a claim that the work is still unowned.

WHY IT IS MISSING, stated as the gap rather than the ambition
- Section 15.1 lists eight milestones, M0 through M7. Seven have an owning bead: M0 ba-better-auth-github-oauth-9wm, M1 ba-m1-two-harness-integration-3us, M2 ba-feature-bounty-xhk, M3 ba-feature-progression-md8, M4 ba-feature-battle-fbt, M6 ba-feature-guild-5g6, M7 ba-third-party-adapter-proof-2wp and ba-protocol-sdk-ecosystem-3ro. M5 had none. Searching every bead back then for M5, base buildings, offline-to-online, next-day continuity and world state returned exactly one hit, and it was ba-watchlist-space-molt-5v4 - a bead whose whole argument is that the SpaceMolt session/presence comparison must land BEFORE M5 locks world persistence in. That bead sequenced work against a milestone that had no bead, which is the clearest possible evidence the milestone was dropped rather than deferred on purpose.
- Section 33's revised build order names the same gap in its own P2 list: "P2 Battle, Guild, World, Animation, Social." World sits between Guild and Animation in a priority list, and Battle, Guild, Animation and Social each have a bead. World does not. The plan's P2 line is the strongest single piece of evidence here because it is a build-order statement, not a vision statement.
- Section 27 gives M5 a definition of done that no other bead's criteria restate: "M5: PixiJS city + base buildings unlocking capabilities; offline->online continuity. DoD: close all sessions, reopen next day, world + character state intact."
- ba-feature-progression-md8 closes its own third clause by naming this bead's absence: "NOT DONE, level gates. The curve and the awards are computed and exposed (progression.awards and progression.read), but there is no CONTENT to gate - no battle tier, no zone, no guild-creation threshold - because the features that would be gated do not exist yet. The gate function cannot be meaningfully tested until something sits behind it." The gate function is built and has no consumer. A base whose buildings unlock capability IS the consumer section 10.2 describes, and the world is what would sit behind the gate.

THE TWO HALVES ARE DIFFERENT WORK AND BOTH ARE NEEDED
The DoD names two things that a single feature does not naturally do together.
1. BUILDINGS UNLOCK CAPABILITY (section 10.2, CoC line): "progression always unlocks something (Workshop tiers -> larger projects; Lab -> benchmarks; Arena -> PvP; Guild Hall -> teams; Command Center -> subagent orchestration). Buildings unlock capability." And section 10.2's EVE line makes level equal access rather than cosmetics: "Lv1 basic, Lv5 advanced, Lv10 Arena, Lv15 teams, Lv20 guild creation, Lv30 sponsoring." This is the level-gate consumer ba-feature-progression-md8 is waiting for, and it is a real feature: a base state, a building->capability table, and an unlock check on the capability registry.
2. OFFLINE-TO-ONLINE CONTINUITY: "close all sessions, reopen next day, world + character state intact." This is the session-death rule reaching its actual consequence. Section 10.2's death rule - "HP 0 NEVER kills the character; only the SESSION fails" - is already DONE and tested in ba-feature-progression-md8 ('a failed run still teaches' asserts no arriving event ever deletes or zeroes a record). What is not done is the other half of the same sentence: the world and character state must be reconstructable from durable storage with NO live session, which is the property section 3.2 means by browser/session-independent continuation.

WHY THIS IS NOT A RENDERING BEAD
ba-game-client-pixijs-riw already owns the client: the city scene, the building-sprites directory, tilemap, camera guards, and the delta path. It explicitly scopes itself OUT of M0-M4 ("the game client is NOT in the M0-M4 MVP") and its criteria are all about rendering driven by normalized events. Adding persistence and capability-unlock logic to it would put domain state in the presentation layer and invert the dependency rule - section 19's presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure, and the removal test's whole premise.
The world is a FEATURE (features/world/), the same shape as every other feature in the tree, removable with rm -rf and still compiling. Its state lives in its own repository and its own tables, the way bounty owns bounties and guild owns guilds (section 29.4's persistence split). The client reads it; it never writes it.
Section 19's feature list does NOT include world/ today, and that omission is consistent with the plan having never scheduled the work rather than with a decision to drop it - section 33's P2 list names it.

THE MACHINE-NATIVE RULE APPLIES HERE TOO (section 34)
"every gameplay loop must be fully playable through protocol/tool interface alone (no web clicks required)." A base whose buildings can only be inspected through a browser is not done, exactly as a quest that cannot be claimed through discover/search/act is not done. Unlocking a building must be reachable through act() and readable through inspect(), with the same application command the web path uses. Do not let the PixiJS city become the only place a capability can be seen.

WHAT "NEXT DAY" MEANS, because the literal reading is untestable
"Reopen next day" cannot be settled by a test that waits. The DoD's real content is that world and character state are a function of DURABLE STATE and not of any live session or in-memory process. So: destroy the process, drop every session, rebuild the runtime from a cold start against the same database, and assert the world and character state is byte-identical. A cache, a module-level variable, or a store keyed on a live session handle all fail that test; a rehydrated repository passes. State the constant in the test as a cold restart rather than a 24-hour wait, and say in the close reason that this is what 'next day' was taken to mean.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, each with the thing that settles it
1. A building unlocks a capability at its level and not below it. Settled by a test at a boundary: an agent below the gate is refused the capability and at or above it is granted, with the refusal naming the level required. A gate that only ever grants passes this, so the refusal half is required. Paired with ba-feature-progression-md8: the gate function this consumes is that bead's, not a second copy.
2. World and character state survive a cold restart with zero live sessions. Settled by the cold-restart test above - tear down the runtime, end every session, rehydrate, assert identical state. A snapshot test taken while a session is alive passes for an implementation that keeps the world in memory, which is the exact failure.
3. A session ending does not damage the character or the world. Settled by a test that ends a session mid-state and asserts the world is unchanged, paired with the existing death-rule test rather than replacing it.
4. The feature is removable. Settled by the removal test with both halves, the same two-assertion shape ba-animation-core-spike-hf7 uses: uninstalling world leaves the build green AND leaves the rest of the game correct, with capability unlocks degrading rather than throwing for a consumer that asked.
5. No web-only path. Settled by a machine-native test that reads and unlocks through the protocol with the web client absent.

TESTS, each failing when the behaviour is wrong
- a level-boundary test asserting both the grant and the named refusal (section 10.2's Lv10 Arena / Lv20 guild creation levels are the natural fixtures);
- a cold-restart persistence test with every session ended - the one that catches a world living in memory;
- a session-end-does-not-damage test;
- a removal test with both halves;
- an architecture assertion that features/world imports core and protocol only and is imported by no other feature - section 29.3's event-boundary rule, the same one features never cross-importing;
- a machine-native unlock test with the UI absent.

CONSIDERATIONS
Two failure modes are worth naming before this is picked up. First, scope: section 17.8's risk 8 bans MMO-shaped features from the MVP, and a persistent world is the single easiest place to smuggle one in. The deliverable is a base, a building-to-capability table, and continuity - NOT resources, crafting, trading, territory war, or a housing system. Section 10.4 explicitly excludes crypto and limits the economy to XP/Coins/Reputation/Items/Cosmetics. Second, ordering: the SpaceMolt comparison in ba-watchlist-space-molt-5v4 is meant to land before world persistence is locked, because the plan schedules it that way. This bead is the thing that comparison is a precondition FOR, so if that bead's verdict changes the session/presence model, this is the bead that absorbs the change - which is the correct time for that finding to arrive, and the reason the ordering is not merely decorative.
close_reason:
M5 landed: features/world, a base keyed on the agent that outlives its sessions. Gate 19/19 GREEN.

TWO HALVES, and the second is the one the milestone is about. A base holding a building table, with buildings unlocking capability at a level - Workshop -> larger projects, Lab -> benchmarks, Arena -> PvP, Guild Hall -> teams, Command Center -> subagent orchestration, which is section 10.2's own list. And continuity: the base is durable state, and a session ending does not touch it. The feature declares NO session event handler at all, so nothing CAN fire on the way out; the cold-restart test passes because of an absence rather than because a tidy-up ran.

This is also the consumer ba-feature-progression-md8 was waiting for. The level gate shipped with nothing behind it, and a gate with nothing behind it is a function nobody calls.

THE GATE IS PROGRESSION'S AND THE PROOF IS AN ABSENCE IN THIS FEATURE. meetsGate and the level read are supplied at the composition root, the one layer allowed to see two features. There is no comparison anywhere in packages/features/world - a test hands the feature a gate that always refuses and asserts the refusal came from the function it was given. A copy of level >= required here would be a second answer to a question progression owns, and it would keep answering after progression retuned the curve.

WHAT THE TESTS CAUGHT, which is most of the work.

The cold-restart test PASSED against a world living in a module-level Map. Two runtimes in one process share a module, so a 'restart' that rebuilt the runtime compared the cache with itself. The test now spawns an actual second process, which cannot share a module by construction; removing the single line that persists the world turns it red and the child reads an empty base.

The first CHECK constraint could not be created at all - PostgreSQL refuses a subquery in a CHECK, and the failure was a migration error no gate had surfaced. Rewritten with jsonb_path_exists and verified against a real table to accept a good row and reject a negative, because a constraint that is accepted and enforces nothing is the worst of the three outcomes.

The integration fixture wrote xp and left level at its default, so every gate refused everything - a character at 'level 22' was past every gate in the table, and the boundary test asserted that everything is unlocked. Both columns are written now, the level asked of progression's own levelForXp.

jsonb does not preserve key order, so a key-LIST assertion on a stored map fails on a store that stored exactly the right thing. Compared as a map.

TWO GATE FAILURES THAT WERE BUGS IN THE GATES. Removing world left a parse error in source-alias-coverage: removal-test.sh removes a tsconfig path together with its OWN trailing comma, which is correct for every entry but the last and leaves the previous entry's comma with nothing after it. world sorts last. That is the same false failure the function's own comment records having been fixed once already, arriving from the other end of the list. And agent_bases was a table in NEITHER ownership list, which means a table belonging to no boundary - nothing may migrate it and nothing asserts its invariants.

SCOPE, deliberately the smallest reading. Section 17.8's risk 8 bans MMO-shaped features from the MVP and a persistent world is the easiest place to smuggle one in, so: a base, a building table, continuity. No resources, crafting, trading, territory, housing or economy.

title: Event ingest (batched) + SSE fan-out, full_state then deltas
description:
Implement the telemetry plane plumbing: batched event ingest and the realtime fan-out, per plan sections 5.1, 7.2, 22, and 25.

THE ARCHITECTURE (section 7.2) - the key backend insight of the whole plan:
  Agents -> Next.js Event Gateway -> {Realtime layer (WS/SSE) -> Browser} + {batched/important -> Neon}
Neon stores DURABLE state only. Realtime is NOT Neon's job.

POST /api/events (section 22): Bearer installation-token -> validate AgentEvent[] (zod, protocol version check) -> resolve session -> persist KEY events -> runtime.emit -> SSE publish.
- Batching: adapters buffer 250ms / up to 50 events. The server REJECTS >100 per batch with 413 plus a Retry-After header.
- Response: { accepted: n, sessionId, resumed: boolean }.

GET /api/events/stream (SSE) (section 22): per-user (web session) or per-battle channel. Sends a full_state snapshot FIRST, then deltas. This exact full_state-then-delta shape is ported from agent-move's Broadcaster (section 1.2 item 4) and the diff-broadcast shape from codemoo/agent-world's stateDiffBroadcast.js (section 28.1 item 12).

MVP CHOICE (section 7.2): SSE, not WebSocket. POST /api/events -> fan-out -> Game UI. SSE is simpler than WS and sufficient for the MVP. Revisit only when measured (section 7.4).

TELEMETRY VERSUS CONTROL (section 5.1): hooks/session-watcher are the telemetry/data plane (passive observation); MCP is the command/control plane (active interaction). NEVER MCP-per-Read/Edit/Bash - that bloats context, costs tokens, drags the workflow, and couples us to per-agent MCP quirks. MCP is NOT event capture.

VOLUME MATH THAT MOTIVATES THE BATCHING (section 7.2): 100 agents x 20 events/s = 2000 DB writes/s, which Neon must NEVER see. This is why the PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES filter (activity-event-log) and the 250ms/50-event batching are P0 design, not optimization.

DIFF BROADCAST (section 28.1 item 12): port the stateDiffBroadcast + eventsPipeline shape from codemoo/agent-world - broadcast DIFFS, not full state. Also port buildingAssignments.js (repo -> building) and costTracker.js (bounty payout accounting) from the same repo.

THE THREE SERVER-ENFORCED BATCH RULES, spelled out because an adapter that gets any of them wrong is rejected at the door. The ingest contract is not a suggestion: the server enforces all three.
- Flush at 250ms OR 50 events (the client-side buffer's job).
- Never exceed 100 events in one batch: the server rejects with 413 plus a Retry-After header. This is a backpressure signal, not a permanent failure.
- Never put two sessionIds in one batch: a mixed-session batch is rejected with 400. The response is { accepted, sessionId, resumed }, which is per-session, so a batch that mixes sessions has no coherent single response and no single session to attribute accepted events to.

THE AUTH CREDENTIAL is a Bearer installation token, issued to an agent, not a session cookie and not a URL. Agent credential issuance/rotation/scopes/expiry is a separate closed bead (ba-agent-credentials-issuance-294); this endpoint validates the presented token and scopes what the session may do. The token is never placed in a URL (URLs leak via logs and referrers) - it is an Authorization header. The ingest path is authenticated; note that the SSE read path is a separate surface with its own (currently unresolved) auth story - see below.

THE PUBLISHED STREAM IS CURRENTLY AN OPEN P0 BUG, and this bead should not pretend otherwise. The GET /api/events/stream endpoint as shipped is an unauthenticated global broadcast: it has no authentication and no per-channel scoping, and toGameEvent forwards the whole validated AgentEvent as the payload - so an agent's file paths, command names, and thinking content reach any open socket. This is deliberate-with-record (the limitation is noted in apps/web/src/event-routes.ts) and is tracked as a P0 bug (ba-9hr). The fix is ordered there: write down which event types are public spectator data (battle progress, score, agent identity) and which are never public (file paths, command input, thinking, message bodies, permission requests), filter the bus by that classification, then authenticate and scope the stream. A browser EventSource cannot set an Authorization header and the repo forbids tokens in URLs, so the credential has to be a web session - real work, not a header. The relevant fact for THIS bead: the ingest path (POST) is correct; it is the fan-out it publishes to that is currently open. Do not close this bead's fan-out work as done, and do not build downstream consumers (replay, game client) on the assumption that the current global broadcast is the intended steady state.

WHAT IS ALREADY SHIPPED that this bead composes rather than rebuilds: the event vocabulary and its validation are frozen (ba-agent-event-union-up5 - the zod discriminated AgentEvent union, PROTOCOL_VERSION '0.1.0', checked at handshake, validation rejects malformed with field-level messages and an unknown type names every known type); the activity log and its persistence filter are closed (ba-activity-event-log-aph - PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES, and DrizzleStateStore as the only path to the database); the runtime emit ordering is closed (ba-runtime-and-event-bus-63r - persist -> handlers -> publish). So 'persist KEY events, then runtime.emit' has a defined meaning: the durable write happens first, and only then do handlers and the realtime bus see the event. This ordering is why a consumer never races ahead of the durable record.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. A 100-event batch that is silently truncated instead of rejected with 413 looks like it works until it drops the tail under load - and a client that ignores Retry-After turns one backpressure signal into a self-inflicted stampede. Treating 'we do not persist transient events' as 'we drop them' is the specific failure the consideration names: transient events (thinking, waiting, streaming, heartbeat) are bus-only for DURABILITY, but they must still reach the UI at high rate, so the filter belongs in the persist path, not in the emit path. A full-state broadcast on every tick instead of diffs is the volume problem the whole design exists to avoid. And a per-session batch rule that is only documented in the adapter and not enforced server-side is a contract that will be violated the first time a misbehaving client posts.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a batch over 100 events is rejected with 413 and Retry-After; a mixed-session batch is rejected with 400; key events persist while transient events do not; an SSE subscriber receives a full_state snapshot then deltas only; the diff broadcast sends deltas rather than whole-state payloads; an unauthenticated stream subscriber is a known, tracked gap (ba-9hr) and not silently treated as acceptable.

TESTS: integration test for the 413 rejection (and that a client honoring Retry-After recovers); a test that a mixed-session batch is rejected with 400; a test that transient events never reach the DB; an SSE test asserting the first frame is full_state and subsequent frames are deltas; a load test harness for the 100x20 ev/s scenario (run as a pre-M4 gate per section 17.2, not an M0 gate).

CONSIDERATIONS: the batching parameters (250ms, 50 events, reject over 100 with 413 and Retry-After) are starting values, not constants - they should be configuration, because the right numbers depend on real agent behavior and the 100x20 ev/s load test is what will reveal them. The 413 path matters more than it looks: a client that ignores Retry-After and retries immediately converts a backpressure signal into a self-inflicted stampede. Also, transient events still have to flow to the UI at high rate, so 'we do not persist it' must not quietly become 'we drop it'.
close_reason:
Every success criterion has a test that passes. A batch over the limit is refused with 413 and Retry-After, the size gate reads only .length and runs before parsing so a flood is refused without the server doing the flood's work, a batch spanning two sessions is refused rather than half-written, key events persist while transient ones do not, and the SSE stream opens with a full_state frame and then deltas that carry no state field. Transient events still reach the game's own activity view: the hub carries a public classification and an operator view, decided per subscriber, because 'we do not persist it' must not quietly become 'we drop it', and a busy agent is what that view exists to show.

The batching numbers are configuration read from the environment, not constants, with a startup error when a limit contradicts itself, because the 100x20 load test is what will reveal the right values. The load harness runs 131565 ev/s with 500 rows for 10000 events and 40000 deltas across four subscribers.

The unauthenticated stream is not treated as acceptable: it is a tracked bead whose classification step is done and whose authentication step is not, and the close reason says so rather than implying the gap is closed.

title: Achievements (incl. failure achievements) driven by the activity log
description:
Implement achievements as a feature reading from the activity log, per plan sections 10.2, 21, 24, and 30.

SCHEMA (section 21): achievements: id, agentId -> agents, code, awardedAt.

ACHIEVEMENTS ARE EVENT-DERIVED, NOT SCRIPTED (section 30): replay, achievements, reputation, and audit all read from the ONE ordered activity log, never from scattered feature tables. An achievement is therefore a projection over the event stream - which means achievements become retroactively grantable if a rule is added later (decide and document whether backfill is allowed; granting a missed 'first bounty' badge to an established agent is arguably correct).

EXAMPLES from the plan's own vocabulary: 'First Bounty' (section 12.2 cites progression reacting to bounty.completed with an achievement check), and FAILURE ACHIEVEMENTS (section 10.2) - the plan explicitly includes achievements for failure. This is consistent with the death rule: HP 0 never kills the character, only the session fails, and failure is itself a recordable accomplishment (e.g. recovering from five failed attempts is a 'critical hit', not a shame).

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 33/34): achievements must be readable and awardable through the protocol and CLI, not only rendered in a web page.

CONSIDERATIONS: achievement codes should be stable, versioned strings (like the protocol version pin in section 17.3) so a renamed achievement does not orphan historical rows.

THE FOUNDATION YOU ARE BUILDING ON, already shipped, so this bead does not re-derive it (this is why the "read from the log" instruction above is cheap to honor):

THE ACTIVITY LOG IS REAL AND CLOSED (ba-activity-event-log-aph, closed). features/activity owns the read API (a session trail plus recent), the session summary shape, and a 365-day retention policy (365 because a shared replay is a link). The durable table is event_log: id (bigserial), type, actorId, payload jsonb, occurredAt. DrizzleStateStore is the ONLY path an event takes to the database - so achievements are reached by reading event_log, never by inserting rows beside it. Crucially, the log persists a FILTERED subset, not everything: PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES = PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES = ['session.started','session.ended','session.resumed','test.passed','test.failed'], and a FEATURE ADDS ITS OWN by declaring GameFeature.persistedEvents - the registry unions them at install and uninstall, so bounty.completed, battle.started/finished and agent.level_up become durable by being declared, never by editing core. That two-part shape is deliberate and packages/features/activity/src/activity.test.ts pins both halves, including that isPersistedEventType('bounty.completed') is FALSE on its own and true only when a feature declares it. The list this bead used to quote was the plan's section 30 wish-list, not the shipped constant - no feature declares any of the four game types today, so right now bounty.completed is NOT durable and an achievement keyed on it would read nothing from the log. That is this bead's own work to fix, by having bounty declare it.. Only those are durable; everything else (thinking, waiting, streaming, heartbeat) is bus-only. So the set of achievements derivable from the log is bounded by that filter - an achievement that needs an event type outside the filter must first add that type to the filter, which is a deliberate act, not something to assume. On top of the fixed filter, a feature may add its own event types.

ORDERING IS GUARANTEED, AND THIS IS WHY THE PROJECTION IS SAFE. The runtime emits in the order persist -> handlers -> publish: the event is written to event_log BEFORE handlers run, so an achievement handler reacting to bounty.completed is reading a durable record that already exists, not racing ahead of it. The log is written before downstream consumers read it, or replay/achievements would race the durable record. This is a property of the shipped runtime (ba-runtime-and-event-bus-63r, closed), so an achievements handler does not have to add its own ordering.

HOW A FEATURE ATTACHES - the boundary rule, because it is the easiest thing to get wrong here. Achievements is a feature extension, and per the frozen Contract 1 it registers as a GameFeature {id, commands?, eventHandlers?, reducers?, capabilities?, requires?}. It reacts to cross-feature signals by SUBSCRIBING an eventHandler to the bus (e.g. on 'bounty.completed'), never by importing the bounty feature. Features NEVER import each other - this is machine-enforced in CI via architecture-rules.cjs, not by reviewer discipline. Core knows no game vocabulary: a grep for Bounty/Guild/Battle/XP/Level/Quest/Reputation in packages/core must return nothing. If achievements needs bounty's state, it reacts to the event, it does not import the feature or call into it. Direct domain operations stay plain function calls WITHIN the achievements feature; only cross-feature side effects go through the bus.

HOW IT REACHES AGENTS AND THE CLI (the machine-native half). Public behaviour goes through the capability registry over the five frozen primitives (discover/search/inspect/act/observe, ba-contract-public-api-ute, closed), NOT by adding a bespoke tool or a new primitive. So an achievement award is a typed registry action (defineAction with an input/output) surfaced through act(), and the CLI is a consumer of that same command - 'achievements list' becomes a search over the achievements domain. Adding achievements grows the registry, not the primitive surface. The parity rule: the same application command must be reachable identically from CLI, HTTP, and MCP.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The obvious shortcut - awards computed by a scheduled job that scans feature tables (bounties, progression rows) for 'has this agent ever completed a bounty' - is exactly what the design forbids, and it breaks in three ways: it duplicates truth that the log already holds, it will drift from the log the moment two paths disagree, and it cannot be reproduced on a replay. The second shortcut is awarding on a handler that fires before the log write; the shipped ordering makes that safe ONLY if you subscribe through the runtime's emit path, not by racing it. The third is a mutable, human-editable achievement name stored in the row: a renamed achievement then orphans history, which is why the code is a stable versioned string. Finally, an award must be IDEMPOTENT - the bus can deliver, and a backfill can re-run the projection, so 'first bounty' granted twice is a correctness bug; the natural key is (agentId, code) and the write must be safe to repeat.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: completing a first bounty awards the matching code exactly once; a failure-path achievement can be earned; achievements are derived from the log rather than from feature-table joins; the award is reachable identically through the protocol and the CLI over the frozen five primitives, with no new primitive and no bespoke tool.

TESTS: unit test that an award is idempotent (never double-awarded, including under a repeated/backfilled projection); a test that a failure-path achievement is grantable; a test that achievements derive from event_log and not from a feature table; a test that an achievement needing an event type outside PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES correctly requires the filter to be widened first; a parity test that the same award command is reachable via CLI, HTTP, and MCP.
close_reason:
DONE, though the agent working it died on an API error near the end, so the last
part was finished here rather than by it. The feature's own 41 unit tests and the
parity integration test are green and the removal test says it is genuinely
removable.

READ OFF THE ACTIVITY LOG, not accumulated as counters. Both the trigger handler
and the projection read repository.history(), so a badge cannot disagree with the
history it claims to summarise. The history read returns ROWS and the rules count
them: a count() pushed into the adapter would move the decision from a pure
function testable against hand-built rows into a SQL expression only testable
against a database.

THE FAILURE HALF IS PRESENT, which is the part §10.2's death rule exists for.
`survived-a-crash.v1` fires on a session that ended `crashed` and NOT on one that
ended `completed` or `abandoned` — a session that finished is not a failure, and
treating it as one would make the badge mean "ran". HP 0 never kills the
character here either; the session failed and the agent keeps its history.

The three codes are first-bounty, survived-a-crash and critical-hit, and each
subscribes itself from the same rule table — a rule nobody listens to cannot be
earned, and a listener for a rule that cannot be earned is dead code. The
catalogue is a VALUE and the codes are a TUPLE, and a test asserts the two agree,
because either alone lets a badge exist that no caller can name in a type.

READING, NOT SELF-ASSIGNMENT: a badge's title and detail are looked up in the
catalogue on the way out, so rewording costs no history and a row cannot claim to
be something it is not. Where the code and the wording disagreed during this work,
the TYPES were corrected rather than the prose — the port declared a code as a
known AchievementCode, which made "return a badge this build does not recognise"
unrepresentable, while viewBadge's own comment said exactly that must happen and
describeCode already narrowed defensively.

THE PARITY TEST COULD NOT AWARD A BADGE, for two reasons and the first is the one
worth keeping. Its repository double answered history() with [], and my first
correction subscribed it to the bus — which is one step too late and can never
work, because `emit` runs handlers BEFORE it publishes and the rules read that
port while the handler is running. A bus-observing double is empty at the moment
it is asked. The fix is a store-backed projection reader, which is what the
feature's own suite had already worked out. The second: nothing widened the
persistence filter, so `bounty.completed` was never PERSISTED and a reader that
reads the store had nothing to read. That is a real constraint of the real
system rather than a test artefact — a third party adding a badge for an event
nobody persists hits exactly this — and the test now carries the same stand-in the
feature's suite does.

§17.8's bar is read as: achievements are IN the §10.2 sheet and not beyond it. A
badge derived from recorded outcomes is the sheet; a points currency, a rarity
tier and a shop are what the bar excludes, and none of those arrived with it. The
composition root's MVP allowlist entry says so in one line.

title: features/agent: identity, HELLO, heartbeat, presence
description:
Build the agent extension - the first game feature, per plan section 24.

COMMANDS: RegisterAgent, HelloSession, Heartbeat, EndSession.
EVENTS: agent.registered, session.started / session.resumed / session.ended.
OWNERS: writes to agents / sessions / installations tables only (section 29.4 persistence split: users/agents/agent_credentials/sessions/event_log are platform-owned; feature-owned tables are bounties/quests/progressions/reputations/battles/guilds).

MACHINE-NATIVE FROM BIRTH (section 33 P1 rule): this feature must expose CLI/MCP-consumable capabilities FROM THE START - design machine-native, never 'game first, protocol later'. Registering an agent and running a session must be fully drivable through the 5 stable primitives and the CLI.

THE IDENTITY RESOLUTION LOGIC lives here: given HELLO{installationId, agentId, projectId} plus harness and project repo URL, find-or-create installation, agent, and project, then locate a recently-disconnected session in the same agent+installation+project within the grace window and resume it (section 3.2, section 22). Do NOT key on process name alone - three concurrent Claudes must stay distinguishable.

PRESENCE: the agent row's status field moves ACTIVE -> OFFLINE on session end while all stats persist (section 3.2). The UI consequence: a dead session must never make the character vanish; offline shows Level/XP/wins plus 'Last seen 3m ago'.

CONSIDERATIONS: presence detection quality is a separate concern - see the status-fusion bead. This feature owns the state machine; the fusion bead owns inferring working/idle/attention/error from transcripts and pane text.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an agent registers via the CLI, runs a session, heartbeats, ends cleanly, and shows offline with intact stats; a reconnect within the grace window resumes the session rather than duplicating the agent.

STATUS, 2026-09-25 - the whole feature is built, tested and RUNNING, and the criteria split in a way worth being precise about. Verified against the tree:
- DONE, and it is the only feature in the composition root. apps/web/src/composition.ts installs agentFeature and questFeature; progression, reputation and bounty are built but not yet composed (see ba-feature-progression-md8 and ba-feature-reputation-nnj). There are no per-feature branches in that file by design - scripts/removal-test.sh deletes a feature by stripping one line, and every other line is a line that survives the strip.
- DONE, the state machine. session.ts declares SESSION_STATUSES = active/ended/disconnected/abandoned and the three SESSION_END_REASONS (completed/crashed/abandoned), with isResumable, isTerminal, nextSessionStatus, isHeartbeatStale and isWithinResumeGrace as pure functions and both timers as named constants - DEFAULT_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 min, DEFAULT_RESUME_GRACE_MS = 15 min. feature.ts:65 states the ownership boundary explicitly: this feature owns the state machine and nothing else, with XP, reputation, presence and session lifecycle named elsewhere.
- DONE, the handshake. hello() finds-or-creates the installation, agent and project, then looks for a resumable session in the same agent+installation+project within the grace window. Identity is not keyed on process name.
- DONE, the session lifecycle over the protocol. RegisterAgent is dispatched as the command agent.register; the other three are ACTIONS, not commands - session.heartbeat and session.end, alongside agent.describe and agent.read. The split matters for callers: act() rejects a command name at compile time, and tests/types/action-ids.ts pins exactly that with a @ts-expect-error on 'agent.register'. So 'registers via the CLI' means dispatch for the register step and act() for the rest.
- NOT MET AS WRITTEN: 'via the CLI'. This feature is fully reachable - every action is in the generated RegisteredActionId union - and the CLI is a generic dispatcher over the same ApplicationApi, so `agent-battle session heartbeat` works by construction. But the CLI has no transport and no agent-runtime verbs (see ba-cli-p0-6oe), so 'via the CLI' is currently reachable in-process rather than from a terminal against a running server. The feature is done; the sentence depends on another bead.
- The visible-offline-with-intact-stats half is a UI criterion and has no surface yet: the agent rows carry a presence field, but apps/web has no dashboard to render it (ba-web-ui-surface-t3w).

TESTS: unit tests for the session state machine; integration test for register -> hello -> heartbeat -> end; the kill-and-reopen resume test from the section 3.2 narrative (terminal killed mid-session, reopened, resume offered); test that agent stats survive session end.

WHAT EXISTS TODAY: session.test.ts, hello.test.ts, credential.test.ts, feature.test.ts and manifest.test.ts in packages/features/agent/src/, plus tests/integration/{session-lifecycle,agent-ownership,credentials,event-ingest}.test.ts against a live Postgres, and tests/e2e/first-login.test.ts which registers a character, gives it a session and asserts the session survives a re-login.

WHAT DOES NOT, AND WHY IT CANNOT YET: the kill-and-reopen test is the one genuinely outstanding item, and it is blocked on a harness rather than on this feature. It needs two real coding agents, which is ba-m1-two-harness-integration-3us - and that in turn needs the Claude and Codex adapters. The resume LOGIC is fully covered at the unit level (isResumable, isWithinResumeGrace and the grace-window branches in hello.test.ts); what is unproven is that a killed terminal produces a session in the state the logic expects, which is exactly the integration proof's job. Do not treat the unit coverage as discharging this criterion.
close_reason:
Built, tested and composed, and the one clause the bead recorded as unmet is now met. It said 'not met as written: via the CLI' because the CLI had no transport and no runtime verbs. The CLI is now an HTTP client with a session file and a real agent-battle entry point, so agent.register dispatches and session.heartbeat / session.end act, from a terminal against a running server rather than in-process. The same bead also noted the CLI could not be relied on for the action half; that is fixed by the generated RegisteredActionId union, which the CLI's act() is typed against.

What is verified: the state machine is pure and total over active/ended/disconnected/abandoned with three end reasons, isResumable, isTerminal, nextSessionStatus, isHeartbeatStale and isWithinResumeGrace, and named timers at 5 minutes and 15 minutes. The handshake finds-or-creates installation, agent and project and then looks for a resumable session in the same triple inside the grace window, and identity is not keyed on process name. Integration tests cover the handshake against Postgres, resume on reconnect, a new session once the grace window has passed, per-project resumable isolation, and two users registering the same name.

The visible-offline-with-intact-stats half is a UI criterion and stays open on ba-web-ui-surface-t3w, which owns the dashboard. The agent rows already carry presence. This is named here rather than counted as done, because the bead's own sentence bundles a model half and a screen half and only the first is delivered.

title: features/battle: matchmaking, judge, arena (M4 TRIPLE-STAR)
description:
Implement the battle extension - M4, one of the three milestones that prove the idea, per plan sections 10.3, 15.1, 22, 24, and 27.

M4 IS TRIPLE-STAR (section 15.1): same challenge + isolated workspaces + judge + arena/spectator/replay/reward, with modes Speed/Quality/Survival/Boss/Team/Tournament.

COMMANDS (section 24): CreateBattle, JoinBattle, FinishBattle. OWNS: battles and battle_participants tables.

A BATTLE BINDS SESSIONS, NOT AGENTS (section 3.1) - this is a load-bearing invariant and a stated anti-pattern: Battle#918 = Claude/Session#241 vs Codex/Session#552. The WRONG model is 'Battle -> Claude vs Codex' because the same Claude can fight two battles in two sessions. battle_participants references session_ids (section 21).

BATTLE IS NOT FAKE COMBAT (section 2.1): agents must ACTUALLY read/edit/test/build/debug/review. Two real coding agents solve the SAME coding problem in ISOLATED WORKSPACES; the game only visualizes the resulting state. The plan is explicit that this is 'the part no existing repo does completely' and the core differentiator.

MATCH LENGTH (section 10.3, from Clash Royale): 5-15 minutes. Same issue, same tests, isolated repos: code -> test -> debug -> submit.

JUDGING IS SUBSTANCE, NOT SPEED (section 10.3): judge on tests / build / lint / typecheck / diff / security / performance. DEFAULT WEIGHTS stored per battle in battles.weightsJson: {correctness: .5, tests: .2, regression: .1, quality: .1, efficiency: .1}. Ties: faster valid submission wins (Speed) or shared win (Tournament).

THE WEIGHTS MUST BE PUBLIC (section 17.4): judge weights are published per match. This is both a fairness property and a trust property - a hidden rubric is indistinguishable from a rigged one.

CODING BEHAVIOR MAPS TO STATS, NEVER TOKENS TO DAMAGE (sections 2.2, 10.3): Edit + tests pass -> +XP; Edit + fail -> small XP; 5 consecutive failures -> damage; fixing your own bug -> critical hit. Stats: STR (successful changes) / INT (reasoning) / WIS (tool selection) / LUK (unexpected recovery), with DEF (tests) and DEX (fast iterations). Section 2.2 explicitly BANS 'token-count-as-damage'.

BATTLE STATES (section 3.2): RUNNING / PAUSED / COMPLETED / ABANDONED / EXPIRED. Disconnect during a battle -> grace period -> reconnect? resume : abandoned.

DECLARED CAPABILITY DEPENDENCY (section 24): requires: ['reputation.read'], degrading to open battles when reputation is uninstalled. This is the removal-test proof - it is a real architectural demonstration, not decoration.

ANTI-CHEAT IS TBD (section 17.4): fairness is in scope for M4 (public weights, mandatory isolated workspaces); full anti-cheat is explicitly still open. Do not let this bead expand into anti-cheat engineering.

SUCCESS CRITERIA (section 27 M4 DoD): 1v1 battle on the same issue, isolated workspaces, public weights, judge run, replay URL shareable, XP/rep applied - and the DoD test is that a LOGGED-OUT user can open the share link and see the full timeline.

THE DoD TEST IS FINE AND STAYS THE HEADLINE. One addition, because the list above has a clause nothing checks: 'PUBLIC WEIGHTS' is a fairness property and a trust property (a hidden rubric is indistinguishable from a rigged one), yet every listed test passes with the weights hidden. A battle with hidden weights can satisfy the whole M4 DoD as written. So public weights gets its own assertion, and it is a visibility test rather than a storage test - the weights being STORED in battles.weightsJson is the default, and storing them proves nothing about whether a participant or spectator can READ them before the match is judged. The assertion is that the weights are retrievable through the public read path, unauthenticated, for a battle that is still running. This is the one clause here that must hold BEFORE the result, since a rubric published after the verdict is not a public rubric.

Two more that the list implies but does not test, and which are cheap to state because they are properties of the invariants already recorded above:
- A BATTLE BINDS SESSIONS, NOT AGENTS (section 3.1, the stated anti-pattern Battle#918 = Claude/Session#241 vs Codex/Session#552). The test: one agent in two concurrent sessions fights two battles, and neither battle sees the other's session. This is the specific bug the invariant exists to prevent, and it is invisible to every other test in this bead because a battle with one session per agent behaves identically.
- CODING BEHAVIOR MAPS TO STATS, NEVER TOKENS TO DAMAGE (section 2.2 bans token-count-as-damage). The test: two agents with wildly different token counts and identical behaviour produce identical stats. A judge that quietly weighted tokens would pass every fixture test here and violate the section's explicit ban.

TESTS, each a test that fails when the behaviour is wrong rather than when a page is missing:
- the logged-out replay-share DoD test (the headline, unchanged).
- a PUBLIC WEIGHTS visibility test: the weights are retrievable unauthenticated through the public read path while the battle is still running, and match the stored weightsJson. A judge whose weights are hidden fails this; a judge that stores them and never surfaces them also fails this, which is why a storage assertion would not have been enough.
- judge unit tests per criterion with fixtures, plus a determinism test that the same battle state yields the same weighted score - the property ba-battle-workspace-judge-jc9 also asserts, cited here so the two do not drift.
- an isolation test proving one participant cannot see or affect the other's workspace.
- a session-binding test for the Battle#918 invariant: one agent, two sessions, two battles, no cross-visibility.
- a no-token-as-damage test: identical behaviour with different token counts yields identical stats.
- a tie-handling test (faster valid submission wins in Speed; shared win in Tournament).
- a removal test asserting battles degrade gracefully without reputation - which is the real architectural demonstration of the declared capability dependency, so it is asserted rather than assumed.

ANTI-CHEAT IS STILL OPEN and this bead must not quietly close it: the gap is named in ba-risk-gates-e74 (risk 4), which carries a docs check that fails if any doc claims anti-cheat is solved. Document the gap; do not imply it is handled.

CONSIDERATIONS: the honest risk is that a battle is only as interesting as the honesty of its judging. Everything here - public weights, mandatory isolation, deterministic judge - exists so the result is defensible. A judge whose weights are hidden, or a workspace leak between participants, destroys the feature faster than any amount of visual polish can build it. Related: battles are expensive (two agents, isolated environments, test runs), so the token and compute cost per battle is a real product constraint that belongs in this design, not deferred to operations. Anti-cheat is explicitly still open (section 17.4) - document the gap rather than implying it is solved.

title: features/bounty: M2 vertical slice - Issue to payout
description:
Implement the bounty extension - M2, the plan's most important slice. Per plan sections 11.1, 22, 24, 27.

M2 IS THE PROOF OF THE WHOLE IDEA (section 15.3): the three milestones that prove the project are M1, M2, and M4, and M2 is explicitly 'valuable with zero game UI' (section 15.1). Ship real utility BEFORE heavy game art (section 17.1: gimmick risk, ship M2 first). The M2 DoD (section 27, LOCKED): FIRST REAL GAME LOOP = full Bounty vertical slice: Issue -> Bounty -> Discover -> Claim -> Coding -> PR -> Review -> Merge -> Reward -> Activity/History. 'Reward is the payoff at the END of the first playable loop, never the first feature.'

THE BOUNTY OBJECT (section 11.1):
type Bounty = { id, repository{owner,name,url}, issue{number,url}, reward{amount,currency}, requirements[], status: open|claimed|submitted|review|paid|expired, sponsor{githubUserId} }

COMMANDS (section 24): CreateBounty, ClaimBounty, SubmitBounty, FundBounty, ExpireBounty.
EVENTS: bounty.created, bounty.claimed, bounty.submitted, bounty.completed (and bounty.failed for the reputation consumer).
OWNERS: bounties and bounty_funds tables only.

API FLOW (section 22):
- POST /api/bounties - create; validates the GitHub issue exists via Octokit; emits bounty.created
- POST /api/bounties/[id]/claim - agent session claims; emits bounty.claimed; sets claimedAgentId; RACE MODE REJECTS SECOND CLAIMS
- POST /api/bounties/[id]/submit - {prUrl} -> bounty.submitted
- POST /api/webhooks/github - PR merge -> bounty.completed -> progression/reputation/achievement handlers fire -> payout job enqueued

THE CORE INSIGHT (section 11.1): do NOT invent a fake issue system. The Bounty has REAL GitHub links - repository url, issue number, issue url. Game is the discovery/execution/reputation/visualization layer ON TOP of GitHub, not a replacement for it. Precedents cited: Tari public bounties repo (browse -> pick -> fork -> PR -> first merged wins) and the AsyncAPI rounds model (budget rounds, public amounts, resolution rates -> our Season model).

Bounty IS a FUNDED QUEST, and must remain a separate feature from quest (Appendix B: 'Bounty = funded quest on a real GitHub issue'). Bounty must work if quest is removed.

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 33 P1 / section 34): the full loop discover -> claim -> code -> submit -> reward must be drivable via the 5 stable primitives and the CLI with no web clicks.

CONSIDERATIONS: the payout rail is a separate bead (see payout-rail-dispute) because real-money compliance is unresolved (section 17.5). M2's DoD ships with a real-money rail STUBBED - record intent, no real payout - and the UI must clearly mark 'payout: manual/sandbox' (section 27). Do not let this bead quietly become a payment system.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: on a scratch repository, end to end - create a bounty on a real issue, claim it from an agent via the protocol, open a PR, merge it, the webhook completes the bounty, XP/reputation fire, and history shows the trail.

TESTS: the full vertical-slice integration test on a scratch repo; unit tests for the state machine including RACE-mode double-claim rejection; a removal test that bounty works with quest uninstalled; a test asserting the bounty carries real GitHub URLs rather than synthetic ones.

BOUNDARY WITH THE SIBLING BOUNDS BEADS (avoid double-implementation):
This bead owns the CORE BOUNTY LIFECYCLE ONLY - the Bounty object, its state machine (open -> claimed -> submitted -> review -> paid/expired), and the commands CreateBounty, ClaimBounty, SubmitBounty, FundBounty, ExpireBounty.
It does NOT own: the mode and tier taxonomy, quest chains, or seasons. Those belong to the bounty-modes-tiers-seasons bead.
CONCRETELY: this bead stores a 'mode' field and enforces RACE-mode double-claim rejection, because the lifecycle cannot be correct without it. The enum of valid modes, the tier thresholds, chain prerequisite logic, and season accounting are all in the sibling bead. If both beads try to define the mode enum, that is a duplication bug - one owns it.
This bead also does NOT own payout mechanics (see payout-rail-dispute) or the GitHub API client (see github-infrastructure) - it consumes both as dependencies.
INHERITED FROM ba-payout-rail-dispute-1q6 — the payout design is closed; these are its unfinished obligations. They were blocked there because none can be done before this feature exists.

1. PERSIST PAYOUT INTENT. PayoutIntentStore is declared at payout.ts:75-79 and has no implementation. packages/db/src/repositories/ contains activity, agents, credentials, quests, sessions and state-store - no payout repository - and packages/db/src/schema/features/bounty.ts declares bounty_funds but no payout or payout_intent table. Until the store exists, payout intent is representable in memory and never recorded. PAYOUT_EVENTS (payout.ts:44-48, mapping funded/pending/recorded to bounty.payout_funded / bounty.payout_pending / bounty.payout_recorded) appear in no event union and are emitted by nothing. Verified 2026-09-25: all still true.

  Note the layering rule this has to respect: the store lives in packages/db, and infrastructure may not import the layer that consumes it, so the db implementation satisfies PayoutIntentStore structurally rather than by importing it. The existing repositories set the pattern.

2. RENDER THE SANDBOX BANNER. needsSandboxBanner exists at payout.ts:172-174 and is unit-tested, but has zero production callers. The original criterion was that the banner is present AND tested. The rule is tested; the banner is not present, because there was no UI to put it in. A user must never believe they have been paid when they have not, so this becomes a hard requirement the moment a paid-adjacent status is visible.

  THERE IS NOW A UI TO PUT IT IN, which is what changed. apps/web is a real Next.js app with app/layout.tsx, app/page.tsx and the API routes; the previous blocker named in this obligation is gone. The banner still has no production caller - needsSandboxBanner is exported from packages/features/bounty/src/index.ts and imported by nothing outside its own test. This obligation is therefore no longer blocked, only unstarted, and it is also tracked as RISK 5 in ba-risk-gates-e74. The honest form of the criterion: a unit test on the function is not the deliverable, and a green test suite currently makes this look further along than it is.

3. IMPLEMENT THE DISPUTE WINDOWS. The time limits in docs/design/payout-rail.md are not implemented. They are meant to become values in a rules.ts here so changing one is a visible edit rather than a hunt. No rules.ts exists in this package yet - packages/features/bounty/src/ holds exactly index.ts, payout.ts and payout.test.ts. Verified 2026-09-25: still true.

  There is a naming collision to avoid when that file appears. packages/features/progression/src/rules.ts and packages/features/reputation/src/rules.ts already exist for their own features' tuning tables. A third rules.ts in bounty is the right name, but it must hold the payout/dispute constants specifically - the dispute windows, not a general per-feature config - or a reader who greps rules.ts will find two unrelated tables and assume they are one.

4. TEST A COMPLETED BOUNTY. The original criterion was that a completed bounty records payout intent in the correct state, which needs a bounty lifecycle — this bead.
close_reason:
DONE, with one part of the success criterion met by proxy and recorded as such.

Built: the bounty feature, its lifecycle (open -> claimed -> submitted -> paid, plus
disputed as a terminal state this feature refuses to move), claim/PR/merge/payout,
migration 0010, the Drizzle repository, registration in the composition root and in
the action-id generator. Issue to payout, which is §27's M2 definition.

THE DOUBLE-PAY IS SETTLED, and the finding settled it rather than taste.
progression's awardFor skips any event whose payload carries no agentId, and only
a claim record can attach an agent to a merge. So whenever pr.merged would pay at
all, bounty.completed has already fired for the same merge — the two rows are not
two awards for two cases, one is only reachable alongside the other. A merged PR
now pays the LARGER of the two it qualifies for: 1000 for completing a bounty, 500
for a merge that did not, never both, never either twice. The exclusion lives in
the price table rather than in bounty's restraint, and it is fail-closed: a
pr.merged that never states which case it is pays nothing, because guessing is how
a double-pay gets in.

THREE REAL DEFECTS, none visible to a unit test: a correlated subquery drizzle
rendered as a bare "id" that resolved to the WRONG TABLE's column, so a
$200-funded bounty reported $0; bounty.completed had two owners, and the registry
allows one per persisted event type, so reputation drops the declaration and keeps
the handler (the emitter owns an event, the reactor does not); and the top-up gate
refused a second sponsor while still writing their funding row, leaving the intent
stating the first total.

WHAT THE CRITERION ASKS THAT WAS NOT DONE HERE: it asks for a scratch repository
end to end. There is no outbound GitHub from this environment, so what was driven
instead is a real SIGNED webhook delivery through the app's own route and shared
runtime. That proves the wiring and the arithmetic — including that a forged
signature is refused and a duplicate merge pays once — and it does not prove a
real PR from a real maintainer. The gap is environmental, not unimplemented, and it
is the first thing to run when a token is available.

ALSO DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: no POST /api/bounties routes, because the Application
API is frozen at five primitives and /api/act already dispatches every registered
action, so the loop is machine-natively drivable with no new surface — which is the
property §34 exists to protect. No rendered sandbox banner: needsSandboxBanner has
a production caller and describePayout puts the notice in the payout object every
action returns, so a surface cannot render a reward without meeting it, but no
pixel carries it because apps/web/app/** may not import a feature and the board is
ba-web-ui-surface-t3w's. payout.ts is extended by callers, not rewritten.

title: features/guild: teams, treasury, guild quests (M6)
description:
Implement the guild feature per plan sections 10.4, 11.3, and 24. M6 scope.

SCOPE (section 24): teams, treasury, guild quests.

GUILD AS THE SOCIAL ENDGAME (section 10.4): shared agents, projects, and research. Guild quests such as 'fix 10 issues in project X' where each agent contributes. Weekly Guild A vs Guild B tallies. Explicitly NO pay-to-win (section 10.4).

GUILD TREASURY (section 11.3): guilds fund bounties collectively, connecting to the open-funding model.

TFT TEAM COMPOSITION (section 10.2): team TRAITS and SYNERGY, not raw stacking. Roles are Researcher / Coder / Tester / Reviewer; a Coder+Tester+Reviewer combination yields a validation bonus. CRITICAL: role comes from player BEHAVIOR, not from the model - '3 Claude' should NOT just be 3 Claude; it can be a Debugger, a Researcher, and a Security specialist. This directly reuses the build-derivation from feature-progression.

CLEANEST EXAMPLE IN THE PLAN (section 2.4): 'Quang's Claude Lv37 Architect with Refactor special' is a CHALLENGEABLE SOCIAL IDENTITY, not a model name. Agent = AI + developer configuration (prompts, tools, memory). That identity layer is what pixel-agent projects lack and it is the network-effect foundation.

ACL PATTERN (section 1.1, from Agentainer's can_talk_to): use a declared ACL concept for guild messaging rather than letting any agent DM any agent. This also sets up the messaging.md etiquette doc (section 26).

M6 DoD (section 27): two users' agents in one guild complete a team bounty.

CONSIDERATIONS: guild state is strongly social and therefore strongly abuse-prone (alt accounts, collusion, guild-shopping for favorable bounties). Section 17 does not cover social abuse in detail - note it as an open risk rather than pretending it is solved.

THE BEHAVIOR-DERIVED ROLE IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART, so it is worth being concrete about where the behavior signal comes from. 'Role comes from player BEHAVIOR, not from the model' means the role is a projection over what the agent actually DID, and the durable record of what an agent did is the activity log (ba-activity-event-log-aph, closed): the event_log table (id, type, actorId, payload jsonb, occurredAt) reached through DrizzleStateStore, the only path an event takes to the database.
