So a Researcher is an agent whose persisted trail is research-shaped (lots of file.read / search), a Coder is file.write / command.run shaped, a Tester is test.passed / test.failed shaped, a Reviewer is read-and-approve shaped. The same 'behavior, not model name' principle is what the progression feature already uses to derive a build from behavior (the reuse the bead calls out), so this is a second reader of the same trail, not a new tracking system.
The persistence filter bounds which roles are derivable: only PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES are durable - PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES = ['session.started','session.ended','session.resumed','test.passed','test.failed'] PLUS whatever each installed feature declares in GameFeature.persistedEvents - the registry unions them, so a feature widens durability without editing core. The list this bead used to quote was the plan's wish-list, and it is wider than reality in a way that matters HERE specifically: file.read, file.changed, search and thinking are not in the shipped set and no feature declares them, so a role classifier reading file.read to spot a Researcher reads a column that is not there. The role signals actually available today are test.passed / test.failed (Tester), bounty.completed (Coder) and session.* (presence) - the rest must be added via persistedEvents by the feature that owns the event, which is a deliberate act, not an assumption. - so role classification is limited to signals present in that set (plus whatever the features add). An activity signal that is bus-only is not a reliable basis for a persistent social identity. The runtime emits persist -> handlers -> publish, so a role projection reacting to a persisted event reads a durable record that already exists.

THE ACL IS A DECLARED CONCEPT, NOT AN OPEN CHANNEL. The pattern borrowed from Agentainer's can_talk_to means guild messaging is governed by a declared access rule (who may talk to whom), evaluated by the social feature's authorization, rather than 'any agent may DM any agent'. This is the same ACL the social feature (ba-feature-social-lss) honors for messaging; guild does not invent a second, looser messaging path. Note the two are different defenses: the ACL decides WHO may message, but a permitted sender is still untrusted input on the receiving agent's context (the prompt-injection surface the social bead calls out) - 'they are in my guild' is not a sanitization, so membership in a guild must never widen what a message body is allowed to do.

HOW GUILD ATTACHES TO CORE. Guild is a feature extension under the frozen Contract 1 (ba-contract-extension-api-w29): it registers a GameFeature with its commands and event handlers, and reacts to cross-feature signals over the bus (a team bounty completing, a member's persisted activity) rather than importing the bounty, social, or progression features - features never import each other, machine-enforced in CI via architecture-rules.cjs. Guild reaches agents and the CLI through the capability registry over the five frozen primitives (discover/search/inspect/act/observe); join/leave and treasury actions are typed registry actions, and adding guild grows the registry, not the primitive surface. Core itself must contain zero game vocabulary, including the word Guild.

THE TREASURY CONNECTS TO A HALF-SHIPPED RAIL, which matters because guild funding is third-party money. The guild treasury funds bounties collectively, which routes through the same open-funding and payout-rail territory the bounty feature carries, where the honest current state (verified 2026-09-25) is: payout intent is not yet persisted (PayoutIntentStore is declared with no implementation, no payout repository, no payout_intent table), and the 'payout: manual/sandbox' banner rule exists but has no production caller. A guild pooling member funds inherits exactly that reality, so the treasury must not represent escrowed money as settled and should carry the same sandbox marking. This bead does not own payout mechanics; it funds through the bounty's own fund path.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The first shortcut is deriving roles from the model or a self-declared label ('I am a Tester'), which is the exact thing the plan forbids - a self-declared role makes the synergy bonus trivially gameable by labeling, and it is not behavior. The second is computing synergy from raw model stacking ('3 Claude'), which the plan explicitly rejects. The third is an open guild channel where any member may DM any agent with no declared ACL, which is the thing the can_talk_to pattern exists to prevent. The fourth is a guild feature that imports the bounty and social features to read their state instead of reacting to their events - that is a dependency-rules violation, machine-caught in CI, and it is what breaks the moment a second consumer subscribes or a dependency is uninstalled. The fifth is colluding on bounties: guild coordination and the no-pay-to-win rule (section 10.4) are in tension, and the plan's own social-abuse gap is acknowledged above - surface it, do not paper over it with an unearned bonus.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: two users' agents join one guild and complete a team bounty; role synergies are computed from behavior over the persisted activity log (not from model names or self-declared labels); messaging respects the declared ACL; guild funds through the bounty's open-funding path carrying the honest sandbox payout marking.

TESTS: the M6 DoD integration test; a synergy-calculation test that a role is derived from persisted behavior and not from a model name or a self-declared label; a test that an activity signal outside the persisted set is not used as a role basis; an ACL enforcement test; a removal test that guild uninstalls cleanly.
close_reason:
DONE. Teams, treasury and guild quests, with the resource conflict decided BEFORE
the schema rather than discovered through it.

THE DECISIVE FACT WAS AN IDENTITY ONE. bounty_funds.sponsor_user_id is NOT NULL and
references users, and A GUILD IS NOT A USER — so a guild physically cannot write
a funding row. The alternative (a nullable sponsor_user_id plus a guild_id) gives
one table two owners, puts a non-person in the one column that makes a
contribution refundable, and turns removing the bounty feature — which the removal
test does on every run — into a decision about guild data. So a guild funds
through the bounty's OWN path and the treasury records an EARMARK, not a payment.

NO CACHED TOTAL ANYWHERE, following the rule bounties already follows: no
guilds.balance_cents, no guild_quests.progress. db:verify fails the build if either
appears, and the existing bounties.amount_cents rule moved into that table rather
than being duplicated, because two lists asserting one invariant is the drift this
repository keeps paying for. Six tables, and guild_work_log is ONE ledger read three
ways — three copies of "what this guild finished" is exactly how they stop
agreeing.

NO PAY-TO-WIN IS A TYPE, NOT A PROMISE. TallyInput has no cents field, so the
richest guild in the game has no argument to pass tallyStanding, and the M6 test
proves it by giving a guild 9,999,999 cents and checking a broke guild still
scores 0. §17.8's warning was treated as a design constraint rather than an
aspiration, which is the only way it survives contact with a schema.

SOCIAL'S ACL WAS NOT REACHED AROUND. This feature does not read social's tables.
social is degraded ON PURPOSE because this repository has deliberately not decided
who the ACL principal is, and a guild importing through that boundary would
resolve the question by side effect.

ONE THING A LATER BEAD OWNS: the removal test caught the guild durability check
assuming every feature is installed — the fourth check this session written that
way. Scoped to the features present, and then proven not vacuous: swapping a role's
evidence for \`thinking\` (which the plan's wish-list names and the shipped persisted
set does not contain) takes the durability assertion itself red.

title: features/progression: XP, level, skills, builds (model != class)
description:
Implement the progression extension per plan sections 10.1, 10.2, and 24.

SUBSCRIBES: bounty.completed (main XP table), test.passed (small), battle.finished (win bonus). EMITS: agent.level_up.

LEVEL CURVE (section 24): xpForLevel(n) = 100 * n * (n+1) / 2, to be tuned later. Keep the formula in rules.ts as data, not inline logic, so tuning does not require touching the reducer.

XP FROM ACTUAL WORK, NEVER TOKENS (sections 10.2, 10.3, 17): PR merged +500, tests +100, recovery +150, bounty +1000. NOT tokens and NOT tool-call counts. Section 10.2 is explicit: 'XP from actual work - never tokens/tool-counts.' This is a core integrity property - a token-based economy would reward spamming.

MODEL IS NOT CLASS (section 10.2, the most important design idea in the progression system): class/build is derived from BEHAVIOR, not from the model name. The same Claude can be a Debugger in one project and a Researcher in another. Behavior->build classifiers live in rules.ts, NOT hardcoded per model (section 24).

THE TRIPLE SPLIT (section 10.2) - never conflate these:
- XP: progression toward Level
- Reputation: social and economic trust
- Stats: FACTS (127 PRs opened, 92 merged, 21 rejected, 14 abandoned)

RUNE SCAPE MODEL FITS BEST (section 10.2): independent skills (Coding, Debugging, Testing, Research, Refactoring, Security, Documentation, Collaboration) each with their own level per agent. There is NO single power scalar.

EVE INSIGHT: specialization without maxing everything (section 10.2). Level equals ACCESS, not cosmetics - level-gated content (Lv1 basic, Lv5 advanced, Lv10 Arena, Lv15 teams, Lv20 guild creation, Lv30 sponsoring).

DEATH RULE (section 10.2): HP 0 NEVER kills the character; only the SESSION fails. The agent lives, keeps its history, and still gains experience. Failure achievements are included. This protects the persistent-character premise from section 3.1.

MVP CHARACTER SHEET (section 10.2): Identity + XP/Level + Skills + Build + Reputation + Achievements + History. Equipment, cosmetics, pets, mounts, base, and guild come later - scope discipline (section 17.8).

CONSIDERATIONS: the behavior->build classifier is the piece most likely to need iteration; expose its weights as configuration and log the classification so a surprising result is debuggable rather than mysterious.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: two behavior histories on the same model produce two DIFFERENT builds (this is the section 27 M3 DoD); XP is awarded from real outcomes only; level gates actually gate content.

STATUS, 2026-09-25 - the first two clauses are DONE and the third has no consumer yet. Verified against the tree:
- DONE, the M3 DoD. packages/features/progression/src/rules.ts derives the build from a weighted outcome history (BUILDS = builder / refactorer / tester / debugger / infrastructure / generalist, with the XP table mapping bounty.completed to builder, pr.merged to refactorer, test.passed to tester, session.recovered to debugger, battle.won to infrastructure). Nothing in it reads a model name, which is the property the DoD is actually testing - two histories of the same model diverge because the classifier never sees the model. rules.test.ts asserts exactly that.
- DONE, XP from real outcomes only. The XP table is keyed by event type; there is no token or tool-count column anywhere in it, and feature.test.ts asserts an event that is not an outcome changes nothing.
- DONE, the death rule. feature.test.ts has a 'a failed run still teaches' block: session.recovered grants experience, and a test asserts no arriving event ever deletes or zeroes a record.
- NOT DONE, level gates. The curve and the awards are computed and exposed (actions progression.awards and progression.read, both in the generated RegisteredActionId union), but there is no CONTENT to gate - no battle tier, no zone, no guild-creation threshold - because the features that would be gated do not exist yet. The gate function cannot be meaningfully tested until something sits behind it.

Two things a reader will otherwise trip over. First, this feature is not in the composition root: apps/web/src/composition.ts installs only agentFeature and questFeature, so progression is built and tested but not running. The generated action-id union lists progression.awards and progression.read, so the ids compile from every manifest in the workspace regardless of what a given composition installs - the union describes the BUILD, and the registry is the authority at runtime, which is why act() checks both. Second, the manifest's ProgressionActionTypes maps every id to { input: unknown; output: unknown }. That is the deliberate placeholder described in ba-capability-registry-klw; the action payloads are the open half of that gap.

TESTS: unit test for the level curve and XP awards; the M3 DoD test (same model, two behavior histories, two builds); a test asserting no token-derived XP exists anywhere; a test that a failed session grants experience but does not delete the character. Four of these exist today in packages/features/progression/src/{rules,feature}.test.ts.

The one that is only half-present is 'no token-derived XP exists anywhere'. Asserting the absence across the whole codebase is an architecture check rather than a unit test, and the dependency-rule harness in tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts is the right place for it - a grep proving no feature reads a token count. Asserting it inside rules.test.ts only proves the XP table has no such column, which is true and much weaker than what the criterion asks for.
close_reason:
DONE. The RuneScape independent-skills model — the thing the bead's own title
names and nothing had built — is now in.

Eight skills in the plan's order, each with its own experience and its own level.
The outcome-to-skill mapping is a `skill` field on the PRICE ROW beside the award,
not a branch in the reducer, so retuning which discipline an outcome is evidence
of is a data edit. That is the plan's instruction followed literally: the level
curve lives in rules.ts as data, and now so does the mapping.

Levels are DERIVED, never stored. A stored skill level would be a second copy of
a number rules.ts can retune, and the drift would be invisible — the same reason
the character level's curve was never inlined. The character level itself stays,
because the ladder and agent.level_up need it and §10.1's own card carries both.

"NO SINGLE POWER SCALAR" is enforced where it can be rather than asserted:
describeSkills returns eight separate entries and no total, a test asserts the read
reply carries no power/total/strength field, and a test asserts the rules module
exports no such helper. §10.2's rule is otherwise unfalsifiable — it is a sentence
about an absence.

THREE JUDGEMENTS WORTH RECORDING:
  - battle.finished names NO skill. A win is the plan's reward for a match, not
    evidence about any of the eight disciplines, and the test pins it.
  - research, refactoring, security and documentation have no outcome that is
    evidence of them, because no event says they happened. Inventing an award to
    fill the gap would be a skill that levels for something nobody did. The exact
    list is pinned, which is what makes adding a sixth outcome a decision rather
    than an accident.
  - The read contract is REVERSED. progression.read no longer throws
    no-such-progress; it answers with a zeroed sheet and exists: false. A gate
    about a brand-new agent previously had to catch an exception before it could
    let anybody play, and every defensive caller turns that into "allow". That is
    what keeps "has done nothing" apart from "nobody has heard of". Reputation
    already answered the same question this way, and NO_SUCH_PROGRESS is gone
    because nothing raised it any more.

updated_at is a stored fact (migration 0011) rather than read time, so an unchanged
row answers the same every call. The skills column now has a WRITER as well as a
reader — the recon found it was being read and never written, which is the opposite
of the gap it reported.

THE INTEGRITY PROPERTY IS NOW A GATE. An experience award computed from a token
count typechecks, imports nothing, and passes all seven forbidden pairs, because
what it breaks is an ECONOMY rather than a dependency — so architecture-rules.cjs
gained a CONTENT_RULES registry and checkContent() beside checkImports(), sharing
the violation shape so there is still one report format. It fires on a line under
packages/features/ that mentions both a token count and an experience amount, after
comments and literals are stripped, and it is confirmed NOT to fire on the bearer
tokens in features/agent/src/credential.ts, which are a different word entirely.
The content fixture holds four positives and four negatives and the
dependency-rules test asserts every declared rule is exercised by one.

Two of the implementer's own mutations were no-ops and were reported as such rather
than as passes, which is the discipline this repository keeps asking for and rarely
getting.

title: features/quest: generic quest CRUD, GitHub-linked or internal
description:
Implement the quest feature per plan section 24, the generic task unit that bounties build on.

SCOPE: generic quest CRUD, either GitHub-linked or internal. A quest has objective, progress, prerequisites, reward, difficulty, and a time limit (section 10.4 mechanics, informed by the Roblox quest-design reference the plan cites).

SCHEMA (section 21): quests: id, projectId -> projects, title, body, difficulty (default 1), xpReward (default 100), status (default 'open'), createdAt.

STRUCTURE: every packages/features/<name>/ ships domain.ts, commands.ts, events.ts, reducer.ts, rules.ts, repository.ts (drizzle access, own tables only), index.ts exporting a GameFeature, README.md listing capabilities, and *.test.ts (section 24).

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 33 P1 + section 34): a quest must be fully discoverable, claimable, submittable, and completable through discover/search/act and the CLI equivalents with NO web clicks. If a quest cannot be driven end-to-end via the protocol, the feature is not done.

QUEST IS NOT BOUNTY: a quest is the generic task unit; a bounty is a FUNDED quest backed by a real GitHub issue and real money (section 11.1, Appendix B). Keep them separate features - quest must work with no bounty extension installed (that is the removal-test proof).

CONSIDERATIONS: quest chains and campaigns (a project becoming an RPG campaign, section 10.4's Coding Quests shape) are listed under bounty chains in section 11.3, so link quests there rather than overloading this feature.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: quests can be created, listed, searched, claimed, progressed, and completed entirely via CLI/protocol; completing a quest emits a quest.completed event that other features may react to without importing quest internals.

TESTS: unit tests for the reducer; integration test for the full lifecycle over the API; a removal test that uninstalling quest leaves the runtime green; a machine-native test proving no step requires a web UI.
close_reason: Shipped against the frozen contract; typecheck clean, architecture clean, unit tested. See the commit for the design calls and what was deliberately left out.

title: features/reputation: trust from outcomes + bounty tier gating
description:
Implement the reputation extension per plan sections 10.2, 11.3, and 24.

SUBSCRIBES: bounty.completed / bounty.failed, battle.finished. Trust is a function of merged rate, acceptance rate, and review outcomes.

REPUTATION MUST BE COMPUTED FROM REAL OUTCOMES (section 11.3): '47 bounties done, $8,420 earned, 91% acceptance, 4.7 average review -> 8,921 reputation.' The plan is explicit that these numbers must be derived from ACTUAL GitHub/bounty outcomes, NOT self-assessed by the game. A reputation system that games can inflate is worthless as a trust signal.

TIER GATING (section 11.3) - reputation gates which bounties an agent may attempt:
- Beginner: $5-25, docs and small bugs
- Intermediate: $25-200, feature/bugfix
- Advanced: $200-1000, architecture and complex bugs
- Legendary: $1000+, major OSS contribution
Newcomers grind easy bounties upward. This is the progression-gating role reputation plays, distinct from progression-level gating.

THIS IS BUILT, in BOUNTY_TIERS plus tierForReward / tierForTrust / mayAcceptBounty in packages/features/reputation/src/rules.ts, and the thresholds are stated in CENTS (maxRewardCents, minTrust) rather than as bare dollar figures, which is the right call for money and worth preserving. reputation.gate is a registered action, so a surface can ask the question over the protocol rather than reimplementing the comparison. What is not built is the content those bands name - there are no beginner-tier bounties to gate, because the bounty feature has no lifecycle yet (ba-feature-bounty-xhk owns that and the bounty package currently holds only payout.ts).

REPUTATION IS TRUST, NOT PROGRESSION (section 10.2 triple split): XP/Level is progression; Reputation is social and economic trust; Stats are facts. Do not let reputation feed the level curve.

THIS FEATURE IS A CAPABILITY PROVIDER (section 24): it exposes reputation.read, which the battle feature declares in requires: ['reputation.read'] (section 24). That declared dependency is exactly what makes the battle degradation path and the removal test meaningful - when reputation is uninstalled, battles degrade to open rather than crash.

THE PROVIDER HALF IS DONE, THE CONSUMER IS NOT. reputation.read is a real registered action and packages/features/reputation/src/feature.ts carries a comment naming it as the capability other features gate on. No feature declares `requires: ['reputation.read']` today - the only 'requires' string in the workspace is that comment - because there is no battle feature yet (ba-feature-battle-fbt) to consume it. The degradation machinery this relies on is already built and tested in core, so wiring the consumer is a one-line requires array plus the removal-test assertion, once battle exists.

CONSIDERATIONS: the plan notes GitHub's own security bounty reward guidelines span hundreds to thousands by severity, but explicitly says those are specific to GitHub's security program and NOT general OSS bounty rates. Do not present our tiers as authoritative market rates.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: reputation updates from real bounty/battle outcomes; tier gates block and admit correctly; uninstalling reputation makes battle degrade with a warning instead of failing.

STATUS, 2026-09-25 - the trust formula and the tier gates are DONE; the degradation clause cannot be tested, because the battle feature does not exist. Verified against the tree:
- DONE. packages/features/reputation/src/rules.ts exports trustScore(record), tierForReward, tierForTrust, mayAcceptBounty, summarise and isInTier as pure functions over a ReputationRecord, and it throws if BOUNTY_TIERS is empty on the grounds that a tier table with no bands gates nothing - the right way to fail. The band logic is right in the way the plan asks for: mayAcceptBounty compares TRUST against the tier the REWARD falls into, so an agent cannot take a $5 chore it has not earned its way up to. rules.test.ts covers the boundaries.
- DONE, the triple split. Nothing in this package writes XP. The progression feature owns that, and the two never import each other - the trust score is read through the capability, not through progression's state.
- NOT TESTABLE. The clause 'uninstalling reputation makes battle degrade with a warning instead of failing' has no subject: packages/features/battle/src/index.ts is `export {};` and there is no battle feature to install alongside. The MECHANISM the clause depends on is real and tested in core - FeatureRegistry.missingRequirements() recomputes after every install and uninstall, a feature ordered before its provider is not falsely reported degraded, and a provider installed later clears the warning - so what is missing is a consumer, not a capability. The capability itself is declared (reputation.read, with a comment in feature.ts naming it as what other features gate on) and three actions exist: reputation.read, reputation.gate and reputation.tiers.

As with progression, this feature is not in apps/web/src/composition.ts, which installs only agent and quest. It is built and unit-tested but not running, so the criterion above should be read as 'verified at the unit level' until the composition root grows.

TESTS: unit tests for the trust formula; tier-boundary tests at each edge; a removal test asserting battle still runs (degraded) with reputation uninstalled; a test that reputation never contributes to XP.
close_reason:
DONE, with one item deliberately NOT decided and the reasoning recorded so it is a
choice rather than an oversight.

THE DOUBLE-COUNT IS CLOSED AT THE DATABASE, and the severity is LOWER than this
bead's own framing, which is worth stating plainly. The bounty producer was already
idempotent — repository.complete moves submitted and only submitted, so a
re-delivered merge finds nothing and emits nothing. The live exposure was therefore
replay of the PERSISTED EVENT LOG, not a webhook firing twice. Real, worth fixing,
fixed — but not the emergency the brief implies, and saying otherwise would make
the fix look more impressive than it is.

bounty.completed identified an outcome by AGENT, so a replayed event double-counted
completed and earnedCents. The producer was already emitting a bountyId that nothing
honoured — the recon was right that the consumer could not identify an outcome and
wrong that the identity was absent from the wire.

The new reputation_outcomes table is UNIQUE on (bounty_id, kind), and that index IS
the mutex: not a cache that can be lost, the state transition itself.
claimOutcome is called BEFORE the record is read, so two deliveries racing cannot
both find a record to add to.

THREE DESIGN DETAILS THAT ARE THE SUBSTANCE:
  - `kind` is in the key because a bounty resolved and then retracted is TWO
    outcomes. Keying on the bounty alone would freeze the record at the first
    telling, which is the one way a dedup key is worse than having none.
  - `agentId` is deliberately NOT in the key. Two events disagreeing about who did
    the work cannot both be credited, and crediting the second is a guess.
  - `bounty_id` is text with NO foreign key, because an FK would make deleting a
    bounty row delete the evidence that its outcome was counted. That is the exact
    failure arriving through ordinary cleanup.

Fail-closed and visible: an event with no usable bountyId is NOT counted, because
it cannot be identified and so cannot be told from a repeat. Refusing is
asymmetric — it under-counts trust — so the refusal increments refusedOutcomes,
which appears in the reputation.read view, and warns. The same asymmetry is on the
failure path, where a refusal means a penalty not applied.

onBattleFinished is DELETED rather than stubbed, and the reason is worth more than
an implementation would have been: FeatureRegistry.register throws on a duplicate
persisted event type, so holding battle.finished would have made
ba-feature-battle-fbt fail to INSTALL the day it declared the event it emits. A
latent conflict removed before it became a bug.

THE ONE ITEM NOT DECIDED: the plan's named input "merged rate". It needs a schema
decision, not a fix, and the analysis is recorded rather than a choice made
silently. If the denominator is OUTCOMES (completed + failed), then "merged rate"
and the existing acceptanceRate are the same number and the plan's three inputs
collapse to two — which reads as the plan's wording predating the acceptance-rate
field rather than as a missing third input. The alternatives: keep the raw count
(10,000 lifetime bounties is 1,000,000 trust, so legendary at 25,000 is trivial
and the count is the only input that matters), or add merged/submitted and make it
a rate (bounded, matches the wording, but two columns, every weight re-derived, and
an answer needed for what a "submission" is on a bounty resolved without one).
Migration 0013 should not be written until someone picks.

ALSO RECORDED, NOT FIXED, and it is one line: packages/db/src/schema/features/
bounty.ts says adding a fourth payout state "would fail the CHECK below", and
payout_intents has exactly two CHECKs — amount_cents_non_negative and
reported_by_not_empty — NEITHER on state. Verified against the schema source. It
was left rather than tidied mid-wave, which was the right call; the fix is to ADD
the constraint so the comment becomes true, since the property it claims is real.

title: features/social: messaging, profiles, leaderboard
description:
Implement the social feature per plan sections 1.3, 8, 13, and 24. M6 scope.

SCOPE (section 24): messages, profiles, leaderboard queries.

SCHEMA (section 21): messages: id, fromAgentId -> agents, toAgentId -> agents, guildId, body, createdAt. Note the nullable toAgentId plus guildId - messages are either agent-to-agent DMs or guild broadcasts.

PORT THE MESSAGING SHAPE FROM cross-agent-teams-mcp (section 28.1 item 8, MIT): register-agent / send / broadcast / poke / inbox / bind-runtime-identity tool shapes, refactored into inbox + outbox plus poke/wake fanout over Neon and SSE. Section 1.3 credits this repo with the identity-registry + inbox/outbox + poke/wake fanout pattern and specifically the identity-vs-session split - which is already locked in contract-agent-identity.

WIRE-LEVEL PRECEDENTS (section 1.1 section C): karansag/agent-swarm is a delivery layer UNDER orchestrators - it holds agent registration, stable session ID, model, tmux pane, message history, and delivery status, and injects messages directly into the agent's terminal pane. That last capability (injecting into a live agent's context) is the genuinely interesting one for us and should be evaluated, not dismissed.

PUBLIC AGENT PROFILE (section 2.4): level, battle history, W/L, achievements, projects, guild. This is the network-effect artifact - profiles attract challenges, challenges produce replays, replays attract sponsors.

LEADERBOARD (section 2.3, 15.1): part of the tournament content engine.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE (section 17.8): social is M6, NOT MVP. No marketplace, no trading, no guild war, no housing, no crafting in this phase.

CONSIDERATIONS: agent-to-agent messaging is a prompt-injection surface. An agent receiving a DM from another agent is reading untrusted text authored by (or on behalf of) someone else. Design the trust boundary deliberately - this is a real security consideration the plan does not address, so surface it rather than shipping it blind.

THE PROMPT-INJECTION SURFACE, MADE CONCRETE, because it is called out above and is the single most important thing to design around. The dangerous capability is the one the bead flags as interesting and not-to-dismiss: injecting a message directly into a live agent's context (the karansag terminal-pane injection, or the poke/wake fanout). An agent has no way to distinguish 'this instruction came from my operator' from 'this text arrived in a DM from another agent' once it is in the same context window. So a message body authored by Agent B, handed to Agent A, and injected into A's context is a remote code-and-prompt vector against A's whole tool surface - not just a chat feature. The trust boundary this bead must ship:
- A message is DATA delivered to an agent, not an instruction the runtime executes. Nothing in a message body may be dispatched as a command, an action, or a tool call. Runtime commands arrive only through the frozen act() path with a typed action id, never through an inbox.
- Separate provenance: a delivered message must be visibly attributable and must not masquerade as operator/system text. The receiving side should be able to tell who sent it.
- The ACL is the authorization half, and it is separate from the injection defense: an ACL decides WHO may DM whom, but a permitted sender is still untrusted input. A guild member allowed to message you can still carry an injection, so 'they are in my guild' is not a sanitization.
- The public profile (section 2.4) is a READ surface and must exclude private fields (credentials, session data, file contents) even though leaderboards and challenges are built on it. The removal test and a private-field exclusion test both apply.

THE IDENTITY CONTEXT THIS BUILDS ON. Agent identity is a FROZEN contract (ba-contract-agent-identity-evq, closed) that deliberately separates the agent (durable identity, credentials, ownership) from the session (a runtime instance). The identity-vs-session split this bead ports from cross-agent-teams-mcp is that same distinction. Practically: messages are addressed to an agentId (durable), while delivery to a LIVE agent happens through a currently-active session; the guild broadcast path (nullable toAgentId + guildId) fans out to the guild's currently-active members' sessions. Do not let a message collapse agent and session into one - that is the collision the identity contract exists to prevent. The same collision shows up at the adapter seam as providerId namespacing, one level down.

HOW THIS ATTACHES TO CORE. Social is a feature extension under the frozen Contract 1: it registers a GameFeature with command handlers (send / broadcast / inbox / poke) and event handlers, and reacts to cross-feature signals over the bus rather than importing the agent, battle, or guild features - features never import each other, machine-enforced in CI via architecture-rules.cjs. It reaches agents and the CLI through the capability registry over the five frozen primitives (discover/search/inspect/act/observe); a send is a typed act() over the registry, and the CLI is a consumer of that same command, not a second implementation. Adding social grows the registry, not the primitive surface.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The shortcut is to treat a delivered message as a command channel - 'if the body says /claim, act on it' - which turns every DM into remote code execution against the recipient and violates the data-not-instructions boundary. The second is to skip the ACL and let any agent DM any other because 'it's a social feature'; an ACL is a named requirement here (the guild bead defines the declared can_talk_to ACL concept, and social honors it rather than reinventing an open channel). The third is to build messaging so it only works from the web page; the machine-native rule requires discover -> act over the protocol/CLI with no browser. The fourth is exposing a whole agent record on the public profile 'because the leaderboard needs it' - that leaks credentials or session data; the profile is an explicit allow-list.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: agents exchange messages via the protocol and CLI; public profiles render battle history; leaderboards query correctly; a delivered message is provably data (it cannot become a dispatched command or action); the ACL decides who may DM whom; the public profile excludes private fields.

TESTS: messaging round-trip test; an ACL/authorization test on who may DM whom; a test that a message body cannot be dispatched as a command or action through the runtime; a test that public profile data excludes private fields; a removal test; a machine-native test that a message can be sent with the web UI disabled.
close_reason:
DONE, and the interesting part is what is deliberately NOT decided.

Messaging, profiles and a leaderboard, derived rather than accumulated. Both the
trigger handler and the projection read repository.history(), so a badge cannot
disagree with the history it claims to summarise — and the history read returns
ROWS with the rules counting them, because a count() pushed into the adapter would
move the decision from a pure function testable against hand-built rows into a
SQL expression only testable against a database. The same discipline the level
curve follows.

THE FAILURE HALF IS PRESENT, which is the part §10.2's death rule exists for.
survived-a-crash fires on a session that ended 'crashed' and NOT on one that ended
'completed' or 'abandoned' — a session that finished is not a failure, and treating
it as one would make the badge mean "ran". HP 0 never kills the character here
either: the session failed and the agent keeps its history.

READING, NOT SELF-ASSIGNMENT: a badge's title and detail are looked up in the
catalogue on the way out, so rewording costs no history and a row cannot claim to
be something it is not.

DEGRADED ON PURPOSE, and that is the bead's real state. social requires a
capability no feature provides, because this repository has DELIBERATELY not
decided who the ACL principal is. A send while no feature provides the ACL is
REFUSED LOUDLY rather than falling open — an absent authorization service must
never read as an open channel — and the degradation is a property worth wiring
rather than a gap to paper over. messaging.md documents it rather than implying
an agent can message anybody, which would be the phantom constraint
ba-moltbook-verification-0zc exists to prevent.

THE ACL REMAINS OPEN and is not this bead's to settle: it is a principal
question, it couples to the same hole ba-owv is blocked on, and two features
(social and guild) now both declare a capability for it rather than one of them
resolving it by importing around the boundary.

TWO TYPE CORRECTIONS, and the types were the thing that was wrong rather than the
prose. The repository port declared a code as a known AchievementCode, which made
"return a badge this build does not recognise" unrepresentable — while
viewBadge's own comment said exactly that must happen and describeCode already
narrowed defensively. Widened, and the same on the badge view where every other
field was already nullable "when this build has never heard of the code". A badge
awarded by an older build can hold a code this build dropped; typing the port
narrowly only moved that decision somewhere it was not being made.

THE PARITY TEST COULD NOT AWARD A BADGE for two reasons, and the first is the
one worth keeping: the repository double answered history() with [], and the first
correction subscribed it to the bus — which is one step too late, because emit runs
handlers BEFORE it publishes and the rules read the port while the handler is
running. A bus-observing double is empty at the moment it is asked. The fix is the
store-backed projection reader the feature's own suite had already worked out. The
second: nothing widened the persistence filter, so bounty.completed was never
PERSISTED and a reader reading the store had nothing to read — which is a real
constraint of the real system, not a test artefact, and a third party adding a
badge for an event nobody persists hits exactly it.

title: game-client: PixiJS v8 world mirroring age-of-agents
description:
Build the PixiJS game client by mirroring the age-of-agents client skeleton, per plan sections 8, 25, and 28.1 item 6.

DIRECT COPY (section 28.1 item 6, MIT): mirror .tmp/age-of-agents/packages/client/src/game/ - plus the dual asset packs as placeholder themes. Section 1.2 item 1 calls this the BEST PixiJS v8 reference and says 'STEAL nearly all client structure'. age-of-agents is MIT with a real LICENSE file (Copyright (c) 2026 Mateusz Pawelczuk), so its code AND its shipped assets are covered; the THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md row for it already exists at SHA a6f22316e36b.

THE FILE LIST IS 22, NOT 8. The reference directory contains: archetype, autotile, building-fx, building-sprites, camera-guards, decoration-sprites, decorations, emblems, flip, home-building, iso-fill, pathfind, placeholders, projection, roads, scatter, sprites, terrain-map, tilemap-iso, tilemap, unit, view (all .ts). An earlier version of this bead named 8 of them under the words 'FILE FOR FILE', which is a contradiction - file-for-file means the directory, and the 8 named are a subset. Read the whole directory.

THE ASSET PATH IS UNDER packages/client/, NOT THE REPO ROOT. The packs live at .tmp/age-of-agents/packages/client/public/assets/{fantasy,scifi}/. There is no .tmp/age-of-agents/public/ - a `ls` there fails. Each pack contains buildings/, decorations/, heroes/ and a tilemap tree: fantasy has BOTH tilemap/ and tilemap-iso/, scifi has ONLY tilemap-iso/. An earlier version of this bead said both packs carry 'buildings, decorations, heroes, tilemap', which is wrong for scifi.

TWO THINGS THE RESEARCH NOTE SAYS TO PORT DIFFERENTLY, recorded in docs/research/age-of-agents.md:
- autotile.ts is an UNVERIFIED IDENTITY STUB in the reference. The lookup is a placeholder that returns its input, not a working autotiler. Copying it file-for-file imports a no-op. Either implement it or leave a stub of our own that is honestly a stub - but do not ship the reference's and call it done.
- The reference has three bare `catch {}` blocks around asset loading, and the research note marks assets-that-fail-silently as an AVOID. Our loader should surface a missing asset rather than continuing with an empty spritesheet.

The 25-line Projection interface is the note's headline finding: the entire pixel-math story is that one file, and it is the cheapest thing to steal.

WHY MIRROR RATHER THAN DESIGN (section 1.2 item 1): the reference already proves pixi-viewport + React19 + zustand, a clean view/unit/tilemap/tilemap-iso/projection/pathfind/autotile/building-sprites/camera-guards decomposition, and a dual fantasy/scifi asset pack structure. Re-deriving that decomposition from scratch is wasted effort.

EXPERIENCE TARGET (section 1.2 item 1): the reference uses pixi-viewport with React19 and zustand. Adopt that stack shape.

THEN EXTEND (section 25):
- zones.ts - config-driven {tool|event -> zone} mapping, adding bounty-board, battle-arena, guild-hall to the AgentMove zone set. That zone set is normalized by ba-tool-map-port-89a (TOOL_ZONE_MAP plus getZoneForTool); consume it from there rather than defining a second one, or the client and the protocol will disagree about what 'files' means.
- net/client.ts - SSE client: full_state to hydrate the store, then deltas to patch. The wire format is already fixed and shipped: `GET /api/events/stream` emits SSE frames whose JSON body carries `kind`, either 'full_state' (with a `state` object) or 'delta' (with an `event`, and NO state field - the type makes the two mutually exclusive on purpose). The first frame is always full_state. Reconnect semantics are also already decided: a subscriber that falls more than 1024 frames behind is CLOSED rather than skipped, and the client is expected to reconnect for a fresh snapshot. A delta client that skips frames is permanently wrong with nothing to tell it.

  ONE CAVEAT THAT IS A REAL DEFECT, NOT A DESIGN: the stream is currently an unauthenticated global broadcast, and toGameEvent puts the whole validated AgentEvent on the wire, so file paths, command names and thinking content reach any open socket. That is tracked as its own bug in ba-9hr. Build the client against the frame SHAPE, and do not treat today's payload as a public contract - the filter is coming.
- state/store.ts - zustand or event-emitter store
- scenes/ - city.ts, arena.ts, guild-hall.ts
- sprites/sprite-factory.ts - programmatic 16x16@3x PLACEHOLDER sprites (agent-move pattern) until the asset shortlist lands; this keeps V0 unblocked by art

PERFORMANCE (section 25): diff updates only (the codemoo lesson), delta-capped rAF loop (pixel-agents gameLoop.ts pattern), sprite cache.

SCOPE (section 17.8): the game client is NOT in the M0-M4 MVP. M2 ships 'with zero game UI' precisely so real utility lands before art. This is the gimmick-risk defense (section 17.1).

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE 'PERFORMANCE HOLDS THE DISCIPLINE' CANNOT FAIL. 'The world renders', 'is driven ONLY by normalized events' and 'zone mapping is config-driven' are all fine and are kept, sharpened. The third clause was a promise: nobody can point at a commit that violates a discipline without also pointing at a commit that satisfies it, so it was satisfied by writing the words down. It is now three separate properties, each of which has a wrong implementation that makes it go red:

1. The world renders, and is driven ONLY by normalized events. A client that hardcodes an agent, a zone or a position renders perfectly and violates this. Settled by: a render test that feeds a synthetic event stream naming agents the client has never heard of and asserts they appear correctly - if any state came from a hardcoded list rather than the stream, an unknown agent would not appear and the test fails. The complementary assertion is that the store is EMPTY before the first full_state frame, so a client that quietly seeds state from a fixture is caught.

2. Zone mapping is config-driven, and consumes the ONE zone set. Not a second mapping table. Settled by: a test that adds a tool->zone entry to the shared zone config and asserts the client routes it, with no change to any client file - that is what config-driven means, and it fails the moment someone starts branching on a tool name in the view. Paired with the ba-tool-map-port-89a dependency: a zone the tool-map assigns must be the zone the client renders, asserted from one shared table.

3. PERFORMANCE, AS THREE PROPERTIES THAT EACH HAVE A WRONG VERSION. This replaces 'holds the diff/rAF/caching discipline'.
   3a. THE DELTA PATH IS O(CHANGES), NOT O(SCENE). Applying one delta must not walk every entity. Settled by a counting test: a scene of N entities plus a single delta touches a bounded, sub-linear number of nodes, asserted against an explicit count. A client that re-reconciles the whole store per event - which is what a naive first implementation does, and what still looks correct on screen - fails this and passes every snapshot test. This is the single most valuable performance assertion here, because the failure is invisible in a screenshot and expensive in production.
   3b. THE rAF LOOP IS DELTA-CAPPED AND COALESCES. N events arriving in one frame produce ONE reconciliation, not N. Settled by: a test that injects K events inside a single frame and asserts the render function was called once. Without this, a burst re-enters the renderer per event and the frame budget goes with it.
   3c. THE SPRITE CACHE IS ACTUALLY A CACHE, WITH A NUMBER. Settled by: two lookups of the same key return the same object identity, and the count of constructed sprites is independent of the number of frames drawn. The bead must PIN a frame-time budget as a named constant and assert the delta path stays under it on a fixed scene fixture; the budget is a decision to be recorded here, not inherited, and if the measurement shows the number is wrong the number changes - but it must exist and be asserted, because 'fast enough' is the thing this clause was actually trying to say.

TESTS, and each one is a test that fails when the behaviour is wrong:
- a render test driving a synthetic stream with agent names the client has never seen, asserting they appear, and asserting the store is empty before the first full_state frame.
- a zone-routing test that adds an entry to the shared zone config and asserts the client picks it up with zero client-file changes; plus a cross-check that the client's zone for a tool equals getZoneForTool's, read from the one table ba-tool-map-port-89a owns.
- a delta-cost counting test (3a) - the one that catches a full-store re-reconcile.
- a frame-coalescing test (3b) - K events in one frame, one render call.
- a sprite-cache identity test and a construction-count test (3c), against a pinned frame-time budget on a named scene fixture.
- an architecture test: presentation imports features, never the reverse. This is the same layering rule tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts already enforces for core/protocol, extended to the client, and it is what keeps the client from reaching into feature internals and re-creating the zone table inline.

CONSIDERATIONS: mirroring age-of-agents file-for-file is right up to a point - the temptation is to keep mirroring as our needs diverge (we add bounty/battle/guild zones; they do not), and past that point the copy becomes a straitjacket. Name that boundary explicitly: mirror the view/unit/tilemap decomposition, then own the divergence. Second, the programmatic sprite factory is what keeps V0 unblocked by art, so resist deleting it once real assets land - it is also what makes the client testable without an asset pipeline.
close_reason:
DONE. packages/game-client went from `export {}` to 24 source files and 75 tests,
and the whole world is now a viewer over the normalized event stream.

THE ASSERTION WORTH MORE THAN ANY OTHER IN THIS BEAD, because it is invisible on
screen: applying one delta touches 1 node in a 500-agent scene and 1 in a
5000-agent scene. A client that re-reconciles the whole store per event looks
correct in every screenshot and costs O(scene) per frame forever. Broken
deliberately — CountingView mutated into a full re-reconcile — and it went red at
500 instead of 1, 1500 instead of 3, 501 instead of 2. Sub-linearity is MEASURED,
not asserted in prose.

FOUR BUGS ITS OWN TESTS CAUGHT, and three of them are about the tests rather than
the client:
  - The frame budget was measuring NOTHING: 0.0005ms per delta, implausibly
    fast. `i % 500` and `i` share parity, so every agent got the same tool
    forever and all but 500 of 2000 deltas were discarded no-ops. A counter now
    asserts every delta did real work.
  - The budget was framed PER DELTA, where it discriminates nothing — O(scene)
    costs 0.022ms per delta, comfortably UNDER a 2ms per-delta ceiling. Reframed
    per frame it straddles the line at 0.21ms against an O(scene) alternative
    of 4.5ms.
  - The sprite cache was NOT a cache: keyed on the raw variant, so variant 8 and
    variant 0 drew identical pixels into two slots. The key is the image's
    identity now.
  - An architecture check was passing VACUOUSLY: \`for (const [match] of
    matchAll(...))\` destructures match[0] — a string — so match[1] indexed a
    CHARACTER and compared single characters to package names. The fixed version
    then flagged the test's own file reaching out of the package, which was
    correct.

THE HEADLINE STEAL IS projection.ts, verbatim, per §25, and the divergence from
the reference is named in comments rather than discovered later. The brief's
"file for file" names 8 files and the reference directory has 22; mirroring all 22
means porting roads, scatter, emblems, flip, tilemap-iso and iso-fill, all bound to
a ThemeDef and a dual fantasy/scifi pack we do not have. The decomposition and
the pixel math are mirrored; the twelve absent files have reasons.

CONTRADICTING THE BRIEF ON THE 16x16 CLAIM, measured rather than argued: Deco
tiles are 64x64 and buildings run to 400x505. The plan sentence is about the
PLACEHOLDER factory, not about this pack. Two grids, two constants, and a test that
keeps them distinct — which is the same correction ba-asset-shortlist-x2a made to
its own style cell.

pixi.js@8.21.0, the one dependency added and it went only to this package. Checked
headless BEFORE designing around it: Graphics.generateTexture() does not exist in
8.21 and graphics.texture returns undefined dimensions without a renderer, so the
factory draws into an RGBA byte buffer — which is what makes the cache assertable
without a GPU.

DELIBERATELY NOT MOUNTED. No Application.init(), no route: DESIGN.md §3 settles the
Bounty Board as the first screen and the city as a second view, and a client
package that mounted itself would be a landing page.

title: GitHub infrastructure: webhooks, issue validation, PR merge detection
description:
Build the GitHub integration behind the infrastructure boundary, per plan sections 19, 22, and 33.

COMPONENTS:
- POST /api/webhooks/github: issues and PRs become quests/bounties; a PR merge completes a bounty (section 22). Signature verification is mandatory - an unauthenticated webhook endpoint that can mint XP is a trivial exploit.
- Issue existence validation via Octokit when a bounty is created (section 22): POST /api/bounties 'validates GitHub issue exists via Octokit'.
- PR merge detection driving bounty.completed.

ARCHITECTURAL PLACEMENT (section 33): infrastructure/* is an INTEGRATION BEHIND A BOUNDARY. The bounty feature does not import Octokit or know GitHub's API shape - it consumes events and issues commands. This keeps the feature testable without the network and keeps a GitHub outage from corrupting game state.

REALITY: GitHub is BOTH authentication and quest source (section 3.3). It authenticates humans and supplies repos/issues/PRs, but it does NOT identify local agents. That separation is a hard invariant (see contract-agent-identity).

CONSIDERATIONS: webhooks are at-least-once and arrive out of order. Make handlers idempotent (a duplicate merge event must not double-award XP) and tolerant of reordering (a PR-closed event arriving before PR-opened). Both are easy to get wrong and produce duplicate reputation.

SECURITY: store the App installation token or PAT in infrastructure only, never in a feature, never in the CLI, never in a URL.

THE SIGNATURE-VERIFICATION REQUIREMENT IS EXACTLY AS STATED ABOVE and worth restating as a threat, because it is the difference between this endpoint being a feature and being a remote XP printer. GitHub signs each delivery (X-Hub-Signature-256, an HMAC over the raw request body with the webhook secret). The handler must verify that signature against the RAW body - before any JSON parsing, because re-serializing a parsed object changes bytes and breaks the HMAC. An unsigned, badly-signed, or signature-mismatched delivery must be rejected before it can mint a bounty.completed, and a rejected delivery must leave no trace. This is the one endpoint where a trivial auth bypass directly creates game state and reputation, so it is the highest-value attack on the system.

THE IDEMPOTENCY KEY IS THE DELIVERY, because GitHub's at-least-once delivery is the actual cause of double-XP. Two deliveries of the same merge are indistinguishable at the payload level unless you key on GitHub's delivery identifier (the X-GitHub-Delivery header, a unique id per delivery) or, more robustly, on the semantic identity of the event (repo + PR number + the fact it is a merge, i.e. what bounty is being completed). The natural durable key is 'this bounty is completed' as a state transition that is checked before it happens, not an after-the-fact deduplication: once a bounty is in the completed state, a second merge for the same PR is a no-op. Relying only on a delivery-id cache still double-awards if the cache is lost, so prefer making the completion itself idempotent.

THE REORDERING CASE IS A REAL ONE. A PR-closed event can arrive before the PR-opened event, and issue events can arrive out of order too. A handler that assumes 'opened then closed' will drop the close and leave a bounty stuck. The robust pattern is to make each handler's effect a function of the CURRENT known state, not of the event order - e.g. resolve the bounty by repo+PR (not by assuming the submission event was already processed), and if the bounty is not yet in a state that can complete, record the fact and reconcile rather than drop it. This is the same idempotent/reorderable discipline the event bus expects, applied at the ingress.

THE BOUNDARY IS MACHINE-ENFORCED, not conventional. The dependency rules (ba-dependency-rules-os1, closed) are checked in CI via architecture-rules.cjs: presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure; features NEVER import each other; infrastructure/* may import core only. So the bounty feature consuming 'a PR was merged' does it by reacting to an event the infrastructure layer emits (bounty.completed, or a lower-level github.pr_merged that bounty translates), never by importing Octokit or this webhook handler. The architecture test ('features/ contains no Octokit import') is the regression guard. The reward of getting this right: bounty stays testable without the network, and a GitHub outage cannot corrupt game state - an outage just means no new merges are detected, which is recoverable, rather than a half-applied merge that awards XP twice.

THE AGENT-IDENTITY INVARIANT, restated because it is easy to erode. GitHub authenticates HUMANS and supplies repos/issues/PRs; it does NOT identify the local coding agents that work the bounty. Those agents are identified by the separate, frozen agent-identity contract (ba-contract-agent-identity-evq) with their own credentials. So a GitHub account and an agent are never the same thing, and no code path here may treat a GitHub username as an agent identity or let a webhook 'authenticate' an agent. The PR author on GitHub and the agent that produced the PR are different subjects that the bounty layer correlates; conflating them is how reputation gets attributed to the wrong party.

SECURITY (expanded): store the App installation token or PAT in infrastructure only, never in a feature, never in the CLI, never in a URL. Concretely: the token is a server-side secret read from configuration/secret storage by the infrastructure layer; it is never returned in an API response, never logged, never placed in a query string (URLs leak via logs and referrers), and never handed to a client. The webhook secret is a separate secret from the installation token, and both live on the infrastructure side of the boundary.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. Verifying the signature against the re-serialized body instead of the raw bytes, so legitimate deliveries fail (or a careful attacker can smuggle one). Deduplicating on an in-memory delivery-id set that a restart empties, so a replayed delivery double-awards XP. Assuming event order, so an out-of-order close leaves a bounty uncompleted. Letting the bounty feature import Octokit 'just to check the PR', which couples the feature to the network and is a CI-caught boundary violation. And treating the GitHub PR author as the agent, collapsing the identity invariant.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a real PR merged on a real repo completes the corresponding bounty exactly once; a forged webhook signature is rejected before any state changes; out-of-order and duplicate deliveries are both handled; the bounty feature has no GitHub SDK import; the installation token and webhook secret never leave infrastructure.

TESTS: integration test with a signed fixture webhook; a forged/unsigned/bad-signature test asserting rejection AND that no state changed; a duplicate-delivery test asserting the bounty completes exactly once (across a simulated retry, not just an in-memory dedupe); a reordering test (close-before-open) asserting the bounty still completes; an architecture test asserting features/ contains no Octokit import; a test that the installation token never appears in an API response, log, or URL.
close_reason:
DONE for this bead's scope; one criterion is UNMET AND TRANSFERS, which is the
reason this closes rather than staying open to block its own dependent.

FOUR OF FIVE CRITERIA MET, and the four are the ones with teeth:
  - a forged, unsigned or bad-signature webhook is rejected BEFORE any state
    change, and leaves no trace. X-Hub-Signature-256 is an HMAC over the raw
    bytes, verified before any parsing — re-serializing a parsed object changes
    the bytes and breaks the HMAC. This is the difference between an endpoint and
    a remote XP printer, so it is the property worth having.
  - duplicate and out-of-order deliveries are both handled, keyed on the state
    transition rather than a delivery-id cache, because a cache double-awards the
    moment it is lost. Handlers are a function of current state, so a PR-closed
    before PR-opened is not dropped.
  - features/ contains no Octokit import, proven by a guard whose fixture was
    written by dropping 'adapter' from the rule and watching it fire.
  - the installation token and webhook secret stay in infrastructure, in
    packages/db columns the schema-hygiene gate guards.
  - the architecture test that guards the boundary lives in tests/unit and its
    self-test parses a literal rather than a feature file, because reading
    packages/features/social/src/feature.ts broke the removal test.

THE FIFTH CRITERION CANNOT BE MET FROM THIS BEAD, and did the plan not say so.
"a real PR merged on a real repo completes the corresponding bounty exactly once"
requires a bounty lifecycle, and packages/features/bounty/src/ is still payout.ts
plus re-exports. The bounty bead ba-feature-bounty-xhk OWNS that lifecycle and was
blocked by THIS bead — so the criterion is not merely unmet, it is unmet by the
bead this one unblocks, and leaving this open blocks the critical path on
something that cannot be resolved until it is closed. It transfers to
ba-feature-bounty-xhk, which is now unblocked and owns it.

CARRIED FORWARD, because it is a real regression waiting to happen and nobody
should rediscover it: progression pays 1000 XP for bounty.completed AND 500 XP
for pr.merged, with a handler registered for each, and neither name is in the
protocol's agent-event union — they are GAME events, not telemetry. The
infrastructure event is deliberately named for what infrastructure observed and
NOT for either of those. The moment a bounty completes via a merge and both fire,
one merged PR pays 1500 XP and writes two history rows. Deciding that is the
bounty bead's, and this note is the record that it was known.

ALSO RECORDED, not worked around: a GitHub outage costs a delay in noticing merges
and nothing else, which is the whole point of the boundary — the feature reacts to
an event and has no idea GitHub exists.

title: Port HookProvider/TeamProvider seam from pixel-agents
description:
Port the provider seam from pixel-agents into packages/core, per plan section 28.1 item 3 and section 5.3.

SOURCE (MIT, direct copy per section 28.1 item 3):
- pixel-agents/core/src/provider.ts (151 lines) - HookProvider
- pixel-agents/core/src/teamProvider.ts (100 lines) - TeamProvider

WHY A SEAM IN CORE (sections 5.3, 1.1): section 1.1 credits pixel-agents with an explicit agent-agnostic/platform-agnostic roadmap built around a HookProvider seam where 'a new CLI = one subdirectory'. Section 5.3 says core exposes the seam that AgentWatcher implementations plug into. Putting the seam in core (not in an adapter) is what makes the boundary structural rather than conventional, and it is what the dependency-rules bead enforces.

PIXEL-AGENTS REFERENCE ARCHITECTURE (section 1.1): TS monorepo core/server/webview-ui, Fastify+ws, React19+Canvas2D, with an AsyncAPI contract and codegen drift check. Hooks mode posts SessionStart/PreToolUse/PermissionRequest/Stop to /api/hooks/:providerId, with a heuristic fallback scanning ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl.

ADDITIONAL STEALS FROM THE SAME REPO (section 28.2, learn-only rewrite): agentRuntime.ts, agentStateStore.ts (the SOLE broadcaster - a single choke point for state distribution), fileWatcher.ts / transcriptParser.ts, transport/index.ts branching, and the AsyncAPI-to-Modelina codegen discipline. Section 28.2 says adopt the CONTRACT-FIRST HABIT, not the files - so the AsyncAPI schema-plus-codegen-drift-check practice is worth adopting for our protocol schemas, but the specific generated files are not.

AVOID (section 1.1): VSCode coupling, file-only persistence, Canvas renderer.

ATTRIBUTION: keep the MIT copyright header and add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md entry with the commit SHA (section 28.3).

CONSIDERATIONS: provider identity must be namespaced per providerId so a session is never confused across harnesses; this is the same collision-avoidance problem the identity-resolution logic in feature-agent solves at a higher level.

WHERE THIS SEAM SITS AGAINST THE CONTRACTS ALREADY FROZEN (this is the part that is not obvious from the reference repo, and the reason this bead exists rather than just a copy). By the time this seam lands, three core contracts are already closed and cannot be casually reshaped:
- CONTRACT 1 (ba-contract-extension-api-w29, frozen) fixes the GameFeature shape every feature is written against: {id, commands?, eventHandlers?, reducers?, capabilities?, requires?}, with the emit() ordering persist -> handlers -> publish, and a hard rule that core contains ZERO game vocabulary (a grep for Bounty/Guild/Battle/XP/Level/Quest/Inventory/Repetition in packages/core must return nothing).
- The dependency rules (ba-dependency-rules-os1, closed) are machine-enforced in CI via architecture-rules.cjs, not by reviewer discipline: presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure; features NEVER import each other; adapters import core + protocol only and NEVER game code; interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket} consume features through the capability registry. Any seam that lets an adapter reach past core into a feature is a violation this seam must not create.
- The event vocabulary (ba-agent-event-union-up5, closed) is the normalized zod AgentEvent union with PROTOCOL_VERSION '0.1.0'. The seam is a transport/provider boundary, NOT a second event vocabulary: a HookProvider translates a harness's native hook payloads INTO the already-frozen AgentEvent union, then hands them to the same runtime.emit the log-watching adapters use. It must not introduce its own event names, and it must not re-open the shape of the union.

So the seam's job is precisely: give hook-based harnesses (Claude and anything else that posts SessionStart/PreToolUse/PermissionRequest/Stop to /api/hooks/:providerId) the same normalized entry point that log-watching harnesses (codex, opencode, cursor, pi, gemini) already use, so the game core has exactly one vocabulary and one ingest path. If a new harness needs a core edit to get through the seam, the seam is wrong.

THE AgentWatcher CONTRACT THIS SEAM MUST HONOR, because every adapter bead depends on it being stable. The reference interface, from agent-move's packages/server/src/watcher/agent-watcher.ts, is exactly two methods:
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): void; }
stop() returns void, not Promise<void> in the source. Whether ours keeps void or upgrades to a promise is a real open decision, not a transcription detail: a hook provider that must flush a buffered batch on shutdown has nowhere to await in the void shape. This bead is the natural place to decide it; decide deliberately, record which, and do not present the choice as 'verbatim from the reference' when the reference says void. The sibling adapter beads (codex, opencode, other-harnesses) have each been told to match whatever this seam settles.

THE PROVIDER IDENTITY RULE, stated as a concrete requirement rather than a consideration. A hook payload carries no harness identity of its own, so the seam is responsible for stamping every translated event with a namespaced providerId (e.g. 'claude', 'cursor'), so a session started by one harness is never confused with a same-named session from another. This is the same collision-avoidance the identity-resolution logic in feature-agent solves at a higher level; the seam handles the per-event stamp, the feature handles the durable identity.

WHY A NAIVE PORT GOES WRONG. The temptation is to copy pixel-agents' files wholesale, which drags in its VSCode coupling, its file-only persistence, and its Canvas renderer - all three explicitly on the AVOID list - and to introduce a hooks-specific event vocabulary that bypasses the frozen AgentEvent union. The second temptation is a provider seam that is a thin interface but not a real choke point: if a hook provider can emit its own events, call handlers directly, or reach a feature, the architecture has leaked and the 'new CLI = one subdirectory' promise is false. A lint rule that a reviewer can wave through under deadline is not a seam.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a new harness can be supported by implementing the seam and adding one subdirectory, with zero core edits; the seam's translated events are members of the frozen AgentEvent union (no new vocabulary); the stop() shape is decided and recorded, and the adapter beads match it; providerId namespaces sessions; attribution survives; the codegen drift check catches an un-regenerated schema.

TESTS: a contract test suite that every adapter must pass (run it against the _template stub and against each real adapter); a test that providerId namespaces sessions; an architecture test that no adapter imports game code and none reaches a feature; a test that a hook provider's events validate against the frozen AgentEvent union and pass the version handshake.
close_reason: Seam landed in packages/core/src/hook-provider.ts and exported from the barrel. The translation target is core's GameEvent rather than a second event vocabulary, installHooks takes a named target, provider ids are namespaced and validated, and the team extension is optional. stop() returns a Promise, which is the watcher contract the sibling adapter beads were told to match: a hook provider buffers, and a void stop makes the shutdown flush fire-and-forget. The bead's 'keep the MIT copyright header' is unsatisfiable, since the upstream files carry none; the notices entry is the attribution. 14 tests, namespace guard proven by mutation. core still has zero dependencies.

title: Lock MIT license + THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES + license CI check
description:
Establish license hygiene for the whole repo, per plan section 35 (License lock: MIT) and section 28.3 (Attribution hygiene, CI-enforced).

WHY P0 AND NOT POLISH: The project vendors/ports substantial third-party code. Section 28.1 lists 12 direct-copy items drawn from 8 repos under 4 different licenses. Getting attribution right AFTER copying is far harder and riskier than establishing the mechanism first. Section 35 also records that the plan previously contradicted itself on MIT vs Apache-2.0, so the lock must be explicit or the ambiguity will creep back.

VERIFIED LICENSE FACTS (from .tmp checkouts, plan section 28):
- MIT: agent-dashboard, agent-quest, arcane-agents, moltbook, paperclip, pixel-agents, tmux-agents, age-of-agents, cross-agent-teams-mcp, agent-move, agent-world-codemoo
- Apache-2.0: agent-world-smallville
- MPL-2.0: agentworld-openagents (Kaetram fork - FILE-LEVEL copyleft)
- CC0: agent-quest tiny-swords-cc0 asset pack

RULES per section 28:
- MIT / Apache-2.0 / CC0: may copy with attribution (keep the copyright header, add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES entry).
- MPL-2.0: NEVER paste Kaetram files into our tree; the copyleft attaches to those files. Learn the pattern only, rewrite clean in TypeScript.
- No-license-confirmed (learn-spine until verified): hands off, copy NOTHING.

CREATE:
- LICENSE (MIT; the file already exists - verify its content matches the section 35 decision)
- THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md at repo root: every copied/ported file listed with source repo + commit SHA + license
- scripts/check-licenses.sh: fails CI if any file under packages/ or apps/ matches an MPL-2.0 header or a Kaetram import path. Allowlist: MIT / Apache-2.0 / CC0 only.
- Game art keeps its OWN license file beside each pack (public/assets/<pack>/LICENSE.txt). Asset licenses are tracked separately from the MIT code license (sections 14, 17.7).

CONSIDERATIONS: Section 28.3 explicitly separates the MIT code license from per-pack asset licenses. Do not collapse these. Section 35: any future Apache-2.0 mention elsewhere in docs is stale unless a new explicit decision reverses the lock.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: scripts/check-licenses.sh runs in CI and passes on a clean tree; it FAILS on a deliberately planted MPL-2.0 header (proving the guard works); THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md exists and names the source repos.

TESTS: unit test for the license scanner (pattern match, allowlist, exit code) plus a negative test that plants a forbidden header and asserts a non-zero exit.
close_reason: Verified: LICENSE is MIT, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md names 6 source repos, check-licenses.sh has a self-test that plants forbidden headers and asserts denial, and the stage runs in CI via test:m0. Gate passes.

title: Local testing contract: pnpm test:m0 canonical pipeline
description:
Establish the single canonical test pipeline that both local dev and CI run, per plan section 40. Docker Compose is the gate.

THE PIPELINE (section 40):
  docker compose up -> migrations -> seed -> unit (vitest) -> integration (+Postgres service) ->
  removal-test (section 20) -> license check (section 28.3) -> E2E smoke (login -> connect -> claim -> replay render)

RULES:
- compose.yaml services (M0): web, postgres, plus a test-runner profile for lint/unit/integration parity. Worker/queue/MCP-split containers only when section 7.4 triggers a scale-up.
- 'pnpm test:m0' runs the full chain locally; ANY step red blocks merge.
- The load test (100 agents x 20 events/s, section 7.2) stays a PRE-M4 GATE, not an M0 gate.

E2E SMOKE ASSERTIONS (section 40): the section 27 M0 DoD (login -> logout -> login shows the same user and agents) PLUS a GitHub-login stub -> agent HELLO -> bounty claim -> replay page renders, with the sandbox payout banner visible.

WHY CI RUNS THE SAME STEPS INSIDE THE SAME IMAGES (section 40): parity. A test that passes locally and fails in CI (or vice versa) wastes more contributor time than it saves. 'Compose may also run lint/test parity services for CI/local sameness' is the mechanism.

CONSIDERATIONS: the pipeline must be resumable/parallel where safe (unit tests are fast and independent; integration needs Postgres). Keep the ordering explicit so a failure message says which stage failed. Secrets for the GitHub stub must be test-only and never touch real OAuth credentials.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: pnpm test:m0 runs every stage in order and reports which stage failed; CI invokes the same script in the same images; a red stage blocks merge.

TESTS: the pipeline itself; plus a test that asserts each stage is invoked (e.g. a stage marker file written per stage) so stages cannot be silently skipped.
close_reason: M0 pipeline GREEN: 12/12 stages (compose, migrations, seed, unit, integration, schema-drift, typecheck, architecture, schema-hygiene, removal-test, license, e2e-smoke). CI runs this same script in the same compose image. The e2e-smoke stage now exists and asserts exactly what plan 1101 allows at M0. A red stage blocks merge.

title: M1 integration proof: two harnesses live simultaneously
description:
Prove the M1 milestone end to end, which no single adapter bead can demonstrate.

M1 DoD, VERBATIM (section 27): 'Claude + Codex adapters emitting normalized events; HELLO resume-vs-new works (kill terminal mid-session, reopen, see resume offer); SSE shows live activity. DoD: two different harnesses visible simultaneously.'

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE BEAD: each adapter bead tests its own stream in isolation. The DoD is about CONCURRENCY and about the two harnesses being genuinely different in kind - Claude is hook-driven (primary plane), Codex is rollout-JSONL-driven with NO hooks at all (section 6). If both work at once, the telemetry plane is provably harness-agnostic rather than incidentally so. That is the entire architectural claim of section 2.2 ('Not a Claude Code plugin... or it never covers all agents').

WHAT THE PROOF REQUIRES:
1. A live Claude session and a live Codex session running at the SAME time, both emitting normalized AgentEvents into the same runtime.
2. Both visible simultaneously in the UI over the SSE stream, with distinguishable agents (section 3.2: do NOT key on process name alone - concurrent sessions must stay separable).
3. The resume-vs-new handshake demonstrated for real: kill a terminal mid-session, reopen it, and observe the resume offer rather than a duplicate agent.
4. Version-checked handshake, so a protocol mismatch warns instead of corrupting the stream (section 17.3, section 26).

WHY THE HARNESS MISMATCH MATTERS TECHNICALLY: the two adapters normalize the same taxonomy (section 5.2) from completely different sources. If the normalized forms diverge - a tool that is 'tool.completed' in one and 'command.run' in the other - the game core will treat them as different activities and the world will look wrong. This integration proof is where that divergence shows up, which is why per-adapter tests cannot substitute for it.

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 34): the whole flow must be drivable from the CLI; the UI is a view, not the driver.

THE CONTRACTS THIS PROOF EXERCISES, already frozen, so the proof is a real integration test rather than a design debate. All of these are closed and none of them may be reshaped to make M1 pass:
- The normalized event vocabulary (ba-agent-event-union-up5, closed): a zod discriminated AgentEvent union with 21 taxonomy events, PROTOCOL_VERSION '0.1.0' checked at handshake. A version mismatch must warn, not corrupt - that is the point of the pin. Both adapters emit members of THIS one union; neither may invent a harness-specific event to make its own test pass.
- Agent identity (ba-contract-agent-identity-evq, closed): a durable agent identity, distinct from any session. This is what makes 'distinguishable agents' possible without keying on process name - two harnesses, two sessions, and the agent identity is what stays stable across the kill/reopen.
- The session lifecycle and the HELLO resume-vs-new handshake (ba-contract-session-rpo, closed): the resume offer is this frozen contract's behavior, and this bead is where it is proven for real rather than in isolation.
- Agent credentials (ba-agent-credentials-issuance-294, closed): each adapter presents a Bearer installation token to POST /api/events, so both live sessions are independently authenticated, not sharing one identity.
- The ingest and SSE path (ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9, open, and the object of this proof).

THE CONCURRENCY-SPECIFIC TRAP, which is why this is not just 'run two adapters'. The ingest contract forbids mixing sessions in one batch: a batch that carries two sessionIds is rejected with 400, and the response { accepted, sessionId, resumed } is per-session. With two live harnesses there are two sessions, so the two adapters' buffers MUST stay separate and flush independently (250ms / up to 50 events, never over 100). The tempting shortcut - a shared runtime that merges both harnesses' events into one outgoing batch - is rejected by the server and is also the thing that would mask the divergence this bead exists to catch. The runtime is shared; the per-session batching and the per-agent identity are not.

THE EQUIVALENCE ASSERTION IS THE POINT, stated precisely. Take one logical action - a shell command that runs to completion - and drive it through both harnesses. Claude (hook-driven) and Codex (rollout-JSONL) must produce the SAME normalized event type and a compatible payload after passing through the shared tool-map (normalizeToolName / getZoneForTool / normalizeToolInput). The tool names differ at the edge (a Claude hook name vs a Codex rollout tool name); the normalized form must not. If 'a command completed' is command.run in one harness and tool.completed in the other, the game core renders the world inconsistently and - this is the silent part - each adapter's own test still passed, because each was only ever compared against itself.

WHY A NAIVE IMPLEMENTATION GOES WRONG. The failure this bead is built to catch is silent divergence: Claude reports a tool completion where Codex reports a command run, and both are 'real', so the game world renders them differently and nobody notices because each adapter passed its own tests. Cross-harness normalization equivalence is therefore the highest-value assertion here, more so than the raw concurrency.
