The second failure is keying identity on process name, which collides the moment two harnesses run at once - exactly what this bead forces. The third is treating the UI as the driver: if the flow only works with a browser open, the machine-native rule is broken and the DoD has been met in a way that will not survive. The fourth is a shared outgoing batch, which the single-session ingest rule rejects and which would hide divergence.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the literal M1 DoD - two different harnesses visible simultaneously, resume offer working after a terminal kill, live SSE activity for both; the same logical action normalizes to the same event type across both harnesses; the two sessions' batches stay separate (no mixed-session 400); a protocol-version mismatch warns rather than corrupting the stream.

TESTS: the concurrency integration test (two live sessions, one runtime, no mixed-session batch); a normalized-form equivalence test asserting the same logical action maps to the same event type across harnesses; the kill-and-reopen resume test asserting a resume offer, not a duplicate agent; a protocol-version-mismatch warning test; an identity-separation test proving two concurrent sessions are not keyed on process name.

CONSIDERATIONS: the interesting failure mode is silent divergence - Claude reports a tool completion where Codex reports a command run, and both are 'real', but the game world renders them differently and nobody notices because each adapter passed its own tests. Cross-harness normalization equivalence is therefore the highest-value assertion in this bead, more so than the concurrency itself. Second: running two real agents means real tokens, so budget this as a deliberately-run integration test rather than something attempted casually during development. Third: the SSE stream this proof reads is the same unauthenticated global broadcast tracked as a P0 bug (ba-9hr); this bead proves the ingest and concurrency, not the stream's public/private policy, and should not be read as accepting the current fan-out as final.

passes for the wrong reason, and a mutation proves it. The public stream carries
exactly session.started from both harnesses and drops every transient event, so
"two harness events appear" is satisfiable. Driving all of Codex and then all of
Claude takes the INTERLEAVING test red while the naive one stays green — which
is the separation the bead actually needs, and it is invisible without a
mutation. Two views, proved on both, with the file saying which is which: public
for the spectator, operator through the SAME hub object the route subscribes
rather than a parallel path, for interleaving and attribution. No operator
assertion is dressed up as a public-surface proof.

FOUR REAL DIVERGENCES THE BEAD DID NOT ANTICIPATE, all found by measuring rather
than by reading, and all left standing rather than papered over:

  - The equivalence criterion is FALSE today. For one `pnpm test`, Claude's hook
    plane emits tool.started, tool.completed and command.run; Codex's rollout
    emits only the first two. deriveOutcomeEvents is hook-plane-only because a
    rollout writes the call and its result as separate lines and pairing them
    needs held state — so it is a CAPABILITY GAP, not a normalization bug, and the
    consequence is concrete: a Codex agent's shell work is not reported to the
    game world as a command. What IS shared, and what is asserted, is the call:
    Bash and shell_command both normalize to Bash in zone terminal on the one
    union, with the negative asserted too — the edge names its zone differently,
    which is what makes the shared map load-bearing rather than decorative.

  - The public view publishes session.started WHOLE, so harness, agentId and
    installationId all travel. The design narrowed a REPLAY and did not narrow
    the live stream the same way, which is ba-9hr's surface rather than this
    bead's, and it is recorded as a finding.

  - Nothing in the tree subscribes 'operator' over HTTP — that view has no route
    at all — so "the operator view" is only reachable in-process, and the file
    says so instead of implying a public surface that does not exist.

  - A module-level buffer genuinely shared by both senders is a NO-OP here, and
    is reported as one: the scenario drives the watchers in sequence and the array
    empties after every post, so a shared buffer never coalesces. The
    one-session-per-batch rule is therefore asserted directly — a hand-built mixed
    batch must 400 — and the mutation that stops the server refusing one is what
    proves that assertion is real. Its own comment overclaimed and was corrected to
    the measured limit.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE, said plainly: it demonstrates ba-9hr rather than
settling it. The public-stream test connects with NO CREDENTIAL and the operator
test subscribes to the same global broadcast unauthenticated, so nothing here
proves anything about access control. The current fan-out is not presented as
accepted.

Also deliberately not done: spawning the real `agent-battle-claude` binary
(this proves the telemetry plane, not the shipped process — that bead is closed),
kill-and-reopen resume (it needs a real terminal kill and would make this the one
assertion in the file depending on a mounted feature), and a CLI driver
(packages/cli is frozen).

title: MCP adapter: 5 stable primitives over the capability registry
description:
Implement the MCP Streamable HTTP adapter, per plan sections 5.1, 22, 26, 32, 33, and 36.

CRITICAL SCOPE CORRECTION (sections 31, 32, 33): MCP is NOT P0. Protocol/API + CLI ship first; MCP is an adapter on the SAME protocol later. Section 33's P3 list puts 'MCP adapter' explicitly in phase 3, and section 36 makes interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket} EQUAL capability consumers rather than MCP-first.

THE SURFACE IS EXACTLY 5 PRIMITIVES (section 32): discover, search, inspect, act, observe. NOT the old domain-operation tool list.

BANNED IMPLEMENTATION (sections 5.1, 32, 33): the section 1.3-era tool list - register_agent, get_world, get_quests, get_opponents, challenge_agent, accept_battle, send_message, inspect_enemy, claim_reward, spawn_agent, quest/party/progress/report/move and so on - describes CAPABILITIES IN THE REGISTRY and must NEVER be implemented verbatim as MCP tools. That verbatim list IS the tool-explosion path section 32 bans. Adding Guild must change the registry, not the tool surface.

WHY THE PRIMITIVES EXIST (section 32): N features x M operations collapses to 100-200 MCP tools, which is undiscoverable and bloats agent context. 'Cover every capability, expose few stable primitives.' discover() is LAZY - top-level domains first, per-domain detail on demand, NEVER the full 200-capability firehose at connect time.

ANTI-GOD-TOOL GUARD: act() dispatches TYPED registry-defined actions (defineAction), never act({action: string, payload: any}). A bogus action id must be a compile error.

MCP IS THE CONTROL PLANE, NOT EVENT CAPTURE (section 5.1, section 5 'MCP khong nen dung de capture moi event'): NEVER make the agent call MCP after every Read/Edit/Bash. That bloats context, costs tokens, drags the workflow, and couples us to per-agent MCP quirks. Hooks/session-watcher carry telemetry; MCP carries commands.

AUTH (sections 3.4, 22, 4): short-lived installation token from the section 4 flow, obtained via MCP OAuth. NEVER put a raw token in the MCP URL (?token= leaks into logs and history) - the plan's own bad example.

ONBOARDING UX this enables (section 4, from mcp-coding-agents): 'claude mcp add agent-battle https://agentbattle.gg/mcp' then browser auth, then a terminal confirmation showing Agent, Account, and Project. This is the proof that 'login -> add MCP -> authorize -> play' needs no separate CLI install.

REVIEW GUARD (section 36): any PR adding interfaces/mcp/* implementation code FOR A SPECIFIC GAME FEATURE (instead of registry entries) fails review.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an agent connects over MCP, discovers domains lazily, performs a full bounty loop via the 5 primitives, and the tool count stays at 5 no matter how many features are installed.

TESTS: a tool-count test asserting exactly 5 primitives regardless of installed features; a lazy-discovery test; a protocol-loop integration test; an architecture test that no per-feature MCP tool modules exist.

CONSIDERATIONS: the pull toward a richer tool surface is strongest right after a real agent struggles with the 5 primitives - and that is precisely the moment the plan's argument applies. If discover is too coarse, the fix is finer-grained REGISTRY metadata, not a sixth tool. A useful forcing function: any proposed sixth primitive must demonstrate a capability that genuinely cannot be expressed as discover/search/inspect/act/observe. Related, keep MCP clearly on the control plane - it is tempting to use it for notifications or telemetry because it is already connected, and that is the exact conflation section 5.1 warns against.
close_reason: Shipped against the frozen contract; typecheck clean, architecture clean, unit tested. See the commit for the design calls and what was deliberately left out.

title: Verify Moltbook claims from source (section 29 correctness pass)

Resolve the unverified Moltbook claims flagged in plan section 29, by reading source or API docs directly.

The old criterion was close to right and is kept in substance; what it lacked is any check that could fail. The distinction matters: a design that still builds around a heartbeat interval nobody confirmed is exactly the phantom constraint this bead exists to prevent, and it survives the label perfectly - the note says UNVERIFIED while the design keeps the assumption. Settled by: for every UNVERIFIED claim, a check that the design docs no longer assert it, so an unverified claim cannot quietly keep doing work in the architecture. Where the PRINCIPLE survives but the citation does not (the Human -> Agent -> Session distinction, per section 29), the note records that split explicitly, so 'keep the principle, drop the certainty' is a recorded decision rather than an accident.

3. The learn-spine question is NOT re-done here. It is already answered - no license, copy nothing - and recorded in docs/research/learn-spine-license.md. 4. The note is dated and carries the staleness section. This is the shape docs/research/README.md already uses for the six existing notes and it is the model worth copying - a research note without a date and a staleness note is a claim with no shelf life.

5. The note lands in the EXISTING research index rather than beside it. Settled by: a Moltbook row in the docs/research/README.md per-repo table, carrying the commit SHA and a headline finding. A seventh standalone note the index does not list is the failure - it exists, satisfies every per-file check above, and is invisible to the next person who reads only the index, which is where the design work actually starts.

TESTS. Not a code test - documentation-accuracy tests, and they are as concrete as the code ones:
- a per-claim verdict check: every Moltbook claim in the note is individually tagged, and every CONFIRMED claim names a file in .tmp/moltbook rather than only the repo. A note asserting 'all claims verified' with no per-claim tags fails this - which is the point, because that note is the failure mode.
- the unverified-claims-dropped check: for each UNVERIFIED claim, the design docs no longer assert it. This is the check that makes the label load-bearing instead of decorative.
- the uncited-claims grep, which is the gate: a design doc asserting a Moltbook implementation detail with no source citation fails. The failure it catches is the one that matters - a design quietly leaning on an unverified Moltbook mechanic, which is how a phantom constraint gets built.
- an index check: docs/research/README.md carries a Moltbook row with a commit SHA and a headline finding, so the note is discoverable from the index.

OUT OF SCOPE, stated so it is not smuggled back in: the same caution applies to any claim sourced only to an unfetched page - the Pi and Paperclip references, the MCP-spec quotes in sections 12-13: keep the principle, drop the citation certainty.

title: Scaffold pnpm monorepo: apps/web + packages/*
description:
Create the pnpm-workspace monorepo skeleton for Agent Battle, exactly as specified in the plan section 19 (Implementation - monorepo layout).

WHY FIRST: The plan locks a specific target layout because several architectural guarantees are enforced by the folder boundaries themselves (section 19 dependency rule, section 33 extension kinds). If the scaffold deviates, the guarantees 'features never import each other' and 'adding a feature never edits core/cli/mcp' become unenforceable conventions instead of structural facts.

CREATE per section 19:
- package.json (pnpm workspaces), pnpm-workspace.yaml, turbo.json (optional)
- .env.example with BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, BETTER_AUTH_URL, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET, DATABASE_URL
- apps/web/ (Next.js 14 App Router: pages, api routes, components, lib)
- packages/core/ (primitives ONLY, no game words)
- packages/protocol/ (versioned AgentEvent union, tool-map, version.ts)
- packages/adapters/{claude,codex,opencode,cursor,pi,gemini,_template}/
- packages/features/{agent,progression,reputation,quest,bounty,battle,guild,social,inventory,animation}/
- packages/game-client/ (PixiJS v8 world)
- packages/mcp-server/ (thin, 5 stable primitives only)
- packages/cli/ (P0 per sections 31/36)
- drizzle/ (schema + migrations), scripts/

DEPENDENCY DIRECTION (enforced separately): presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure. Features NEVER import each other (only core + protocol). Adapters import core + protocol only.

CONSIDERATIONS: Docker lives in the infrastructure layer only (section 37) - features must never import Docker/Compose/Postgres-container concepts, only repository/capability interfaces (section 33). Folders may start near-empty; this bead establishes structural boundaries, not contents.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: pnpm install succeeds; pnpm -r build runs (each package may be a stub); folder graph matches section 19 exactly; no package imports outside its allowed direction.

TESTS: a scaffolding test that walks packages/* and asserts each has package.json with the correct @battle-agents/* name and no cross-boundary imports.
close_reason: Scaffold verified: 24 packages, pnpm build and pnpm -r typecheck green, architecture and removal-test gates pass

title: Web app dựng hai runtime với hai bus riêng, nên event từ API không tới SSE
description:
Fixed in bc6bd6b. apps/web/src/shared-runtime.ts now owns the pool, the runtime and the bus; sharedApi() and sharedEventGateway() both draw from it.

The condition event-gateway.ts set for this fold was met: its own header said folding the two runtimes together "belongs with the work that makes the act path a first-class publisher". MCP is that work and ba-4to is closed, so the deferral was executed rather than re-litigated.

CHOSE: runtime and bus became OPTIONAL dependencies of createEventGateway rather than being removed. The ingest integration test constructs a gateway with no runtime and gets an isolated one, so it keeps asserting against a runtime it fully controls and did not have to be rewritten. Only the app passes the shared ones.

DID NOT: fold the three closers into one function. closeSharedApi, closeSharedEventGateway and closeSharedRuntime each drop their own cache; the pool is closed once by closeSharedRuntime. Three entry points where one would do is untidy, but each is a correct shutdown of a different layer's state and collapsing them is a cleanup rather than a fix.

REGRESSION GUARD: identity, not equality. The assertion is that gateway.bus IS the shared bus by reference, so two structurally identical buses fail it. A deep comparison would have passed while every event went missing. Watched failing: restoring the gateway's own bus makes the stream assertion report "expected +0 to be 1" and the identity assertion report two different buses.

ALSO: the paragraph in event-gateway.ts that argued FOR two runtimes was a stale claim once the fold landed. Replaced, per AGENTS.md's "comments are claims". api.observe(), fixed in ba-4to, now actually delivers because sharedApi() is built over a bus something else can see.

title: Vercel + Neon cloud deploy and per-PR preview branches
description:
Stand up cloud deployment, per plan sections 7.1 and 37.

THE STACK (section 7.1): Next.js App Router on Vercel (git push -> deploy; no Docker, Nginx, PM2, Postgres VM, DB backup, DB scaling, or Kubernetes required FOR DEPLOYMENT) plus Neon Postgres. MCP endpoint lives in Next.js at https://agentbattle.gg/api/mcp; split into a standalone gateway ONLY if long-lived streaming demands it.

CLARIFY THE EARLIER PHRASING (section 7.1 supersedes): Docker is the LOCAL DEVELOPMENT/TEST environment (section 37), never a production dependency. Do not let the old 'no Docker' wording cause someone to strip the compose setup.

THE BEGINNER TRAP THIS BEAD EXISTS TO AVOID (section 7.1): never construct a new Client() and connect() per query. Always use a POOLED driver - the Neon serverless driver in cloud, pg-pool against the local container in Docker dev. The conversation explicitly identified this as the mistake a beginner makes.

NEON IS NEVER A LOCAL-RUN DEPENDENCY (section 37): default local is container Postgres (offline-capable); cloud/preview uses a Neon branch per-developer/per-PR via the neonctl link/checkout/env pull workflow.

WHY DEPLOY-EASE WON: the conversation explicitly prioritized deploy simplicity, and this stack wins from MVP to mid-scale. Phase 1 (MVP) is Vercel Next.js (Web+API+Auth+MCP+SSE) + Neon. Phase 2 happens ONLY AFTER A BENCHMARK PROVES event throughput is the bottleneck: Agents -> Gateway -> {Next.js/Vercel, Realtime service, Queue} -> Neon.

DO NOT ADD REDIS/UPSTAZ PREEMPTIVELY (section 7.4) - the plan's exact words: 'don't choose Redis just because realtime might need Redis'. Measure first.

CONNECTION MANAGEMENT vs WRITE VOLUME (section 7.2): Neon is perfectly capable of handling many requests; the danger is write VOLUME from agent telemetry (2000 writes/s at 100 agents x 20 ev/s). The batching and persist-filter are the mitigation, not a bigger database.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE 'PUSH TO MAIN DEPLOYS' CANNOT FAIL. A deploy is not observable from inside the repo - a green pipeline that deploys a broken build, or deploys nothing at all, satisfies the old first clause. All three clauses now name a command whose exit code settles them.

1. A merge to main produces a working deployment. Settled by: an automated smoke test against the deployed URL on every main build, which must FAIL the build when it fails. The test asserts a real response, not a reachable host - specifically that the app serves its root, that the Better Auth mount responds at /api/auth/*, and that the event ingest route answers on a batched request with the documented status for that batch. A deploy that 404s or serves a shell with no working API is the failure this catches, and it is not hypothetical: the auth and events routes are the real surface, and a Next.js shell with no API behind it renders fine. Exit 0 means deployed AND serving; there is no "deployed" state that passes without a working endpoint.

2. Each PR gets an isolated preview with its OWN Neon branch. Settled by two assertions, because either alone is satisfiable by a lie: (a) the preview environment is bound to a branch whose name derives from the PR number, asserted by reading the deployment's env, and (b) a migration run against that branch leaves the PRODUCTION branch's schema untouched. The second is the one that matters and the one easiest to claim without checking - a preview wired to the production database satisfies "each PR gets a preview" and corrupts shared data on merge. The check is: run the migration against the preview branch, then assert the production branch's migration ledger is unchanged. Two PRs running concurrently against one database is the failure this prevents, and it is exactly what per-PR branches exist to stop.

3. Local development never requires Neon. Settled by: a local test run with no Neon credentials present at all - DATABASE_URL unset, no neonctl config - which must still pass, because the local default is container Postgres (section 37). This is the assertion that catches a stray Neon import or a hardcoded connection string, and it is the only clause here checkable in CI without a cloud account, so it is the one to wire into .github/workflows/m0.yml first.

4. The pooled driver is used; no per-request Client construction. Settled by: a grep-level guard rejecting a new Client() constructed inside a request path, PLUS - because the grep is easy to satisfy wrongly - a test asserting the Neon serverless driver is a pooled singleton in cloud and pg-pool against the local container in Docker dev. The grep alone is defeated by a single hoisted Client that reconnects per query under load, which is the exact failure the bead was written to prevent: it looks correct in code review and exhausts connections in production at 2000 writes/s.

TESTS, each a command with an exit code:
- a smoke test against the deployed URL on every main build, asserting the root, the /api/auth mount and the events ingest route all respond - failing the build when they do not, not warning.
- a preview-isolation check: the preview's Neon branch name derives from the PR number, AND running migrations against it leaves the production branch's migration ledger byte-identical.
- the no-Neon local check: the full local test suite passes with DATABASE_URL unset and no neonctl config, wired into m0.yml.
- the pooled-driver guard: a lint rejecting per-request Client construction, plus a test asserting the pooled driver is a reused singleton rather than a per-query connection.

STILL BINDING, and worth restating because it is the discipline this bead exists to protect: Phase 2 (a realtime service, a queue) happens ONLY after a benchmark proves event throughput is the bottleneck. Adding Redis/Upstash because realtime seems to need it is the failure - section 7.4's exact words are 'don't choose Redis just because realtime might need Redis'. The right-hand side of criterion 4 is what makes that checkable: if event throughput is not the bottleneck, none of these tests should ever ask for a queue.

CONSIDERATIONS: the discipline this bead must protect is 'measure before scaling'. The plan is unusually explicit that Redis/Upstash must NOT be added just because realtime seems to need it (section 7.4), and that a queue is Phase 2 only after a benchmark shows event throughput is the bottleneck. It is cheaper to hold a simple architecture under a proven load than to debug a speculative one. Second: preview branches per PR are the mechanism that keeps shared staging data from corrupting parallel work - worth the setup cost even before anyone needs it, because retrofitting it mid-project is painful.

title: test:m2 / test:m4 milestone pipelines + wire the pre-M4 load test
description:
Add the `pnpm test:m2` and `pnpm test:m4` milestone pipelines, and wire the pre-M4 load test into a gate that can actually fail the build.

WHAT THE PLAN SAYS, QUOTED
Section 40, added 2026-09-24: "The bounty-claim and replay-render assertions are NOT M0: bounty is M2 and replay is M4, so asserting them in the M0 smoke made `pnpm test:m0` impossible to pass before M2 and M4 were complete. They move to `pnpm test:m2` and `pnpm test:m4` respectively (added 2026-09-24)."

Those two commands are named in the plan as the reason the M0 smoke is allowed to be small. Neither exists, and nothing in the tracker will build them.

WHY IT IS MISSING, verified 2026-09-25
- package.json scripts are: architecture, build, codegen, db:generate, db:migrate, db:seed, db:verify, format, license-check, load:events, lint, removal-test, schema-hygiene, test, test:e2e, test:integration, test:m0, test:unit, typecheck. There is no test:m2 and no test:m4.
- The pipeline that would be extended is real and good: scripts/test-m0.sh with a CANONICAL_STAGES array, scripts/stages.manifest, and scripts/check-stage-manifest.sh asserting THREE-WAY agreement between the manifest, the array, and the run_stage dispatch, so a stage cannot be dropped, added in one place only, or left with no implementation. Per-stage markers land under .tmp/m0-stages/ and the gate may only report green when a marker exists for every stage. The M0 machinery is the thing to copy, not reinvent.
- ba-local-testing-contract-gmi is CLOSED and its close reason is about test:m0 only: "M0 pipeline GREEN: 12/12 stages ... A red stage blocks merge." It did not build, and was not asked to build, the M2/M4 pipelines.
- No bead mentions test:m2 or test:m4. Searching all 61 beads for those strings returns nothing.
- The gap is not cosmetic. The M2 and M4 DoDs in section 27 are among the plan's most important claims - "Three most important milestones to prove the idea: M1, M2, M4" (section 15.3) - and the bounty bead's own success criterion is an end-to-end vertical slice on a scratch repo. A DoD with no command that settles it is a claim, not a gate.

WHAT test:m2 MUST SETTLE
Section 27's M2 DoD: "end-to-end on a scratch repo with real money rail stubbed (record intent, no real payout until 17.5 resolved - mark clearly in UI 'payout: manual/sandbox')." The pipeline asserts the LOOP, end to end, on a real scratch repository: a bounty is created on a real GitHub issue, claimed by an agent through the protocol, a PR is opened, the merge webhook fires, the bounty completes, XP and reputation are awarded, and the history shows the trail. The payout leg asserts INTENT RECORDED and the sandbox marking rendered - never a real transfer. ba-payout-rail-dispute-1q6 closed with the type-level no-real-transfer guarantee mutation-verified, and ba-feature-bounty-xhk owns the loop; this pipeline is the command under which both are proven, not a second implementation of either.

WHAT test:m4 MUST SETTLE
Section 27's M4 DoD: "share replay link with a logged-out user and they see the full timeline." So: 1v1 battle on the same issue, isolated workspaces, public weights readable while the battle runs, judge run, replay URL shareable, XP/rep applied - and the logged-out read, which is the specific clause and the one that actually distinguishes M4 from "a battle page exists."

THE LOAD TEST, WHICH IS A GATE THAT DOES NOT CURRENTLY GATE ANYTHING
Section 17.2 and section 40 both require it: 100 agents x 20 events/s, run as a PRE-M4 gate, not an M0 one. Section 7.2 is explicit that the number reaching the database must be a small fraction of the number crossing the wire - that gap is the whole thesis of the batching design.
The good news: the harness EXISTS. scripts/load-test-events.ts is implemented, `pnpm load:events` runs it, it drives the real ingest handler in-process, and it deliberately reports generated / accepted / rows-written as three separate numbers. The bad news, and the reason this is in scope: it is referenced by no gate. It is not in scripts/stages.manifest, not in CANONICAL_STAGES, and not in any CI job. ba-risk-gates-e74 states the requirement - "a load test simulating 100x20 ev/s, run as a pre-M4 gate rather than an M0 one (section 40), so it must be runnable before feature-battle closes" - and then says in its own considerations: "a gate nobody runs is a comment." By that bead's own standard the load test is currently a comment with a script attached. Two beads name the load test as a test (ba-risk-gates-e74 and ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9) and neither runs it.

WHAT TO BUILD
- scripts/test-m2.sh and scripts/test:m4, following test-m0.sh's shape: a manifest, a stage array, a run_stage dispatch, per-stage markers, and a red stage that names itself in the summary and the exit code. Extend the EXISTING three-way check rather than adding a second convention - if a stage is added to a milestone pipeline it must appear in all three views or the pipeline is not trustworthy, and the check-stage-manifest.sh self-test already proves that check catches a dropped stage.
- Wire `load:events` into test:m4 as a stage, with a PASS THRESHOLD, not just an exit code. A load test that prints numbers and always exits 0 gates nothing. The threshold is a decision to be recorded here and asserted; if the measurement shows the number is wrong, the number changes - but it must exist, because "the batching held" is prose. The natural assertion is on rows-written versus events-generated, since that ratio is what section 7.2 actually claims, plus an explicit assertion that the harness exceeded its target rate (a load test that quietly ran at 5 events/s passes any threshold).
- Keep the M2 and M4 pipelines honest about what they may assert: bounty is M2, replay is M4. A pipeline asserting a later milestone's surface makes itself unpassable, which is exactly the mistake section 40's amendment was written to undo.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, each with the thing that settles it
1. `pnpm test:m2` exists, runs the M2 vertical slice against a real scratch repository, and exits non-zero when a stage of that slice is broken. Settled by deliberately breaking one stage of the loop and asserting the command goes red - a pipeline that has never been seen red is not known to gate.
2. `pnpm test:m4` exists, runs the M4 DoD including the LOGGED-OUT replay read, and exits non-zero when it is broken. The logged-out read is the clause; assert the timeline renders with no Better Auth session, and that the same request with a session also works (the public path must not be a logged-in-only path with the session stripped).
3. The load test runs inside test:m4 and FAILS on a threshold breach. Settled by a test that runs the harness with a deliberately raised write-ratio and asserts the stage goes red. Without the deliberate-breach half this is a script in a pipeline that always passes.
4. Stage parity with test:m0. Settled by the three-way manifest check passing for the new pipelines, so a stage cannot be added in the dispatch only and left out of the manifest.
5. CI runs both, on the same terms as test:m0. Settled by the CI configuration naming them; a local-only pipeline is the "gate nobody runs" failure this bead exists to end.

CONSIDERATIONS
The tempting wrong turn is to fold the M2 and M4 assertions back into the M0 smoke, which is precisely the change section 40's amendment reversed: it made `pnpm test:m0` impossible to pass before M2 and M4 were done, and a permanently-red M0 gate trains people to ignore red. Separate commands, each asserting only its own milestone. Second, the scratch repository must be a real one with real GitHub URLs - ba-feature-bounty-xhk already requires a test asserting real GitHub URLs rather than synthetic ones, and a pipeline that mints fake issues would let a broken GitHub integration pass. Third, the load-test threshold should be recorded as a number with a rationale, not copied from the plan's 100x20: that figure is the SCENARIO, and the PASS CRITERION is how many of those events may reach the database, which is a different number the plan does not state.
close_reason:
DONE. Both milestone pipelines exist, the load test is wired, and the choice of
what to assert was the whole judgement.

WHAT test:m2 AND test:m4 ASSERT is §27's own words, not a copy of m0's stages. A
milestone pipeline that runs the same eighteen checks as m0 asserts nothing about
a milestone — it asserts the repository still builds, which was already true and
would stay true with the milestone unbuilt. So: a bounty reaching payout with the
sandbox banner carried, and a replay readable with NO CREDENTIAL and no session id
anywhere in the page. Both are now real, so a pipeline that stops describing its
milestone is a pipeline that can go green while the milestone is not.

check-stage-manifest.sh now covers all THREE pipelines rather than one, and that
is a correction rather than tidying. A copy per pipeline is a second convention
with its own bugs and no relationship to the first: fixing the sed range in the
m0 copy would leave the milestone copies accepting a dispatch that names a runner
nobody registered, and a stage quietly dropped from one pipeline would be
invisible. §40 moved the bounty and replay assertions OUT of the m0 smoke; it did
not say the m0 smoke's definition of a trustworthy stage set stops applying.

THE PRE-M4 LOAD TEST (RISK 2, §17.2) at last has its CI job, in its own workflow
because §40 says so and because a load test is not a correctness gate. The job
asserts on the GAP between generated, accepted and rows-written rather than on a
throughput number — that gap is the entire thesis of the persistence filter, so a
gate on raw events-per-second would pass while the thing the harness exists to
measure got worse. Thresholds are a named constant in scripts/load-thresholds.ts,
so a number that turns out wrong changes in one visible place.

§7.4's standing prohibition held: no Redis, no Upstash, no queue, because realtime
"might need" one. Nothing here measures a bottleneck, because there is none to
measure, and adding a queue in order to watch it not exist is the failure the rule
exists to prevent.

title: Payout rail + dispute path for real-money bounties (design before promising)
description:
DESIGN (and stub) the payout rail and dispute path for real-money bounties. This is the unresolved blocker flagged in plan section 17.5, and it must be settled BEFORE the product ever promises real amounts.

THE OPEN RISK (section 17.5): 'Payment/compliance for real-money bounties: M2 needs payout rail + dispute path design (not yet specified in conversation - must design before promising amounts).' The conversation never settled this. It is a genuine gap, and the plan correctly says so.

M2 SCOPE (section 27): the DoD ships with real money STUBBED - 'record intent, no real payout until section 17.5 resolved - mark clearly in UI payout: manual/sandbox.' The UI banner is a hard requirement, not a nicety: users must never believe they have been paid when they have not.

WHAT THIS BEAD MUST PRODUCE:
1. A payout rail decision: which provider(s), escrow vs direct transfer, KYC/AML posture, tax/reporting obligations, minimum bounty size, refund policy.
2. A dispute path: who adjudicates, what evidence is required (the activity log is the audit trail - section 30), time limits, refund to multiple co-sponsors when a bounty is cancelled or a maintainer rejects a valid PR.
3. A compliance checklist: what legal exposure does accepting money for OSS work create, and at what scale does it require counsel.
4. A stub interface so the bounty feature records payout INTENT (bounty_funded -> payout_pending -> payout_recorded) without moving money.

WHY THE ACTIVITY LOG MATTERS HERE: section 30 lists audit and anti-abuse as reasons the ordered, attributed event trail exists. A dispute is resolved by replaying what actually happened, so the log must be sufficient evidence. If the log cannot settle a dispute, the design is incomplete.

CONSIDERATIONS: the refund-on-cancel case is the hardest, because open funding (bounty-open-funding) means multiple sponsors with different expectations. Decide proportional refund semantics.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a written design exists and is referenced from the bounty feature; the stub interface records intent with no money movement; the sandbox banner is present and tested; nothing in the product claims a real payout.

TESTS: test that a completed bounty records payout intent in the correct state; test that the sandbox banner renders whenever a bounty is in a paid-adjacent state; a test that the payout stub cannot be invoked in a mode that implies real transfer.
close_reason:
The design half is done and good: 265 lines settling all four section 17.5 questions with reasoning rather than deferral, including a rejection table for four payout providers derived from a hard external constraint (Vercel Hobby counts payment processing as commercial, so escrow is unavailable on the current plan). The type-level no-real-transfer guarantee is real and mutation-verified: removing the intent.mode refusal from payout.ts turns the smuggle test red, and PayoutMode is a single-member union with a separate structural test.

The three obligations that were not met are moved to ba-feature-bounty-xhk, which this bead blocked. They could not be done here: a PayoutIntentStore implementation needs a database repository, a rendered banner needs a UI to render in, the dispute windows need a rules.ts, and a completed-bounty test needs a bounty lifecycle. Keeping them here was a deadlock, and the risk they guard against is impossible today because no bounty surface exists at all.

Three present-tense sentences in docs/design/payout-rail.md claimed the events are persisted, the windows live in rules.ts, and the README reports manual/sandbox. None was true. Corrected to say what is declared and what is not built.

title: External extension packages + public protocol/SDK (M7)
description:
Open the ecosystem per plan sections 16 and 33 (M7).

WHAT M7 IS (section 15.1): open ecosystem via MIT protocol/SDK covering adapters, agents, clients, and arenas - the contributor flywheel.

LICENSE POSTURE (sections 16, 35): MIT everywhere, whole repo, public from day one. Rationale: a fun-game OSS flywheel maximizes stars, forks, and contributions; MIT is simpler than Apache-2.0 and avoids copyleft fear; it is commercial-use safe. THE MOAT IS COMMUNITY + AGENTS + BOUNTIES + HISTORY + REPUTATION + GUILDS, NOT SOURCE. Precedents cited: Kubernetes, Kafka, Spark, TensorFlow, Android - forks cannot fork ecosystems; LiveKit - open core to hosted cloud value. Custom 'MIT + no-compete' licenses were REJECTED (they are not OSS). Trademark, brand, and domain are protected separately, since MIT/Apache grant no trademark rights beyond attribution.

FORKS ARE WELCOMED (section 16): forks like 'Agent Arena' or 'Coding Wars' are welcome IF protocol-compatible - and that compatibility is precisely what would make us the standard.

THE FLYWHEEL NEEDS MORE THAN A LICENSE (section 16): docs, easy dev, clear architecture, good-first-issues, fun visible results (adapter, reporter, or battle-mode PRs), a useful protocol, and active maintainers. A permissive license alone does not produce contributors. This bead is where that non-license work happens.

BANNED (section 29.2): a plugin MARKETPLACE, a plugin INSTALLER, dynamic/remote plugin loading, distributed event infrastructure, and microservices. The extension model is EXPLICIT COMPOSITION via createRuntime({extensions: [...]}), not a dynamic loader. Do not build an installer here.

PACKAGE SHAPE (section 33): features/extensions declare capabilities and know NOTHING about MCP/CLI/REST/Web. External packages install the same way internal ones do - as GameFeature objects. A third-party world or battle mode is just another extension.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, and the second clause is the one that decides whether this bead worked:

1. An external package can be published and consumed as a GameFeature without patching core. Settled by: the out-of-tree extension test, which installs and uninstalls through the public API only. 'Without patching core' is the load-bearing half and it needs a real assertion, not a convention - the test runs against a core with a diff guard, so an extension that reaches into core internals fails rather than merely being discouraged. The removal half matters as much as the install half and is easy to omit: a feature that installs but whose handlers, commands, actionDefs, capabilities and persistedEvents are not all given back is a leak that survives into every later test.

2. The protocol/SDK is documented well enough to write a client from scratch. [REWRITTEN] 'Well enough' has no wrong version - a doc set that omits the handshake, or gets the auth model wrong, still reads as documentation and still passes a completeness check. It is now the property that makes it a real test: a client written from the PUBLISHED DOCUMENTATION ALONE, with no access to the repo source, compiles and completes a real exchange against a running server - register, authenticate, call each of the documented capabilities, and parse the responses. The assertions that make it fail when the docs are wrong: the client builds using only what the docs state, its requests authenticate under the documented credential model (the agent Bearer token, never the human web session), and every response it parses matches the documented shape. A doc gap produces a client that cannot compile or cannot authenticate, and THAT is the failure being looked for.

   The published-package half is the same property from the other side, and it is the half THIS BEAD owns: the extension is consumed the way a third party would consume it - from a package, through public exports only - so 'published' means consumable rather than merely uploadable.

   THE DOCS-SUFFICIENCY CLAIM IS NOT THIS BEAD'S, and the duplication is worth naming because two beads claiming one property is how it ships half-proved. The claim "a third party with no repo access can build a working client from the published documentation" is a single property, and ba-skill-md-protocol-72x owns it: that bead publishes the four docs and discharges it with a fresh-agent conformance test. This bead already depends on ba-skill-md-protocol-72x, so the ordering is right - the point is only that the reader should not also build a docs-only client here. What is genuinely distinct and genuinely this bead's is the out-of-tree extension test: an external PACKAGE installed and uninstalled through public exports, with the core-diff guard. A package is a shipped artifact; a doc set is prose. They fail differently - a package fails on a missing export or a leaking registration, docs fail on an omitted step - which is exactly why they are two beads rather than one criterion twice.

TESTS, and each fails when the behaviour is wrong rather than when a file is missing:
- the out-of-tree extension test: installs and uninstalls through the public API only, with a core-diff guard so 'without patching core' is asserted rather than assumed, and an uninstall assertion covering every registration kind (handlers, commands, actionDefs, capabilities, declaredCapabilities, eventHandlers, persistedEvents) - runtime.test.ts already asserts the give-back property for internal features, and this is that same assertion for an external one.
- the removal test for the external extension: uninstalling it leaves the runtime with no trace, and the surrounding features keep working.
- the docs-only client test, the criterion-2 test: a client built from the published docs with no repo access, compiling and completing register -> authenticate -> each documented capability -> parse. A completeness check on the docs cannot substitute for this, and passing this while the docs are wrong is impossible by construction - the client has nothing else to go on.
- a versioning/compatibility check, because the moat argument cuts both ways: breaking protocol compatibility is expensive, so the published PROTOCOL_VERSION and the handshake's expected version are asserted to agree, and a client presenting the wrong version is refused rather than silently admitted. This is the mechanical half of 'forks are welcome IF protocol-compatible' - without it, 'protocol-compatible' is a wish.

WHAT THIS BEAD STILL CANNOT PROVE: a docs-only client that works proves the documentation is SUFFICIENT, not that it is good. Do not read a green run as evidence the protocol is ergonomic to build against.

CONSIDERATIONS: the plan's moat argument is worth restating as an engineering constraint rather than a slogan - the defensibility is community, agents, bounties, history, reputation, and guilds, NOT source code. That has a practical consequence: breaking protocol compatibility is expensive, so versioning and compatibility guarantees deserve more care here than typical feature work. Second, resist building the ecosystem tooling early. Section 29.2 bans a plugin marketplace, a plugin installer, and dynamic loading; explicit composition is the model. Publishing packages and documenting the protocol is enough until real third parties force otherwise.

title: Run reference implementations locally to internalize PixiJS + AgentWatcher
description:
Plan section 18 build order item 1 - the FIRST thing to do, and it is currently unowned.

PLAN SECTION 18, VERBATIM: 'Re-clone learn-spine cleanly; run age-of-agents demo + agent-move locally to internalize PixiJS + AgentWatcher behavior.'

WHY THIS IS A BEAD AND NOT A NICE-TO-HAVE: the plan explicitly instructs reading source, not just cloning it (section 9.5). Running the two best references locally is how the porting beads (tool-map-port, hookprovider-seam, game-client-pixijs, adapters-template) get grounded in observed BEHAVIOR rather than code reading alone. Porting a PixiJS client or a watcher interface from source you have only skimmed is how subtle behavioral details get lost.

TASKS:
1. Re-verify the learn-spine checkout (the stale 'empty/broken HEAD' caveat in sections 79/28.2/17.6 is now outdated - the repo is cloned and valid) and determine its LICENSE, which is currently unconfirmed. Until the license is known, copy NOTHING from it.
2. Run the age-of-agents demo locally and study packages/client/src/game/ as the PixiJS v8 reference (section 1.2 item 1): pixi-viewport + React19 + zustand, the view/unit/tilemap/projection/pathfind/autotile decomposition, and the dual fantasy/scifi pack structure.
3. Run agent-move locally and study watcher/ per-CLI parsers, the AgentStateManager 30s idle rule, the Broadcaster, full_state-then-delta, and the OpenCode WAL-polling CAUTION (sections 1.2 item 4, 28.2).
4. Read .tmp/agent-quest's mapping config (the TOOL -> activity table, section 28.2) since tool-map-port depends on the same idea.

ALSO WORTH A PASS (they are already cloned): agent-world-codemoo for the stateDiffBroadcast + permission-queue + costTracker patterns (section 28.1 item 12), and arcane-agents for the 1061-line status-fusion decider (section 28.1 item 5).

DELIVERABLE: a short study note per repo recording the concrete behaviors worth porting and the ones to avoid, so the porting beads do not each re-derive the same reading. The plan's Appendix A already maps repo to lesson; this note fills in the BEHAVIORAL detail that a static map cannot.

NOTE: all 14 reference repos are already cloned into .tmp/ (gitignored, ~4.3GB). No re-cloning is needed.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: each porting bead can cite an observed behavior rather than only a source snippet; learn-spine's license is determined.

TESTS: not code - the study note is the artifact. Add a dated note so future readers can judge staleness.

CONSIDERATIONS: the value of this bead decays. Read the sources while the specific porting question is live, not speculatively - a study note written a month early will be confidently wrong about behavior it never observed. Keep the notes dated and tied to a porting bead, so a reader can tell which claims were verified and against which commit. And resist cloning repos 'just in case': the plan already names what was not cloned and why (Appendix A backlog), and a .tmp full of unread checkouts is a false sense of coverage.
close_reason:
Six dated, SHA-pinned notes. age-of-agents and agent-move were genuinely run with recorded evidence (229 tests passing, HTTP 200, four watchers live). learn-spine's licence determined NONE by five independent checks, which resolves the plan's open 'copy NOTHING' item. The three NOT RUN notes say so in three places each, which is honest rather than a shortfall: the bead named two repos to run and both were run.

The notes corrected two plan errors rather than agreeing with them: the idle rule is 45s, not the 30s the plan states, and agent-world-codemoo is AMBIGUOUS rather than MIT (package.json says MIT, the LICENSE file does not exist). Caveat carried forward: ba-status-fusion-presence-5zk and ba-animation-core-spike-hf7 have no observed material behind them.

title: Removal test: every feature removable without breaking the build
description:
Turn the REMOVAL TEST into an executable CI gate, per plan section 12.2 and section 20.

WHAT IT IS: Section 12.2 states 'Removal test is architectural principle #1: rm -rf features/guild must still compile/run.' This bead makes that principle an automated check so the pluggability property cannot silently regress as features are added.

MECHANISM (section 20): scripts/removal-test.sh - for each packages/features/*, temporarily move it away, then run 'tsc --noEmit && vitest run'. The tree must stay GREEN except for capability-degraded warnings. This is also the mechanism by which the Battle feature proves its requires: ['reputation.read'] degradation (section 24).

WHY IT MATTERS: The entire extension architecture (sections 12, 33) is justified by 'add feature without touching others'. If removal breaks the build, the architecture has quietly become a God Engine and section 29.2's 'thin core, rich edges' claim is false. Catching that in CI rather than at M6 is the entire value of this bead.

CONSIDERATIONS: the script MUST restore the moved directory even on failure (trap/finally), or a crashed run leaves the tree broken. It must be reasonably fast so it runs in CI and not just locally. Capability-degraded warnings (a feature whose requires[] become unsatisfied after removal) are EXPECTED and must not fail the run; only type errors and test failures do.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: 'pnpm removal-test' passes with all features present; passes with any single feature removed; fails when a feature illegally imports a sibling feature (cross-check with the dependency-rules bead).

TESTS: the script is itself the test. Add a fixture feature that illegally imports a sibling and assert the removal-test run fails.
close_reason: Script checks all 10 removable features + extensions[] stripping; self-test proves the strip is sound and was mutation-verified against the exact bug it guards. Gate runs in CI via test:m0.

title: Risk gates: gimmick, event volume, adapter sprawl, fairness, scope
description:
Encode the plan's documented risks (section 17) as verifiable gates rather than prose warnings.

RISK 1 - GIMMICK TRAP (section 17.1, also section 2.3): 'Claude/Codex/OpenCode -> pixel characters -> XP -> battle with no real utility' produces a 'haha cool' reaction then churn. DEFENSE: ship M2 real utility (bounties paying real money) BEFORE heavy game art. GATE: the game client and art beads must not be scheduled to complete before the bounty vertical slice.

  STATUS, and it is the one risk that has actually bitten: the art and game-client work is moving ahead of the slice. packages/game-client/src/index.ts is `export {};` and apps/web has no public/assets directory, so nothing visual has been BUILT - but ba-game-client-pixijs-riw and ba-asset-shortlist-x2a are both active open beads with detailed instructions, and the Next.js shell in apps/web now means a contributor can see a running app. The gate as written ('must not be scheduled to complete before') is therefore already being strained. The stronger form of the gate, and the one worth enforcing, is that the bounty vertical slice (ba-feature-bounty-xhk) CLOSES before either art bead starts producing files - not merely before they complete, because completing-in-order is trivially satisfiable by writing art first and declaring it unfinished.

  THE GATE IS NOW AN EDGE, not a sentence. Both art beads now carry an explicit dependency on ba-feature-bounty-xhk: br dep add ba-game-client-pixijs-riw ba-feature-bounty-xhk and br dep add ba-asset-shortlist-x2a ba-feature-bounty-xhk. That is deliberate and it is not redundant with this text - if you are reading this and the two edges are missing, the gate has been quietly deleted, and that is the failure this risk exists to prevent. Do not remove them as over-constraining: the plan defense is to ship M2 real utility BEFORE heavy game art, and an ordering edge is the only form of gate an agent swarm actually obeys.

  ONE HONEST TENSION, recorded rather than smoothed over. Gating the asset shortlist behind M2 also delays RISK 7, whose per-pack license tracking is downstream of exactly that shortlist. The plan explicit ordering was chosen over that convenience, because risk 1 is the one risk that has already bitten and risk 7 gate is only needed before art ships, not before the shortlist is researched. If a future reader disagrees, the asset-shortlist edge is the one to reverse; the game-client edge is not.

RISK 2 - EVENT VOLUME (section 17.2): 100 agents x 20 events/s = 2000 DB writes/s. DEFENSE: enforce the section 7.2 batching from day one. GATE: a load test simulating 100x20 ev/s, run as a pre-M4 gate rather than an M0 one (section 40), so it must be runnable before feature-battle closes.

  STATUS: THE HARNESS ALREADY EXISTS AND RUNS. scripts/load-test-events.ts is written and wired as `pnpm load:events`; its defaults are exactly LOAD_AGENTS=100, LOAD_EVENTS_PER_SECOND=20, LOAD_SECONDS=5, LOAD_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS=4. It drives the real ingest handler in-process against the real EventStreamHub, and it reports generated / accepted / rows-written as three separate numbers - the gap between the last two is the whole thesis of the persistence filter. So this risk's deliverable is DONE; what remains is running it and wiring it somewhere visible, because a harness nobody invokes is the exact failure this bead exists to prevent. It is deliberately NOT in .github/workflows/m0.yml, and per section 40 it should not be: add it as its own pre-M4 job when M4 work starts.

RISK 3 - ADAPTER SPRAWL (section 17.3): third-party adapter PRs must not break core. DEFENSE: keep the AgentEvent union versioned with a skill.json-style pin, and check the version on every handshake. GATE: a CI check that a protocol version bump forces regeneration of schemas and updates skill.json.

  STATUS: THE DEFENSE IS BUILT, THE CI CHECK IS NOT. PROTOCOL_VERSION lives in packages/protocol/src/version.ts; the ingest route rejects a mismatched version with a 400 naming both the expected and the received value; `pnpm codegen` regenerates packages/protocol/src/generated/action-ids.ts from each feature's manifest, and tests/types/action-ids.ts pins the union at compile time with @ts-expect-error in both directions. What does NOT exist is a CI job that fails when the generated file is stale relative to the manifests, or that a version bump moved skill.json. The codegen is a script a human runs; nothing verifies it was run. That gap is the live part of this risk and it is small: a job that runs codegen and fails on a dirty diff closes it. (skill.json itself is ba-skill-md-protocol-72x's deliverable and does not exist yet, so that half of the gate is blocked on that bead rather than on this one.)

RISK 4 - BATTLE FAIRNESS (section 17.4): judge weights must be public per match; isolated workspaces mandatory; ANTI-CHEAT IS TBD. GATE: assert that weights are stored and surfaced per battle, and that the anti-cheat gap is documented rather than silently assumed solved.

RISK 5 - PAYMENT/COMPLIANCE (section 17.5): unresolved; see the payout-rail-dispute bead. GATE: no UI may imply a real payout before that design lands; the sandbox banner is enforced by test.

RISK 6 - LEARN-SPINE CHECKOUT (section 17.6): RESOLVED, and the answer is a prohibition rather than a permission. docs/research/learn-spine-license.md records the determination dated 2026-09-24: learn-spine has NO LICENSE - no license file, no license field in package.json, and GitHub's own API reports none - confirmed five independent ways. The checkout is present and readable at .tmp/learn-spine; reading it is how we know this. Standing instruction: copy nothing, not one line. An unlicensed repo may be READ for architectural ideas and that is what ba-animation-core-spike-hf7 should do, but no file may be copied and no code derived from it may be vendored. This risk is CLOSED, not pending; the verify step this bead used to carry is done.

RISK 7 - ASSET LICENSING (section 17.7): track per-pack licenses; decide the game-asset license separately from the code MIT license.

RISK 8 - SCOPE DISCIPLINE (section 17.8): NO MMO, and no equipment/pets/trading/guild-war/housing/crafting/marketplace/tournament/boss/season/achievements in the MVP beyond the section 10.2 MVP character sheet and the M1/M2/M4 slice. GATE: a scope check in review - the tempting failure mode is gold-plating while M2 is still incomplete.

WHY ENCODE AS GATES: section 17 calls these 'documented', but documentation alone does not prevent the failure. Each should have an executable or reviewable check.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE THE OLD CRITERION CONTRADICTED THE BEAD'S OWN REASONING. The old wording was 'a named, runnable OR REVIEW-ENFORCED gate', and this bead's own closing line says 'a gate nobody runs is a comment'. A review-enforced gate is the one form nobody runs - it is satisfied by writing a checklist, which is the exact failure the bead exists to prevent. So the three-way disjunction is removed and replaced with a single rule.

THE RULE: a gate is DONE only when a COMMAND exists whose exit code settles it, and that command runs somewhere that is not a human's memory. Concretely, per risk, a gate is done when at least one of these holds, and the risk's entry must name which:
  (a) it is a script or test in the tree, named by its command, and
  (b) it is WIRED - invoked by a CI job, or by a br dependency edge, or by a pre-commit/CI check that fails the build.
  (a) without (b) is a harness nobody runs and does NOT count. This is exactly risk 2's current state: pnpm load:events exists and is real, and is deliberately not yet an M0 job, so risk 2 is NOT done even though its harness is written. Writing the harness was the work; wiring it is the gate.
  A 'review-enforced' gate is acceptable ONLY as a fallback for a risk that genuinely cannot be mechanized yet, and it must name the file and line where the checklist item lives and who reviews it - and it is recorded as PARTIAL, never as done. A review gate with no named location is a comment, by this bead's own reasoning.

THE HONEST TALLY as of 2026-09-25, with each entry naming the command that would settle it, because a state description that names no command is the thing being fixed here:
- risk 1 GIMMICK: enforced by dependency edge, and that IS a command - br dep list showing ba-game-client-pixijs-riw and ba-asset-shortlist-x2a both blocked on ba-feature-bounty-xhk. DONE as a gate. But the M2 slice it protects is still outstanding, so risk 1's DEFENSE is unbuilt; the gate and the defense are different states and the tally must not merge them.
- risk 2 EVENT VOLUME: harness built and runs (pnpm load:events), NOT wired. PARTIAL - fails the (b) test until it is a pre-M4 job.
- risk 3 ADAPTER SPRAWL: defense built (PROTOCOL_VERSION, the ingest 400, the generated action-ids union pinned by @ts-expect-error both ways), CI check MISSING. PARTIAL. The settling command is a CI job that runs pnpm codegen and fails on a dirty diff; skill.json's half is blocked on ba-skill-md-protocol-72x, not on this bead.
- risk 4 BATTLE FAIRNESS: no gate, depends on the battle bead. NOT DONE.
- risk 5 PAYMENT/COMPLIANCE: the RULE is tested and the BANNER IS NOT RENDERED. needsSandboxBanner is unit-tested in packages/features/bounty/src/payout.ts with ZERO production callers, so a green test suite says nothing about the UI. NOT DONE, and this is the sharpest illustration of the whole bead: a passing unit test on an uncalled function is the definition of a gate that settles nothing.
- risk 6 LEARN-SPINE: CLOSED, and the answer is a prohibition. The settling check is the negative one - docs/research/learn-spine-license.md plus a check that no file under packages/ or apps/ contains code derived from .tmp/learn-spine. Copy nothing, not one line.
- risk 7 ASSET LICENSING: no gate, depends on the asset shortlist. NOT DONE. [its CI check is specified in ba-asset-shortlist-x2a and must be a LICENSE.txt-per-directory check; see the scope-lint form below for why a directory-existence check is the wrong shape]
- risk 8 SCOPE DISCIPLINE: no gate. NOT DONE - needs the scope lint below.
And the M1/M2/M4 slice ships before any MMO-shaped feature.

FOR RISK 4, THE ANTI-CHEAT CLAUSE WAS ALSO A COMMENT. 'The anti-cheat gap is documented rather than silently assumed solved' is satisfied by typing the words 'anti-cheat is a gap' into a file, which is the opposite of what it means - the risk is precisely that a reader ASSUMES it is solved. It is now a check that fails in both directions: a docs check asserting the anti-cheat gap is still described as open in the battle docs, AND failing if any doc claims anti-cheat is solved. A doc asserting a solution is a finding, not a completion. The gap stays an open named bead, cited by id from the battle docs, so 'TBD' has an owner.

TESTS, each of which is a command with an exit code, per the rule above:
- risk 2: pnpm load:events exists AND is referenced by a CI job definition. The reference is the assertion - grepping for the script alone is what let a wired-up-looking gate pass unwired.
- risk 3: a CI job that runs pnpm codegen and fails on a dirty git diff. Exit 0 means the generated schemas are in sync; exit 1 means someone bumped a manifest and did not regenerate.
- risk 5: a test that asserts needsSandboxBanner is CALLED from a rendered component, not merely that it returns the right boolean for a given input. Production callers > 0 is the assertion. This is the check that would have caught the current state.
- risk 6: a negative check that no source file contains code derived from .tmp/learn-spine, plus the dated determination in docs/research/learn-spine-license.md.
- risk 8: the scope lint below.
- a per-risk completeness check: every one of the eight risks names a settling command in this bead, and a risk whose command is a review checklist is recorded PARTIAL rather than done. This is the check that stops the tally from drifting back into prose - it fails when someone adds a ninth risk without a way to tell it is safe.

WHAT THIS BEAD STILL CANNOT PROVE: a green gate says the encoded risk is covered, not that the risks were the right eight. The list comes from section 17 and a risk nobody thought of is invisible to every check here.

THE SCOPE LINT HAS A CONCRETE FORM HERE, because the placeholder directories already exist: packages/features/ contains battle, guild, social, animation and inventory, each holding only `export {};`. A lint that fails when a non-empty implementation appears in an out-of-phase feature is the check; a lint that fails on the directory's existence would fail today for reasons that are intentional. The M6 features (social, guild) and the M4 battle feature are all past their milestone as empty placeholders, which is fine and is what the placeholder is for.

CONSIDERATIONS: a gate nobody runs is a comment. Each of these should be runnable (a load test, a version CI check, a banner assertion) or attached to an explicit review checklist item, not left as prose in a document nobody re-reads. The one that will get the most pushback is scope discipline (risk 8) - the MMO-shaped features are individually appealing, and the M1/M2/M4 slice is the whole reason the project avoids the gimmick trap. Treat a scope expansion during MVP as a change to the plan, not a small feature addition.
