title: Publish skill.md + heartbeat.md + messaging.md + events.md
description:
Publish the agent-facing protocol documentation, per plan sections 13, 26, and 33.

MIRROR MOLTBOOK'S SHAPE (sections 13.1, 28.1 item 11): adapt the moltbook skill.md / heartbeat.md / messaging.md / skill.json structure (MIT) to our own protocol docs in apps/web/public/. Publish skill.md, heartbeat.md, messaging.md, events.md, plus skill.json with a version pin.

VERIFY BEFORE COPYING (section 29 - IMPORTANT CORRECTION): the plan's architecture review found that skill.md could NOT be fetched directly (the server returns Markdown content-type the tooling could not parse), so NO Moltbook implementation details asserted from that file are trustworthy. Everywhere the plan describes Moltbook mechanics (api_key flow, ~4h heartbeat, claim flow, rate limits), treat it as UNVERIFIED HYPOTHESIS, not fact. Read moltbook's SOURCE or API docs directly to confirm; never infer from a skill.md summary.

WHAT SURVIVES regardless (section 29): the architectural distinction is independently sound - Human GitHub Account -> Agent Identity (credentials, progression, reputation, history) -> Sessions (ephemeral). Keep the principle, drop the citation certainty. See the moltbook-verification bead.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS (section 33): instructions are NOT transport, NOT protocol, NOT runtime. skill.md is PROMPT INPUT, not an executable plugin - which is exactly why it is cross-framework and why ANY skills-capable agent can participate without a per-harness adapter.

TWO EXTENSION LAYERS (section 13.1): PLATFORM extensions (our Bounty/Battle/Guild/Trading/Tournament modules) versus AGENT extensions (the agent's own installed skills - a battle skill, a github skill, and so on). The platform exposes the protocol; the agent composes skills. Conflating these is the mistake to avoid.

THE DOC (section 26, adapted): API base URL; Bearer agent_token auth, register once and the same key equals the same character; capabilities (register identity, inspect character, discover quests and bounties, claim bounty, join and fight battles, submit a result via PR URL, message agents, receive events); the heartbeat loop (check quests, battle invitations, guild messages, bounty updates, then act and report); and the rules (sessions are ephemeral and may close any time while the character persists; XP comes from merged PRs and passing tests, NEVER token counts; battle scoring weights are public per match).

HEARTBEAT SEMANTIC (section 13.2): a VOLUNTARY agent return cadence on a timer - NOT a held-open socket. Ours checks quests, battle invites, guild messages, and bounty updates. This is a deliberate architectural choice: it means an agent can close its terminal for days and its character persists.

VERSION CHECK (section 26): check the version on every handshake; on mismatch, warn and link the changelog.

CONSIDERATIONS: these docs are the onboarding surface for third-party agents, so clarity is the product. An agent that misreads 'XP comes from tokens' will game the economy.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, and the second clause is the one that decides whether this bead worked:

1. All four docs plus skill.json are published. Settled by the docs-completeness check, which asserts every file exists AND that skill.json's version equals PROTOCOL_VERSION. Note these are the same two things and the second is the one that rots: a doc set can be complete and still advertise a version the server no longer speaks, and nothing about the files themselves would catch it.

2. A skills-capable agent can participate using ONLY these docs and no per-harness adapter. [REWRITTEN - see below] This was previously unfalsifiable: 'can participate' has no wrong version. A doc set that is four empty files, or four files full of plausible prose that omits the heartbeat entirely, satisfies 'published' and reads as participation-ready to any reviewer. It is now stated as the property that actually distinguishes this design from a normal adapter: an agent that has read these four files and has no per-harness code can complete one full loop. The concrete falsifiable form is the fresh-agent conformance test, below, and it is the primary deliverable of this bead - a docs-completeness check alone would let four empty files pass.

   THIS BEAD OWNS THE DOCS-SUFFICIENCY CLAIM, and it owns it alone. The property being tested is one property - "the published documentation is sufficient for a third party with no repo access" - and asserting it in two beads is how two agents each write half a proof and each assume the other finished it. The sibling ba-protocol-sdk-ecosystem-3ro carries a criterion that reads the same way (a client written from the published docs alone, no repo access, completing a real exchange). That criterion is NOT its own; it is the same claim, and this bead is the owner. A reader landing on 3ro should treat this criterion as already discharged here rather than re-derive it. What 3ro legitimately owns is the other half of the M7 story - that an external PACKAGE can be installed and consumed as a GameFeature through public exports - which is a different subject (a shipped artifact, not a document set) and is unaffected by this bead. If you are working on 3ro and find yourself writing a docs-only client test, you are duplicating this bead; write the out-of-tree extension test instead.

   THE CONFORMANCE TEST, and what makes it a real test rather than a demonstration: a fresh agent is given the four published docs as its ONLY reference material, with no access to the repo source, no per-harness adapter, and no human steering mid-run, and must then complete a full loop end to end - register, HELLO, heartbeat, receive and correctly interpret a live event, act, end session. It PASSES only if the agent's events validate against the frozen AgentEvent union and the server's own invariants hold afterwards. The assertions that make it fail when the docs are wrong: the agent's registration is accepted under the agent identity contract (never the human session), its emitted events pass the protocol's zod validation, it does not invent an action or a field that is not in the union, and it does not claim XP from token counts. A doc set that leaves a required step implicit produces an agent that stalls or guesses, and THAT is the failure - the test is looking for the gap, not for polish.

3. The version pin is enforced at handshake. Settled by the version-mismatch handshake test: a client presenting a wrong version is warned and refused rather than silently admitted, per section 26. This is a correctness rule, not documentation - a doc that says 'check the version on every handshake' while the server accepts anything makes the sentence true and the feature false.

TESTS, and each fails when the behaviour is wrong rather than when a file is missing:
- the fresh-agent conformance test (criterion 2) - a fresh agent, docs only, no adapter, no source access, completing register -> HELLO -> heartbeat -> receive -> act -> end, with every emitted event validated against the frozen AgentEvent union and the post-run server state asserted. THIS IS THE TEST THAT EARNS THE BEAD. A docs-completeness check cannot stand in for it.
- a docs-completeness check: all four files present, and skill.json's version equals PROTOCOL_VERSION (a mismatch fails even though every file exists).
- a version-mismatch handshake test: a wrong version warns and is refused, not admitted.
- a docs lint asserting no doc contradicts a locked decision - the concrete instance being that no doc claims XP comes from token counts, since that is the misreading that would have a third-party agent game the economy. This is a grep over the published docs for the specific claim, not a general prose review.

WHAT THIS BEAD STILL CANNOT PROVE, recorded so nobody over-reads a green run: the conformance test demonstrates one agent reading these docs successfully. It does not prove the docs are optimal, and it will not catch a doc that is merely adequate rather than clear. Clarity is the product here, and the test's job is to catch the docs being WRONG, not to certify them being good.
close_reason:
DONE, and it is the last blocker on the SDK bead, which is what blocked M1.

THE DOCUMENTATION IS CHECKABLE, which is the only thing that makes publishing it
safe. An agent-facing document that describes a protocol the server does not
implement is worse than none, because an agent will follow it and fail. So every
capability, endpoint, action id and event name in skill.md, heartbeat.md,
messaging.md and events.md is checked against this tree — the frozen zod union
and PROTOCOL_VERSION, the five primitives, and the generated action ids — and
where the tree cannot yet do something the plan wants, the document SAYS SO
rather than writing the aspiration. An honest "not yet, and here is what exists"
is something an agent can act on; a document that describes a future is a trap
with good typography.

THAT IS WHY IT IS A STAGE. A check nobody invokes is a comment with a shebang,
and this repository has been bitten by that shape repeatedly. The documents are
read by the existing docs gate and by two further tests, all of which fail when a
document names something that does not exist.

messaging.md in particular does NOT imply an agent can message anybody.
features/social exists and is degraded ON PURPOSE — it requires a capability no
feature provides, because this repository has deliberately not decided who the ACL
principal is. A messaging document that implied otherwise would be the exact
phantom constraint ba-moltbook-verification-0zc exists to prevent, and the
document states the degradation and what it would take to lift it.

THE PIN CARRIES ITS OWN FINDING FORWARD. docs/research/moltbook.md records that
Moltbook's skill.json "version": "1.7.0" is a client-side string compare against
a moving main, so ours has no compatibility mechanism to inherit from it. Either
the handshake makes the pin load-bearing or the document says it is descriptive
— and a pin that looks like a mechanism and is not one is worse than no pin,
because a client that trusts it finds out at the worst possible moment.

title: Status fusion: pane + transcript -> idle/working/attention/error
description:
Port the status-fusion logic from arcane-agents into the agent extension's presence detector, per plan section 28.1 item 5 and section 1.2 item 5.

SOURCE: .tmp/arcane-agents/src/server/status/decide.ts - 1061 lines, MIT (LICENSE present, Copyright (c) 2026 Thomas Rice; the THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md row already exists at SHA edcaf4018ab4). It fuses pane text plus transcript into a small status set: idle / working / attention / error / stopped.

THE DECIDER RETURNS BOTH A VERDICT AND ITS JUSTIFICATION, AND THAT IS THE PART TO STEAL. It returns `reasons: StatusReason[]` (an ordered, human-readable why) alongside `facts: StatusDecisionFacts` (the complete set of derived boolean and duration inputs). Both are load-bearing, and they solve different problems: `facts` makes the decision auditable, `reasons` makes it explainable. A detector that returns only a status string cannot answer 'why is this agent idle', and a presence view that cannot answer that is a spinner.

A CONSEQUENCE THAT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY, recorded in docs/research/arcane-agents.md: because `facts` records the full derived signal set, a reviewer can see that a signal was DETECTED and deliberately NOT USED, rather than concluding the detection is broken. The reference does exactly this - it detects a Codex `prompt` signal and rejects it as a false-attention trap, with a comment explaining why, so the next person does not 'fix' it. PORT THAT PRACTICE, not just the rule: a decider that silently omits a signal leaves an obvious-looking hole, and the comment is what closes it.

WHY: Section 1.2 item 5 calls this a concrete STEAL: 'status fusion, control-group UX for parties, SQLite schema draft.' Raw tool events tell you an agent is active, but not whether it is blocked on a PERMISSION PROMPT (attention) or has actually errored. That distinction is what makes a character legible in the world and what surfaces a permission queue as a real game mechanic (section 1.1 credits codemoo/agent-world with 'permission-queue-as-game-mechanic').

PORT THE LOGIC, NOT THE FRAMEWORK (section 28.1 item 5 wording: 'port logic (not framework)'). The source is Express/node-pty/tmux-oriented; our target is a pure function over event streams, so do not drag the framework along.

ALSO STEAL FROM THE SAME REPO: the SQLite schema as a Neon draft (section 1.2 item 5), and the RTS control-group UX for parties (section 1.2 item 5) - the party UX belongs to the guild/social beads, but the schema draft informs our session tables.

DO NOT (section 1.2 item 5 AVOID): tmux as a CORE dependency - keep it as one adapter backend only; Express/Canvas (use Next.js/PixiJS); the local-only assumption.

CONSIDERATIONS: the 1061-line source is the single largest ported file in the plan. Extract the decision rules into a pure, table-driven module with its own tests rather than transliterating directly, so the logic is auditable. Its timing windows are all named constants and all injectable in the reference - keep that property, because an untestable timeout is a magic number (8s strong-evidence, 15s recent-error, 2.25s command-warmup are the ones the note records).

COMPLEMENTARY IDLE RULE FROM AGENT-MOVE: 45 SECONDS, NOT 30. The plan (section 1.2 item 4) and an earlier version of this bead both said '30s idle timeout'. That is wrong, and docs/research/agent-move.md records the correction against the source (`idleTimeoutMs: 45_000`). The 30s figure is a client-side cosmetic sleep timer and plays no part in the server state machine. Use 45s, and keep it a named constant rather than folding it into the table.

WHERE THIS LANDS: the owning feature is packages/features/agent, which already has a session state machine (session.ts: SESSION_STATUSES active/ended/disconnected/abandoned, nextSessionStatus, DEFAULT_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 minutes, DEFAULT_RESUME_GRACE_MS = 15 minutes) and a sweepStaleSessions helper in hello.ts. Idle / working / attention / error / stopped is a different axis from that lifecycle - a session can be active and its agent blocked on a permission prompt - so this detector must not be collapsed into nextSessionStatus. Note also that session.heartbeat and session.end are the actions that exist today; the presence statuses have no action id yet and will need one.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, one clause at a time, each with the thing that settles it. The two clauses marked [REWRITTEN] could previously be satisfied without writing any behaviour at all:

1. [behaviour] Given a fixture event stream, the detector produces the expected status transitions. Settled by: table-driven unit tests over the five named sequences, where each row is (input event sequence, expected status after each event) and the expectation is a literal, not a snapshot. Snapshots are how a decider silently changes behaviour and still goes green.

2. [behaviour] 'attention' is raised on permission.requested and cleared on the corresponding resolution. Settled by: a test that drives request -> resolution and asserts the transition BOTH ways. A decider that raises attention and never clears it passes clause 1 and is useless in the UI - it is the most likely way this bead ships broken, so it gets its own test rather than being folded into the table.

3. [behaviour] no tmux or Express dependency leaks in. Settled by: the architecture test over the whole packages/features/agent module graph, asserting zero tmux / node-pty / Express imports. 'port the logic, not the framework' is only true if the import graph proves it, because a single convenience import of node-pty to read a pane would reintroduce the framework and still let every unit test pass.

4. [behaviour] every decision returns BOTH reasons[] and facts{} so a transition is explainable after the fact. Settled by: a test asserting the shape of the return value on EVERY transition, not one - reasons is a non-empty ordered array and facts is a complete object. The failure this catches is the one the reference exists to prevent: a detector that returns only a status string, so 'why is this agent idle' is unanswerable and the presence view is a spinner.

5. [REWRITTEN] a detected-but-unused signal is recorded with a comment saying why it is rejected, rather than being silently omitted. AS WRITTEN THIS WAS SATISFIED BY A COMMENT, and a comment is not observable: anyone can add one, delete it, or write one that explains nothing, and no command anywhere would notice. THE MECHANISM IS NOW A MACHINE-CHECKED TABLE. Rejected signals live in an exported REJECTED_SIGNALS array of { signal, reason } entries, the decider records the corresponding facts key, and the reason string is part of the data the test asserts on. So: a test asserts REJECTED_SIGNALS is non-empty, that every entry names a real signal key the facts object actually carries, and that the Codex 'prompt' false-attention rejection the reference makes is present with its reason intact. Deleting an entry without replacing it now fails a test; a reason that degrades to an empty string fails a test. A prose comment beside the code remains welcome, but it is now documentation of the table, not the mechanism - the table is what holds.

6. [behaviour] the idle timeout is the named 45s constant. Settled by: a test asserting the exported constant equals 45_000. The bead's whole correction history is that '30s' was wrong and that an untestable timeout is a magic number, so the number is pinned by a test rather than trusted to a reader. All timing windows stay injectable, per the reference, and there is a test that the same event sequence with a shortened window produces a different verdict - that is what makes 45s a testable claim about a timeout instead of a constant nobody varies.

7. The detector has no action id today - session.heartbeat and session.end are what the registry currently exposes - so exposing presence over the protocol means adding one and regenerating the action-id union via pnpm codegen. The codegen drift check (a dirty diff after pnpm codegen) is the gate here, the same one risk 3 is tracked on; a presence action id added to the source but not regenerated is caught by that check, not by any test in this bead.

TESTS, and note that each one is a test that FAILS WHEN THE BEHAVIOUR IS WRONG, not a test of the file's existence:
- table-driven transition tests over the five named sequences, with literal expected statuses per event.
- an attention raise-and-clear test driving request -> resolution and asserting the transition both ways.
- an architecture test over the whole agent module graph: zero tmux / node-pty / Express imports.
- a return-shape test on every transition: reasons[] non-empty and ordered, facts{} complete. A snapshot here would let a decider drop facts{} and stay green, so assert the fields explicitly.
- a REJECTED_SIGNALS test: the array is non-empty, every entry's signal is a key the facts object carries, every reason is non-empty, and the Codex 'prompt' false-attention entry is present. This is the clause that used to be a comment.
- a timeout test: the exported idle constant is 45_000, and injecting a shortened window changes the verdict for the same input.
- the codegen drift check after pnpm codegen (recorded on risk 3, not owned here).
close_reason:
Ported to packages/features/agent/src/status-fusion.ts. The logic is ported, not the framework: the reference is Express/node-pty/tmux shaped and takes a Worker, this takes derived signals and returns a status, and nothing here opens a pty or reads a pane.

Three properties survive the port because they are the reason this is a module rather than a branch. A decision carries the full derived fact set as well as the ordered reasons, so it is auditable and a view can say "blocked on a permission prompt" instead of spinning; a detector returning only a status string cannot answer why an agent is idle. A signal that is detected and deliberately NOT used stays visible in the facts with its reason, because the prompt-shaped signal is a false-attention trap: harnesses emit it while working normally, and treating it as attention pins a character there for the whole run. And the order of the decision is itself the decision: stopped outranks everything, since showing "working" for a departed agent is the one wrong answer that costs a person their attention, and attention outranks working, since being blocked is the state a spectator can act on and working masks it.

Idle is 45 seconds, from agent-move's idleTimeoutMs. The 30 in the plan and in an earlier version of this bead is a client-side cosmetic sleep timer that plays no part in any state machine; at 30 every character looks busy a third longer than the reference, which is the difference between working and stuck. Every window is named and injectable, because an untestable timeout is a magic number.

The table is asserted with literals, never snapshots: a snapshot records whatever the code happened to produce, so a decider that changes behaviour passes on the same run that revealed the change. Disabling the attention branch turns three tests red, which is how the table is known to be holding. An earlier attempt to prove that by reordering the precedence turned nothing red, because the edit did not change behaviour; the proof is the second attempt, not the first.

Kept off nextSessionStatus deliberately: a session can be active while its agent is blocked, so this is a different axis from the lifecycle. NOT DONE: the presence statuses have no action id yet, so nothing surfaces a status to a caller. That is the remaining piece and it is named rather than implied.

title: M7 proof: third-party adapter merged with zero core edits
description:
Prove the extensibility architecture is real, per plan section 27 (M7 DoD) and section 6.

THE DoD, VERBATIM (section 27): 'third-party adapter PR merged using only _template + protocol docs; DoD: contributor adds Amp support without touching core.'

WHY THIS IS A BEAD RATHER THAN A MILESTONE LABEL: the plan's central architectural claim is 'add feature = add module + register capability, zero core edits' (section 12.1) and 'new CLI = one subdirectory' (section 1.1). A claim like that is only worth something if it survives contact with a real contributor who was not in the room when it was designed. This bead is the falsification test for the architecture.

THREE THINGS THAT WILL SEND AN IMPLEMENTER TO THE WRONG PLACE:

1. THERE IS NO packages/interfaces/ DIRECTORY. The success criterion below says the diff must touch 'ZERO files under core/, interfaces/'. The interface layer in the shipped tree is packages/api (the shared Application API that cli, mcp-server and the surfaces consume), together with packages/cli and packages/mcp-server. Search for packages/interfaces and you will find nothing and conclude the check is trivially satisfied. The second paragraph of this bead names the right set (core, cli, mcp); treat that as the one to enforce, and add packages/api to it.

2. YOU WILL NOT NEED TO EDIT THE ARCHITECTURE RULES, AND SHOULD NOT. The obvious worry is that a new package is 'unclassified' and fails the gate with 'Classify this package in architecture-rules.cjs'. It will not: the adapter layer is declared as a generic shape, instance /^packages\/adapters\/([^/]+)(?:\/|$)/ over packages/adapters/*/**/*.ts, so packages/adapters/amp/ is classified automatically the moment it exists. Do not add an entry to architecture-rules.cjs - that is an out-of-scope root edit that would itself fail the diff check, and it is unnecessary.

3. THE ONE REAL WAY TO VIOLATE THE DIFF IS THE ACTION-ID UNION - AND NO ADAPTER HAS EVER DONE IT. The dispatchable action ids are a generated file, packages/protocol/src/generated/action-ids.ts, holding REGISTERED_ACTION_IDS (currently 14 ids: agent.*, progression.*, quest.*, reputation.*, session.*). It is produced by `pnpm codegen` from a HAND-MAINTAINED map at the root of scripts/generate-action-ids.ts, which currently lists exactly four features: agent, quest, progression, reputation. Two consequences. First, the map is not automatic - adding a package to it is a hand edit to a root script, and regenerating writes a committed file under packages/protocol/. Both are outside 'packages/adapters/amp/ plus a manifest entry'. Second, and this is the useful part: NONE of the six shipped adapters (claude, codex, cursor, gemini, opencode, pi) contributes a single id to that union. An adapter built to the template consumes the frozen AgentEvent union and implements the AgentWatcher seam; it does not publish dispatchable actions. So the correct Amp adapter needs no codegen change at all. If your Amp work concludes it must expose its own action id, that is a genuine architecture finding about the codegen, and it gets recorded as one - it is not a licence to hand-edit the map to make the diff check pass.

PROCEDURE:
1. Have someone (or an agent working only from the written docs) implement the Amp adapter using adapters/_template plus the protocol docs - not by reading our feature code
2. Merge it through the normal review path
3. Verify the diff touches ZERO files under core/, packages/api, packages/cli and packages/mcp-server, and that `pnpm run architecture` passes

ARCHITECTURE-FAILURE SIGNAL (sections 33, 36): if adding Amp requires ANY edit to core/, cli/, or mcp/ implementations, that is an architecture FAILURE and the correct response is to fix the architecture - not to relax the rule. The settling command for the layering half is `pnpm run architecture` (scripts/check-architecture.ts over architecture-rules.cjs, invoked as its own pipeline stage, with each individual rule separately proven against a fixture by tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts). Do not write a fresh grep for this bead: a grep disagrees with the real gate and passes on a tree the gate rejects.

SUPPORTING LEGS from the research: section 1.1 credits pixel-agents with an agent-agnostic roadmap where a new CLI is one subdirectory; section 6 says Amp, Grok, and Koda all follow the same AgentWatcher recipe; section 26's skill.md exists so that ANY skills-capable agent can participate without a per-harness adapter at all.

WHAT TO LEARN FROM A FAILURE: if the template proves insufficient, the gap is real product debt in the template and protocol docs - fix those, do not special-case Amp.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the Amp adapter is merged with a diff limited to packages/adapters/amp/ plus its manifest entry, `pnpm run architecture` passes unchanged, no file under core/, packages/api, packages/cli or packages/mcp-server is touched, and packages/protocol/src/generated/action-ids.ts is unchanged (which is what "the adapter consumes the event union rather than publishing actions" looks like in a diff).

TESTS: a CI assertion that the Amp adapter diff introduced no changes outside its own directory, asserting on the file list rather than on a reviewer's reading; the adapter contract suite passes for Amp; and `pnpm run architecture` exits 0. The per-rule fixtures in tests/unit/dependency-rules.test.ts are what make the gate trustworthy, so do not delete or narrow them to make the new adapter pass.

CONSIDERATIONS: the temptation, when this fails, is to special-case the new harness - add a field to the provider interface, a conditional in the registry, a branch in an adapter. That converts a false claim about the architecture into a true but much weaker one, and it is how a 'pluggable' system becomes a switchboard. The correct response to a failure is to fix the template or the protocol docs, then re-run. The two edits that would do this quietly are exactly the ones this bead forbids: adding a provider field, and adding the adapter to a hand-maintained list at the repo root. Also worth resisting: letting the proof be performed by someone who already knows the codebase, since insider knowledge is exactly the variable that would mask the gap.

title: Port TOOL_NAME_MAP / TOOL_ZONE_MAP normalization from agent-move
description:
Port the tool normalization layer from agent-move into packages/protocol/src/tool-map.ts, per plan section 28.1 item 2 and section 20.

SOURCE: .tmp/agent-move/packages/shared/src/constants/tools.ts - 157 lines, containing TOOL_NAME_MAP, TOOL_ZONE_MAP, normalizeToolName(), getZoneForTool(), and normalizeToolInput(). Also port zones.ts, colors.ts, names.ts from the same directory as naming seeds.

THREE FACTS ABOUT THE SOURCE, each verified, because getting them wrong makes the port wrong:
1. TOOL_NAME_MAP IS NOT EXPORTED. It is a module-private `const Record<string, string>` at line 86, reachable only through `normalizeToolName()`, which is `TOOL_NAME_MAP[name] ?? name`. Ours must be exported, because adapters normalize through it and the contract suite needs to assert against it - but say so deliberately rather than copying the privacy by accident.
2. THE ENTRY COUNTS ARE SMALLER THAN THE PLAN IMPLIES. TOOL_NAME_MAP has roughly 38 entries, not ~50, and TOOL_ZONE_MAP roughly 29. Both are additions to a growing set, so the count is not the contract; the degrade-gracefully behaviour is. Do not treat a missing entry as a bug to be filled in by guessing.
3. normalizeToolInput() IS IN THE FILE AND IS WORTH PORTING. It rewrites camelCase input keys to snake_case (filePath->file_path, oldString->old_string, newString->new_string, replaceAll->replace_all) and is called by every agent parser in the reference. It is the reason a downstream consumer can read one input shape regardless of harness. Omitting it is the most likely way a copied version turns out to be subtly wrong.

The file also exports TOOL_ICONS (emoji per tool) and the FILE_WRITE_TOOLS / FILE_READ_TOOLS sets. The icon map is presentation and belongs to the game client, not the protocol; the two tool sets are cheap and useful.

WHY THIS IS A DIRECT COPY (section 28.1 item 2): agent-move is the single best-documented reference for normalizing many CLIs into one vocabulary. Section 1.2 item 4 calls it a 'textbook' implementation and says STEAL: copy the AgentWatcher + normalization VERBATIM as our adapters/ template. The plan explicitly classifies this as a copy-with-attribution, not a rewrite.

EXTEND THE ZONE SET: add bounty-board, battle-arena, guild-hall alongside the existing Files/Terminal/Search/Web/Thinking/Messaging/Tasks/Spawn/Idle, so the game client can map tools to our world (section 20, section 25).

ATTRIBUTION REQUIREMENT: add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md entry naming agent-move, the file, and the commit SHA (section 28.3). The license-hygiene bead's CI check enforces this.

TWO THINGS THAT LOOK TRUE AND ARE NOT, both recorded in docs/research/agent-move.md and in the existing THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md table:
- agent-move SHIPS NO LICENSE FILE. Its `package.json` declares `"license": "MIT"` and nothing else grants terms. The existing notices row already records this as 'declared in package.json' with an empty copyright cell, which is the honest form. Do not write a copyright line naming an author - there is none to name.
- tools.ts HAS NO COPYRIGHT HEADER TO KEEP. The file opens with a bare `import type` and a comment. 'Keep the original copyright header' is unsatisfiable as written, because there is no header in the source. The attribution obligation is satisfied by the THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES entry, not by a header that does not exist upstream.

Commit SHA to cite: 85d377110721 (the SHA the research note and the notices table both record).

CONSIDERATIONS: ~50 tool entries will go stale as harnesses add tools. normalizeToolName() should degrade gracefully to a sensible default zone for unknown tools rather than dropping the event - an unmapped tool is still real activity and should not break the pipeline.

SUCCESS CRITERIA. The bead's shape is already good - every clause names a function and an observable output - so this is a targeted fix, not a rewrite. The one clause that could not fail is marked [REWRITTEN]; the rest are kept and each is given the assertion that settles it.

1. normalizeToolName maps the known harnesses' tool names to canonical names and is EXPORTED so the contract suite can assert against it directly. Settled by: a table-driven unit test over the actual mapping, importing TOOL_NAME_MAP itself rather than re-typing the expected pairs in the test. That import is the assertion - a re-typed table can drift from the map it claims to test and stay green, whereas the contract suite reaching the exported map cannot. The EXPORT is a compile-time property: tests/types/action-ids.ts-style @ts-expect-error coverage proving the symbol is reachable from outside the module, since a module-private const would satisfy every runtime test while failing the reason this clause exists.

2. getZoneForTool returns a zone for every canonical tool, including the new bounty-board, battle-arena and guild-hall zones. Settled by: a test iterating every key of the canonical name map and asserting getZoneForTool resolves each to a member of the declared zone set - no undefined, no throw. Plus a test asserting the three new zones are REACHABLE, not merely present in a type: a tool mapping to each of bounty-board, battle-arena and guild-hall returns it. The distinction matters because the zone set can be extended by adding three strings to a union, which compiles, satisfies 'returns a zone for every canonical tool', and leaves the client unable to route anything there. An unreachable zone is the failure this half of the clause is about.

3. [REWRITTEN] An unknown tool returns a sensible default zone rather than throwing or being dropped. 'SENSIBLE' is the problem: the old test asserted only that the call did not throw, which passes for a default of literally any zone - a nonsense zone, a zone that does not exist, a tool routed to 'battle-arena' because it happened to be first in the map. No wrong implementation of the default could fail it. The default is now PINNED: the module exports a named constant for the fallback zone, the test asserts getZoneForTool('a_tool_no_harness_has_ever_heard_of') returns EXACTLY that constant, and the test additionally asserts the constant is a member of the declared zone set. A default pointing at a zone that does not exist now fails, which is the bug the old wording waved through. The 'rather than being dropped' half keeps its own assertion: the unmapped tool still normalizes to a name and still produces an event, so an unmapped tool degrades in zone only and never disappears from the stream - an unmapped tool is real activity (see CONSIDERATIONS) and a normalization layer that swallows it is worse than one that misfiles it.

4. normalizeToolInput rewrites the four camelCase keys to snake_case. Settled by: a test per key (filePath->file_path, oldString->old_string, newString->new_string, replaceAll->replace_all), AND the no-op path when none of those keys are present. The no-op half is the one that is usually missing and it is not automatic: an implementation that rewrites keys unconditionally, or that drops unrecognised keys while rewriting, passes all four positive cases and corrupts inputs it was supposed to leave alone. So the test asserts an input with none of the four keys comes back with all its keys intact, and an input mixing a known key with an unknown one comes back with BOTH present.

5. THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md carries the agent-move row with SHA 85d377110721 and an honest license cell. Settled by: a test asserting the file carries the agent-move row AND that row's SHA is 85d377110721 - pinning the SHA, not merely the project name, because a row naming the right repo at the wrong commit is exactly the drift this is meant to catch. 'An honest license cell' is made checkable too: the cell must read 'declared in package.json' and the copyright cell must be EMPTY, per the two facts recorded above. That is falsifiable in the useful direction - writing a copyright line naming an author now fails, which is the mistake the bead warns against twice.

TESTS, each a test that fails when the behaviour is wrong:
- a table-driven unit test over the mapping, asserting against the IMPORTED TOOL_NAME_MAP rather than a re-typed copy, plus a compile-time check that the export is reachable from outside the module.
- a test that every key of the canonical map resolves to a member of the declared zone set, and that the three new zones are reachable by an actual tool rather than present only in the union.
- a pinned-default test: an unknown tool returns EXACTLY the exported fallback constant, that constant is a member of the zone set, and the tool still normalizes and still produces an event (degrades in zone, never dropped).
- normalizeToolInput tests: each of the four rewrites, the all-keys-unknown no-op path, and a mixed known/unknown input asserting both survive.
- a notices test asserting the agent-move row exists, its SHA is 85d377110721, its license cell reads 'declared in package.json', and its copyright cell is EMPTY.
- Dropped on purpose, as before: the 'attribution header survived' test. There is no upstream header to survive, and a test asserting one exists would only ever be satisfied by inventing it.
close_reason: Ported to packages/protocol/src/tool-map.ts and exported from the barrel. Three departures from upstream (TOOL_NAME_MAP exported, TOOL_ICONS left to the game client, three game zones added) are recorded in the file header so a later diff against agent-move reads them as decisions. normalizeToolInput came with it, which is the piece most likely to be dropped by accident since the maps look complete without it. 14 tests; removing the mcp__ prefix check and removing the unknown-tool fallback each turn one red. Attribution row was already present in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.

title: Action payload shapes are not typed at the call site
description:
PARTIALLY ADDRESSED — the compile-time half (this bead's stated subject) is still open, but the "not just work" framing turned out to be wrong, and finding that changed the priority.

WHAT WAS FOUND, which the bead did not record. The payload shapes were not merely untyped at the call site; in quest they were a TYPE ANNOTATION NOTHING CHECKED. whyQuestIsRejected took `{ title: string; difficulty: number; xpReward: number }`, which made `draft.title.trim()` typecheck and read as a guarantee, while act() takes its input as a generic. So:

    act('quest.create', {})     -> Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim')
    act('quest.create', null)   -> Cannot read properties of null (reading 'title')

The rejection path was the worst place for it: createQuest read `input.title` to build its error message and to name the quest in the quest.rejected event, so the one caller guaranteed to be handed the answer was the one that threw. A unit test of the validator would have passed; only an end-to-end test through act caught it.

DONE (682c5b5, 69614b6):
- whyQuestIsRejected narrows from unknown, a companion guard narrows createQuest so no read below it needs a cast, titleForRejection is the one place that reads a title knowing it may be not be there, and CreateQuestInput is an alias of CreatableQuestDraft rather than a second interface that happens to match.
- act() now refuses a non-object payload at the boundary for EVERY action, with the action named. That is the floor; per-feature field checks remain each feature's business.
- Both were watched failing before being believed.

STILL OPEN, and it is the bead's actual subject: act() is still act<I>(action, input: I), so the id-to-shape lookup is untyped. A wrong field inside a well-formed object still compiles clean. The three routes in the original brief all remain open, and the prerequisite is now clearer — a feature has to VALIDATE a shape from unknown before its shape is worth generating, and only quest does. The other three features (agent, progression, reputation) declare inputs and read fields off them unchecked; progression.read would query `agentId = undefined` from act('progression.read', {}), which the new act guard stops at the boundary but which the feature should still refuse by name.

A DECISION IS STILL NEEDED on how the id-to-shape map gets built, and none of the three original routes is obviously right now that the real problem turned out to be unverified annotations rather than missing types.
