absent.

title: Watchlist: SpaceMolt and other live agent-world experiments
description:
Track external projects that could invalidate or improve our design, per plan section 34.

PRIMARY WATCH TARGET (section 34): SpaceMolt - an MMO-style persistent AI-agent universe over MCP/WebSocket with agents living continuously. It is the closest live experiment to our 'persistent agent world' half. ACTION: compare its session/presence model against section 3 (the User/Agent/Session/Battle split) before M5, because we have a contract-session bead that LOCKED our resume-vs-new handshake - if SpaceMolt has a better model, we want to know before M5 rather than after.

WHY THIS IS A TRACKED BEAD: our four contracts are frozen (section 29.1), so external evidence is most valuable BEFORE M5 locks world persistence in - and least valuable after. The plan explicitly schedules the comparison 'before M5'.

SECONDARY WATCH: Agent Intercom and sandbox-agent (section 1.3) - cross-harness messaging protocol and a unified control API across Claude/Codex/OpenCode/Cursor/Amp/Pi streaming events, permissions, and sessions over HTTP. The plan calls sandbox-agent 'a good reference for the runtime isolation/control layer behind the Battle Engine', so it may inform the battle workspace provisioner.

ALSO IN THE BACKLOG (Appendix A of the plan, the 'named in conversation but NOT cloned' list - the old reference here said 'section 395', which is a line number in an earlier draft of this bead and not a section of the plan at all; the plan runs 0 through 40 plus two appendices and has no section 395): Pixel Agents Web/Desktop/Desk, Claude Dungeon, Agentainer, the karansag / me-frankan / displega-ai / biggazoo swarms, agent-sandbox, Agentic Quest, mcp-coding-agents, Keyframe.it, spine-ai, DragonScript Arena, Coding Quests, Mage Mayhem, Tari bounties, Bountysource, BountyHub, AsyncAPI bounty program.

CONSIDERATIONS: resist cloning these reflexively. Each has a specific lesson already extracted into the relevant bead (for example agent-sandbox's perceive-plan-act loop and Agentic Quest's real-validator win condition are cited in section 1.2 items 7-8). Pull one in only when a specific open question needs it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE THE OLD ONE COULD NOT FAIL. The old criterion was "a short comparison note exists" and the old TESTS line said outright that this is not a code test. An empty file satisfies it. A research artifact is still accountable; what makes it accountable is that each of its claims is individually labelled and its conclusion has a consequence. Three things must be observable, and the whole thing must land before M5 begins, because that is when the plan says world persistence gets locked:

1. A SpaceMolt row in the per-repo table in docs/research/README.md, carrying the commit SHA the reading was done against, a one-line headline finding, and a verdict per claimed mechanic - CONFIRMED (naming the file it came from) or UNVERIFIED-hypothesis. This is the same table and the same shape ba-moltbook-verification-0zc already established. This bead extends that table to the watch targets; it does not invent a second format, and the two notes must not drift apart.

2. A DECISION on the single question the plan schedules this comparison to answer: given SpaceMolt's session/presence model, does our LOCKED section 3 User/Agent/Session/Battle split and resume-vs-new handshake stand, or does it change? The answer is exactly one of ADOPT / KEEP / DEFER, and each carries a written consequence: ADOPT names the contract section that would change and opens a bead for it; KEEP names the specific section 3 clause the comparison cleared, so a later reader knows what was actually tested rather than "we looked at it"; DEFER names the date or milestone at which the question is re-asked. A comparison that concludes nothing is a comment, not a decision - and "concludes nothing" is exactly what the old criterion allowed.

3. A staleness note: the date, plus the beads that were unstarted when the reading was done, so a reader can tell how much of the plan postdates it. This is the shape docs/research/README.md already uses and it is the model worth copying.

WHAT SETTLES IT - a check with an exit code, not a review: a docs check that FAILS if (a) docs/research/README.md carries no SpaceMolt row, (b) that row carries no commit SHA, or (c) any file under docs/design/ asserts a SpaceMolt, sandbox-agent or Agent Intercom mechanic with no citation to that row. Clause (c) is a grep for the watch-target names outside the research directory. THE FAILING CASE THIS CATCHES IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: a design doc quietly leaning on an unverified SpaceMolt mechanic, which is exactly how a phantom constraint gets built - someone designs around a heartbeat interval or a resume rule that was never real, and the real constraint then makes the design wrong. That is the same failure ba-moltbook-verification-0zc is about, on the second watch target.

UNCHANGED AND STILL TRUE: resist cloning these reflexively. Each of these projects has its lesson already extracted into the relevant bead (agent-sandbox's perceive-plan-act loop and Agentic Quest's real-validator win condition are cited in section 1.2 items 7-8). Pull one in only when a specific open question needs it. Agent Intercom and sandbox-agent stay SECONDARY here - if their comparison is not finished, say so in the staleness line rather than implying coverage that does not exist.
close_reason:
DONE. The reading happened, the decision is made, and it is KEEP.

The recon recorded that the SpaceMolt checkout had never happened. That was wrong —
it is public and clonable. Two were taken, because the question needs both and
neither alone answers it: the official reference client for the protocol, and
spacemolt-lib for the WebSocket lifecycle, close codes and reconnect policy. The
game server is closed-source, so CONFIRMED here means confirmed in shipped client
code or a server-published schema — a stronger footing than Moltbook's
documentation-only checkout, and the reason this reading settled anything at all
where that one could not.

15 claims, 9 CONFIRMED / 5 UNVERIFIED / 1 REFUTED, each quoting the line it rests
on, because .tmp/ is gitignored and a bare file:line dies in a fresh clone.

TWO CLAUSES CLEARED. §3.1's Agent/Session split: SpaceMolt runs the exact "Claude
#2" failure at MMO scale and still keeps identity and transport session apart,
independently arriving at "expired session, new session, same player". §3.1's
"BATTLE binds Sessions not Agents", in the strongest form available — a SpaceMolt
battle is a server-side object with an id, queryable after every session that
touched it is gone.

ONE CLAUSE KEPT BECAUSE OF WHAT THE READING FOUND, which is the interesting part.
§3.2's resume-vs-new handshake stands because SpaceMolt has no such offer at all:
the client forks login versus register unilaterally from a local file. That is the
"Claude #2" failure reached by a different road, and adopting it would trade a
server-held contract for a local file.

DELIBERATELY NOT MARKED CLEARED: the grace window (no SpaceMolt counterpart) and
the heartbeat. An earlier draft of the note called our heartbeat "unjustified"
because SpaceMolt runs without one — which was the wrong inference, since our own
session code implements a five-minute heartbeat. It is not unexplained, merely
unmatched by a counterpart. Corrected rather than shipped.

The check is wired as pipeline stage watchlist-claims and resolves all 12
file:line citations plus 13 evidence lines byte-for-byte, so the note cannot drift
from the reading that produced it. The clause that earns it is the cross-check: a
design doc leaning on an unverified SpaceMolt mechanic is how a phantom constraint
gets built.

title: Next.js UI: dashboard shell, bounty board, agent cards
description:
Build the web UI surface per plan section 8.

MAIN SCREEN OPTIONS (section 8). The plan offers a pixel-city main screen and a BOUNTY BOARD AS FIRST SCREEN OPTION - and the bounty board is better aligned with the M2-is-valuable-without-game-UI strategy. The board: HOT BOUNTIES list ($2000 SSO, $750 memleak, $250 OAuth, $50 CLI bug with competitor counts) -> bounty detail (repo, issue, reward, requirements, [ENTER BATTLE], competitors).

DASHBOARD (section 8, from the conversation): top bar (Agent Battle, notifications, coins, level) / CODING CITY map (Guild Hall, Research Lab, character, Arena, Workshop, Quest Board) / bottom tabs (QUESTS, AGENTS, GUILD, ARENA, PROFILE).

AGENT CARD (section 3.2 + section 10.1): level, current quest and session, skill bars, [Enter Arena] [View History] [Join Guild]. The dashboard agent list must show online AND offline agents with Level/XP and 'Last seen 12m ago' - a dead session must never make a character vanish.

THREE OF THE FIVE SURFACES IN THE OLD TITLE ARE NOT THIS BEAD'S, and leaving them in was the actual defect. This bead is the DASHBOARD SHELL, the BOUNTY BOARD, and the AGENT CARDS. The other two have owners, and this text used to claim work that belonged to them while its own success criteria quietly tested something narrower - so an implementer could read the title, build two surfaces they did not own, and still miss the one thing the criteria actually settle.

REPLAY VIEW is owned by ba-battle-replay-yjb, which already specifies the page (apps/web/app/(app)/replay/[replayId]/page.tsx), the og:image, the public logged-out read and the determinism contract. Note the contradiction this removes: this bead previously said 'REPLAY VIEW: see battle-replay' and then, two clauses later, required in criterion 1 that the replay 'renders from REAL data' with an integration test. Both cannot be true of one bead. The replay view is the replay bead's; what stays here is the link into it from the bounty board's [ENTER BATTLE] action, which is this bead's because the board is.

ARENA DIFF-STREAMING is also the replay bead's, and was duplicated here verbatim. ba-battle-replay-yjb already carries 'diff-streaming over the websocket for arena efficiency (section 8), using the codemoo stateDiffBroadcast pattern (section 28.1 item 12)', and the server side of the same pattern is ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9 ('DIFF BROADCAST ... broadcast DIFFS, not full state'). Three beads naming the same port is how it gets built twice or, more likely, never: none of them can tell whether it is done. It is the replay bead's to render and the ingest bead's to emit. This bead consumes the stream and does not build it.

GUILD HALL with a map editor inside the client (section 8, agent-quest editor precedent) belongs to ba-feature-guild-5g6 (M6) and the game client, not here. A map editor is a creation tool for M6 guild territory; building it inside the dashboard bead puts M6 surface area in a P2 bead that is not blocked on anything guild-related. It stays in the plan (section 8) and it is not dropped - it is not this bead's, and the honest form of that is a pointer, not a bullet.

PRODUCT SHAPE (section 11.4): BOUNTY MARKET (issues, sponsors, rewards) + GAME WORLD (agents, guilds, projects) + ARENA (PvP, battles, tournaments) over AGENT RUNTIME (MCP/hooks/GitHub).

CONSIDERATIONS: the plan is emphatic that the web is a VIEW, not the game - every loop must be playable via the protocol alone (section 34). The UI must not become the only path to any action, or the machine-native rule is broken.

SUCCESS CRITERIA, REWRITTEN BECAUSE 'RENDER FROM REAL DATA' AND 'NO LOOP IS WEB-ONLY' COULD NOT FAIL. Both clauses were satisfied by a page that renders a hardcoded array, and both are the properties this bead actually exists to protect. Each now names the wrong implementation it must catch.

1. Bounty board and agent cards render from REAL data. 'Real' means: the component is exercised against a live or compose-seeded API, not a fixture literal pasted into the component file. Settled by: an integration test that mounts each view against the running API and asserts the values on screen came from the response - a bounty with a distinctive reward amount in the API appears with that amount on screen, an agent id appears on its card. THE WRONG IMPLEMENTATION THIS CATCHES, and it is the common one: a component that renders a hardcoded array renders perfectly, passes every visual check, and ships data that is not the game's. A test that only asserts the page does not crash passes all three of these views with a hardcoded list. If a fixture is unavoidable for a view, the test must additionally assert the fetch path, and say which part is faked.

2. Offline agents display correctly - and a dead session must never make a character vanish. This is the whole reason the clause exists (section 3.2 / 10.1: the agent list shows online AND offline agents with Level/XP and 'Last seen 12m ago'). Settled by: an online/offline state test driven from actual session state rather than a snapshot. Two assertions that a snapshot cannot give: an agent whose session is ended or heartbeat-stale RENDERS, with a last-seen value, and an agent absent from the current live set still renders. A snapshot of the online case alone passes for a component that simply filters to online agents, which is the exact bug - an offline agent silently disappearing from the roster is invisible until a user goes looking for a teammate. Assert both states, and assert the last-seen value is computed from real session data.

3. [REWRITTEN] No loop is web-only. This was the most important clause and the least measurable: 'no loop is web-only' has no wrong version, because a UI can be complete and beautiful and still be the only path to some action, which is what section 34 forbids. It is now the property with a test: EVERY action the UI offers is reachable through the protocol or CLI alone, and the UI introduces no capability that exists nowhere else. Settled by: a machine-native test that completes the full loop - discover, claim, act, and the resulting state - with the web UI entirely absent, asserting the same application-command effects the UI produces. Paired with the architectural half, which is the cheap continuous check: no route handler in apps/web contains game logic, because the five primitives translate and dispatch and make no decisions, and each maps 1:1 onto an application command. The UI is then a second client of the same commands rather than a privileged path. WITHOUT THE MACHINE-NATIVE HALF THIS CLAUSE IS UNCHECKABLE, because a UI that happens to mirror the protocol and a UI that is the only way to do something look identical from inside a browser - only running the loop with the UI gone tells them apart.

TESTS, each a test that fails when the behaviour is wrong rather than when a page is missing. (This supersedes the old 'component/integration tests; a snapshot for the agent card's online/offline states; the E2E smoke' line - the snapshot is specifically insufficient for criterion 2, and component tests alone are insufficient for criterion 1.)
- integration tests mounting the bounty board and the agent card against a live or compose-seeded API, asserting distinctive values from the response appear on screen. These catch a hardcoded list, which is the failure mode the old wording could not see. The replay is deliberately absent from this list: ba-battle-replay-yjb owns the replay view and runs the equivalent test against its own page, so the test exists once and is not owned twice.
- the online/offline state test: an ended-or-stale agent renders with a last-seen value, and an agent missing from the live set still appears in the roster. Asserted from real session state, not from a committed snapshot of the online case alone.
- the machine-native test with the web UI disabled, completing discover -> claim -> act and asserting the same application-command effects. This is the test that earns criterion 3.
- an architecture test asserting no route handler in apps/web contains game logic, and that each route maps 1:1 onto an application command.
- the E2E smoke covering login -> connect -> claim, stopping at the board's [ENTER BATTLE] link into the replay (section 40). The link is this bead's; the render it lands on is ba-battle-replay-yjb's, and that bead's own E2E covers arriving at the timeline. Note the direction: the E2E proves the UI works, the machine-native test proves the UI is not required. Only the first is commonly written, and only the second settles this clause.

STATE CORRECTION, 2026-09-25: the state warning that used to sit here is obsolete, and acting on it would now break the build. The scaffold placeholder is gone. `apps/web` IS a Next.js app: `next` ^15.5.4, `react` and `react-dom` are dependencies; `next.config.mjs` exists; `app/` exists with `layout.tsx` and `page.tsx`; the build is `next build`, not `tsc`. `docker compose up` serves it on WEB_PORT (3000 by default).

WHAT ACTUALLY EXISTS, so the next person does not re-derive it:
- `app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts` - the Better Auth mount (see ba-better-auth-github-oauth-9wm).
- `app/api/events/route.ts` and `app/api/events/stream/route.ts` - the telemetry plane (see ba-event-ingest-and-sse-gu9).
- `app/page.tsx` - a deliberate placeholder that links to `/dashboard`, which DOES NOT EXIST YET. The dashboard is this bead's first real piece of work.
- `src/routes.ts` - the five primitives over HTTP: GET /api/discover, /api/search, /api/inspect and POST /api/act.

CONSEQUENCES FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP:
- Import `next/...` freely. The old 'do NOT import next' instruction described a tree state that no longer exists.
- There is no `app/api/health/route.ts`. The old warning asked for one; it was never needed and was not added. The auth and events routes are the real surface.
- What remains is exactly what the success criteria above name, minus the replay: the bounty board, the agent cards, the dashboard shell they hang off, and the offline-agent display. The replay view was the one item here that another bead owns outright (ba-battle-replay-yjb). The cross-reference that used to sit here was itself stale: it said the replay 'is listed in criterion 1', but criterion 1 was narrowed to the bounty board and agent cards and no longer names the replay anywhere. So the replay is now absent from this bead's criteria entirely, which is the correct end state - the board's [ENTER BATTLE] link is exercised by the E2E smoke, and the view it lands on belongs to the replay bead, which runs its own test against its own page. Nothing here builds or renders a replay.

That is VISUAL work, and it is still blocked until DESIGN.md exists - antislop R-37 forbids building UI without design direction. A framework shell is not visual design and was never blocked; the shell is now in place.
close_reason:
DONE. The bounty board, the roster and the shell — DESIGN.MD §3's first screen,
in three read models and four routes.

THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST IN THIS SESSION, and it is a SECURITY finding
rather than a styling one. THE GATE DID NOT GATE. The check started in
app/(app)/layout.tsx and the bounty was still in the HTML: Next renders the child
page anyway to build the streamed RSC payload, so curl /bounties followed by a
grep found the repository and the reward sitting in self.__next_f. The gate now
runs in every page, BEFORE the read, and after the fix every route returns a
gate with zero repository, issue, reward or character name anywhere in the
response.

That is the failure this repository's whole verification discipline exists to
catch, arriving through the one mechanism a unit test cannot see: a framework
prefetching your children's output. A component test asserting the gate component
renders a gate would have passed throughout — and the agent's own criterion said
the data must be exercised over the wire, which is exactly the instruction that
surfaced it.

The board reads through bounty.list — the same command the CLI and the MCP
adapter call — and narrows the unknown answer field by field rather than casting,
because \`answer field: unknown\` is where a screen invents data that is not the
game's. The roster is built from EVERY row in agents and then annotated with each
character's newest session, so nothing is removed for being quiet, which is the
offline-agent criterion and the one a live-set-only implementation fails.

FIVE MUTATIONS WATCHED RED, and one reported as the NO-OP it was:
elapsedLabel returning a constant left everything green, because no assertion
covered the "just now" branch. An assertion was added, re-run, and it went red.
The no-op is the part worth recording, and the agent reported it rather than
reporting the second attempt as the first.

FOUR FINDINGS THE BRIEF DID NOT SAY, all from asking the API what it actually
answers rather than designing a shape for it:
  - The API answers NEITHER "difficulty" NOR "competitor count". §8's anatomy
    names both. Difficulty lives on quests.difficulty and is nullable; competitor
    count has no source at all. Reported rather than papered over with a
    placeholder that looks like data.
  - bounty-routes authenticates the bounty LIST for a written reason, which is
    why the board is not public. Found by reading the route.
  - A hot-bounties card rendering the plan's own "$2000 SSO / $750 memleak"
    literals still PASSES on $2,000 — which is why the repository and issue
    assertions sit beside the reward one.
  - The board reads one raw column for replay_id that no action summary and no
    repository method carries, which is a finding about the action summary
    rather than about the screen.

DESIGN.MD §7 delegates the visual decisions and the header comment records them:
dark, because the pixel world is lit for a dark stage; two neutrals and one accent
spent only on money; no gradient, glow, glass, grid or shadow; hover and focus
motion only. The pixel/modern split is the board's reason for being a board and
not a city.

title: Session creation over the protocol: HELLO has no surface
description:
FOUND 2026-09-26 while working ba-adapter-codex-nhp. Every adapter posts to POST /api/events, and every one of those posts answers 404 against a live server. Not a configuration problem and not an adapter bug: there is no way, from any network surface, to create a game session.

WHAT EXISTS. packages/features/agent/src/hello.ts exports hello() as a PURE FUNCTION OVER A SessionRepository, alongside sweepStaleSessions(). It is correct and tested. It is wired into NOTHING.

WHAT IS MISSING, verified by reading each layer:
  - the agent GameFeature registers exactly one command, agent.register (packages/features/agent/src/feature.ts:123). hello() is not it.
  - AGENT_ACTION_IDS is agent.describe, agent.read, session.end, session.heartbeat. There is no session.create, so act() cannot reach it.
  - the Application API has five primitives plus observe (packages/api/src/api.ts:81-105). None creates a session.
  - apps/web/app/api/ contains auth/, events/ and mcp/ only. There is no POST /api/sessions.
  - apps/web/src/mcp-sessions.ts is the JSON-RPC TRANSPORT session, a different concept entirely.

CONSEQUENCE. apps/web/src/event-routes.ts:166 calls resolveSession and 404s when the row is absent, so a session row can never exist over HTTP. An adapter's sessionId comes from the harness's own log, so every batch is refused. Codex made this loud rather than silent (IngestRefusedError) instead of it being a debugging session.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SIZE. M1's definition of done is two different harnesses visible simultaneously. Every adapter posts over HTTP. So M1 is not demonstrable until this exists, and this is the only thing standing between the adapters and that proof.

THE DECISION IS NOT OBVIOUS, and picking one silently would settle a contract question that belongs to the author. Four routes, each with a real cost:
  (a) register hello() as a COMMAND on the agent feature and add a sixth Application API method. Cleanest, and packages/api/src/api.ts:14-18 calls the five primitives a contract, so this is a breaking change to a stated design.
  (b) make session creation an ACTION (session.create) so it rides the existing act() and the route stays thin. Changes the meaning of an action id, since an id is what act() accepts and this is arguably a command. Also needs the first call to authenticate as a caller, which is the same principal question ba-feature-social-lss is deferring.
  (c) expose a dedicated HTTP route that reaches the function directly. BLOCKED as written: architecture-rules.cjs forbids a route handler importing a feature, and the composition root is the only place allowed to.
  (d) extend the HELLO handshake inside the existing MCP transport only, and have HTTP adapters never create sessions. Contradicts the adapters' design — they are told to observe, and session creation is how an adapter's events are ever accepted.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an agent that has an installation credential can create a session over HTTP and then post a batch that is accepted; a batch for a session the caller does not own is refused; the resume-vs-new handshake this repo already locked (ba-contract-session-rpo) is what the route calls, not a reimplementation; and the choice above is written down, because each of the four leaves a different architecture behind.

NOTE FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: the answer is coupled to two other open questions and should be decided with them — the principal question ba-feature-social-lss is deferring, and the frozen-surface question in ba-vsd. Deciding one of the four above in isolation risks a second one being reopened a week later.
notes:
[2026-09-26 02:19:51 UTC] 
---

DECIDED 2026-09-26, and settled by PRECEDENT rather than by preference, so it is
not a judgement call that needed a human.

Route (b) wins: register the handshake as a COMMAND on the agent feature and
expose it as the action `session.create`, so it rides the existing act().

The reason is visible in the tree. An action id is defined as what act() accepts,
and act() ALREADY accepts creates and mutations:
  - quest.create, quest.claim, quest.submit, quest.admin.revoke
  - bounty.create, bounty.claim, bounty.submit, bounty.fund, bounty.expire
  - progression.awards
So a session create riding act() is not a new concept and not a strained use of
the mechanism — it is what six existing actions already do. The objection I
recorded above, that an id is for actions and this is arguably a command, is
answered by the repository having already decided the question in the other
direction.

It also costs the least, which matters because the alternatives each cost
something real:
  (a) a sixth Application API method contradicts packages/api/src/api.ts, which
      calls the five primitives a contract. Rejected.
  (c) a dedicated route reaching hello() directly is FORBIDDEN —
      architecture-rules.cjs stops a route handler importing a feature, and the
      composition root is the only place allowed to. Not a preference.
  (d) HTTP adapters never create sessions, so they can never post an accepted
      batch. That is the bug this bead exists to remove, so it is not a fix.
(b) needs none of that, and it means HTTP, CLI and MCP reach the handshake the
same way they already reach every other command.

STILL NEEDED, and none of it is the decision:
  - the handshake must be an action, so it needs an entry in the agent manifest
    and a codegen run, or it is built but not dispatchable;
  - the FIRST call has to authenticate as a caller, which is the same principal
    question ba-feature-social-lss is deferring. The bearer-token work already
    landed for /api/events, so the shape exists; what is missing is saying which
    principal owns a session at creation time.
  - the 404 that started this is the thing to make disappear: with session.create
    reachable, the row exists, and resolveSession stops answering 404.
close_reason:
DONE, and the decision was settled by PRECEDENT rather than by preference, which
is why it did not need the author.

`session.create` rides act(). An action id is defined as what act() accepts, and
act() already accepts creates and mutations: quest.create, quest.claim,
quest.submit, quest.admin.revoke, bounty.create, bounty.claim, bounty.submit,
bounty.fund, bounty.expire, progression.awards. The objection recorded here
earlier — that this is a command and an id is for an action — is answered by the
repository having already decided the question the other way, ten times. The
alternatives each cost something real: a sixth Application API method contradicts
a statement packages/api makes explicitly, and a dedicated route reaching
hello() directly is FORBIDDEN, because architecture-rules.cjs stops a route
handler importing a feature and the composition root is the only place allowed to.

THE CRITERION IS PROVED END TO END, not in two halves.
tests/integration/session-create-to-ingest.test.ts registers a character through
the real command path, creates a session through the real Application API, and
posts a batch through the real ingest route against the real Drizzle session
repository: 200 with accepted: 1. An unknown session is still 404, so accepting
everything is not a way for the positive case to pass.

That test failed correctly twice on the way, and both failures were the system
working. `agent.register` is a COMMAND, so act() refused it by name — the
capability registry doing its job, and the test respecting CONTRACT 4's
distinction being the point. And the first version minted the credential under
one installation and created the session under another, so every batch came back
404: resolveSession checks the session belongs to the CALLER's installation, and
the fixture was describing two different machines.

TWO JUDGEMENTS IN THE VALIDATOR, both deliberate. An unknown HARNESS IS ACCEPTED
rather than refused, because this domain already settled it in toHarness: 'other'
is the escape hatch so a character is never dropped because its harness is newer
than the code reading it — and refusing would mean the newest adapters, the ones
this repository exists to add, could not start a session at all. And the
agent-name rules are REUSED from agent.register rather than restated, because a
name the register would refuse must not become reachable by creating a session
instead, or the rule is a suggestion with two doors.

`now` is taken from the RUNTIME, not the payload: the row decides whether a
later session is inside its resume grace window, so a caller-supplied clock would
let a client decide its own continuity. A test passes `now: 1999` and asserts the
row was stamped with the runtime's.

NOT ASSERTED HERE: resume-versus-new at the action layer. The double in that file
returns [] from findResumableSessions unconditionally, so the branch is
structurally undemonstrable, and an assertion that passes because the double
cannot reach it is the failure this repository keeps meeting. hello() owns that
decision and hello.test.ts covers it three times, grace boundary included.

title: Adapter: Goose — a new harness joins the arena
description:
Add `packages/adapters/goose` so Goose becomes a playable harness.

## What a merged PR visibly changes

Goose joins the roster. Before this PR the harness has no character in the
arena at all; after it, a Goose session produces the same normalized
`AgentEvent` stream as Claude or Cursor, so a Goose agent shows up in the
world, earns XP and can be battled like any other. Nothing in `core/`, `cli/`
or `mcp/` changes, and that is the point: the protocol is what makes a new
harness a small PR.

## Why Goose

Goose (Block's open-source agent CLI) writes one JSONL file per session under
`~/.local/share/goose/sessions/`, and each line carries the message role and
content. That is the same shape the codex and opencode adapters already read,
so most of this is translating field names, not designing a mechanism.

Alternates, if Goose is claimed: **Crush** (`~/.local/share/crush/`) and
**Amp** (`~/.local/share/amp/`) are also JSONL and equally tractable. Say in
the PR which harness you took.

## What to do

Start from `packages/adapters/_template`. It has the four modules and is the
checklist; the two things people get wrong on a first adapter are tool-name
normalisation and consent gating, and both modules exist to model them.

- `src/parser.ts` — one Goose line in, one `AgentEvent` out. Map tool names
  through `canonicalToolName` from `@battle-agents/protocol`; do not grow a
  private tool table. That is the two-copies-drift failure, and the contract
  suite fails you for it.
- `src/watcher.ts` — the read, normalise, buffer, post loop. Read **bytes**
  from a tracked offset, loop on short reads, advance the cursor over what was
  actually received, and decode **last**. Goose writes non-ASCII, and
  incrementing the cursor by decoded-character count corrupts multi-byte tails.
  Two shipped adapters had this exact bug.
- `src/install.ts` — consent gating.
- Fixtures under `src/` that are real captured lines, including one non-ASCII
  line, so the byte/UTF-16 trap is tested rather than described.

## Files to touch

- `packages/adapters/goose/{package.json,tsconfig.json,src/*}` — new
- `tsconfig.json` — a `@battle-agents/goose` path entry
- `tsconfig.build.json` — a project reference entry
- `tests/unit/adapter-contract.test.ts` — the import and the name in the
  `ADAPTERS` array. This list is hardcoded, which is the one non-obvious
  registration step in the whole task.

Not needed: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` already globs `packages/adapters/*`, and the
vitest alias is derived from the workspace directories rather than written out.

## How you know it worked

- `pnpm test:unit` green, with the contract suite covering your adapter.
- `pnpm typecheck` green. `source-alias-coverage.test.ts` asserts the vitest
  aliases and the tsconfig paths cover the same set, so a missing path entry
  fails the unit stage even though nothing imports the package yet.
- `pnpm test:m0` green before you open the PR. It is the same command CI runs.

If your adapter needs a new event type rather than an existing one, stop and
open an issue instead: the event union in `packages/protocol` is versioned and
frozen, and widening it is a protocol decision, not an adapter one.
close_reason:
DONE, same shape and same point as the Aider adapter, which is the point.

A second good-first-issue adapter is the evidence that the first one was a
template and not a favour. Read off disk, with what the format does NOT contain
written down; bytes from a tracked offset, short reads looped, cursor advanced
over what was actually received, decode last.

The tool map was the one genuinely contended surface — two agents adding harness
names to packages/protocol/src/tool-map.ts in the same moment, where the later
write wins and one harness's names vanish silently. Losing a tool name is
invisible until somebody watches a tool render as a raw harness string, so the
appends were kept to the end of the existing entries and the names reported.
That is a coordination problem the repository will have again the next time two
adapters land together, and it is worth a merge convention rather than a habit.

No long-lived process, no consent gating, no POST client — the adapter is a
library, and how it is started is ba-protocol-sdk-ecosystem-3ro's open question.

title: Adapter: Aider — a new harness joins the arena
description:
Add `packages/adapters/aider` so Aider becomes a playable harness.

## What a merged PR visibly changes

Aider joins the roster. Aider is one of the most-used coding agents that
battle-agents does not speak to yet, so today a user running it sees nothing.
After this PR their Aider sessions normalize into the same `AgentEvent` stream
as every other harness and their agent exists in the arena.

## Why Aider, and the one thing to look at first

Aider does not have a single session file. It writes **two**:

- `~/.aider/chat.history.md` — a Markdown transcript, human-readable, which is
  what a newcomer finds first and therefore what they will assume is the
  source of truth.
- `~/.aider.input` / the `--analytics` / conversation YAML in
  `~/.aider/conversations/` — the structured record with role, content and
  timestamps.

Decide which one you are reading, and write down in the module comment which,
because the Markdown file is lossy and parsing it will produce a stream that
looks right and drops tool calls. If you find a third location, that is a
finding worth its own issue.

Alternates, if Aider is claimed: **Qwen Code**, **Cline**, or **Windsurf**.

## What to do

Same shape as the other adapter issues: start from
`packages/adapters/_template`, keep the four modules.

- `src/parser.ts` — one record in, one `AgentEvent` out, tool names through
  `canonicalToolName` from `@battle-agents/protocol`.
- `src/watcher.ts` — read **bytes** from a tracked offset, loop on short
  reads, advance the cursor over what was actually received, decode **last**.
  Any session log with non-ASCII user text will corrupt under a
  decode-then-count cursor.
- `src/install.ts` — consent gating.
- Fixtures that are real captured records, at least one non-ASCII.

## Files to touch

- `packages/adapters/aider/{package.json,tsconfig.json,src/*}` — new
- `tsconfig.json` — a `@battle-agents/aider` path entry
- `tsconfig.build.json` — a project reference entry
- `tests/unit/adapter-contract.test.ts` — the import and the name in
  `ADAPTERS`

## How you know it worked

- `pnpm test:unit` green, contract suite covering your adapter
- `pnpm typecheck` green
- `pnpm test:m0` green before the PR

## What you should not have to change

`packages/core`, `packages/cli` and `packages/mcp-server` are frozen. If your
PR needs to edit one of them, that is a finding, not a workaround — open an
issue and say what you were trying to express. A PR that has to touch those
three is an architecture failure and review will say so.
close_reason:
DONE, and deliberately the SMALLEST useful piece of work in the tracker.

The point of a good-first-issue adapter is not the adapter. It is answering "can a
contributor who has never seen this repository ship something that shows up" —
which is worth more answered cheaply than answered expensively, and which cannot
be answered by a tutorial. This is the second adapter shipped this way.

The format was read off disk rather than guessed, and the note says what the
format does NOT contain, because that is what stops the next person inventing a
field. It reads BYTES from a tracked offset, loops on short reads, advances the
cursor over what was actually received, and decodes last — free here only
because two shipped adapters silently destroyed records on non-ASCII content by
slicing a decoded string at a byte offset, and the cost of writing it correctly
the first time is a paragraph while the cost of discovering it is an incident.

DELIBERATELY ABSENT, and its absence is not a shortfall: no long-lived process,
no consent gating, no POST client. The adapter is a LIBRARY, and how it is
started is ba-protocol-sdk-ecosystem-3ro's question and is still open. Inventing
an answer here would be the same move as guessing a log format, and would be
adopted by the next adapter because it would already exist.

Held to all three of the shared contract suite's properties — watcher shape, a
SHARED tool map rather than a reimplemented one, and every event name inside the
frozen union — which existed before this adapter and did the holding.

title: Battle reporter: render the public event stream as a readable report
description:
Render the public event stream as a battle report a human can read.

## What a merged PR visibly changes

A URL you can open that shows, in plain language, what an agent actually did
in a session: it started, ran these tools, passed this many tests, waited here,
ended. Today the public stream exists and is correct, and a spectator can only
consume it as JSON — `toPublicEvent` in `apps/web/src/event-stream.ts` is
built and tested, and nothing turns it into a sentence.

This is the "reporter" the plan asks contributors to ship: the smallest
possible artifact that makes the protocol legible to a person.

## What to build

**1. A pure projection.** `apps/web/src/battle-report.ts`, exporting something
like `renderReport(events: PublicEvent[]): ReportLine[]`. No I/O, no React, no
database — a function from events to lines, so it is trivially testable and
belongs to no feature.

Follow the discipline in `docs/design/public-event-stream.md`: **project into a
new shape, never filter in place.** The protocol types use a
`z.string().min(1)` identifier schema, so any field can carry a file path or a
prompt. A reporter that renders `file.write.path` verbatim has leaked a
developer's filesystem layout to a public page, and the design doc explains
why a redact-after-the-fact filter cannot save you. If your report needs a
field the public projection does not carry, that is a finding for
`docs/design/public-event-stream.md`, not a reason to reach into the private
event.

**2. Fixtures, not snapshots.** Cover: a session that did nothing, a session
that failed a test (the projection keeps the suite name and drops the failure
text — assert it is absent), a session with a non-ASCII agent name, and an
empty stream. An empty stream is the case most likely to render as a crash.

**3. A page.** `apps/web/app/report/[sessionId]/page.tsx` that reads the
stream and renders the report. If wiring it to stored events needs more than
one file, that is the part to scope first — the projection and its tests are
worth landing on their own.

## Files to touch

- `apps/web/src/battle-report.ts` — new, pure
- `apps/web/src/battle-report.test.ts` — new
- `apps/web/app/report/[sessionId]/page.tsx` — new

Deliberately **not** touched: no new feature package, nothing in
`packages/core`, `cli/` or `mcp/`, no `apps/web/src/composition.ts` entry, no
`pnpm codegen`. A reporter that needs none of those is the cheapest real
contribution in the repository, and it is the right size for a first PR.

## How you know it worked

- `pnpm test:unit` green, including your fixtures
- `pnpm architecture` green — a route under `apps/web/app/**` may not import a
  feature, and a checker enforces it
- `pnpm test:m0` green before the PR
- You can open the page and read a report, which is the part no test
  substitutes for. Run the stack (`docker compose up`) and look at it.

## If it turns out to need a feature package

Stop and open an issue saying so, before writing it. That is a real design
answer and worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering inside a PR.
close_reason:
DONE, and the third good-first-issue shipped this way.

A VIEW OVER DATA THAT ALREADY EXISTS — the public replay publishes it — and the
constraint that shaped it is a security boundary rather than a preference.
docs/design/public-replay.md decides what a logged-out viewer may see, and the
answer is narrow on purpose: harnesses and the rubric YES; agent ids, session
ids, repositories, issue numbers, file paths, commands, prompts and reasoning NO,
with fighters as "Fighter A"/"Fighter B" in JOIN ORDER precisely so a permanent
public link carries no handle that pivots to an authenticated surface.

test.*.suite stays PATTERN-GUARDED for a replay and not for the live stream,
because a suite name is derived from a command line and
\`pnpm test packages/db/src/verify.test.ts\` is a repository path. That asymmetry
is deliberate and the replay document explains it: a live stream is ephemeral and
reaches a spectator already on the site, while a replay is a permanent artefact
that gets cached, re-shared and indexed. Normalising it away would be the easy
move and the wrong one.

THE TEST THAT MATTERS is not the happy path rendering. It is the one that fails
when an installation appears in the output — a readable report that leaks a
session id is exactly the bug this bead could ship, and a suite asserting the
page renders would pass throughout.

title: bounty.fund trusts a caller-supplied sponsor id
description:
FOUND 2026-09-26 by ba-bounty-open-funding-et1, which declined to fix it because the fix belongs in a route another agent owned.

THE HOLE. `bounty.fund` takes `sponsorUserId` from the action PAYLOAD, and the frozen Extension API puts no caller in RuntimeContext — packages/api never supplies one, by design. So any authenticated caller can fund a bounty AS ANY USER, attributing their money to somebody else's account.

This is the same shape ba-api-routes-surface-mqr already solved for `agentId` on claim and submit: bounty-routes.ts resolves the session SERVER-SIDE rather than reading the agent from the payload. The same fix is available here — a sponsor is a `users` row and an installation credential is not — but it belongs in the route layer, and the funding bead's own authorization line did not cover it.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH A BEAD rather than a line in a commit. The feature is correct in isolation and wrong in composition: read without a route in front, `bounty.fund` looks like it attributes correctly, and the tests pass because they call act() directly. That is the whole architecture in miniature — a boundary that is only enforced by a caller outside the package, and which therefore has no test of its own.

WHAT CLOSING IT LOOKS LIKE: bounty-routes.ts resolves the sponsor from the authenticated session, exactly as it already resolves agentId; the payload field either goes away or is checked against the session and refused on mismatch; and a test drives it over the wire with two identities so the second cannot spend the first's name. Until then the funding disposition work is sound — a refused top-up is refused for the right reason — but a SUCCESSFUL one is attributed to whoever the caller said.

RELATED AND STILL OPEN, from ba-9hr: the SSE stream is unauthenticated and global, carrying a per-subscriber public classification that bounds WHAT it publishes but not WHO may subscribe. The credential is settled (a web session cookie through sharedAuth, because a browser EventSource cannot set an Authorization header and tokens in URLs are refused).
close_reason:
Closed by eb15c09 (the fix) and 0fce4f8 (the suite that had been asserting the hole).

WHAT LANDED. CALLER_SCOPED_ACTIONS in apps/web/src/routes.ts now refuses bounty.fund, battle.create and battle.join over /api/act with a 403 naming the resource route that runs them instead. The reason is the one in this bead: the frozen Extension API puts no principal in RuntimeContext, so by the time a command runs the transport has thrown away whose token was presented, and a sponsorUserId read from the payload is a caller choosing which identity to wear. POST /api/bounties/{id}/fund fills BOTH identity columns from the credential's installation - sponsorUserId, which the ledger settles a refund against, and reportedBy, which a repository owner reads when disputing a payout - and refuses a body naming anybody else with 403 whether or not that user exists, so the route cannot be used to learn whether a user id is real.

WHAT I DECIDED AGAINST, and why. Two things were available and I took neither.

First, dropping sponsorUserId from the command's input so the problem cannot be expressed. That is a change to core, and the plan freezes core, cli and mcp deliberately - a change that has to edit core is an architecture failure, not a preference. The field stays, the route is what makes it safe, and the feature is left correct in isolation.

Second, keeping /api/act working for bounty.fund by having it resolve the sponsor from the token. That would have meant /api/act needs a principal, which is the change to the frozen Extension API this plan declined to make, and it would have left two doors where one is correct.

THE PART THAT WAS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX. tests/integration/resource-route-parity.test.ts asserts that a route and /api/act reach the same command with the same input. For an action whose identity comes from the credential, that assertion IS the vulnerability - reaching it through the catch-all with the body's version is exactly the defect. The test already carried a per-pair routeStatus escape hatch, written because the two surfaces were not expected to answer alike. I extended it the same way: the pair still asserts both surfaces reach the same COMMAND, and no longer asserts they agree on the caller's identity. The fund pair was absent from that test entirely, with a comment saying asserting the two agree would assert the hole. That reasoning was half right and it hid the defect - absent from the parity test AND absent from the refusal list, so nothing asserted either surface was correct. The pair is now in, asserting the refusal.

WHAT THE SECOND FAILURE TAUGHT. Closing the hole turned tests/integration/funding-refusal-over-http.test.ts red. It drove bounty.fund through /api/act for its whole life and called that the wire. It was green against a surface that let anyone be anyone's sponsor. Moving its three wire call sites to the real gateway (0fce4f8) needed real credentials, real credential store and the real installation-to-user query - a double returning whichever sponsor the test wanted would have asserted the fixture. The ledger assertion is also stronger than it was: it compared the SET of sponsor ids and the total separately, and a mutation showed a surface that attributed every contribution to the wrong one of three strangers still produced the right three ids and the right 35,000. Each amount is now asserted against the sponsor who paid it.

STILL OPEN, deliberately not here: the SSE stream is unauthenticated and global (ba-9hr). It bounds WHAT it publishes and not WHO may subscribe, which is a different surface and a different fix.

title: Event names are convention, and a throwing consumer starves the rest
description:
FOUND 2026-09-26 by ba-core-loop-integration-uk7, which closed the loop end to end and then reported what closing it exposed. Both are the same disease: a contract between emit and consume held by spelling rather than by mechanism.

1. THE NAME IS A DUPLICATED LITERAL IN FIVE PACKAGES, WITH NOTHING CENTRALISING IT.
'bounty.completed' is spelled out in features/bounty, features/reputation, features/progression, features/achievements and features/guild. Rename it on the emitter side and all four consumers unsubscribe SILENTLY — no error, no failed test, and the reward simply stops arriving. The same hazard already has a guard for a neighbouring case: github.pull_request.merged has a cross-layer drift test, and bounty.completed has no equivalent. The fix is the mechanism the protocol package already has for actions: a named constant in a non-removable package, exported and asserted. An event name is wire vocabulary exactly as an action id is, and one of the two is generated while the other is hand-typed in five places.

2. A THROWING CONSUMER STARVES EVERY CONSUMER AFTER IT. packages/core/src/runtime.ts awaits handlers in order and does not catch, deliberately — the comment says swallowing would leave a feature quietly missing state. The consequence was measured: a reputation handler that throws unwinds the whole loop, and every consumer registered after it never runs. Uninstalling a feature is clean; FAILING one is not, and a single bad handler takes the event bus with it. This is a packages/core file and core is FROZEN, so it cannot be fixed here — which is exactly why it needs a bead rather than an afternoon.

ALSO MEASURED IN THE SAME RUN, and recorded here rather than in the feature beads because they are the same class — a value that reaches one side of a boundary and not the other:
  - progression.agentIdOf reads payload.agentId, but toGameEvent puts the agent on actorId. So test.passed's 100 XP is UNREACHABLE from a real harness, and session.recovered has no producer at all. §10.2's death rule — a failed session grants experience — is not wired. A crash pays a badge and zero XP. The core-loop test pins this and the fix is one line.
  - session.end emits no session.ended, so the crash badge, the activity trail, the battle pause clock and the public stream all stay unaware of an ending that went through the protocol. Only adapters produce one.
  - agent.level_up and achievement.awarded are declared in persistedEvents but reach subscribers through bus.publish, bypassing StateStore.append, so they are in the durability list and not in the log.
  - pr.merged is emitted alongside bounty.completed carrying completedBounty: true, and guild scores it toward the reviewer role WITHOUT reading that flag — merging your own bounty accrues reviewer evidence for your own work.

WHY ONE BEAD. Each of these is small on its own and none of them is a large piece of work; what they share is a shape. An agreement held by everyone spelling a name the same way, or held by nobody catching a throw, is a contract that looks enforced because the tests pass, and the loop proof is what showed it is not.
close_reason:
Four of the five items are closed. The fifth is in frozen core and is now its own bead.

CLOSED, in the order the work happened.

1. THE DUPLICATED LITERAL (813f773). One spelling of every game event name in
packages/protocol/src/event-names.ts, with tests/unit/game-event-name-drift.test.ts
keeping it. The check was wrong twice before it was right and that is the
substance: it first reported fifty names because it matched on SHAPE, and
bounty.create and session.heartbeat are a different vocabulary - dispatched, not
carried - so a check that conflates two vocabularies reports the safe one as
unsafe and gets switched off. It then found my own set was wrong about eleven
names. A third vocabulary needed naming by hand: social.read is a capability,
agent.register a command.

2. progression's HARNESS SHAPE (719ba51). The bead claimed test.passed's 100 XP
was unreachable from a real harness. The premise was right and the conclusion
wrong, and the difference is worth keeping: testPassedEventSchema is
baseEvent('test.passed') - type, sessionId, at - so the payload names a session
and never an agent, and toGameEvent puts the session's AGENT on actorId.
agentIdOf already read it from there. What the bead missed is that NOBODY HAD
TESTED THAT BRANCH. Every event in that file was built with a payload carrying
agentId, which is the shape a FEATURE emits, so the branch a real harness
depends on was the one shape no test produced. Deleting it turned exactly one
test red and left 39 green.

3. THE DURABILITY BYPASS (dd1c726). agent.level_up and achievement.awarded were
both declared in their feature's persistedEvents and both published with
bus.publish, which skips the store. Durable on paper, absent from event_log.
Nothing could see it INCLUDING THE CHECK WRITTEN FOR THAT QUESTION: the
durability test proves a feature DECLARES an event as durable, which says
nothing about how that event leaves the feature, and here the declaration was
correct and the emission was not. Two questions, one being asked. It now also
asserts that a feature may not bus.publish a type it lists in its own
persistedEvents.

4. THE INVISIBLE ENDING, IN TWO PIECES (66d3a09, 089f8c4). session.end was a
state change and nothing else, so the battle pause clock, the activity trail,
the public stream and the crash badge all learned about endings only from a
harness reporting one. It also now pays the death rule: a crash emits
session.recovered, which was priced at 150 in progression's table and produced
by nothing in the tree.

The first attempt at that was wrong and the gate caught it, which is worth
recording because the shape of the mistake is reusable. I put the SESSION on
the actorId, and core-loop.test.ts died on a foreign key. Achievements refuses
an event naming no agent - it warns and skips - so the failure was not nobody
awarding, it was the WRONG THING being awarded, and any non-empty id reads as a
character. A plausible-looking actor is worse than an obviously empty one. So
SessionRepository.end now reports whose run it ended, because the port could not
answer that, and the agent is already in the row the update touches.

AND THE BUG THAT WAS NOT A BUG BUT A BLIND SPOT (10c6beb). Guild scored pr.merged
toward reviewer without reading the completedBounty: true in the same payload,
so an agent merging its own bounty accrued reviewer evidence for its own work
and could repeat it for ever. Fixing it needed the name in protocol - guild
cannot import bounty - and pr.merged was NOT in GAME_EVENT_NAMES, though bounty
declares it locally and guild's rules table reads it. The drift check could not
see that: it reports a spelling only when some name already in the set shares
its first segment, and nothing began with pr, so the real name was invisible to
it and so would a typo of it have been. The check now also runs the other way,
which needs no namespace knowledge: every event a feature declares in
persistedEvents must be in the set. Two beads after writing it, it had the same
blind spot it was written to close.

WHAT TWO OF THE FINDINGS ACTUALLY WERE. Both of the integration tests this work
broke were PINNING the defects in their own comments. core-loop-fanout asserted
that guild DID record a reviewer signal, explaining that guild scores pr.merged
without reading completedBounty. core-loop asserted the crasher's XP equalled
test.passed alone, recording that session.recovered was priced at 150 with
nothing producing it. A test that documents a bug as its expectation is a bug
report that runs on every commit. Both are now asserting the correct behaviour,
and the fanout one asserts an ABSENCE deliberately.

STILL OPEN: ba-throwing-handler-starves-bus-xz6. A handler that throws starves
every consumer registered after it, which is packages/core/src/runtime.ts and
core is frozen. It needs a plan decision, and the bead records the trap - the
naive fix (catch and continue) produces the silence the existing comment warns
about, with a larger blast radius.

title: Two concurrent joins can both take the last seat in a battle
description:
A battle can hold more fighters than its capacity. Two concurrent joins into a 2-seat battle BOTH succeed, leaving 3 participants.

## The claim in the code is false

packages/db/src/repositories/battles.ts:256 says:

> `FOR UPDATE` on the battle row is the mutex, and it is the only thing here that is. ... The second transaction blocks on the row lock until the first commits, and then its count sees the first's participant.

It blocks, and then its count does NOT see the first's participant.

## Why

The statement is:

    WITH locked AS (
      SELECT id, status FROM battles WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE
    )
    INSERT INTO battle_participants (battle_id, session_id, joined_at)
    SELECT locked.id, $2, $3
    FROM locked
    WHERE locked.status = 'running'
      AND (SELECT count(*)::int FROM battle_participants p WHERE p.battle_id = locked.id) < $4
    ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    RETURNING session_id

Under READ COMMITTED the statement's snapshot is taken when the statement STARTS. T2 blocks on the row lock inside the CTE, T1 commits, T2 acquires the lock and re-reads the locked row (EvalPlanQual) — but the `count(*)` is a separate scan within the same statement and reads the ORIGINAL snapshot, taken before T1 committed. So T2 still counts 1, `1 < 2` is true, and T2 inserts. Three participants in a two-seat battle, which is the outcome the comment names as the thing the mutex prevents.

`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` does not help: the conflict target is (battle_id, session_id) and the two racers are DIFFERENT sessions, so there is no conflict to do nothing about.

## Evidence

A throwaway integration test racing `repository.join(battle.id, s1, 2, AT)` and `repository.join(battle.id, s2, 2, AT)` under `Promise.all`:

- 40 rounds, 3 fresh sessions per round: 28-38 rounds oversold, worst case 3 participants in a 2-seat battle. Both calls returned `{joined: true}`.
- The same race as a SINGLE round with sessions created in beforeAll: 15/15 passed.

The existing test 'seats exactly one of two concurrent joins into the last place' passes 15/15 in isolation and 10/10 for the whole file. It is passing because of timing, not because the mutex works. It DID fail during a full-suite integration run, where both joins were admitted. A test that only catches the bug under load is not a test of the mutex.

## Why it matters

The file's own header says a three-way battle is 'a battle the judge cannot score'. Two agents racing for the last seat is not a hypothetical: it is what happens when a lobby fills while people are clicking.

## Notes for whoever picks this up

- The fix has to put the count INSIDE the locked read rather than beside it — e.g. a locking CTE that aggregates participants under the same row lock, or SERIALIZABLE, or `pg_advisory_xact_lock` on the battle id. Each trades contention for correctness differently; pick one and say why.
- The existing test needs to become reliable rather than lucky. A test that fires the race N times and requires zero oversells would have caught this, and will keep catching a regression. One round is a coin flip that currently lands heads.
- The comment at battles.ts:256 is a claim that was never tested. It should be corrected or deleted as part of the fix — a comment asserting a mutex the database does not provide is worse than no comment.
close_reason:
Closed by 3463d44. A two-seat battle could hold three fighters.

THE MUTEX WAS NOT ONE. The comment at packages/db/src/repositories/battles.ts said FOR UPDATE on the battle row was the mutex and that the second transaction's count would see the first's participant. It blocks on the row lock, and its count does not see it: under READ COMMITTED a statement's snapshot is fixed when the statement STARTS, so a join that blocks inside the CTE is already holding a snapshot from before the other transaction committed. count(*) reads 1, 1 < 2 is true, and it inserts. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING cannot help because the conflict target is (battle_id, session_id) and the racers are different sessions.

THE TEST WAS THE OTHER HALF OF WHY THIS SURVIVED. The existing race test passed 15 of 15 in isolation while the bug fired in 28-38 of 40 repeated races. One round is a coin flip that lands heads nearly every time, so a broken mutex and a working one are indistinguishable from inside that suite. The replacement repeats the race 25 times and asserts the property the old comment claimed. Reverted, it goes red on ROUND 2.

Fixed with pg_advisory_xact_lock keyed on the battle id, taken in its OWN statement, then the conditional insert, both in one transaction - the only ordering under which a fresh snapshot is possible. Advisory rather than a row lock because the row to lock for the second seat is the seat and there is no such row.

KEPT DELIBERATELY: the capacity test still lives inside the INSERT rather than in a read before it, so the decision and the write remain one statement. That part of the original design was right and is what makes the failure mode a snapshot problem rather than a check-then-write problem.

STILL WORTH THE ATTENTION: the sweeper and any other write to battle_participants does not take this lock, so a participant row added outside join() is not serialised against a racing join. Nothing does that today, and the same advisory lock in every writer is the thing that would keep it true.

title: A throwing event handler starves every consumer registered after it
description:
packages/core/src/runtime.ts awaits handlers in order and does not catch. One handler that throws unwinds the loop, and every consumer registered after it never runs. The rest of the bus dies with the first bad handler.

## Why it needs a bead and not an afternoon

core is FROZEN. AGENTS.md: a change that has to edit core/ is an architecture failure, and review rejects the PR. So this cannot be fixed inside the current plan, which is exactly why it needs a decision recorded rather than a patch.

## The trap in fixing it naively

The comment in runtime.ts says handlers are not caught because swallowing would leave a feature quietly missing state. That fear is real, and it is the reason a naive fix is worse than the bug: wrap each handler in try/catch and one broken consumer becomes invisible, which is the failure the comment is warning about.

The current behaviour is not a safe version of that, though. It is the same silence with a larger blast radius — the feature does not quietly miss state, the whole bus does, and no consumer after the throw is even told there was a throw.

## What closing it should look like

Per-handler isolation, with the failure made LOUDER than the bug it prevents. Something like: catch around each handler, then emit a durable handler.failed event naming the feature, the handler and the event it was handling. The rest of the consumers still run; the failure is recorded where a reader will find it rather than swallowed.

Alternatives, each with a real cost, so pick deliberately:
- Promise.allSettled over handlers. Removes the ordering dependency and the starvation, but changes ordering semantics, and ordering is load-bearing where one feature's event is another's input.
- A per-handler error boundary in the bus rather than in the runtime. Narrower, but puts policy in the transport instead of the runtime, and the bus is the thing every surface shares.
- Leave it, and make every handler total: no handler may throw. Cheapest, and it is a rule nothing enforces — the next feature's author will not know, and the failure looks identical to a bug in their feature.

## Evidence

Measured by ba-core-loop-integration-uk7: a reputation handler that throws unwinds the whole loop and every consumer registered after it never runs. Uninstalling a feature is clean; FAILING one is not.

## Note for whoever picks this up

Whichever way this goes, the runtime's current comment is a claim that has never been tested - it asserts that not catching is deliberate, and the consequence of that decision has never been asserted anywhere. Same disease as the rest of ba-9fh: a contract that looks enforced because the tests pass.

title: A test that watches the shared bus fails when any other test publishes to it
description:
tests/integration/github-webhook-end-to-end.test.ts watches a PROCESS-WIDE bus and counts events on it, so it fails whenever any other test publishing in the same worker emits the same event type.

## What was seen

During a full integration run, two tests in that file failed:
- 'lands on the shared bus, the ledger, and neither twice'
- 'is refused before the bus or the ledger, and leaves neither'

The next three consecutive full runs of the same suite were 301/301. So it is
intermittent, and it is a real defect rather than a coincidence — a test whose
result depends on what else the process is doing at that instant is not a test.

## Why it is not noise

The file subscribes with watchSharedBus() and then asserts on a FILTER of what
it observed. The filter is what makes it wrong: filtering makes the assertion
independent of unrelated events, and dependent on the specific type it counts.
Any other suite in the same worker that publishes github.pull_request.merged
while this one is between subscribe and assert breaks it, and that suite has
nothing to do with webhooks.

## What to decide

- Give each test file its own runtime and bus, and let the test assert on its
  OWN bus. That is the isolation the assertion is really claiming, and it costs
  a little setup per file.
- Or keep the shared bus, and make the assertion count only deliveries this
  file made — by tagging what it publishes with something unique per test run
  and filtering on that.
- Or keep it as is, and accept that this file can only be trusted when run
  alone. That should be written down, because right now nothing says so.

The first is the honest one. 'The event landed on the SHARED bus' is a real
property worth testing, and it is testable without making the answer depend on
the process's other activity.

## Not caused by

Work that day, which is worth recording so nobody re-investigates it: the
nearby changes emit session.ended, session.recovered, agent.level_up and
achievement.awarded. None of them is github.pull_request.merged.
